case_name: DARSAN JITENDRA JHAVERI v LAKSHMI ANIL SALGAOCAR suing as the Administratrix of the ESTATE OF ANIL VASSUDEVA SALGAOCAR (India Passport No.HXXXXXXX),deceased
subject_tags: ["Contempt of Court — Civil contempt"]
court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 27 February 2026 Case summary Darsan Jitendra Jhaveri v Lakshmi Anil Salgaocar suing as the administratrix of the estate of Anil Vassudeva Salgaocar, deceased [2026] SGCA 6 Court of Appeal/ Civil Appeal No. 19 of 2025 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Court of Appeal (delivered by Justice Belinda Ang Saw Ean): Outcome: The Court of Appeal upheld the lower court’s decision finding the appellant in contempt of court and sentencing him to five months’ imprisonment for breaching a prohibitory injunction (“PO”). Pertinent and significant points of the judgment: • The Court of Appeal explained that when interpreting a court order, the court will discern from the plain language of the order the purpose which informed the grant of the order. It is this purpose that guides the court’s determination as to the effect of the order. Any ambiguity in the order’s purpose will be resolved in favour of the person who is required to comply with the order. • The Court of Appeal disagreed with the appellant’s narrow interpretation of the PO ( ie , that as trustee he was only restricted from disposing of the shares of special purpose vehicles (“SPVs”) and not their assets). Based on the wording of the PO and the context in which it was made, it was clear that the PO was to protect shareholder equity; therefore it restricted the appellant from disposing of the net asset value of the SPVs. The appellant’s breach of the PO was in reducing the net asset value of the SPVs by disposing of the assets held by the SPVs without the corresponding account of all the sale proceeds to the SPVs. Accordingly, the Court of Appeal upheld the lower court judge’s decision finding the appellant in contempt of court. 1 CA/CA 19/2025 (“CA 19”) was an appeal against the decision of a judge in the General Division of the High Court of Singapore (“Judge”) which found the appellant guilty of contempt of court and sentenced him to 5 months’ imprisonment for breaching a prohibitory injunction restraining him from disposing of trust assets. The Court of Appeal dismissed CA 19 with costs fixed at $50,000 (all-in) to be paid by the appellant to the respondent. Background to the appeal and material facts 2 The appellant and respondent were, respectively, the first defendant and first plaintiff in HC/S 821/2015 (“Suit 821”). In Suit 821, the respondent claimed that the appellant had, in his capacity as trustee, been appointed sole director and sole shareholder over special purpose vehicles (“SPVs”) that held the respondent’s monies and investments. The appellant had thus acted in breach of trust by, among other things, misappropriating the assets of those SPVs: at [3] and [4] . 3 The trial judge in Suit 821 found in favour of the respondent. The trust as described by the respondent indeed existed, and the respondent’s claims were made qua beneficiary of the trust and thereby not barred by the reflective loss principle. Accordingly, he ordered that the appellant was to (among other things) “cause or procure the delivery up, transfer of possession or title or ownership to the [respondent] of all the trust assets”, and, in the meantime, that the appellant was to be restrained from disposing of the trust assets ( ie , the PO). These trust assets were defined as the “equity” in the SPVs, which “include[d]” the shares in certain named SPVs. The trial judge’s decision in this regard was upheld on appeal: at [8] , [11] and [13] . 4 The reliefs ordered by the trial judge were then cast into a formal judgment which was extracted on 17 March 2023 (“JUD 98”). The language of the orders in JUD 98 remained the same, save that “trust assets” were defined as “the shares in the BVI SPVs and the Singapore SPVs”: at [12] . 5 On 26 June 2023, after negotiations fell through, the respondent filed an application in HC/SUM 1897/2023 for a stay of execution of JUD 98 pending his intended appeal. In his supporting affidavit, the appellant claimed that he was “concerned about the [respondent’s] ability to return the full value of the ‘Trust Assets’ to the [appellant] if the shares of the various SPVs are transferred to the [respondent] pending the Appeal”, noting that “[o]nce this transfer takes place, there is nothing to stop the [respondent] from taking steps to substantially diminish the value of the SPVs’ asset holdings”: at [14]–[16] . 6 It was subsequently discovered that between the date of the trial judge’s judgment on 28 February 2023 and 16 May 2023, while the appellant was negotiating an amicable stay of execution of the orders in JUD 98, the appellant had sold ten properties owned by some SPVs (“Properties”) for a total of $23,169,300. The appellant had also made payments totalling $10.5m to himself, purportedly as director’s dues, from the SPVs (“$10.5m Payments”) on 14 March 2024: at [19] . Decision on appeal Issue 1: The $10.5m Payments 7 The Court of Appeal found that there was no breach of O 52 r 5(3) as alleged in the appellant’s written submissions. At the hearing of the appeal, the solicitor for the appellant clarified that the $10.5m Payments were made from the sales proceeds of the Properties. The respondent’s complaint in her O 52 statement was not limited to just the sale of the Properties, but also covered the broader assertion that the appellant had converted and dissipated those sale proceeds. As the $10.5m Payments were made from the sales proceeds of the Properties, they were properly considered as part of the respondent’s complaint about conversion and dissipation: at [ 31] . Issue 2: The interpretation of the PO 8 The Court of Appeal clarified and amplified the principles relating to the interpretation of a court order as set out in PT Sandipala Arthraputra v STMicroelectronics Asia Pacific Pte Ltd [2018] 4 SLR 828 . Specifically, the court will first discern from the plain language of the order the purpose which informed the grant of the order. It is this purpose that then guides the court’s determination as to the effect of the order. Any ambiguity in the order’s purpose will be resolved in favour of the person who is required to comply with the order: at [34] and [37] . 9 According to the appellant, the wording of JUD 98 was intended to restrict the definition of the trust assets to the shares in the SPVs. Given the literal interpretation of the word “shares”, the appellant’s disposal of the assets of the SPVs was not a disposal of the shares and he was thus not in breach of the PO. The Court of Appeal rejected this narrow interpretation of the PO, and concluded that on a proper interpretation, the PO restricted the appellant from disposing of the net asset value of the SPVs: at [4 0] and [5 2] . a. It was significant that the trial judge defined the trust assets as the “equity in the [SPVs]”. The term equity would refer to shareholder equity, or the net asset value of a company. Given that the “equity in the [SPVs] … include[d] the shares in the [SPVs]”, this “equity” was evidently intended to encompass more than just those shares and was capable of including shareholder equity: at [4 2]–[43] . b. The fact that the wording of JUD 98 differed from that used by the trial judge was of no consequence. First, JUD 98 did not and could not have altered the meaning or scope of the trial judge’s orders. Second, the interpretation of the court order must take into account the trial judge’s purpose in making the order. It was clear from the use of the word “equity” that the trial judge’s purpose in making the PO was to preserve the value of the shares ordered to be returned to the respondent. Third, this purposive interpretation accords with the plain meaning of the word “shares”; the shares represent not only units of ownership in a company, but also a bundle of rights, including the right to participate in the company’s net assets upon its winding up. The Court thus concluded that the prohibition in the PO extended beyond the mere disposal of the shares to include disposal of underlying assets which would diminish the net worth of the company: at [3 8] and [4 4] . c. The appellant’s narrow interpretation of the PO in JUD 98 ( ie , that the trust assets referred only to the shares in the SPVs and the restriction only extended to disposal of those shares) was nothing more than a convenient afterthought designed to escape the consequences of his breach. In his affidavit filed in support of his application to stay execution of JUD 98 pending appeal, the appellant demonstrated his clear understanding that the effect of the PO in JUD 98 was to safeguard the net asset value of the SPVs rather than simply to prevent him from disposing of the shares in the SPVs. His narrow interpretation adopted in the contempt proceedings and the appeal was therefore an about turn that was contrived and designed to resist contempt proceedings: at [4 6] . 10 The sale of the Properties (without the corresponding account of all the sale proceeds to the SPVs) and the making of the $10.5m Payments without substantiation would necessarily reduce the owning company’s total assets and thus its shareholder equity in the absence of any reduction in total liabilities. The appellant had not demonstrated such a reduction in total liabilities. Accordingly, the appellant had breached the PO: at [4 5] . Issue 3: The sentence to be imposed 11 The Court found that a custodial sentence of 5 months’ imprisonment was appropriate. The appellant had knowingly and repeatedly breached the PO. In so doing, he had caused grave harm to the respondent. In these circumstances, the sentence of 5 months’ imprisonment was evidently warranted, and in fact was on the low side: at [5 1]–[54] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.

case_name: XKU v XKT
subject_tags: ["Family Law — Maintenance — Wife", "Family Law — Maintenance — Child — Apportionment of maintenance", "Family Law — Matrimonial assets — Division — Dual-income or single-income marriage"]
court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 27 February 2026 Case summary XKU v XKT [2026] SGHC(A) 7 Appellate Division of the High Court – Civil Appeal No 44 of 2025 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Appellate Division of the High Court (delivered by Debbie Ong Siew Ling JAD): Outcome: The Appellate Division of the High Court dismissed the appeal against a decision on ancillary matters following a divorce, although it reached a different conclusion on the classification of the parties’ marriage. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment • This judgment addresses the classification of a marriage, whether dual-income or single-income, and the consequent applicable approach for the division of assets in s 112 of the Women’s Charter 1961 (2020 Rev Ed). It serves as a reminder that TNL v TNK [2017] 1 SLR 609 should be understood as representing an exception to the application of the approach in ANJ v ANK [2015] 4 SLR 1043 without diminishing the application of the latter’s “structured approach” in most cases . 1 This was an appeal against the decision of a judge in the Family Division of the High Court (“ Judge ”) on ancillary matters (“ AM ”) following a divorce. Background to the appeal 2 The appellant (“ Husband ”), aged 48 at the date of the AM hearing, was the sole listed director and shareholder of [B Pte Ltd] which was in the business of procuring beef products from Australian cattle farmers and/or abattoirs and selling them to distributors in Asia. The respondent (“ Wife ”), aged 49 at the date of the AM hearing, was an estate agent with [K Pte Ltd]. An interim judgment of divorce (“ IJ ”) was granted on 24 January 2024, ending the parties’ marriage of nearly 24 years. The parties had three sons who were 21 years old (“ C1 ”), 17 years old (“ C2 ”) and 13 years old (“ C3 ”) at the date of the AM hearing. C2 and C3 were collectively referred to as the “ Minor Children ”. By the parties’ consent, the parties had joint custody of the Minor Children, with the Wife having care and control and the Husband having access. 3 The Judge identified and valued the pool of matrimonial assets at S$1,698,386.99. She ordered that the assets be divided in the ratio of 70:30 in favour of the Wife. The Judge found that the Husband dissipated sums to his business partner and the Wife’s cousin and added these sums into the matrimonial pool. The Judge also rejected the Husband’s claim that the moneys in certain disputed accounts belonged to [B Pte Ltd] and/or his business partner – these moneys were found to be matrimonial assets and hence included in the matrimonial pool. The Judge found that the marriage was considered a single-income marriage and an equal division of the pool of matrimonial assets was just and equitable. An adverse inference was drawn against the Husband which was to be given effect to by way of a 20% uplift to the Wife’s share. The Judge ordered that the Husband pay a lump sum maintenance of S$20,000 to the Wife. As for maintenance for the Minor Children, the Judge ordered that the Husband pay 75% and the Wife pay 25% of the Minor Children’s reasonable expenses. Decision of the Appellate Division 4 The court dismissed the appeal. It rejected all the grounds of appeal raised by the Husband, save that it agreed that the marriage was a dual-income marriage. However, applying the ANJ v ANK structured approach, the court arrived at the same ratio of division as the Judge. 5 In determining whether a marriage was a single-income or dual-income marriage, the focus only on whether a spouse was the “primary homemaker” or the “primary breadwinner” misse d the rationale of the holding in TNL v TNK . It was observed that it would not be uncommon that in dual-income marriages, one working spouse may also take on the bulk of homemaking responsibilities while the other spouse focuses on his or her career . 6 It was also necessary to consider whether, due to taking on the homemaking role, that spouse did not earn income which could have been credited as his or her contributions in the structured approach and was thereby disadvantaged because of the role undertaken. This was the rationale for the holding in TNL v TNK that the structured approach does not apply to single-income marriages. It was explained in TNL v TNK at [44] that the ANJ v ANK approach tends to unduly favour the working spouse over the non-working spouse – the working spouse would be accorded 100% (or close to 100%) of direct contributions and a substantial percentage for indirect contributions by virtue of the working spouse’s indirect financial contributions. Such an inquiry was a fact-sensitive one that required, amongst other things, a qualitative assessment of the roles of the spouses relative to each other. 7 The court found that in the present case, although the main breadwinning responsibility lay with the Husband and the main caregiving responsibility lay with the Wife, both parties were working spouses. 8 The Wife had worked as a cabin crew for the first six years of the marriage and as an estate agent with [K Pte Ltd] for the rest of the marriage. The only indicator of the nature and extent of the Wife’s real estate work was the income she earned, which, on her own evidence, was an average of S$3,000 per month for 16 years. This was significantly more than what could reasonably be described as a “side income” of a homemaker. While the quantum of the Wife’s income was not determinative, it was an indicator to be taken into account when considering the nature of her work and the amount of time invested in the work. The Wife also had the assistance of a domestic helper throughout the marriage. Although this did not diminish the value of her role as a homemaker, the presence of a domestic helper enabled her to carry out her work whenever necessary. 9 The parties agreed that the direct contributions ratio was 80:20 in the Husband’s favour. As for the parties’ indirect contributions, the Wife managed the caregiving and the family’s affairs in Singapore without much help from the Husband while the Husband was frequently abroad for substantial periods. Thus, an indirect contributions ratio of 80:20 in her favour was fair. The average ratio reached in the third step of the structured ANJ v ANK approach was therefore 50:50 – the same result reached by the Judge. 10 The 20% uplift awarded to the Wife’s share was affirmed. While a 20% uplift is of itself a relatively high percentage, the absolute quantum of S$339,644.88 is not out of proportion to a reasonable estimate of the undisclosed assets. The court upheld the final division ratio of 70:30 in the Wife’s favour. 11 As for the other grounds of appeal, the Husband was unable to show that the Judge erred on her factual findings in including the assets in question in the matrimonial pool or in making the maintenance orders. 12 The appeal was dismissed. This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.

court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 12 February 2026 Case Summary DNO v DNP [202 6] SGHC(I) 2 SIC/OA 4/2025 --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Singapore International Commercial Court (delivered by Anthony James Besanko IJ): Outcome: The Singapore International Commercial Court (“SICC”) ordered costs of $106,123.37 to be paid by the applicant, DNO, to the respondent, DNP. Background 1. In SIC/OA 4/2025 (“OA 4”), DNO brought an application seeking to set aside an arbitral award made in favour of the respondent, DNP. The proceedings were commenced in the General Division of the High Court on 21 October 2024, and later transferred to the SICC on 3 March 2025 and converted into OA 4. 2. This judgment on costs followed from: a. the dismissal of OA 4 in DNO v DNP [2025] SGHC(I) 24; b. the grant of SIC/SUM 25/2025 (“SUM 25”), in DNO v DNP [2025] 4 SLR 362, an application brought by DNO in OA 4 for leave to file a further affidavit on the issue of its standing in OA 4; and c. the resolution of SIC/SUM 20/2025 (“SUM 20”), an application brought by DNP in OA 4 for an increase in security for costs. The SICC’s decision Pre-transfer costs 3. The court accepted that it could exercise its discretion to award indemnity costs on the basis that a case was bereft of merit. DNO’s case in OA 4 was “so devoid of merit” that an order for indemnity costs was warranted: [28]–[3 3], [36] . 4. DNP’s claim for $14,000 in pre-transfer costs (exclusive of GST) was not unreasonable: [40] . 5. Even if the costs were assessed on a standard basis, the total costs claimed by DNP ($15,260, inclusive of GST) was reasonable, taking into account, among others, the complexity of the case arising from the volume of evidence in the affidavits, the lengthy arbitral award, and the numerous arguments raised by DNO: [41] . 6. DNO did not challenge the reasonableness of disbursements incurred by DNP in the pre-transfer stage. The court considered that each disbursement was both reasonable in amount and reasonably incurred. Accordingly, DNP’s claim for disbursements in the pre-transfer stage, in the sum of $4,381.35, was allowed: [42] . 7. The court assessed and fixed DNP’s pre-transfer costs in the amount of $19,641.35 (inclusive of GST and disbursements): [43] . Post-transfer costs 8. By filing its costs schedule, DNP had discharged the legal burden of establishing that its post-transfer costs claimed, in the sum of $77,400 (exclusive of GST), were reasonable. Accordingly, DNO had an evidential burden to adduce evidence showing that the costs claimed were not reasonable. In this respect, DNO’s own costs schedule, which pertained only to costs incurred in relation to the limited issue of standing, did not assist its case. DNO did not refer to comparable cases: [48] –[50] . 9. The length of a judgment was not a reliable guide as to the complexity of a case. Neither was the number of legal practitioners necessarily a reliable guide: [54], [56] . 10. The post-transfer costs claimed were not unreasonable. DNO had not discharged its evidential burden of showing that the costs were unreasonable: [57] . 11. DNO was not entitled to set off any costs (in respect of SUM 25 and SUM 20) against the post-transfer costs awarded to DNP: [72 ] . a. Although a successful party would ordinarily receive its costs, SUM 25 was an application by a party to be relieved of an obligation it failed to comply with. There was also extensive delay in bringing SUM 25, and DNO did not provide a clear explanation for the delay. Further, the delay was a result of a failure to consider the matter carefully. Accordingly, the court rejected DNO’s application for costs on SUM 25: [61], [67] . b. DNP did not act unreasonably in filing SUM 20 when it did, having regard to a direction made by the Court. Accordingly, the court made no order as to costs on SUM 20: [72] . 12. DNO did not challenge the reasonableness of disbursements incurred by DNP in the post-transfer stage. The court considered that each disbursement was both reasonable in amount and reasonably incurred. Accordingly, DNP’s claim for disbursements in the post-transfer stage, in the sum of $2,116.02, was allowed: [ 73] . 13. The court assessed and fixed DNP’s post-transfer costs in the amount of $86,482.02 (inclusive of GST and disbursements): [ 74] . Conclusion 14. In total, costs of $106,123.37 (inclusive of GST and disbursements) were to be paid by DNO to DNP: [75] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s judgment. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s judgment.

court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 3 February 2026 Case summary Low Woon Hong v Lim Chun Yong (alias Lin Junxiong) (suing through his deputy and litigation representative Fung Wui Mang Janet) and other appeals [20 26] SGHC(A) 4 Appellate Division of the High Court — Civil Appeals Nos 54, 55, 56 and 92 of 2024 and Summons No 11 of 2025 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Appellate Division of the High Court (delivered by Debbie Ong Siew Ling JAD): Outcome: The Appellate Division of the High Court (“Appellate Division”) allowed the appeals in part in respect of damages awarded to a victim who was seriously injured in a road accident. The Appellate Division reduced the award for loss of future earnings by 30% and adjusted the award for the costs of future nursing care based on the rates for a four-bedder ward at Orange Valley Nursing Home. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment •  In assessing the loss of future earnings, the court applied a 30% discount to account for uncertainties associated with the future employment of the respondent, Mr Lim Chun Yong (“Mr Lim”). Given the gaps in his employment history, there was significant uncertainty as to whether Mr Lim would have remained employed at the Society for the Aged Sick (“SAS”) where he had worked for only three days before the accident, or whether he could obtain employment offering similar remuneration in the long term until the age of retirement: at [3 4] and [48] to [53] . •  Employment references provided by former employers to assist job applications do not automatically fall within the business records exception under s 32(1)( b )(iv) of the Evidence Act 1893 (2020 Rev Ed). In the present case, it was not shown that the references were made in the ordinary course of business of either former employer: at [4 2] to [46] . •  When assessing the costs of future nursing care, the relevant inquiry is whether the proposed care option is reasonable for the needs of Mr Lim. Institutionalised nursing care in a four-bedder ward was reasonable in the present case to meet Mr Lim’s long-term medical and nursing needs. On the present facts, a four-bedder ward could achieve the same level of effective care as a two-bedder ward for Mr Lim: at [7 7] to [79]. Background to the appeal 1 Mr Lim sustained serious injuries including traumatic brain injury in a chain collision involving three motor vehicles in Malaysia on 12 February 2018. He was 38 years old and had just started work (and was still on probation) as a finance executive at the SAS only three days before the accident. 2 The trial judge (the “Judge”) found all defendants (except the insurer who was added as the sixth defendant) jointly and severally liable to Mr Lim for the injuries he sustained as a result of the accident. Liability was apportioned as follows: the first and second defendants at 30%, the third defendant at 20%, and the fourth and fifth defendants at 50%. Total damages of $4,700,960.28 were awarded. 3 The defendants appealed against the Judge’s award of damages for various heads of claim, including: loss of future earnings; pre-trial loss of income; future nursing care costs; and several other awards. The insurer also appealed the costs order made against it. Decision Loss of future earnings 4 The court reduced the award for loss of future earnings by 30% to $1,116,602.70. The multiplier-multiplicand approach was used, and a discount was warranted given the uncertainties associated with Mr Lim's future employment. He had worked only three days at his new job at the SAS. Having regard to Mr Lim’s earlier chequered employment history, there was significant uncertainty as to whether he would have remained employed at the SAS or in a role offering similar remuneration in the long term until the age of retirement: at [ 26] to [34], [48] to [53] . Future nursing care costs 5 The court reduced the award for costs for future nursing care from $1,869,944.40 to $1,172,747.70 by using the rates in a four-bedder ward at Orange Valley Nursing Home instead of a two-bedder ward. While long-term institutionalized nursing care was reasonable to meet Mr Lim’s long-term medical and nursing needs, a four-bedder ward could achieve the same level of effective care for him as a two-bedder ward: at [7 6] to [79] . 6 The court rejected the appellants’ proposal to adopt the lower rates of another nursing home (ECON Nursing Home) as there was insufficient evidence as to whether that nursing home could provide effective care for Mr Lim's condition and needs: at [7 5] . Other awards 7 The court dismissed the appeal against the award for pre-trial loss of income. There was no reason to exclude Mr Lim’s yearly increments, bonuses and wage supplements from this award: at [57] to [58] . 8 The court agreed that an award for costs of future occupational therapy was reasonable because it is beneficial to Mr Lim. However, it reduced this award by 30% from $111,240 to $77,868 due to the uncertainties regarding whether Mr Lim would continue to require these occupational therapy sessions or require them at the same frequency in the future: at [ 98] to [99] . 9 The court set aside the award of $11,124 for future caregiver services when Mr Lim is on home leave. The award for future nursing care already contemplates a full stay at Orange Valley Nursing Home until the projected end of Mr Lim’s lifespan. Compensating Mr Lim for future caregiver services would mean that he is compensated for both the expenses incurred during the home leave and the expenses incurred at the nursing home: at [ 106] to [107] . 10 The court dismissed the appeal with respect to the costs of caregiver services provided before Mr Lim’s admission to Orange Valley. The Judge did not err in not requiring proof of loss of income by the caregiver. Whether damages may be awarded for caregiving by a family member remains a fact-specific enquiry: at [119] to [122] . 11 The court dismissed the appeal of the sixth defendant, the insurer, who contended that the Judge ought not to have ordered costs against it. The court found that costs against it were warranted; it had essentially conducted the defence of the insured defendants to protect its own interests: at [1 37] to [139] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.

court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 30 January 2026 Case summary Jethanand Harkishindas Bhojwani v Devin Jethanand Bhojwani and others and another appeal [2026] SGHC(A) 5 Appellate Division of the High Court/ Civil Appeal Nos. 3 and 4 of 2025 --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Appellate Division of the High Court (delivered by Justice See Kee Oon): Outcome: Save for certain adjustments to the remedies, t he Appellate Division of the High Court (the “Appellate Division”) dismissed AD/CA 3/2025 (“AD 3”) as brought by Jethanand Harkishindas Bhojwani (“Sajan”) and allowed AD/CA 4/2025 (“AD 4”) as brought by his three sons, Devin, Sandeep and Dilip (collectively, the “Brothers”). Pertinent and significant points of the judgment • Aside from some adjustments to the remedies awarded to the Brothers, the Appellate Division dismissed AD 3 because the Judge’s decision in respect of the issues raised in that appeal was not plainly wrong or unsupported by the evidence: at [164] . • The Appellate Division allowed AD 4 and held that the “conversion” of a founder’s share that formed part of the trust property (the “Founder’s Share”) amounted to a breach of Sajan’s custodial stewardship duty as there had been an unauthorised disposal of trust property. The “conversion” permanently eliminated valuable rights attached to the Founder’s Share that should rightly be regarded as assets of the trust. Consequently, the Appellate Division ordered that the disposal of the Founder’s Share be falsified: at [83] and [107] –[120] . Background to the appeal 1 The appeals arose against the backdrop of a protracted family dispute between Sajan and his three sons, Devin, Sandeep and Dilip. Sajan was the trustee of a testamentary trust (the “Trust”) created under the last will and testament (“Will”) of his late father, Harkishindas Ghumanmal Bhojwani (“Harkishindas”). In the proceedings below, the Brothers brought claims against Sajan for breach of trust, which were largely allowed by a judge of the High Court (the “Judge”). The Judge’s decision was subject to cross-appeals by Sajan in AD 3 and by the Brothers in AD 4. The material facts 2 In October 2006, Harkishindas executed the Will. Clause 5.2 of the Will provided for Sajan’s powers of appointment during the trust period, and stated that they could be exercised “in his absolute discretion”. Under cl 3 of the Will, Sajan was given specific powers that he could exercise in making an appointment under cl 5.2. This included, pursuant to cl 3(h), the power to do or omit to do all such acts or things as Sajan in his absolute discretion considered to be for the benefit of the estate or any one or more of the beneficiaries. 3 Clauses 5.1(iv) and 7(b) of the Will specified certain assets that would form the property of the Trust (the “Trust Assets” or “Trust Property”). The Trust Assets included shares in several companies which were run as a family business loosely known as the “Shankar’s Group” (referred to as the “Trust Shares” either separately or collectively). These companies included: a. Shankar’s Emporium (Private) Limited (“SEPL”); b. Sharrods (Private) Limited (“Sharrods”); c. Shankar’s Pte Ltd (“SPL”); d. Sovrein (Private) Limited (“Sovrein”); and e. Liberty Merchandising Pte Ltd (“LMPL”). The Trust also had a founder’s share in SEPL (the “Founder’s Share”). This was one of two founders’ shares in SEPL. 4 Following Harkishindas’s passing in March 2007, Sajan and the four other second-generation shareholders of SEPL voted to “convert” the two founders’ shares in SEPL into two ordinary shares. Next, in 2010, Sharrods, SPL and Sovrein (the “Three Struck Off Companies”) were struck off, the assets of these companies realised and the proceeds therefrom returned to the shareholders. Finally, in February 2021, Sajan executed two deeds in which he declared that the Trust Shares in SEPL and LMPL (collectively, the “Two Live Companies”) were to be sold to his brothers. The transfers of the Trust Shares were effected in that same month. The Brothers thereafter commenced the present claims against Sajan and contended that Sajan had breached several duties owed as a trustee. Decision of the Appellate Division Preliminary issue: Sajan’s appeal against the Judge’s decision to dismiss an application to admit the evidence of a witness 5 The Court rejected Sajan’s attempt to appeal against the Judge’s decision to refuse to admit the affidavit of evidence-in-chief of Mr Abdul Khader Mohamed Ismail (“Mr Ismail”), or for Mr Ismail’s oral evidence-in-chief to be adduced during the trial itself. This was because the Judge’s decision was an interlocutory order made at the hearing of an interlocutory application. Accordingly, permission to appeal was required pursuant to s 29A(1)( c ) of the Supreme Court of Judicature Act 1969 (2020 Rev Ed) read with para 3( l ) of the Fifth Schedule . Sajan, however, had not applied for and obtained such permission, and was now out of time to do so. Consequently, the Court was not seised of jurisdiction to hear Sajan’s appeal against the Judge’s decision to dismiss the application to admit Mr Ismail’s evidence: at [ 37]–[40] and [45]. Sajan’s challenges against the Judge’s decision on matters not directly related to the Trust Shares 6 The Court dismissed Sajan’s challenges against several of the Judge’s holdings on matters not directly related to the Trust Shares. First, the Court regarded as unmeritorious Sajan’s challenge against the Judge’s finding that he had concealed the Trust from the Brothers. Not only was there no documentary evidence indicating that Sajan had informed the Brothers of the Trust until 16 September 2016, but the timeline of events surrounding the Brothers’ alleged discovery of the Trust was also consistent with the fact that they did not discover the Trust until that date (at the earliest): at [ 47]–[51] and [57]. 7 The Court also rejected Sajan’s argument that he was not obliged to inform the Brothers about their rights under the Trust. A trustee owes a duty to take reasonable steps to inform discretionary beneficiaries of their rights under the trust as long as those discretionary beneficiaries have a realistic and reasonable prospect of benefitting under the trust. In this respect, as the Brothers were three of the four named beneficiaries under cl 5.1(ii) of the Will, they clearly had a realistic or reasonable prospect of benefitting under the Trust the moment the Trust came into existence. Sajan therefore breached his duty as trustee in failing to inform the Brothers of their rights under the Trust: at [58] –[61]. 8 Second, the Court rejected Sajan’s argument that he had not committed a breach of trust even though he had initially commingled the Trust moneys with his own moneys. Sajan himself accepted that there had been improper commingling and mismanagement in that he had failed to maintain proper trust accounts. His intention was immaterial to liability for breach of trust as well as the remedies that would flow from this breach of trust. The “absolute discretion” given to Sajan under cl 5.2 read with cl 3 of the Will did not permit him to deal with the Trust moneys without segregation. While Sajan was a lay trustee, there was nothing sophisticated about requiring him to maintain a separation between the trust assets and his personal assets: at [ 62]–[66]. 9 Third, the Court agreed with the Judge that Sajan had executed certain deeds (the “Exclusion Deeds”) to exclude Devin and Sandeep from the Trust in bad faith. Sajan had executed three deeds in April 2021 wherein he declared that Devin and Sandeep had no further interest in any of the remaining Trust Assets and would receive no distribution from the same, and that he held the remaining Trust Assets only for the benefit of Dilip. The chronology of proximate events leading up to the execution of the Exclusion Deeds strongly supported the conclusion that Sajan had executed those deeds in response to Devin and Sandeep’s questioning of his mismanagement of the Trust. Consequently, the execution of the Exclusion Deeds constituted fraud on the power and the Exclusion Deeds were held to be void. As a result, Devin and Sandeep both had standing to bring the present claims against Sajan: at [ 17], [67]–[70] and [74]. The “conversion” of the Founder’s Share 10 The Court disagreed with the Judge’s conclusion that Sajan had breached his management stewardship duties through the “conversion” of the Founder’s Share . The Court instead held that the “conversion” amounted to a breach of Sajan’s custodial stewardship duty as there had been an unauthorised disposal of Trust Property. To “convert” the Founder’s Share, Sajan and the other shareholders of SEPL had passed a shareholder’s resolution to remove cl 5 of SEPL’s Memorandum of Association, which had conferred several rights on a holder of a founder’s share. This included the right to 10% of SEPL’s annual net profits in perpetuity. Since the Founder’s Share represented a distinct bundle of rights that were qualitatively different in terms of benefits, privileges and control from ordinary shareholding rights, the “conversion” permanently eliminated valuable rights that should rightly be regarded as Trust Assets: at [9], [11] and [83]. 11 Furthermore, Sajan was not empowered to dispose of the Founder’s Share. Clause 5.1(iv)(j) of the Will was not an empowering provision since it merely stated that the Trust Property could comprise any shares that the Founder’s Share may be converted to. It did not specifically empower Sajan as the trustee to “convert” the Founder’s Share. Additionally, the powers vested in Sajan pursuant to cl 3(h) read with cl 5.2 of the Will could only be exercised in the context of or in relation to his making an appointment of a beneficiary. The “conversion” of the Founder’s Share did not occur in such a context: at [90]–[92]. 12 Even if the power vested in Sajan via cl 3(h) read with cl 5.2 of the Will was applicable to the “conversion” of the Founder’s Share, he could not invoke it since cl 3(h) provided that the power had to be exercised in the interest of the estate or for any one or more of the beneficiaries. The Court found that the justifications provided by Sajan for agreeing to the “conversion” were either mere afterthoughts or never genuinely considered at the time of the “conversion”. In those circumstances, Sajan could not be considered to have exercised his discretion under cl 3(h) read with cl 5.2 in the interests of the estate or for any one or more of the beneficiaries: at [93] –[96]. 13 The Court also held that Sajan’s “conversion” of the Founder’s Share amounted to a breach of the no-conflict and no-profit rules. By agreeing to extinguish the rights attached to the Founder’s Share, Sajan failed to ensure that the assets in the Trust were preserved and had lowered the value of the Trust, and also personally stood to benefit from the receipt of additional dividends in his capacity as an ordinary shareholder of SEPL: at [ 100]–[104]. 14 Consequently, the Court ordered that the disposal of the Founder’s Share be falsified through the payment of a monetary sum in lieu of reconstitution in specie of the Founder’s Share . The appropriate substitutive award was best measured by the value of the Founder’s Share as at 1 December 2023, as well as the profits (and interest accrued on those profits) until the date of the Judge’s decision that the Trust ought to have received on account of the Founder’s Share. This amounted to a substitutive award of $26,954,933.43: at [107] –[120] . The sale of the Trust Shares in SEPL and LMPL 15 The Court agreed with the Judge that Sajan had breached his statutory duties under the Trustees Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed), his duty of care under common law and his custodial stewardship duties as a trustee. Sajan’s explanation that he had sold the Trust Shares as part of a defensive strategy motivated by concerns of declining share value amid adverse market conditions was not credible. The Court also did not accept Sajan’s alternative explanation that he had sold the Trust Shares in response to the Brothers’ expressed wishes in 2017 for the Brothers, Sajan and Lakshmi to divest from the family business, as this was irrelevant to whether Sajan had breached any of the aforesaid duties in arranging the sale: at [123]– [124] and [129]–[130]. 16 The Court also generally agreed with the valuation methodology utilised by the Brothers’ expert in valuing the Trust Shares in SEPL and LMPL as at the date of sale (although certain adjustments needed to be made to the expert’s valuation of the Trust Shares in SEPL). In particular, the Court disagreed with Sajan’s submission that the Judge erred in refusing to apply a discount for lack of marketability (“DLOM”) and discount for lack of control (“DLOC”) to the valuation of the Trust Shares. In addition to accepting the Judge’s reasoning on why applying a DLOC and DLOM was not apposite to the specific valuations done in this case, the Court also reasoned that applying a DLOC and DLOM would be inappropriate given the nature of the remedy of falsification. The objective of such a remedy is to reconstitute the trust in circumstances where it is the wrongful act of the trustee that results in the exit from the relevant companies: at [135] , [ 138]–[140] and [142]. The realisation of the Trust Shares in the Three Struck Off Companies 17 The Court dismissed Sajan’s challenge against the Judge’s finding that the realisation of the shares in the Three Struck Off Companies was done at an undervalue in breach of his trustee duties. The Court held that the threshold for appellate intervention in findings on expert evidence had not been met in respect of the Judge’s acceptance of the valuation used by the Brothers’ expert. It was reasonable for the Judge to have accepted the methodology put forward by the Brothers’ expert: at [147] –[148]. 18 Leaving aside the challenges against the valuation methodology of the Brothers’ expert, the fact remained that the Brothers’ expert had substantially relied on the net asset value (“NAV”) of the Three Struck Off Companies as stated in the companies’ balance sheets (as at 30 June 2009, ie , one year before the striking off) to derive his valuation. Sajan had refused to explain the substantial discrepancy between the NAV stated in the balance sheets and the actual sums returned to the Trust. Similarly, with respect to Sharrods and Sovrein, he had refused to explain the potentially significant differences between the amount that ought to have been returned according to the Brothers’ expert and the capital purportedly returned to the Trust as stated in the companies’ statement of affairs. In the circumstances, the Judge was entitled to accept the valuation of the Brothers’ expert. It followed that the Judge was correct to conclude that Sajan had failed to ensure that the realisation of the Trust Shares in these companies resulted in the appropriate amount of capital being rightfully returned to the shareholders. Sajan could not escape the conclusion that he had acted in breach of trust: at [149] –[152]. The award of pre-judgment interest and the removal of Sajan as trustee 19 The Court was not persuaded by Sajan’s objections to the grant of pre-judgment interest: at [155] . 20 The Court agreed with the Judge that Sajan was to be replaced with a professional trustee. Sajan had committed multiple serious breaches of trust involving bad faith and incompetence, and three of the four named beneficiaries of the Trust had called for his removal. The considerations of the beneficiaries’ welfare and the safeguarding of trust property militated in favour of his removal: at [159] –[163]. This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.

court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 28 January 2026 Case summary Ng Soon Kiat v Public Prosecutor [2026] SGCA 3 Court of Appeal / Criminal Appeal No 5 of 2025 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Court of Appeal (delivered by Justice of the Court of Appeal Belinda Ang Saw Ean): Outcome: The Court of Appeal allowed the appellant’s appeal in part. The Court dismissed the appeal against the sentence imposed for the drug trafficking charge but allowed the appeal on the commencement date of the disqualification period imposed for the drink driving charge. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment • Under s 67(2) of the Road Traffic Act (Cap 276, 2004 Rev Ed) (“RTA”), the court can only order the disqualification period to commence upon the offender’s date of release from prison if the offender is sentenced to imprisonment for an offence under s 67(1) of the RTA. Where a fine is imposed, the date of commencement of the disqualification period is the date of conviction: at [73] . 1 This was an appeal against the decision of a Judge of the General Division of the High Court (“Judge”) in respect of the sentence imposed for the drug trafficking charge and the commencement date of the disqualification period for the drink driving charge. Background to the application 2 The appellant pleaded guilty and was convicted of three charges: a. trafficking not less than 166.99g of methamphetamine under s 5(1)( a ) of the Misuse of Drugs Act (Cap 185, 2008 Rev Ed) (“MDA”) (“Drug Trafficking Charge”); b. rioting under s 147 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed) (“Rioting Charge”); c. drink driving under s 67(1)( b ) read with s 67(2)( a ) of the RTA (“Drink Driving Charge”). 3 The Judge imposed the following sentences: a. Drug Trafficking Charge: 13 years’ imprisonment and 10 strokes of the cane. b. Rioting Charge: 1 year and 6 months’ imprisonment and 3 strokes of the cane. c. Drink Driving Charge: A fine of $6,000, and in default of payment, 2 weeks’ imprisonment. The appellant was also disqualified from holding or obtaining a driver’s licence for all classes of vehicles for a period of 34 months, to commence only on the appellant’s release from prison. 4 The prison sentences for the Drug Trafficking Charge and the Rioting Charge were to run consecutively. This resulted in an aggregate sentence of 14 years and 6 months’ imprisonment and 13 strokes of the cane. Facts pertaining to the Drug Trafficking Charge 5 Sometime in August 2020, the appellant began working for one Lim Jun Ren (“Jun Ren”), who was trafficking drugs for a Malaysian supplier known as “Ah Cute”. The appellant’s role was to rent a POPStation locker operated by Singapore Post with his mobile number, place drug parcels in the locker and forward location details to Jun Ren in exchange for $50 to $80 per delivery. On 8 September 2020, he deposited a parcel containing methamphetamine at a POPStation locker. Jun Ren was arrested on 8 September 2020. This led to the discovery and seizure of the parcel on 14 September 2020. The appellant was arrested on the same day. Facts pertaining to the Drink Driving Charge 6 On 30 August 2020, the appellant drove whilst intoxicated. The breath analysing device test showed that the appellant had 65 microgrammes of alcohol in 100 millilitres of breath, exceeding the prescribed limit of 35 microgrammes. He was arrested and released on station bail the same day. 7 The appellant committed the drink driving offence while on bail for the Rioting Charge, and subsequently committed the drug trafficking offence while on bail for the Drink Driving Charge 8 The appellant appealed against two aspects of the Judge’s decision: a. First, the custodial sentence of 13 years’ imprisonment and 10 strokes of the cane imposed for the Drug Trafficking Charge was manifestly excessive. The Judge did not accord weight or appropriate weight to his low culpability and other mitigating factors raised by him. b. Second, the disqualification order of 34 months should commence on the date of conviction and not the date of release from prison as the Judge had ordered. Decision Whether the custodial sentence of 13 years’ imprisonment and 10 strokes of the cane for the Drug Trafficking Charge was manifestly excessive 9 The Judge’s downward adjustment of the indicative starting sentence of 15 years’ imprisonment and 11 strokes of the cane by 0.5 years and 1 stroke of the cane, taking into consideration all relevant circumstances including the appellant’s culpability and the presence of aggravating and mitigating factors, was entirely appropriate: at [45] . 10  The appellant’s role, while limited, was not minor. He was a vital part of the distribution channel as he facilitated the delivery process without which drugs could not reach end users. His lack of knowledge and contact with the end users did not assist him, as it was a feature of the remote system of delivery which he played a part in. Even though the appellant did not attempt to evade detection, he had leveraged upon his personal information to tap into and abuse the POPStation system, which was intended for the remote collection, post and return of legitimate parcels. This facilitated the remote handover of drugs which offered some degree of anonymity and refuge for those involved in the drug trade. Regardless of the quantum of payment, he acted out of self-interest: at [46] to [50] . 11 The appellant’s commission of the offence on bail was an aggravating factor, and the seriousness of the Drug Trafficking Charge represented a marked escalation in criminality: at [51] –[52] . 12 The appellant’s contention that the Judge may have showed restraint in awarding a downwards adjustment to the sentence based on the actual quantity of drugs trafficked was speculative. The Judge had expressly said that the actual quantity of drugs trafficked was not regarded as an additional aggravating factor, and it is not shown how this played a role in the Judge’s sentencing decision: at [53] . 13 The Judge correctly assessed the relevance and weight of the various mitigating factors and had rightly accorded the maximum discount of 10% to the appellant’s sentence for his plea of guilt: at [54] to [55]. 14 The comparison with Vasentha d/o Joseph v Public Prosecutor [2015] 5 SLR 122 (“ Vasentha ”) did not assist the appellant. In Vasentha , the offender had lower culpability as she merely delivered drugs to pre-arranged locations, received only $20 per delivery and was exploited due to her naivety and low intellect. Some weight was also accorded to the offender’s cooperation with the authorities in their investigations. In contrast, the appellant was promised more money ($50 to $80 per delivery), there was no suggestion that the appellant was exploited or otherwise disadvantaged, and the appellant had the significant aggravating factor of reoffending on bail. No weight was accorded to the appellant’s cooperation with the police: at [5 6] to [59] . 15 The parity principle did not assist the appellant. The appellant compared his sentence as against Jun Ren’s sentence of 16 years’ imprisonment and 11 strokes of the cane for his own charge of trafficking 166.99g of methamphetamine, and submitted that the difference of three years’ imprisonment and one stroke of the cane was inadequate. The court agreed with the Prosecution that the difference in sentences sufficiently accounted for the disparate circumstances and culpabilities of Jun Ren and the appellant. Jun Ren was of greater culpability than the appellant as the appellant had acted on Jun Ren’s instructions while Jun Ren sold a variety of drugs to customers for profit, Jun Ren’s charge of possession of 166.99g of methamphetamine for trafficking was also committed on bail and Jun Ren faced 17 TIC charges involving drug offences. The difference of three years’ imprisonment and one stroke of the cane was significant, and the appellant could not be said to have suffered injustice: at [60] to [64] . 16 The sentence of 13 years imprisonment and 10 strokes of the cane was not manifestly excessive on the facts: at [65] . What is the commencement date of the disqualification period under s 67(2) of the RTA 17 The issue turned on an interpretation of s 67(2) of the RTA – whether the court can order a disqualification period under s 67(2) of the RTA to commence on the date of an accused person’s release from prison, when that person was not sentenced to imprisonment under s 67(1) of the RTA. The appellant was not sentenced to imprisonment under s 67(1) of the RTA and was sentenced to imprisonment for a different offence under the MDA: at [66] –[68]. 18 Section 67(2) was clear and unambiguous. The power to order disqualification to commence upon release from prison only applies where the offender is sentenced to imprisonment for the drink driving offence itself under s 67(1). The provision stated “where the person is sentenced to imprisonment” in the context of “a court convicting a person for an offence under this section”, referring specifically to s 67(1) offences: at [69] –[72]. 19 The Judge incorrectly ordered the disqualification period to commence on the appellant’s release from prison. The starting point under s 67(2) of the RTA is that the court can only order the disqualification period to commence upon the offender’s date of release from prison if the offender is sentenced to imprisonment for an offence under s 67(1). Where a fine is imposed, the starting point for the date of commencement of the disqualification period is the date of conviction. Since the appellant was not sentenced to imprisonment for the Drink Driving Charge under s 67(1), the court ordered the disqualification period to commence on the date of conviction, namely, 3 February 2025: at [73] . 20 Neither the appellant nor the Prosecution argued for the application of the “special reasons” proviso in s 67(2) of the RTA. No special reasons were established on the facts: at [74] . Conclusion 21 The court allowed the appellant’s appeal in part and ordered the period of disqualification of 34 months in respect of the Drink Driving Charge to commence on the appellant’s date of conviction on 3 February 2025. The appellant’s appeal against the sentence imposed in respect of the Drug Trafficking Charge was dismissed: at [78] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 13 January 2026 Case summary Law Society of Singapore v K V Sudeep Kumar and another [2026] SGHC 9 Originating Application No 2 of 2025 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Court of 3 Supreme Court Judges (comprising Tay Yong Kwang JCA, Steven Chong JCA and Ang Cheng Hock JCA) (delivered by Justice Ang Cheng Hock): Outcome: The Court of 3 Supreme Court Judges (“C3J”) imposed sanctions on the respondents, who allowed a disbarred lawyer to represent himself as an advocate and solicitor and to take conduct of a case for which they were the solicitors on record. The C3J imposed a term of suspension of five years on the first respondent and ordered that the second respondent be struck off the roll of advocates and solicitors. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment • There are broader public interest considerations at play in cases involving the practice of law by unauthorised persons. These considerations assume greater force when an unauthorised person who has been determined to be unfit to practise is allowed to do precisely that : at [36]–[38] . • The C3J did not accept the Law Society’s submission that the distinction between ss 83(2)( b ) and 83(2)( h ) of the LPA was relevant when it came to the appropriate sanction to be ordered. Once due cause was shown, the specific facts of each case would be scrutinised to determine the appropriate sanction to be meted out: at [66]–[70] . • The C3J had some misgivings as to whether the interpretation of s 83(1)( b ) of the LPA in Law Society of Singapore v Yap Bock Heng Christopher [2014] 4 SLR 877 – that it cannot impose a consecutive suspension period in a case before it if doing so would, when added to a previous suspension period imposed on the errant solicitor, result in him serving a total suspension period of more than five years – is a correct one: at [75] . 1 The respondents, Mr K V Sudeep Kumar (the “first respondent”) and Mr Dhanwant Singh (the “second respondent”) each faced a charge under s 83(2)( h ) of the Legal Profession Act 1966 (2020 Rev Ed) (“LPA”), for allowing one Udeh Kumar s/o Sethuraju (“Mr Kumar”), a disbarred lawyer, to represent himself as an advocate and solicitor and to have de facto control over the conduct of a case for which the respondents were the solicitors on record. 2 The respondents pleaded guilty to the charges before the Disciplinary Tribunal (“DT”). At the conclusion of the proceedings, the DT found that there was cause of sufficient gravity for the matter to be referred to the C3J. Accordingly, the Law Society of Singapore applied for an order that the respondents be sanctioned under s 83(1) of the LPA. 3 Before the C3J, the respondents agreed that the respective charges were proven beyond a reasonable doubt, and that there was sufficient cause for the imposition of sanctions under s 83(1) of the LPA. Thus, the only issue before the C3J was the appropriate sanctions to be imposed. Facts 4 From 2018 to 2020, the respondents practised at S K Kumar Law Practice LLP (“the Firm”). At the material time, they were the only two lawyers with practising certificates at the Firm. Mr Kumar, also known as “S K Kumar”, had been struck off the roll of advocates and solicitors on 23 March 2017. At the time of his striking off, Mr Kumar had been in practice for about 29 years and was the founder and managing partner of the Firm, which was named after him. 5 In or around December 2017, Mr Wong Yiat Hong (“the complainant”) was introduced to Mr Kumar. He met Mr Kumar at the Firm’s premises on 13 March 2018, where they discussed the merits of an action, DC/DC 2662/2016 (“DC 2662”), brought against the complainant. During this meeting, the Firm was appointed to take over the conduct of DC 2662 from the complainant’s previous solicitors. 6 The respondents were the solicitors on record for the complainant in DC 2662 for around two years, from March 2018 to around February 2020. Throughout the Firm’s conduct of DC 2662, Mr Kumar had de facto control over the conduct of DC 2662. At no point did the respondents inform the complainant that Mr Kumar had been struck off the roll of advocates and solicitors and was hence no longer a practising lawyer. 7 After judgment was entered against the complainant in DC 2662, the complainant made a complaint to the Law Society. On 16 February 2024, the Law Society furnished its Statement of Case and applied to the Chief Justice for the appointment of a disciplinary tribunal to hear and investigate the Complaint. In its Statement of Case, the Law Society brought one main charge under s 83(2)( b ) of the LPA, and an alternative charge under s 83(2)( h ) of the LPA, against each respondent. 8 The DT was constituted on 26 March 2024. The first and second respondents filed their Defences on 14 April and 2 May 2024 respectively. On 6 November 2024, the Law Society amended its case to proceed with only the alternative charge under s 83(2)( h ) of the LPA against each of the respondents. 9 On 19 November 2024, a day before the respondents were due to file their amended Defences, the respondents informed the DT that they would be pleading guilty to the charges and would not be filing amended Defences. The second respondent added that he would be withdrawing the Defence he filed. 10 On 22 April 2025, the DT issued its report, finding that there was cause of sufficient gravity to refer both respondents to the C3J for disciplinary action. Parties’ submissions on the appropriate sanctions 11 The Law Society submitted that a substantial period of suspension should be imposed on both respondents – four years for the first respondent, and four-and-a-half years for the second respondent. The Law Society argued that the gravity of the respondents’ misconduct was comparable to that of the respondent in Law Society of Singapore v Yeo Siew Chye Troy [2019] 5 SLR 358 (“ Troy Yeo ”). 12 Both respondents were undischarged bankrupts at the time of the hearing. The Law Society submitted that the period of suspension imposed on the first respondent should commence upon the discharge of his bankruptcy. As the second respondent was already subject to a suspension period of five years imposed in Law Society of Singapore v Dhanwant Singh [2025] 4 SLR 1443 (“ Dhanwant Singh (2025) ”), the Law Society submitted, following the case of Law Society of Singapore v Yap Bock Heng Christopher [2014] 4 SLR 877 (“ Christopher Yap ”) ,  that the second respondent should be struck off the roll. 13 The first respondent contended, in his written submissions, that a period of suspension of between 18 months and two-and-a-half years should be imposed. The second respondent argued that striking off was “not mandated nor warranted”, and that any suspension period imposed in these proceedings ought to run concurrently with the suspension period imposed on him in Dhanwant Singh (2025 ) . He did not, however, specify what the length of his suspension period ought to be. The C3J’s decision 14 The C3J considered that the gravity of the respondents’ misconduct was greater than that of the misconduct in Troy Yeo , notwithstanding that Mr Yeo faced additional charges and that the financial harm caused to his clients was on a greater scale : at [35] . a. The respondents’ conduct of knowingly allowing Mr Kumar to practise when they knew that he had been struck off the roll was far more serious than the conduct of failing to properly supervise an employee in Troy Yeo : at [ 36]–[38] . b. The respondents were acutely aware of Mr Kumar’s status as a disbarred lawyer but nevertheless permitted him to have de facto conduct of DC 2662 : at [ 39]–[40] . c. The respondents were unable to point to any significant effort on their part to supervise Mr Kumar’s conduct of DC 2662 or to stop him from having conduct of the case: at [ 42] . Sanction imposed on the first respondent 15 After considering the gravity of the first respondent’s misconduct and his lack of antecedents, the C3J found it appropriate to impose a period of suspension of five years on the first respondent: at [43] . 16 The various mitigating factors identified by the first respondent did not assist his case: at [44]–[48] . 17 The C3J ordered that the first respondent be suspended from practice for a period of five years, with the period of suspension to commence from the date of his discharge from bankruptcy: at [49] . Sanction imposed on the second respondent 18 The C3J considered that the second respondent’s conduct, taken together with the relevant aggravating and mitigating factors, warranted that he be struck off the roll: at [52] . a. There were two critical aggravating factors which militated against any sanction other than a striking off being imposed on the second respondent: i. The second respondent had two antecedents which were fairly recent, and which pertained to misconduct and/or breaches of the professional rules while he was practising in the Firm: at [53]–[61] . ii. The second respondent was an advocate and solicitor of at least 32 years’ standing, and the managing partner of the Firm. He was more senior than the first respondent both in terms of their length of time in practice, and in his position in the Firm. Thus, the second respondent’s seniority carried more aggravating weight as compared to the first respondent: at [62]–[63] . b. Minimal weight was placed on the second respondent’s plea of guilt, as it came late in the DT proceedings: at [ 65] . 19 The C3J disagreed with the Law Society’s submission that the second respondent was not dishonest. The second respondent’s dishonesty lay in his false representation, through his acts and omissions, to a member of the public (the complainant) that Mr Kumar was a practising lawyer: at [64] . 20 In any event, the second respondent’s conduct was also reflective of a fundamental lack of respect for the law, which was a character defect that rendered a solicitor unfit to be a member of the legal profession. In such a case, striking off would be the presumptive penalty: at [65] . 21 The C3J did not accept the Law Society’s submission that the distinction between ss 83(2)( b ) and 83(2)( h ) of the LPA was relevant when it came to the appropriate sanction to be ordered. Once due cause was shown, the specific facts of each case would be scrutinised to determine the appropriate sanction to be meted out: at [66]–[70] . 22 The C3J ordered that the second respondent be struck off the roll of advocates and solicitors with effect from the date of their decision ( ie , 12 November 2025): at [71] . Coda: Observations on Christopher Yap 23 In Christoper Yap , the C3J expressed the view that it would not be able to impose a consecutive suspension period on the same solicitor in a different case while that solicitor is already serving a period of suspension, if the duration of suspension in total would exceed five years. As the second respondent’s conduct was sufficiently serious to warrant being struck off the roll, there was no need to consider the Law Society’s reliance on Christopher Yap . However, the C3J expressed some misgivings as to whether the observation in Christopher Yap reflect ed a correct interpretation of s 83(1)( b ) of the LPA : at [72]–[79] . a. There was nothing on a plain reading of the LPA which would lead to the conclusion that the C3J could not impose a consecutive suspension period in a case before it if doing so would, when added to a previous suspension period imposed on the errant solicitor, result in him serving a total suspension period of more than five years: at [75] . b. There was also nothing in the legislative history of s 83(1)( b ) of the LPA which support ed the interpretation in Christopher Yap : at [76] . c. Such a reading of s 83(1)( b ) might, in some cases, operate unfairly in practice : at [77]–[78] . 24 Nevertheless, the C3J did not make any definitive determination on the correctness of the observation in Christopher Yap as it was unnecessary to do so in this case: at [79] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.
