court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 12 January 2026 Case summary Valency International Pte Ltd v JSW International Tradecorp Pte Ltd and others and another appeal [202 6] SGCA 1 Civil Appeal Nos 31 and 32 of 2025 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Judgment of the Court of Appeal (comprising Steven Chong JCA, Belinda Ang Saw Ean JCA, Ang Cheng Hock JCA) (delivered by Steven Chong JCA): Outcome: The Court of Appeal (the “CA”) dismissed one appeal but allowed another against the decision of a Judge of the General Division of the High Court (the “Judge”) that was made in relation to a claim for the wrongful conversion of a parcel of cargo (the “Cargo”). Pertinent and significant points of the judgment • In a case where the alleged act of conversion takes the form of an instruction for another party to act in a certain way, the claimant must prove the factual chain of causation between the instruction and the conversion of the good. A bare denial of title remains an inchoate act in the absence of proof that it had caused the event which ultimately crystallised the injury to the claimant’s interest: at [56] , [58] , [62] . • To determine whether a pledge is retained despite the redelivery of the pledged asset to the pledgor, the court will consider whether the redelivery occurred in circumstances which constituted a voluntary surrender of the pledgee’s special interest in that asset. Should the pledgee return the asset to the pledgor to deal with as his agent , this may be indicative of the former’s intention to retain his interest in the asset; however, it is certainly not the sole factor that the court considers when assessing the circumstances surrounding a redelivery: at [84] . Background to the appeal 1 These were appeals against the decision of the Judge in Valency International Pte Ltd v JSW International Tradecorp Pte Ltd and others [2025] SGHC 50 (the “Judgment”) that related to the claims brought by Valency International Pte Ltd (“Valency”) in the tort of conversion. There were two key issues in the appeal: a. whether the Judge correctly dismissed Valency’s claims in conversion against JSW International Tradecorp Pte Ltd (“JSW”) and Oldendorff Carriers GmbH & Co. KG (“Oldendorff”) for want of standing to sue (the “Standing Issue”); and b. Whether the Judge correctly found that (i) JSW’s instruction to the discharge port agent to release the cargo to the end-buyer was not an act of conversion; but (ii) Oldendorff’s instruction to the same agent to release the cargo was such an act of conversion (the “Act of Conversion Issue”). Facts 2 In May 2018, K.I. (International) Limited (“Kamachi”) contracted to purchase the Cargo (made of non-coking steam coal) from JSW. On Kamachi’s request, Valency agreed to finance the purchase by establishing a letter of credit in JSW’s favour. This letter of credit was subsequently opened via the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation (“HSBC”) in August 2018 (the “Valency LC”). 3 Separately, JSW voyage chartered a vessel (the “Vessel”) from Oldendorff to facilitate the carriage of the Cargo to any port of India. Oldendorff had voyage chartered the Vessel from Cara Shipping Pte Ltd (“Cara”), who in turn time chartered the Vessel from its owner. On JSW’s nomination, Unicorn Maritimes (India) Pvt Ltd (“Unicorn”) was appointed as the discharge port agent for the Vessel. 4 In early June 2018, a shipment of coal was loaded onto the Vessel, including the 55,000MT of Cargo that was relevant to the appeals. The parcel of Cargo that is material to the appeals was represented by “Initial BL No 1”. 5 The Vessel arrived at Gangavaram Port, India (“Gangavaram Port”) on 26 June 2018. On 29 June 2018, Unicorn sent a letter to JSW, undertaking to release the Cargo to Kamachi only upon JSW’s written instructions (the “Unicorn-JSW Undertaking”). 6 Between 19 and 21 August 2018, the Vessel discharged part of her laden cargo at Gangavaram Port, not including the Cargo that was represented by Initial BL No 1. The Vessel then set sail for Krishnapatnam Port, India (“Krishnapatnam Port”). The discharge of the Cargo to the storage area at Krishnapatnam Port 7 The Vessel arrived at Krishnapatnam Port on 23 August 2018. Several key events occurred upon the Vessel’s arrival: a. JSW requested for Initial BL No 1 to be switched into 22 bills of lading, each for 2,500MT of coal (the “22 BLs”). b. On 24 August 2018, Kamachi requested JSW to deliver the Cargo to itself “without production of the [22 BLs]”. Kamachi undertook to indemnify JSW against any loss that it might incur by result of complying with this request (the “Kamachi-JSW Discharge LOI”). Thereafter, JSW issued a back-to-back letter of indemnity to Oldendorff, and Oldendorff issued a back-to-back letter of indemnity to Cara, on largely the same terms as in the Kamachi-JSW Discharge LOI. c. Between 27 and 31 August 2018, the Cargo was discharged at Krishnapatnam Port into a storage area without production of the 22 BLs. The Control Letters 8 On 31 August 2018, Valency requested that Kamachi procure letters from Unicorn and JSW confirming that they would only release the Cargo from the Storage Area against presentation of the 22 BLs (collectively, the “Control Letters”). Kamachi responded to say that the Control Letters could only be provided after JSW had been paid for the Cargo. Nevertheless, the following letters were prepared by Kamachi, JSW and Unicorn on the same date (the “Control Letters”): a. Kamachi prepared a letter, addressed to Valency, stating that it would not physically move the cargo from the storage area until it received written instructions or a fresh delivery order from Valency or Valency’s agent (the “Kamachi Letter”). b. JSW prepared a letter, addressed to Unicorn, instructing Unicorn to take Valency’s instructions regarding the issuance of delivery orders and the delivery of the Cargo to Kamachi, and stating that delivery orders were only to be issued against the surrender of the 22 BLs to the Vessel’s agents (the “JSW Letter”). c. Unicorn prepared a letter addressed to Valency, acknowledging that the Cargo would only be released upon surrender of the 22 BLs or on Valency’s written instructions (the “Unicorn Letter”). 9 Separately, on 30 August 2018, JSW had discounted the Valency LC with its negotiating bank, Standard Chartered Bank (“SCB”). On 3 September 2018, SCB presented various relevant shipping documents – including the 22 blank-indorsed BLs – to HSBC, to collect payment under the Valency LC. 10 Payment on the Valency LC was remitted by HSBC to SCB on 10 September 2018. Thereafter, Valency requested again (see [8] above) for the urgent issuance of the Control Letters. The Letters were sent to Valency several days thereafter. The Trust Receipt and the Pledge 11 On 10 September 2018, Valency applied to HSBC for the sum outstanding on the Valency LC to be repaid by way of an import loan (the “Import Trust Receipt Loan”) and pledged the 22 BLs to HSBC as security for this Loan (the “Pledge”). 12 At the same time, Valency applied to retake physical possession of the 22 BLs on trust receipt terms in order for it to control delivery of the Cargo (the “Trust Receipt”). The Trust Receipt provided that Valency would hold the 22 BLs the Cargo, and/or the proceeds of any sale thereof, on trust for HSBC and solely to HSBC’s order. On 11 September 2018, HSBC granted the Trust Receipt application and Valency collected the 22 BLs. The delivery of the Cargo 13 Prior to issuing the JSW-Oldendorff Discharge LOI, JSW originally asked Oldendorff to hold off on releasing the Cargo to Kamachi because it had yet to receive payment for the demurrage incurred at Gangavaram Port (see [5]–[6] above). 14 While Oldendorff initially agreed to this request, it later wrote to JSW on 13 September 2018 to say that it was being pressured by Kamachi for release of the delivery orders. Oldendorff informed JSW that it would instruct Unicorn to issue these orders unless JSW clearly indicated otherwise. In spite of JSW’s request for more time, Oldendorff proceeded to instruct Unicorn, on the same day, to “release delivery order for [the Vessel]” and “issue delivery order for both ports” (the “Oldendorff Release Instruction”). 15 On 17 September 2018, upon receiving word from Oldendorff that Unicorn had already been instructed to issue the delivery orders to Kamachi, JSW instructed Unicorn to “release [d]elivery order for [the Cargo]” (the “JSW Release Instruction”). 16 Thereafter, between 17 September and 15 November 2018, Unicorn issued a total of 14 delivery orders (the “Delivery Orders”), and Kamachi took delivery of the entire Cargo from the storage area at Krishnapatnam Port. Events leading to the commencement of the action below 17 On 24 September 2018, the Import Trust Receipt Loan fell due. Valency thus took out further loans from HSBC (on 24 and 25 September 2018) by discounting the 22 BLs with HSBC with recourse to Valency. In other words, the Pledge was brought to an end by 25 September 2018. 18 In November and December 2018, Kamachi paid for 5,000MT of the coal that was represented by BL-1 and BL-2. Payment for the remaining 50,000MT of the Cargo (represented by BL-3 to BL-22) remained outstanding to Valency. 19 From December 2018 to August 2019, Unicorn informed Valency multiple times that the closing balance for the Cargo was 52,500MT. This was untrue, given that Kamachi had already taken delivery of all the Cargo by 15 November 2018. It was not until 29 January 2020 that Valency learned of the delivery of the Cargo to Kamachi in late 2018. 20 In March 2020, Valency commenced the action below, claiming, inter alia , damages against JSW, Unicorn and Oldendorff for conversion of the Unpaid Cargo. In gist, Valency’s case was that these parties had instructed and/or allowed and/or facilitated the delivery of the Cargo to Kamachi. 21 The Judge (a) dismissed Valency’s claim against JSW and Oldendorff because it lacked the standing to sue these parties in conversion. Additionally, (b) the Judge took the view that the JSW Release Instruction was not an act of conversion; however, (c) the Oldendorff Release Instruction was such an act. 22 Valency appealed against the Judge’s findings at [21(a)] and [21(b)] above. Oldendorff, in turn, appealed against the Judge’s finding at [21(c)] above. Decision on appeal The Act of Conversion Issue 23 On appeal, Valency argued that although JSW and Oldendorff had issued their Release Instructions on 17 and 13 September 2018 respectively, they should remain liable for conversion until Unicorn had completed issuing the Delivery Orders on 15 November 2018. It was, however, unclear at best whether Valency had indeed taken this position in the proceedings below, and it was apparent that Valency had changed tack in the course of the trial: at [ 52]–[54] . 24 For Valency to establish that JSW and Oldendorff were liable for the misdelivery of the Cargo to Kamachi, it had to prove the chain of causation between the respective Release Instructions and the issuance of the Delivery Orders by Unicorn. The respective Release Instructions had to be acted on before liability in conversion could attach: at [56] , [58] . 25 The JSW Release Instruction had to be understood with regard to the context of communications leading up to the instruction. a. At the time of the JSW Release Instruction, Unicorn remained bound by the Unicorn Letter, pursuant to which it had undertaken to Valency not to release the cargo without Valency’s instructions. It was unlikely that Unicorn would have understood the JSW Release Instruction as an instruction to breach its obligations to Valency or to supersede its obligation to Valency. b. Additionally, Unicorn had lied to Valency about the closing balance of the Cargo. This showed that Unicorn knew it still needed Valency’s instructions before issuing the Delivery Orders. c. Lastly, prior transactions between the same parties were indicative that Unicorn was aware of the need to wait for Valency’s instructions before releasing the Cargo. These facts militated against a finding that the JSW Release Instruction caused Unicorn to issue the Delivery Orders: at [64] . 26 There were greater difficulties with finding that the Oldendorff Release Instruction caused Unicorn to issue the Delivery Orders since that instruction had been given four days earlier than the JSW Release Instruction. On its face, the Oldendorff Release Instruction was not an instruction or direction for Unicorn to either deliver the Cargo without presentation of the 22 BLs or Valency’s written consent: at [66] –[67] . 27 There was insufficient evidence to shed light as to which of the two release instructions Unicorn had chosen to follow (if any), and it would be arbitrary to find that one but not the other had been operative on Unicorn’s decision to release the Delivery Orders. Additionally, the fact that the Delivery Orders were released progressively over a period of two months would militate against any inference that either or both of JSW’s or Oldendorff’s Release Instructions had been operative on Unicorn’s mind: at [68] . 28 The CA therefore allowed Oldendorff’s appeal in CA 32 and its findings on this issue were dispositive of Valency’s appeal in CA 31: at [71] . The Standing Issue 29 The CA agreed with the Judge that Valency had no standing to sue JSW and Oldendorff in the tort of conversion: at [ 72] . 30 It was well-established that a party would have the right to sue in conversion if and only if he had, at the time of the alleged conversion, either (a) actual possession of; or (b) the immediate right to possess the relevant goods: at [75] . 31 It was undisputed that Valency did not have actual possession of the Cargo at the time of the alleged conversion. The question, therefore, was whether Valency was entitled to immediate possession of the Cargo at the material times: at [75] . 32 In particular, it was necessary to identify the test for determining if a trust receipt arrangement sufficiently preserved the pledgee’s special property in the pledged good, such that the pledgee reserved the standing to sue in conversion vis-à-vis the pledgor : at [75] , [79] . 33 The CA rejected Valency’s argument that the pledge could only have been preserved if the terms of the trust receipt established an agency relationship between pledgor and pledgee. The creation of an agency relationship was not the logical or legal foundation for the retention of the pledgee’s special interest in the good: at [ 79], [82]–[84] . 34 Instead, it was necessary to examine the terms of the trust receipt and other circumstances surrounding the redelivery to determine if the pledgee intended to surrender its interest in the pledged assets or if the pledge was otherwise extinguished: at [87] . 35 In that connection, the terms of the Trust Receipt between Valency and HSBC made it clear that the latter did not intend to surrender its special interest in the 22 BLs despite the redelivery to Valency. HSBC had no intention of relinquishing it special interest in the Cargo, and the Trust Receipt secured the continuance of the Pledge: at [ 88]–[90] . 36 In any event, the CA was satisfied that Valency in fact obtained redelivery of the 22 BLs in its capacity as HSBC’s agent. HSBC and Valency had both agreed to the terms of the Trust Receipt, the net effect of which was to permit Valency to deal with the Cargo on behalf of HSBC and in HSBC’s name: at [ 91]–[92] . 37 The mere fact that Valency physically held the 22 BLs and was entitled to demand delivery of the Cargo from the carrier would not have sufficed to give it the standing to sue in conversion. This was because Valency could only have done so as HSBC’s agent, and it would have been bound by the terms of the Trust Receipt: at [ 93]–[95] . 38 The CA therefore dismissed Valency’s appeal and allowed Oldendorff’s appeal: at [96] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.

court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 12 January 2026 Case summary XIT v XIS and another matter [2026] SGHC(A) 2 Appellate Division / Civil Appeal No 17 of 2025 and Summons No 44 of 2025 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Appellate Division of the High Court (delivered by Judge of the Appellate Division Debbie Ong Siew Ling): Outcome: The Appellant Division of the High Court (“Appellate Division”) partially allowed the Husband’s appeal on, amongst other things, the drawing of an adverse inference against him, and dismissed the rest of the appeal. The Appellate Division allowed in part the Husband’s application to admit further evidence. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment • The starting point is that the date of the ancillary matters (“AM”) hearing is the operative date that should be adopted for valuing matrimonial assets. The court retains a discretion to depart from that date where warranted. However, any decision to depart from this date should be accompanied by cogent reasons, such as where there is evidence of dissipation of assets by one party: at [33] to [42] . • The purpose of drawing an adverse inference was not to punish the non-disclosing party for concealment but to account for the fact that assets were not placed before the court for a just and equitable division. Therefore, it is not necessary to accord any uplift if the acts of dissipation have already been addressed by adopting a valuation date which precedes the period when the acts of dissipation had taken place : at [62] to [63]. • The Appellate Division’s holding in WOS v WOT [2024] 1 SLR 437 (“ WOS v WOT ” ) at [61] should be read in its context. The holding did not stand for the proposition that indirect contribution of spouses during the period of separation should be discounted simply because parties had lived apart for a large part of the marriage: at [93] to [95] . Background to the application 1 The Husband brought an appeal against the decision of a Judge in the Family Division of the High Court (“Judge”) in respect of ancillary matters following the parties’ divorce. 2 The Husband and Wife were married on 16 January 1993 and have three adult children. The Husband was a director of Company [A], Company [C] and Company [D]. He had beneficial interests in these companies, and another Company [B], collectively referred to as the “Companies”. 3 In November 2000, after nearly eight years of marriage, the Husband moved out of the matrimonial home. After close to 17 years living apart, the Wife commenced divorce proceedings on 22 June 2017. An interim judgment of divorce (“IJ”) was granted on 9 January 2018. 4 In the lead up to the AM proceedings, the Wife filed a suit in the High Court to seek a declaration of the Husband’s beneficial ownership of the Companies and two patents registered in his name. The Husband was found to be the beneficial owner of shares in the Companies, but not of the patents. The value of the Husband’s shares in the Companies, amongst other things, was put into issue in the AM proceedings. 5 The Husband appealed against eight aspects of the Judge’s decision on the division of matrimonial assets. The issues which arose for determination were classified into five categories: a. First, whether the Judge erred in departing from the default position by adopting the valuation of the Husband’s shares in the Companies as at 31 December 2018, which was close to the IJ date, instead of 30 September 2023, which was close to the AM date (“Valuation Issue”); b. Second, whether the Judge erred in drawing an adverse inference against the Husband for failing to make full and frank disclosure, and according a 5% uplift to the Wife’s share in the division of matrimonial assets (“Adverse Inference Issue”); c. Third, whether the Judge erred in not finding that the Husband had taken a loan of S$544,702.03 from Company [A], such that this sum was not taken into account as part of his liabilities (“Loan Issue”); d. Fourth, whether the Judge erred in including certain assets in the matrimonial pool (“Inclusion Issue”), namely: i. The moneys the Husband used to purchase Property [F]; ii. The funds in Account 3612; iii. The sum of RM413,000 (S$136,290) in Account 8336; iv. The Husband’s contribution to Property [G]; v. The dividends paid by Company [A] in 2017 and the dividends paid by Company [A] and Company [B] in 2018; and e. Fifth, whether the Judge erred in his finding that the ratio of indirect contributions was 80:20 in the Wife’s favour (“Indirect Contributions Issue”). 6 The Husband also applied to admit 15 pieces of additional evidence comprising eight pieces of documentary evidence and seven clarificatory statements. Decision Application to admit additional evidence 7 The eight pieces of documentary evidence were admitted as they were pertinent to the issues in the appeal and apparently credible. The principles in Ladd v Marshall [1954] 1 WLR 1489 did not apply strictly to AM hearings: at [28] to [30] . 8 However, the seven clarificatory statements were not admitted as they were not supported by documentary evidence: at [31] . Division of matrimonial assets 9 The court dismissed the appeal in respect of the Valuation Issue, the Inclusion Issue with respect to the moneys the Husband used to purchase Property [F], Account 3612, Account 8336 and Property [G], and the Indirect Contributions Issue. The court allowed the appeal in respect of the Adverse Inference Issue, the Loan Issue and the Inclusion Issue with respect to the dividends paid by Company [A] in 2017: at [32] . The Valuation Issue 10 The starting point was to use the date of the AM hearing as the operative date for the valuation of matrimonial assets. The court retained a discretion to depart from that date where warranted. Any decision to depart from this date should be accompanied by cogent reasons, such as where there is evidence of dissipation of assets by one party: at [33] to [ 42] . 11 The Judge did not err in valuing the Husband’s shares in the Companies as at 31 December 2018, a date closer to the IJ. The Husband’s payment of legal fees and dividends for the benefit of himself and his relatives constituted a dissipation of assets as the Wife had a putative interest in these sums and had not consented to such expenditures. It was not possible to arrive at an appropriate figure to add the moneys dissipated back into the matrimonial pool as not all payments of dividends and legal fees were accounted for. Further, the court could not conclude from the email evidence that the Companies’ contracts with [S], a major client, and its related entities had indeed been terminated. The court also had doubts about whether the value of the Companies could decrease by almost half just by losing [S] as a client and the emails did not adequately explain the drop in the Companies’ value and other aspects of the Companies’ accounts: at [43] to [53] . The Adverse Inference Issue 12 An adverse inference may be drawn where there was a substratum of evidence that established a prima facie case against the person against whom the inference is to be drawn and some evidence suggesting that the person had sought to conceal or deplete assets which should be included in the matrimonial pool. That person must have had some particular access to the information he was said to be hiding: at [60] to [61] . 13 Drawing an adverse inference was not to punish the non-disclosing party for concealment but to account for the fact that some assets were not placed before the court for a just and equitable division. The Wife’s argument that the Husband’s initial attempt to dissipate his assets by transferring his shares in the Companies should be considered negatively appeared to focus on penalising the Husband. It was not necessary to accord any uplift to the Wife’s share of the pool on account of the Husband’s dissipation of assets, as this was already addressed by adopting a valuation date which preceded the period when the acts of dissipation had taken place: at [62] to [63]. 14 No adverse inference should be drawn in relation to the Husband’s Australian superannuation fund and Singapore bank accounts. The Husband provided sufficient evidence that his superannuation fund was closed and that his bank accounts were credit line accounts. There was no evidence that he was wilfully trying to conceal monies: at [64] to [75]. The Loan Issue 15 The Husband’s loan from Company [A] should be taken into account as a liability in the matrimonial pool. Company [A]’s financial statements and management accounts supported the existence of the Husband’s liability to Company [A] in respect of the loan: at [76] to [83] . The Inclusion Issue 16 The Judge did not err in including the moneys the Husband used to purchase Property [F], the funds in Account 3612, the sum of RM413,000 in Account 8336 and the Husband’s contribution to Property [G] in the matrimonial pool. In respect of the dividends paid by Company [A] and Company [B] in 2018, these were also properly included in the matrimonial pool as the Husband was the beneficial owner of the shares. As for the Judge’s inclusion of RM292,000 in dividends paid out by Company [A] in 2017, the appeal was allowed as RM220,000 had been properly accounted for and only RM72,000 should be returned to the matrimonial pool: at [84] to [92]. The Indirect Contributions Issue 17 The Husband relied on the holding in WOS v WOT at [61] for the proposition that the Wife’s indirect contributions should be reduced as the parties were separated for the majority of the duration of the marriage, about 17 years out of a 25-year marriage. The court held that WOS v WOT was distinguishable, and its holding should be construed in its proper context. WOS v WOT did not involve a dual-income marriage to which the structured approach in ANJ v ANK [2015] 4 SLR 1043 applied. WOS v WOT concerned a single-income marriage where the homemaker wife submitted that theirs was a long single-income marriage to which equal division ought to apply. It was in this context that the court held that the indirect contribution of spouses who are separated for a large part of the marriage may not be as substantial as those maintaining a shared home and caring for the family in the factual context of long single-income marriages to which equal division was envisaged to apply. The holding did not stand for the proposition that the indirect contributions of spouses during the period of separation should be discounted simply because parties had lived apart for a large part of the marriage: at [93] to [95] . 18 The Judge did not err in ascribing an indirect contributions ratio of 80:20 in the Wife’s favour. In the present case, the structured approach applied. The Wife brought up three children while working full-time and was the children’s primary caregiver for 17 years. The Husband did not live with the Wife and children and was not involved in caring for the children. The Wife did not receive financial support from the Husband in the first four years of parties’ separation, when the children were in their formative years at the young ages of four, six and seven. Accordingly, the indirect contributions ratio of 80:20 in the Wife’s favour should not be disturbed: at [96] . Conclusion 19 After making the appropriate adjustments, the total matrimonial pool was $10,848,043.30. The Husband was entitled to 53% and the Wife was entitled to 47% of the matrimonial pool: at [97] to [98] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.

court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 9 January 2026 Case Summary DNZ v DOA and another [2026] SGHC(I) 1 SIC/OA 2/2025 --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Singapore International Commercial Court (Joint Judgment of Andre Maniam J, Dominique Hascher IJ and Vivian Ramsey IJ): Outcome : The Singapore International Commercial Court rejected the claimant’s application to set aside an arbitral award on the grounds that there was no valid arbitration agreement, the award was in conflict with the public policy of Singapore, and the award was made in breach of natural justice. Background 1. The claimant (“State”) is a Member State of the European Union (“EU”). The defendants (“UK Investors”) were two companies incorporated in the United Kingdom (“UK”). The second defendant (“UK Direct Holding Company”) is a wholly owned subsidiary of the first (“UK Indirect Holding Company”), and owned a majority of the shares in a company incorporated in the claimant (“Project Company”), which undertook the Project in question. The remaining shares in the Project Company were owned by a company from “State X” (“State X Holding Company), which wholly owned the UK Indirect Holding Company, and was wholly owned by another State X company (“State X Ultimate Parent Company”): [ 2]–[4]. 2. Pursuant to a bilateral investment treaty between the State and State X, State X Holding Company commenced arbitration against the State (“BIT Arbitration”), and pursuant to Art 26 of the Energy Charter Treaty (“ECT”), the UK Investors also commenced arbitration against the State the next day (“ECT Arbitration”). The same tribunal heard, and awarded damages against the State in, both arbitrations: [5]–[8]. 3. In SIC/OA 2/2025 (“OA 2”), the State applied to set aside the award issued in the ECT Arbitration (“ECT Award”) on the grounds that there was no valid arbitration agreement, the award was in conflict with the public policy of Singapore, and the award was made in breach of natural justice under s 24 of the International Arbitration Act 1994 and s 3 of the same read with Art 34(2) of the Model Law. Issues before the Court 4. The Court considered the five objections the State raised against the ECT Award: a. Jurisdictional Objection 1: Intra-EU Objection; b. Jurisdictional Objection 2: Subject-Matter Objection; c. Jurisdictional Objection 3: Fork-in-the-Road Objection; d. Breach of public policy; and e. Breach of natural justice. Jurisdictional Objection 1: Intra-EU Objection 5. The State submitted that Art 26 of the ECT was invalid and/or inapplicable in the present case because the disputed submitted to arbitration was an “Intra-EU Dispute”, ie , one in which the relationship between the two states (being the State and the UK) was governed by EU law, and EU Member States were precluded under EU law from arbitrating a dispute with a national of another EU Member State: [11]–[15]. 6. The Court accepted that the rule precluding EU Member States from arbitrating Intra-EU Disputes was already part of EU law at the time that the ECT Arbitration was commenced, and EU law applied in the UK then. However, whether the Tribunal was bound to apply EU law depended on the law governing the arbitration agreement: [ 15]–[24]. 7. Parties were agreed that, under the three-stage test in Anupam Mittal v Westbridge Ventures II Investment Holdings [2023] 1 SLR 349, international law governed the arbitration agreement; however, they disagreed on the application of EU law as part of international law: [25]–[2 9]. 8. The Court held that EU law did not apply in the way that the State suggested: a. The State submitted that under EU law, the principle of EU law primacy applies as a conflict of laws rule to give the rule precluding arbitration of Intra-EU Disputes over Art 26 of the ECT. The Court disagreed, holding that the principle of EU law primacy only operated within the EU system, and not on the broader international plane, and that it was not obligated to apply the same: [30]–[3 7]. b. The Court also rejected the State’s argument that, notwithstanding the multilateral nature of the ECT, the dispute between itself and the UK Investors was bilateral as recourse to the dispute settlement mechanism within the ECT was implemented bilaterally; they were therefore at liberty to disapply Art 26 of the ECT in case of a conflict with EU law. The Court held that Art 26 was a multilateral obligation owed by each Contracting Party to all other Contracting Parties, and the fact that only two parties would be in dispute did not mean that the obligation should be construed as though it was bilateral: [38]–[41]. c. The Court also held that Arts 1(3) and 25 of the ECT, which recognises the EU as a Regional Economic Integration Organization to which its Member States have conferred competence to examine any question relating to the interpretation and application of international agreements concluded by the EU, could not have meant that the relationships between EU Member States were governed by EU law under the ECT as if they had not independently ratified the ECT. The Court had regard to, in particular, the 1998 Statement submitted by the European Communities to the Secretariat of the Energy Charter, which makes clear that the Member States have concluded the ECT independently and are responsible for the obligations incurred in accordance with their respective competences: [42]–[43] . 9. The Court then held that Art 26 of the ECT applied to an Intra-EU Dispute: a. Article 16 of the ECT, which deals with the conflict between the ECT and other international agreements, gives priority to the provision that is more favourable to the investors. The Court held that the possibility of pursuing arbitration under Art 26 of the ECT, as contrasted with the prohibition against arbitration under EU law, provided an additional and therefore more favourable protection to investors: [4 5]–[47]. b. The State submitted that the rules of interpretation under Art 31 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (“VCLT”), which required regard to be had to the ECT’s object and purpose, supported its view that Art 26 of the ECT was inapplicable in an Intra-EU Dispute. Because the ECT was an EU-driven initiative, and (according to the State) did not have investment as its only objective but was also designed to promote East-West energy cooperation, the EU Member States could not have intended that the ECT to supersede their obligations under EU law. The Court  disagreed, noting that Art 26, on its ordinary meaning, applied to all investor-State disputes equally, and the purpose of the ECT, as defined in Art 2, did not make any distinction between the investor’s geographical origin that would deviate from the ordinary meaning of Art 26: [48]–[49 ]. c. The State also submitted that pursuant to Art 31(3)(a) and (b) of the VCLT,  Art 26 of the ECT could be modified inter se between EU Member States by subsequent agreement or practice . In this regard, it relied on two declarations, the first signed in 2019 by 22 EU Member States including the State and the UK, and the second signed in 2024 by 26 EU Member States. The effect of both declarations was to affirm that EU law precluded the arbitration of Intra-EU Disputes. The Court did not find this persuasive, as both declarations were not agreed within the EU Member States, and even met opposition. The conditions of subsequent agreement or practice were therefore not met: [50]–[52 ]. d. Finally, the State relied on Art 30 of the VCLT, which gives priority to a later treaty over an earlier treaty relating to the same subject matter. It submitted that the ECT, which entered in force between the State and the UK, applied earlier than the Treaty on European Union (“TEU”) and the Treaty of Lisbon (which birthed the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (“TFEU”)), and that Art 19(3) of the TEU and Arts 267 and 344 of the TFEU (which prohibit the arbitration of Intra-EU Disputes) related to the same subject matter as Art 26 of the ECT. The Court disagreed that these provisions relate to the same subject matter, as the ECT dealt with the long-term promotion of cooperation and protection of investments in the energy sector whereas the TEU and TFEU dealt with the organisation of the functioning of the EU: [5 4]–[60]. 10. The Court observed also that any jurisdictional objection relating to an Intra-EU Dispute would have been removed for any arbitration proceedings commenced by the UK Investors after 1 January 2021, pursuant to UK’s withdrawal from the EU. In such circumstances, any jurisdictional defect which existed at the time that the ECT Arbitration was commenced would have been cured at the time that the ECT Award was issued, pursuant to Mavrommatis Palestine Concessions (Greece v. Great Britain) (Jurisdiction) PCIJ Rep Series A. No 2: [61]–[63]. Jurisdictional Objection 2: Subject-Matter Objection 11. The State submitted that the Tribunal did not have jurisdiction because the UK Investors did not have a protected “Investment” under Art 1(6) of the ECT and they were therefore not “Investors” under the ECT: [64]. 12. The Court identified two sub-issues: [65]. a. What criteria are applicable in determining whether an asset qualifies as a protected “Investment”? b. Do the UK Investors’ alleged investments relating to the Project qualify as protected “Investments” under the applicable criteria? 13. The Court held that an “Investment” under the ECT need not satisfy the criteria set out in S alini Costruttori S.p.A. and Italstrade S.p.A. v. Kingdom of Morocco [I] , ICSID Case No. ARB/00/4, Decision on Jurisdiction (16 July 2001) (“ Salini criteria”) . The ECT provides its own definition of “Investment”; the Salini criteria originated from an interpretation of the term “investment” in a treaty which did not provide its definition . The UK Investors’ direct and indirect shareholdings in the Project Company, as well as other assets within the State, satisfied the definition under the ECT, and the UK Investors were therefore “Investors” with a protected “Investment”: [ 70]–[79], [90]–[93]. 14. The Court went on to hold that, in any event, the Salini criteria were satisfied on the facts : [80]. a. The State submitted that the Salini criteria , which required a contribution of money or assets, were not satisfied as the documents indicated that it was the State X Holding Company that paid for the UK Direct Holding Company’s shareholding in the Project Company. The State contended that the evidence in the ECT Arbitrations did not prove that the UK Investors paid for their shareholding; the UK Investors should be precluded from admitting further evidence in OA 2; and even if further evidence were admitted, this did not prove that payment was made: [ 81]–[82]. b. The Court observed that the UK Investors had, in their Post-Hearing Brief in the ECT Arbitration, stated that they were prepared to adduce further evidence of payment if the Tribunal considered it necessary, but did not because the Tribunal was prepared to accept that payment had been made on the available evidence. It was therefore not the case that further evidence was only being introduced before the Court but not offered to the Tribunal. Having regard to the broad principles of relevance, reason for prior-non admission, and credibility ( Sanum Investments Ltd v Government of the Lao People’s Democratic Republic [2016] 5 SLR 536 at [102]–[103]) , the Court admitted the UK Investors’ further evidence, which reinforced the evidence given in the ECT Arbitration: [84]– [87]. Jurisdictional Objection 3: Fork-in-the-Road Objection 15. The State submitted that, pursuant to the “fork-in-the-road” provision in Art 26(2) and (3) of the ECT, read with Annex ID of the ECT, the State had expressly withheld its consent to arbitrate the dispute with the UK Investors, which had already been submitted for resolution in the BIT Arbitration: [ 95]–[97]. 16. The Court held that, in order for the “fork-in-the-road” provision to apply, the Triple Identity Test needed to be met, ie , the two proceedings must have the same parties, cause of action and object . Applying this test, the dispute submitted to the ECT Arbitration was not the same dispute submitted to the BIT Arbitration, for the ECT Arbitration concerns allegations of breach of Arts 10 and 13 of the ECT, whereas the BIT Arbitration concerns allegations of breach of the BIT between State X and the State. Moreover, State X was not a party to the ECT: [119]–[121]. 17. However, even applying the Fundamental Basis Test (which requires the two disputes to have the same fundamental basis, ie , the same subject matter) put forth by the State, the Court held that the Fork-in-the-Road Objection failed because there was no identity of parties: [122]. Breach of Public Policy 18. The State submitted that the ECT Award was contrary to Singapore’s public policy because: [124]. a. The ECT Award violated the autonomy of EU law, which was part of the fundamental constitutional norms of the EU applicable to the parties at the material time. b. If the ECT Award were upheld, it would place the State in the unfair and prejudicial position of having to breach EU law and expose it to infringement proceedings and significant sanctions by the European Commission (“EC”). c. It would be a breach of international comity to uphold the ECT Award as the Court of Justice of the European Union had found that such awards would be invalid. 19. The “public policy” objection is a narrow one, applying where upholding an award would “shock the conscience”, “violate the forum’s most basic notions of morality and justice”, be “clearly injurious to the public good”, or be “wholly offensive to the ordinary reasonable and fully informed member of the public”: [125]. 20. The Court held that the mere fact that the ECT Award might be contrary to EU law or EU public policy did not mean that upholding the ECT Award would be contrary to Singapore’s public policy. In similar vein, a breach of international comity did not mean that, absent the type of criminal activity that would violate the most basic notions of morality and justice or shock the conscience, public policy should be engaged: [126]–[1 31]. 21. The Court also held that Mercuria Energy Group Limited v Republic of Poland Case No.1:23-cv-03572 (TNM), which was the subject of further submissions by parties, did not assist the State. In that case, the United States District Court for the District of Columbia (“USDC”) declined to enforce an award that had been annulled by the Svea Court of Appeal (“SCA”) based on the Intra-EU Objection. The USDC, did not consider whether the SCA’s application of Komstroy to annul the award was correct, but found that the SCA’s decision was not contrary to American public policy, and so it denied enforcement of the award. OA 2 was distinguished on the basis that the Court was not considering the enforcement of an award that has been set aside by the seat court: [132]–[135]. 22. The Court did not agree that the State could rely on its contradictory obligations that it now faced: this was simply a function of the State entering into the relevant treaties, and it was not for the Singapore court to relieve the State of the consequences of its own actions. Moreover, the Court was not satisfied that the State did face the risk of infringement proceedings by the EC if it satisfied the ECT Award, as the State had not pointed to any infringement proceedings brought by the EC against an EU Member State in similar cases, whereas the UK Investors had identified similar cases which did not attract any infringement proceedings: [139] –[140]. Breach of Natural Justice 23. The State submitted that the Tribunal breached the rules of natural justice, specifically the right for the State to be heard: a. The Tribunal determined the quantum of damages in the ECT Award by making its own adjustments to an outdated/inaccurate Excel spreadsheet containing a sensitivity analysis (“BR-218”), which was prepared by the State’s expert, Brattle, in its first report, which was submitted in response to the first report by UK Investors’ expert, Secretariat, which included a discounted cash-flow (“DCF”) valuation model of the Project. Brattle’s first report raised criticisms of the pricing assumptions in Secretariat’s first report, and produced its own version of Secretariat’s DCF valuation model using BR-218, which was intended to provide the Tribunal with a model which allowed changes to be made to various pricing assumptions and inputs, and which reflected the impact of each potential change to Secretariat’s pricing assumptions and DCF valuation: [142]. b. Secretariat accepted some criticisms raised by Brattle and updated its DCF valuation. Brattle submitted a second report which raised further criticisms of Secretariat’s updated DCF valuation, but did not include a further sensitivity analysis, like BR-218 based on that updated DCF valuation. At the hearing of the ECT Arbitration, Secretariat accepted a correction and further updated its DCF valuation: [145]. c. In the ECT Award, the Tribunal held that Secretariat’s DCF model was a “reliable and robust calculation” on which it could quantify the UK Investors’ losses with reasonable confidence. However, some of the criticism raised by Brattle were justified so as to warrant modifications to the DCF calculation. It therefore applied various discounts based on Brattle’s sensitivity analysis in BR-218: [146] –[151]. d. The State submitted that the Tribunal erred in its calculation by using BR-218, which led to a significant overstatement of damages. While it accepted that it cannot set aside the ECT Award merely because the Tribunal had made certain errors in calculating the quantum of damages, it complained that the Tribunal should have sought the parties’ input on the appropriate calculation methodology or invited the parties to submit updated DCF valuation models and sensitivity analyses, and those errors arose because of the Tribunal did not accord the State its proper right to be heard and present its case in relation to the quantum of damages: [152]–[ 167]. 24. The Court found that the State had a full opportunity to be heard and to present its case: a. The State had decided to respond to the DCF valuation in Secretariat’s first report by submitting BR-218, which provided the Tribunal the very means to adjust the DCF valuation produced by Secretariat. Although the State was seeking to undermine the DCF valuation method, it had emphasised in its Post-Hearing Brief that (and was therefore on notice that) if the Tribunal adopted the DCF valuation method and took a different view on some of the inputs and assumptions, the Tribunal would be able to adjust them in the DCF model: [ 170]–[173]. b. When Secretariat updated the DCF valuation in its second report, the State did not respond by providing another sensitivity analysis or suggest that the sensitivity analysis in BR-218 could not be used on an updated or further updated DCF valuation. While Secretariat did not submit an updated excel spreadsheet in respect of its final DCF valuation, the State did not raise any concerns at the time: [174]. c. It was not clear why the Tribunal should raise any concerns or query the parties on the matter. If BR-218 was no longer applicable to the updated or further updated DCF valuations then it was for the State to point that out. Having not submitted a revised version of BR-218 after the updated DCF valuation in Secretariat’s second report, it was for the State to make the appropriate submissions and not for the Tribunal to raise any concerns or query the parties: [175]–[178]. Conclusion 25. The Court dismissed OA 2 in its entirety. This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s judgment. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s judgment.

case_name: YIT CHEE WAH v FULCRUM DISTRESSED PARTNERS LIMITED
subject_tags: ["Insolvency Law — Bankruptcy — Proof of Debt\nCompanies — Directors — Duties"]
court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 7 January 2026 Case summary Yit Chee Wah (as private trustee of the estate of Chan Siew Lee Jannie, a bankrupt) v Fulcrum Distressed Partners Ltd [202 6] SGHC(A) 1 Appellate Division of the High Court — Civil Appeal No 11 of 2025 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Judgment of the Appellate Division of the High Court (delivered by Justice of the Court of Appeal Ang Cheng Hock): This case concerned a proof of debt filed by the liquidators of Timor Global Pte Ltd (“TGPL”), a Singapore-incorporated company, and pursued by the assignee of TGPL’s debt, Fulcrum Distressed Partners Ltd (“FDPL”), a company incorporated in the British Virgin Islands (“BVI”). The proof of debt was based on alleged breaches of fiduciary duties by the bankrupt, Ms Jannie Chan Siew Lee (“Ms Chan”). Ms Chan’s private trustee in bankruptcy (“PTIB”), Mr Yit Chee Wah (“Mr Yit”), rejected the proof of debt. FDPL thus applied to court to appeal against Mr Yit’s rejection. A Judge of the General Division of the High Court (the “Judge”) allowed FDPL’s claim without ordering a trial or cross-examination of witnesses. Mr Yit appealed against the Judge’s decision. The Appellate Division of the High Court (“ADHC”) allowed the appeal and ordered a trial of the matter before the Judge to determine the claims against Ms Chan. Pertinent and significant points of the GD • The proof of debt regime is designed for adjudicators to decide straightforward claims efficiently based on clear written and/or documentary evidence. In claims involving complex disputes of fact requiring examination of witnesses, the adjudicator should reject the claim or seek directions from the court rather than attempt summary determination: at [6] and [59]–[62] . • If the matter comes before the court, the paramount consideration would be whether oral examination of witnesses and/or discovery is “necessary for fairly disposing of the particular issue”. The other factors which the court ought to consider would include the presence of complex disputes of fact, gaps in the documentary or affidavit evidence, conflicting documentary or affidavit evidence, as well as the gravity of the allegations against the bankrupt: at [63]–[64] . • The court will holistically assess all the relevant factors to decide the appropriate directions to be given for the disputed claim to be resolved. This may involve a full trial of the claim, or perhaps only limited cross-examination of key witnesses and only on certain issues. The court may also encourage parties to attempt mediation or some form of neutral evaluation, especially where the value of the bankrupt’s estate might be unduly burdened by the costs of litigation: at [ 65] . Background to the appeal and the material facts 1 TGPL was incorporated in Singapore on 16 February 2005. Its sole shareholder at all material times was Ms Chan. Ms Chan and Mr Lay Ni Suig Bobby (“Mr Lay”) were directors throughout, with Mr Tan Tjo Tek (“Mr Tan”) serving as director from 2005 to August 2016. Ms Chan also held between 60 to 70% of the shares in another company, Timor Global (TL) Pte Ltd (“TL”), a Timor-Leste company registered in 2005. Mr Lay was the sole director of TL 2 TGPL and TL were in the business of agricultural trading. From 2006 to 2008, TGPL and TL were involved in a joint venture arrangement with Intraco Trading Pte Ltd (“Intraco”) for the processing and trading of coffee beans, and for the profits to be shared between TGPL and Intraco. To that end, TGPL, TL and Intraco entered into a joint venture agreement on 1 July 2007 (“2007 JVA”). The recitals of the 2007 JVA referred to an earlier agreement dated 27 March 2006 (“2006 JVA”), but only the 2007 JVA was produced as part of the documentary evidence before the court below. According to the recitals of the 2007 JVA, the latter covered substantially the same subject matter as the 2006 JVA, but there were some changes to Intraco’s trading commitment and the way profits were to be shared. 3 The arrangement under the 2007 JVA involved Intraco making advance payments to TL, to enable TL to purchase and process raw coffee beans, which were then sold to Intraco who then sold them to TGPL at cost for onward sale to third parties. Profits were split 60:40 or 70:30 between TGPL and Intraco depending on profit levels, with TGPL bearing all losses. 4 The parties deviated from the 2007 JVA’s terms. Notably, TL’s invoices directed Intraco to pay TGPL’s bank accounts instead of TL’s. From 31 July to 17 October 2007, Intraco paid S$8,638,389.92 to TGPL, who transferred S$8,142,398.70 to TL (from 3 August 2007 to 18 October 2007). 5 Disputes arose in relation to the joint venture agreement, which led Intraco to bring arbitration proceedings in 2009. Eventually, Intraco obtained arbitration awards in its favour in March and November 2015 respectively against TGPL. In April 2015, Intraco obtained leave to enforce one of the awards as an order of court and took out examination of judgment debtor proceedings against TGPL (the “Intraco EJD Proceedings”). Ms Chan filed three affidavits in those proceedings (the “Intraco EJD Affidavits”) and was also examined in court. TGPL was wound up in March 2018. Ms Chan was declared bankrupt in May 2019 on an unrelated debt. 6 On 14 October 2019, TGPL’s liquidators filed a proof of debt against Ms Chan’s estate in bankruptcy for four sums, including sums described as the TL Sum and the Finished Goods Sum. The proof of debt was revised and the eventual amount of the TL Sum claimed was S$15,766,460. This sum referred to the receivables allegedly owed by TL to TGPL as at 31 December 2014. The Finished Goods Sum referred to a sum of US$2,301,767.43 (or S$3,161,247.39 using the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s exchange rate for 27 May 2019). This sum represented sales proceeds from coffee beans sold by TGPL in 2008, which were allegedly paid directly by TGPL’s customers to TL between 19 June 2008 and 14 November 2008. The claim for both sums were based on alleged breaches of Ms Chan’s fiduciary duties as TGPL’s director. 7 Mr Yit was subsequently appointed as the PTIB of Ms Chan’s estate in bankruptcy on 9 June 2020, and he rejected both the claims for the TL Sum and the Finished Goods Sum on 3 November 2022. On 24 November 2022, FDPL commenced proceedings in court to appeal against Mr Yit’s decision to reject the claims for both sums. FDPL filed both an Originating Application (“OA 797”) and a Summons (“SUM 4314”) to appeal Mr Yit’s rejection of the claims, due to uncertainty about which legal regime applied - the IRDA or the repealed Bankruptcy Act. 8 The Judge allowed FDPL’s claim: a. Despite a prior dispute on the position, the parties eventually agreed that a claim for damages for breach of fiduciary duty, regardless of whether the breach was of a custodial or non-custodial nature, was provable as an unliquidated claim arising by breach of trust. The Judge held that the TL Sum and the Finished Goods Sum were capable of being provable debts, if established by the evidence b. The Judge held that the TL Sum should be admitted in full. He found that the TL Sum comprised three components: (i) the 2007 Payments (S$8,142,398.07) which arose from transfers from TGPL to TL in 2007; (ii) the Opening Balance (S$6,662,009.44) which was the amount recorded as due from TL as at 31 December 2006; and (iii) Sum 3 (S$962,051.84), which the Judge found to be payments made by TGPL purportedly for TL’s operating expenses. c. For the 2007 Payments, the Judge found that they were genuine debts owed by TL to TGPL. First, the 2007 Payments were recorded as “related party receivables” or “amounts due from related parties” in TGPL’s management accounts and financial statements. Second, Ms Chan had stated in the Intraco EJD Affidavits that TGPL had lent money to TL by way of a “cash loan” and the total amount owed by TL in 2013 was S$15,343,006. This amount corresponded to the receivables recorded in TGPL’s books as of 2013, which included the 2007 Payments. Third, the 2007 JVA could not satisfactorily explain the payment patterns. The Judge found that Ms Chan had breached her fiduciary duties through the disbursement of the 2007 Payments to TL, her failure to pursue repayment from 2007 to 2014 and her approval of the write down of the TL Sum in the accounting records of TGPL. d. For the Opening Balance, the Judge held that Ms Chan had similarly breached her fiduciary duties by allowing the loans to be made to TL for no commercial benefit, failing to pursue repayment, and approving the writing down of the TL Sum. For Sum 3, the Judge held that Ms Chan was also in breach of her fiduciary duties as the payments lacked commercial purpose. e. For the Finished Goods Sum, the Judge found Ms Chan knew or should have known about this substantial diversion (32% of TGPL's 2008 revenue) given her control and oversight of the company. Her failure to seek repayment was a breach of her fiduciary duties. f. The Judge held that the claim for both the TL Sum and Finished Goods Sum was not time-barred, as Ms Chan's breaches constituted “fraudulent breach of trust” under s 22(1)(a) of the Limitation Act. Decision on appeal 9 The ADHC expressed tentative views that the Bankruptcy Act regime applied to this case as the applications below were made “in relation to” Ms Chan’s bankruptcy application filed in November 2018, which predated the 30 July 2020 cut-off date: at [20] . 10 Although the overarching substantive issue was whether Ms Chan is liable to TGPL for the TL Sum and the Finished Goods Sum because of her breach of fiduciary duties as a director of TGPL, there was an anterior issue to be determined. This was whether FDPL’s claims for the TL Sum and Finished Goods Sum ought to have been determined simply by way of affidavits, documents and submissions by the parties, without the need for a trial, or at least cross-examination of witnesses. For the following reasons, the ADHC held that the evidence before the Judge did not clearly establish that Ms Chan was in breach of her duty to act honestly and bona fide in TGPL’s interests in respect of the TL Sum and the Finished Goods Sum. The material disputes of fact in relation to FDPL’s two claims rendered them unsuitable to be decided without a trial : at [66]–[67] . 11 The following key issues could not be satisfactorily resolved on the available affidavit and documentary evidence alone: Whether the TL Sum was a genuine debt 12 The ADHC could not conclude that the 2007 Payments were indeed debts due and owing from TL to TGPL. The period in which TGPL paid the 2007 Payments to TL (between 3 August 2007 and 18 October 2007) roughly coincided with the period in which TGPL received around the same amount from Intraco (between 31 July 2007 and 17 October 2007). This suggested that those inflows and outflows were connected. If the moneys paid by Intraco to TGPL were intended to be passed on to TL as the advance payments due to TL from Intraco under the joint venture arrangements, then there would be no issue of any breach of fiduciary duty in respect of these payments by TGPL to TL. If Ms Chan, Mr Lay and Mr Tan, or a staff who had knowledge of the reasons for these 2007 Payments, had given evidence and been cross-examined, they might have been able to shed some light on some of the issues regarding these transfers of funds: at [74]–[77] . 13 The Judge placed too much weight on the TL Sum appearing as a receivable in TGPL’s management accounts. The reliability of the management accounts was questionable given that TGPL’s auditors, L W Ong & Associates LLP (“L W Ong”), had disregarded more than S$9.7m of the receivables from TL recorded in the management accounts of TGPL in 2008. Although it was unclear whether LW Ong could provide any meaningful evidence on why they wrote down the receivables recorded in the management accounts as they no longer had TGPL’s books and records in their possession, Ms Chan, Mr Lay and Mr Tan, as directors of TGPL, or some staff who had been handling the accounts for TGPL, ought to be in a position to clarify why they decided to maintain that amount of receivables in TGPL’s management accounts from 2009 to 2014 despite the auditors writing the amount down significantly in 2008: at [78]–[79] . 14 Although Ms Chan admitted the existence of the loans under oath in the Intraco EJD Affidavits, she later made statements contrary to those admissions under oath in related proceedings that were also heard by the Judge together with FDPL’s application. She claimed that she was only a “financial investor” in the company, and that she left all the affairs of TGPL to Mr Lay and Mr Tan, the other two directors. She claimed that Mr Lay could confirm that she had no knowledge of and control over the operations of TGPL, and that TGPL’s liquidators had confirmed on affidavit that Mr Lay had informed them that Ms Chan had no “working knowledge of TGPL”. Hence, Ms Chan, Mr Lay and Mr Tan (or any of TGPL’s staff with knowledge of its management and operations) ought to have been examined: at [80]–[83] . 15 Just because Ms Chan’s signature appeared on the management accounts did not establish that those management accounts were reliable or that she acknowledged the existence of the receivables owing from TL. Ms Chan had stated on affidavit that, because she was travelling 90% of the time, her staff had her digital signature which they used when necessary. This was another dispute of fact that called for witnesses to be examined: at [78]–[79] . 16 For similar reasons, the ADHC found it difficult to conclude, without the examination of witnesses such as Ms Chan, Mr Lay, Mr Tan, staff from TGPL who handled the accounts, or someone from Intraco, that the Opening Balance was indeed a genuine debt owing to TGPL: at [89]–[90] . 17 There was no objective evidence to support the Judge’s finding that Sum 3 pertained to payment for TL’s operating expenses. TGPL’s liquidators failed to investigate the specific entries which purportedly supported Sum 3’s purpose as being “Operating Expenses”. This meant that the purpose of Sum 3 was far from clear, and this would affect any finding of a breach of fiduciary duty by Ms Chan in relation to Sum 3. This too called for an examination of witnesses such as Ms Chan, Mr Lay, Mr Tan, staff from TGPL and TGPL’s liquidators: at [91]–[95] . The quanta of the TL Sum and the Finished Goods Sum 18 Mr Yit argued on appeal that TGPL’s audited financial statements for the year 2008 excluded approximately S$9.7m in receivables that had been recorded in the management accounts, yet this “Excluded Amount” was carried forward in subsequent years' management accounts and ultimately became part of the TL Sum. The ADHC concluded that the audited financial statements could not be dismissed outright. That meant that the Excluded Amount would raise questions as to the quantum of the TL Sum – questions which would be best answered by witnesses, such as Mr Lay, Mr Tan, Ms Chan and staff from TGPL who handled its accounts: at [98]–[99] . 19 Mr Yit also argued there was double counting between the TL Sum and Finished Goods Sum. He demonstrated that eight of nine entries totalling US$2,002,292.93 recorded in TL’s 2008 general ledger as part of the Finished Goods Sum, corresponded precisely with entries in TGPL's general ledger, as they were matching in quantum and proximate in timing. The ADHC held that it was possible that FDPL was claiming the same amounts under both categories, and this warranted investigation through witness examination: at [100]–[106] . 20 The above two arguments were new points raised on appeal. Nonetheless, applying the principles on when a new point may be raised on appeal, the ADHC allowed these arguments as Mr Yit was merely asking the court to draw reasonable inferences from the evidential record, no witness examination had occurred below, and FDPL suffered no prejudice as they could and did respond to the arguments on appeal: at [108]–[109] . Whether Ms Chan had authorised or caused TGPL to grant the TL Sum and instruct customers to transfer the Finished Goods Sum to TL and whether that was a breach of her fiduciary duties to TGPL 21 The available evidence did not support the Judge’s finding that Ms Chan had known of the various payments making up the 2007 Payments, the Opening Balance and Sum 3, or that TGPL’s customers had made payments directly to TL instead, at the time these payments were made . Hence, the available evidence did not suffice to prove that Ms Chan had actually caused or authorised TGPL to extend the TL Sum as loans and instructed TGPL’s customers to pay the Finished Goods Sum to TL: at [110]–[111] . 22 During the appeal hearing, FDPL referred to Ms Chan’s response in the Intraco EJD Proceedings where she appeared to agree that she had authorised loans exceeding S$15.3m from TGPL to TL. This point did not appear to have been brought to the Judge's attention. This admission had to be weighed against Ms Chan’s contradictory statements in her affidavit for the proceedings below, where she disclaimed knowledge of TGPL’s operations and asserted that Mr Lay was the director with management and control of TGPL. Ms Chan ought to have been cross-examined on these apparent contradictions: at [112] . Whether Ms Chan breached her fiduciary duties by failing to cause TGPL to recover the TL Sum and the Finished Goods Sum and/or by causing TGPL to write off the TL Sum in 2015 23 A director's duty to act bona fide and honestly in the company ’s interests contains both subjective and objective elements. The subjective element requires examining whether the director exercised discretion bona fide in what he considered (not what the court considers) to be the company’s interests. The objective element involves assessing whether an intelligent and honest person in the director’s position could reasonably have believed the transactions benefited the company. The court may infer dishonesty where transactions were not objectively in the company’s interests: at [115] . 24 A director’s fiduciary duty to act in good faith requires him to act in circumstances where he knows that the interests of the company are at risk of harm. The focus is on whether the director should have acted in the circumstances, not on whether the director achieved a particular outcome; the decision to act or not act must be made honestly and in good faith for the benefit of, and in the interests of, the company. Hence, one situation where a director is in breach of her fiduciary duties is: (a) where a director comes to know about the transaction that is against the interests of the company, (b) believes (in the part-subjective and part-objective sense) that the transaction is against the interests of the company, and (c) but does nothing to try to prevent the transaction from being carried out if she has prior knowledge of it, or fails to take steps to try to reverse the transaction if she learns of it only later: at [116]–[11 8] . 25 The available evidence could not establish Ms Chan’s liability for the entirety of the TL Sum arising from her failure to cause TGPL to pursue recovery of the same. First, the reasons for Ms Chan's inaction required examination, eg , if TL was unable to pay, this could constitute a legitimate reason for not pursuing recovery. Second, causation issues arose regarding whether TGPL could have recovered the full amount if it had pursued repayment, eg , whether TL had the financial capacity to fully repay. If Ms Chan were liable only for a non-custodial breach of her fiduciary duties, the burden would fall on FDPL to show that, even if Ms Chan had caused TGPL to pursue recovery of the loans, TGPL would still have suffered loss. Third and relatedly, the evidence was lacking regarding the time at which Ms Chan knew about the respective components of the TL Sum and TL's assets at those respective points of time. Further evidence would be necessary to determine this question, including but not limited to an examination of witnesses: at [121]–[124] . 26 The act of writing off the TL sum could not, by itself, cause TGPL any loss, as it was an internal accounting exercise and did not prevent TGPL from pursuing the sum: at [125] . 27 The available evidence did not permit the court to infer that Ms Chan knew of the Finished Goods Sum, particularly given her affidavit statements denying management of TGPL. There was no evidence that Ms Chan was aware that customers had been instructed to pay TL instead of TGPL, much less that she had given such instructions. The ADHC distinguished between a director failing to notice large receivables and having knowledge of specific ledger entries showing diverted payments. There was no evidence Ms Chan was aware of or signed off on the relevant ledger entries: at [128] . 28 Even assuming Ms Chan learned of the payment diversions from financial records, there was no evidence she procured them. Her potential liability would stem from failing to pursue recovery, which raised the same concerns at para 25 above. These concerns necessitated further investigation and the examination of witnesses: at [129] . Whether FDPL’s claims were time-barred 29 The ADHC took the tentative view that the available evidence was insufficient to support a finding that Ms Chan had acted dishonestly. That question was extremely fact-intensive and could only be answered after all the relevant evidence, including from the examination of witnesses, was considered: at [1 34]. Orders and Conclusion 30 The ADHC allowed the appeal. It set aside the Judge’s orders requiring Mr Yit to admit the TL Sum and Finished Goods Sum. It also set aside the costs order made below in relation to FDPL’s claims, while remitting to the Judge for his determination the issue of costs for other claims not subject to the appeal: at [135]–[136] . 31 The ADHC ordered a trial before the Judge to determine whether Ms Chan breached her fiduciary duties and the extent of any liability for the TL Sum and the Finished Goods Sum: at [137] . 32 Both parties had erred in taking the position that the matter could be decided solely on affidavit and documentary evidence. Hence, the ADHC found it unjust to determine that FDPL had not proven that its claims should be admitted as debts in Ms Chan’s bankruptcy estate. Rather, a trial of FDPL’s claims was ordered for it to establish its claims. At the same time, it would also be unfair to penalise FDPL by making it pay the costs of this appeal and the costs below in relation to FDPL’s claims that were the subject of this appeal. The ADHC ordered parties to agree on costs, failing which to submit on the matter: at [140]– [145] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.
