case_name: PURWADI v MBF NORTHERN SECURITIES SDN. BHD. (IN LIQUIDATION)
subject_tags: ["Civil Procedure — Appeals — Leave — Whether permission to appeal required", "Civil Procedure — Judgments and orders — Enforcement — Whether stay of enforcement amounts to stay of proceedings", "Civil Procedure — Jurisdiction — Paragraph 3(l) Fifth Schedule Supreme Court of Judicature Act 1969 (2020 Rev Ed)"]
court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 15 December 2025 Case summary Purwadi v MBF Northern Securities Sdn Bhd (in liquidation) [2025] SGHC(A) 25 Civil Appeal No. 38 of 2025 and Summons No. 41 of 2025 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Appellate Division of the High Court (delivered by Justice Ang Cheng Hock): Outcome: The Appellate Division struck out the notice of appeal on the ground that no permission to appeal has been obtained. 1 This was an appeal against an order for a stay of enforcement of a registered foreign judgment pending a setting aside application before a foreign court. The central issue was whether permission is necessary to appeal against a decision of a High Court judge on such applications. Background to the appeal 2 The respondent obtained three judgments in its favour in Malaysia (the “Malaysian Judgments”): at [ 5] . 3 In HC/OA 130/2022, the respondent applied and obtained an order (the “Registration Order”) for the registration of the Malaysian Judgments as judgments of the General Division of the High Court of Singapore under the Reciprocal Enforcement of Commonwealth Judgments Act 1921 (2020 Rev Ed): at [ 6] . 4 Before the High Court judge, the appellant was granted a conditional stay on the enforcement of the Registration Order, pending the disposal of the appellant’s application in Malaysia to impeach those Malaysian Judgments on account of fraud (the “Impeachment Application”): at [2] and [16] . 5 The appellant appealed in AD/CA 38/2025 (“AD 38”), contending that an unconditional stay should have been granted instead. In support of AD 38, the appellant also filed AD/SUM 41/2025 (“SUM 41”) seeking to adduce further evidence on the developments in the Impeachment Application and other related applications in Malaysia: at [2] and [17] . 6 The respondent submitted that the Notice of Appeal in AD 38 should be struck out because permission to appeal was required pursuant to s 29A(1)( c ) read with paragraph 3( l ) of the Fifth Schedule to the Supreme Court of Judicature Act 1969 (2020 Rev Ed) (the “SCJA”) . The appellant contended that an application to stay the enforcement of an order was an interlocutory application for a “stay of proceedings”, for which no permission to appeal was required under the SCJA: at [ 19]–[20] . The court’s decision 7 The court struck out the Notice of Appeal in AD 38. Correspondingly, no order was made as to SUM 41: at [ 3] . 8 An appellate court was a creature of statute. It was hence seised of the jurisdiction conferred upon it by the statute that created it or by such other statute which may confer upon it additional jurisdiction: at [23] . 9 Under s 29A(1)( c ) of the SCJA read with paragraph 3( l ) of the Fifth Schedule to the SCJA , subject to any exception specified, permission was required to bring an appeal against a decision of the General Division of the High Court for “an order at the hearing of any interlocutory application”. One such exception was an application for a “stay of proceedings” as stated in paragraph 3( l )(x) of the Fifth Schedule: at [2 3] . 10 To determine if permission to appeal was required under paragraph 3( l ) of the Fifth Schedule, the court would first consider if the application was an “interlocutory application”, and if so, whether the “order” made was an “interlocutory order”: at [25] . 11 Here, the application for a stay of enforcement of a judgment was an interlocutory application, as its outcome would not finally determine the parties’ rights in the cause of the pending proceedings in which the application was brought. The “cause of the pending proceedings” in this case referred to the parties’ rights to the judgment debt under the Registration Order, which was dependent on the outcome of the Impeachment Application in the Malaysian courts: at [26(a)] and [30] . 12 The determination of the stay application did not finally determine the cause of the pending proceedings. If a stay were granted, all that meant was that the respondent’s rights to enforce the Registration Order would be delayed. But if a stay were refused, the respondent may start or continue with enforcement proceedings in respect of the Registration Order. But those enforcement proceedings merely permitted the respondent to recover the amount due under the Registration Order, which had not been set aside. The respondent’s entitlement to retain the judgment debt was ultimately dependent on the outcome of the Impeachment Application in Malaysia: at [31] . 13 A conditional stay order was an interlocutory order. It delayed the respondent’s rights to enforce the Registration Order and did not conclusively determine the parties’ substantive rights to the judgment debt. Their substantive rights to the judgment debt depended on the validity of the Malaysian Judgments which was to be determined in the pending Impeachment Application: at [26(b)] and [32] . 14 None of the exceptions to permission to appeal were applicable. Contrary to the appellant’s submission, an application for a stay of enforcement of the Registration Order did not amount to an application for a “stay of proceedings”: at [26(c)] and [34] . 15 There was a conceptual distinction between a stay of proceedings and a stay of enforcement. An order for a stay of enforcement prevented the party in whose favour the judgment had been made ( ie , the judgment creditor) from relying on the coercive effect of the judgment to recover, through legal processes, what was due under the judgment to the judgment creditor. On the other hand, an order for a stay of proceedings halted the progression of the action from that point when the order was made. A stay of proceedings did not necessarily affect the enforceability of orders or judgments that had already been made: at [36] . 16 The distinction between a stay of proceedings and a stay of enforcement was also evident from the differing statutory provisions and principles governing each application. The power to grant a stay of enforcement may be found under O 22 r 13 of the Rules of Court 2021 (“ROC 2021”). The power to grant a stay of proceedings, on the other hand, may be found in a specific statute, or in the absence of a directly applicable statutory power, the general power of the court under O 3 r 2(2) of the ROC 2021 may be invoked. Broadly speaking, the central consideration behind a stay of enforcement was the risk of injustice if the judgment is immediately enforced, while a stay of proceedings primarily concerned considerations of proper case management, abuse of process, and ultimately, the fair and efficient resolution of the dispute between the parties: at [37] –[39] . 17 Moreover, O 22 r 2(3) of the ROC 2021 required an application for an enforcement order to be brought by summons without notice, and not by an originating process. As stated in O 6 r 1(1) of the ROC 2021, “proceedings” may be commenced by an originating process. As such, enforcement actions, which were to be commenced by way of a summons, were not “proceedings” within the meaning of the ROC 2021. Since the ROC 2021 was subsidiary legislation issued under the SCJA, a consistent meaning should be adopted for the use of the term “proceedings” in paragraph 3 of the Fifth Schedule of the SCJA: at [41] . 18 Finally, the express language in the SCJA and the ROC 2021 drew a distinction between a stay of proceedings and a stay of enforcement: at [43] . 19 As the application in the present case did not concern a “stay of proceedings”, there was no applicable exception to the requirement for permission to appeal. Given the appellant’s failure to seek and obtain such permission, the Court was not seised of the jurisdiction to hear AD 38: at [47] . 20 The appellant’s failure to obtain permission to appeal was a jurisdictional defect of AD 38 and rendered the Notice of Appeal in AD 38 invalid. There was thus no merit in the appellant’s objection that the respondent should have filed a separate striking out application: at [48] . 21 Costs of $14,000 (all-in) were ordered against the appellant. The usual consequential orders applied: at [50] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.

court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 4 December 2025 Case summary Pritam Singh v Public Prosecutor [2025] SGHC 242 Magistrate’s Appeal No 9023 of 2025/01 --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the General Division of the High Court (delivered by Justice Steven Chong): Outcome: The General Division of the High Court (“High Court”) dismissed the appellant’s appeal against his conviction of two charges under s 31( q ) read with s 36(1)( b ) of the Parliament (Privileges, Immunities and Powers) Act . The High Court agreed with the District Judge below that the appellant had wilfully made false answers to questions material to the subject of inquiry put during examination before the Committee of Privileges. Background to the appeal 1 This was an appeal against the appellant’s conviction on two charges under s 31( q ) read with s 36(1)( b ) of the Parliament (Privileges, Immunities and Powers) Act (Cap 217, 2000 Rev Ed) (the “ PPIPA”). 2 On 3 August 2021, Ms Raeesah Begum bte Farid Khan (“Ms Khan”) told a lie in Parliament as a Member of Parliament (“MP”) of the Workers’ Party (“WP”). She repeated the lie in Parliament on 4 October 2021. In essence, Ms Khan fabricated an anecdote by falsely claiming that she had accompanied a rape victim to make a police report, and that the police officers handling the case exhibited inappropriate behaviour (referred to below as the “Anecdote” or the “Untruth”, as the context requires). The appellant, who was the Secretary-General of the WP and the Leader of the Opposition, learned on 7 August 2021 that Ms Khan had lied. 3 The Untruth was eventually revealed in Parliament, which led to an inquiry by the Committee of Privileges (“COP”). While Ms Khan’s conduct was the subject of the COP proceedings, the appellant appeared before the COP to assist in the investigations by giving evidence. In doing so, he purportedly gave the false answers that are the subject of the two charges. 4 The appeal turned on the findings of the District Judge (the “Judge”) in relation to two statements allegedly made by the appellant. Each of the statements corresponded to the two charges against the appellant: a. The first statement, which was the subject of the first charge, was whether the appellant had told Ms Khan on 8 August 2021 to take the Untruth to the grave (the “Grave Statement”). The Judge found that the appellant did make this statement. b. The second statement, which was the subject of the second charge, contained the phrase “I will not judge you” or “I won’t judge you” (the “Judgment Statement”). It was common ground that the appellant did say the Judgment Statement to Ms Khan on 3 October 2021, and the dispute at the trial concerned only its proper meaning: was it that the appellant would not judge Ms Khan if she decided to maintain the narrative ( ie , the Untruth)? Or did the appellant mean, as he so claim ed, that he would not judge Ms Khan for taking ownership and responsibility for the Untruth ( ie , to clarify the Untruth if the matter were to be raised in Parliament the next day)? The Judge found that it was the former and rejected the appellant’s contention as to the latter. 5 In essence, the main issues on appeal were to do with whether the Judge erred in making the findings as described above. There was also a separate, preliminary issue concerning whether the charges were defective. The appellant submitted that the Prosecution was required to identify the specific question that was asked of the appellant, and that the answer to that question must be false. The appellant further argued that the Prosecution was not entitled to frame the two charges by amalgamating the appellant’s responses and summarising the gist of his answers to the COP . 6 Having considered the evidence and the parties’ submissions, the Court dismissed the appeal. Preliminary issue: the framing of the charges 7 Section 31( q ) of the PPIPA provide d that no person shall wilfully make a false answer to any question material to the subject of inquiry put during examination before Parliament or a committee: at [ 60]. 8 There was no basis to adopt a restrictive interpretation of s 31( q ). To begin with, s 2 of the Interpretation Act 1965 (2020 Rev Ed) provided that words in the singular include the plural. This principle applied unless the statutory context indicated otherwise: at [6 3]. 9 Where multiple false answers are given, those multiple answers could be the subject of a single charge where those multiple answers are in substance the same. This would be so even if the multiple false answers are not identical. This interpretation of s 31( q ) accord ed with the inherent nature of witness testimony, which involved questions, responses, clarifications and follow up questions: at [64] and [68]. 10 In this case, each of the appellant’s exchanges with the COP independently conveyed the same false answer which was able to ground the charges. In other words, they spoke with one voice. More importantly, it had never been alleged by the appellant that he did not have sufficient notice of the charges which were brought against him. There was therefore no merit in the appellant’s suggestion that the charges brought against him were defective: at [65]–[67]. The First Charge: the Grave Statement 11 The appellant, Ms Lim Swee Lian Sylvia (“Ms Lim”) and Mr Muhamad Faisal bin Abdul Manap (broadly referred to as the “WP leaders”) met Ms Khan during a meeting on 8 August 2021 (the “8 August Meeting”). It was during this meeting that Ms Khan told Ms Lim and Mr Faisal about the Untruth. The appellant had found out about the Untruth the day before: at [ 11] and [75]. 12 The First Charge concerned the appellant’s testimony before the COP that at the conclusion of the 8 August Meeting, he wanted Ms Khan to, at some point, clarify in Parliament that the Anecdote was untrue. As a matter of common sense and logic, if the Judge was right in finding that the appellant had made the Grave Statement to Ms Khan ( ie , telling her to take the Untruth to the grave), it had to follow that what he said to the COP at the 8 August Meeting ( ie , that he wanted Ms Khan to clarify the Untruth) could not be true: at [ 72]. 13 Based on the evidence, the Court agreed with the Judge that the appellant made the Grave Statement. Two key planks undergirded this finding: at [7 3]. a. First, an important contextual fact was that the WP leaders, including the appellant, held the hope or belief at the 8 August Meeting that the Untruth might not be raised in Parliament again. This was based on Ms Khan’s unchallenged evidence that during the 8 August Meeting, Ms Lim said that the Untruth “probably… wouldn’t come up again”. The appellant did not expressly disagree with Ms Lim’s view or say anything to distance himself from Ms Lim’s statement. In choosing not to contradict Ms Lim’s statement, the appellant appeared to have shared Ms Lim’s view or belief that the matter of the Untruth would probably not come up again. The 8 August Meeting therefore had to be examined in light of the appellant’s hope or belief that the Untruth may not surface again: at [7 5]–[76]. b. Second, and keeping this crucial context in mind, the various pieces of evidence showed that the appellant did not want Ms Khan to clarify the Untruth as at 8 August 2021. This comprised mainly of (a) Ms Khan’s contemporaneous messages and (b) the appellant’s own conduct: at [7 3]. The 12.41pm Message 14 A vital piece of evidence was a WhatsApp Message sent by Ms Khan to Ms Loh Pei Ying (“Ms Loh”) and Mr Yudhisthra Nathan (“Mr Nathan”) on 8 August 2021 at 12.41pm (the “12.41pm WhatsApp Message”). In this message, Ms Khan told Ms Loh and Mr Nathan that the appellant had said to her to take the Untruth to the grave: at [ 81]. 15 It was very significant that the 12.41pm WhatsApp Message was sent shortly after the 8 August Meeting, and there was no reason to disbelieve the accuracy of this message. The only two ways that the appellant could dispute the accuracy of this message was either to say that (a) Ms Khan had lied to Ms Loh and Mr Nathan, or that (b) Ms Khan, Ms Loh and Mr Nathan had conspired to bury the Untruth and pin it on the appellant: at [81]–[82]. 16 Neither argument was defensible. There was no reason for and no evidence that Ms Khan was misrepresenting what the appellant had said during the 8 August Meeting to Ms Loh and Mr Nathan in this message. As for the conspiracy case theory, this was bereft of factual basis, and Ms Khan had never made any concession of its existence. Crucially, the appellant had also failed to put this conspiracy theory to Ms Loh and Mr Nathan in cross-examination, in order to give them a chance to respond. This was a clear breach of the rule in Browne v Dunn (1893) 6 R 67 : at [ 83]–[87]. 17 The appellant’s argument that the 12.41pm WhatsApp Message was not reliable as it was derived from Ms Khan herself was also rejected. There was no rule of law that corroborative evidence from the same witness had to always be given less weight. Instead, the weight to be given to such evidence from the same witness must be assessed on the facts of each case . This case, the Court had already dismissed the various discrete suggestions by the appellant as to the possible lack of reliability of the 12.41pm WhatsApp Message. There was there no basis for diminishing the weight to be accorded to the 12.41pm WhatsApp Message simply because it emanated from Ms Khan herself: at [90]. 18 As there was no reason for this Court to disturb the weight which the Judge had attached to the 12.41pm WhatsApp Message, this message was strong corroboration of Ms Khan’s account of the 8 August Meeting. It served as the anchoring piece of evidence that showed that the appellant did, in fact, tell Ms Khan to take the Untruth to the grave : at [ 91] . Ms Khan’s three versions of her discussions with the appellant were not materially inconsistent 19 Ms Khan provided three accounts of the 8 August Meeting before the COP and the court below. While there were some differences between these three accounts, these differences were not material as they did not contradict each other but merely provided different details. The common and key thread in all three of her accounts was that there was no need for Ms Khan to proactively clarify the Untruth: at [9 4]. 20 More importantly, Ms Khan’s seemingly inconsistent answers provided in December 2021 could not retroactively undermine or dilute the corroborative value of the 12.41pm WhatsApp Message sent contemporaneously in August 2021, approximately ten minutes after the 8 August Meeting: at [9 6]. The appellant’s inaction after 8 August 2021 supported the Grave Statement 21 The appellant’s inaction after the 8 August Meeting was another weighty factor supporting the Prosecution’s case. The appellant’s complete failure to follow-up with Ms Khan or the other WP leaders on the Untruth for around two months following the 8 August Meeting, until 3 October 2021, was probative of the Grave Statement and the appellant’s prevailing understanding that there was no need to proactively clarify the Untruth in Parliament. This was especially since the matter of the Untruth was a significant event for the WP, given the potentially serious fall-out if it were not properly managed. Yet, nothing was said between the appellant and Ms Khan or among the WP party leaders between 8 August and 3 October 2021 about the Untruth: at [98]–[99]. 22 The appellant’s inaction stood in stark contrast to his conduct when he eventually did decide to take steps to clarify the Untruth on or around 11 October 2021. On Ms Khan’s evidence, a total of nine drafts of her clarificatory personal statement were prepared, with multiple in-person meetings between the appellant and Ms Khan to review the statements: at [ 100]. 23 The appellant sought to provide two explanations for his inaction, both of which were rejected by the Court: at [101] –[104]. a. First, the appellant claimed that he was waiting for Ms Khan to get back to him on whether she had spoken to her parents about her prior sexual assault incident (which he termed the “condition precedent”). But even taking the appellant’s account at its highest, his case was that on 3 October 2021, he had asked Ms Khan to clarify the Untruth on 4 October 2021. Yet, when the appellant met Ms Khan on 3 October 2021, he did not even ask Ms Khan if she had spoken to her parents. The “condition precedent” appears to be an afterthought devised to explain away what was in truth an inexplicable omission to follow up with Ms Khan if he had, as he claimed, wanted her to clarify the Untruth at some point in time as at the 8 August Meeting. b. Second, the appellant claimed that he had been busy and “lost sight” of the Untruth. While the Court did not doubt that an opposition member occupying the office of the Leader of the Opposition would be busy, that did not explain the appellant’s complete failure to follow up with either Ms Khan or the other WP leaders on the Untruth. This also stood in contrast to the appellant’s active monitoring of Ms Khan’s other parliamentary work during this same period. 24 Taken together, the circumstantial evidence amply corroborated Ms Khan’s account that the appellant had told her to take the Untruth to the grave. They supported a strong chain of inferences – that the appellant had no explicable reason for his inaction on the Untruth; that this inexplicable inaction continued for two months; and that it continued in the backdrop of a prevailing mindset that the Government might not discover the Untruth. This was all underpinned by the anchor point of the 12.41pm WhatsApp Message which explained the reason for such inaction. These pieces of evidence grounded a significant portion of the case that was accepted by the Judge and was distinct from Ms Khan’s testimony. By extension, there was no need to apply the “unusually convincing” standard to Ms Khan’s testimony: at [10 7]. 25 Accordingly, the Court affirmed the appellant’s conviction on the First Charge: at [10 8]. The Second Charge: the Judgment Statement 26 The Second Charge concerned the appellant’s answer to the COP that at the 3 October Meeting, he wanted to convey to Ms Khan that she had to clarify the Untruth if the issue were to come up in Parliament the next day. If the Judge was correct to find that the appellant told Ms Khan at the 3 October Meeting that he would not judge her if she decided to retain the narrative, it necessarily followed as a matter of logic that the appellant’s answer to the COP was false: at [ 111] 27 The Court was of the view that the Judge did not err in accepting the Prosecution’s version of the Judgment Statement, for the following reasons: at [11 5] . 28 First, the phrase “I will not judge you” was ordinarily used when the statement-maker was telling the recipient that he or she would not be judged for taking a course of action normally considered to be objectionable: at [11 7] . 29 Second, the appellant’s own evidence indicated that he was giving Ms Khan a choice on what to do if the Anecdote was raised in Parliament. This included the undisputed evidence that at the Disciplinary Proceeding session held on 29 November 2021, the appellant reminded Ms Khan that on 3 October, he had told her that it was her “call”. The provision of a choice necessarily included the option of maintaining the Untruth, and contradicted the appellant’s submission that when he told Ms Khan to take ownership and responsibility, he had given Ms Khan no choice but to clarify the Untruth if it came up during the 4 October Parliamentary Sitting: at [ 131]–[133]. 30 Third, the appellant did not react to Ms Khan’s e-mail on 7 October 2021, when she asked the WP leaders for advice on the Singapore Police Force’s (“SPF”) request for an interview, and then thanked the WP leaders for guiding her without judgment. The appellant did not respond even though, on his account, Ms Khan’s conduct in Parliament on 4 October had been in direct contradiction to his earlier advice and instruction: at [12 5]–[130]. 31 Fourth, there was a sudden flurry of activity after the appellant’s meeting with Mr Low Thia Khiang on 11 October. When compared to the complete inaction and lack of preparation for Ms Khan to clarify the Untruth before 4 October, this indicated that there was an about-turn only around 11 October 2021: at [13 7]–[142] . 32 Fifth, Ms Khan’s account of the 3 October Meeting (and specifically, the Judgment Statement) was corroborated by Ms Loh’s and Mr Nathan’s evidence of their meeting with the appellant on 12 October 2021. Ms Loh and Mr Nathan testified that on 12 October 2021, the appellant had discussed the 3 October Meeting with them, which included the same version of the Judgment Statement as testified to by Ms Khan. Their testimony was also corroborated by messages sent by Mr Nathan to Ms Loh and Ms Khan on 23 November 2021 in response to news that Ms Khan had been reprimanded by the appellant. In these messages, Mr Nathan recounted the Judgment Statement as communicated to them on 12 October 2021. The appellant did not succeed in challenging the corroborative value of those messages as there was no suggestion that they were fabricated: at [1 43]–[151]. 33 Sixth, there was no reason to impeach Ms Khan’s credit. The main discrepancy in question was derived from Ms Khan’s statement to the SPF on 12 May 2022, when she said that the appellant told her on 3 October that the matter of the Anecdote might come up. Comparatively, in the trial below, Ms Khan testified that the appellant told her that he did not think the matter would come up the next day. In the Court’s view, this was an innocent discrepancy because neither version made Ms Khan’s account of the Judgment Statement any more or less believable: at [15 7]–[159]. 34 Finally, given the Court’s decision to uphold the Judge’s finding that the appellant did make the Grave Statement, the Prosecution’s interpretation of the Judgment Statement was only consistent with the appellant’s making of the Grave Statement. Given that nothing of note occurred between the 8 August Meeting (where the appellant made the Grave Statement) and the 3 October Meeting, it appears that the appellant’s approach to addressing the Untruth remained unchanged in this period. Seen in this light, the Judgment Statement was a reiteration of the appellant’s position in the earlier Grave Statement: at [1 62]–[163]. 35 For the reasons above, the Court affirmed the appellant’s conviction on the Second Charge: at [1 64]. This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.

court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 3 December 2025 Case summary Muhammad Izwan bin Borhan v Public Prosecutor and another appeal [202 5] SGCA 55 Criminal Appeal Nos 11 and 12 of 2022 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Judgment of the Court of Appeal (comprising Sundaresh Menon CJ, Tay Yong Kwang JCA, Belinda Ang Saw Ean JCA) (delivered by Tay Yong Kwang JCA): Outcome: The Court of Appeal (the “CA”) dismissed appeals against the appellants’ conviction and sentence for drug trafficking offences punishable by death under the Misuse of Drugs Act Significant points of the judgment •  The CA held that a ny change in intention relating to the amount of drugs for trafficking that comes about after the point of possession cannot change the trafficking offence into a less serious one in relation to the quantity of drugs meant for trafficking, in particular, by reducing a capital charge into a non-capital one . What is material is the intention of the offender when he comes into possession of the drugs: at [ 155] . •  The CA held that the defence of “bailment” contemplates that the drugs in question are returned to a person “who originally deposited those drugs with him”. Where a person moves the drugs towards their ultimate consumer, that act would constitute trafficking under s 2 of the MDA: at [ 160] and [161] . •  The CA held that an unreliable witness is not necessarily an untruthful one. Even if a witness’ credit has been impeached, it does not necessarily entail a total rejection of all his evidence. The court must scrutinise the whole of the evidence to determine which aspect might be true and which aspect should be disregarded: at [ 183] . Background 1 These were appeals against the appellants’ conviction and sentence in Public Prosecutor v Muhammed Izwan bin Borhan and another [2022] SGHC 40 (the “First Judgment”) for drug trafficking offences under the Misuse of Drugs Act (Cap 185, 2008 Rev Ed) (“MDA”). Additional evidence was subsequently taken pursuant to a Criminal Motion, with the Judge delivering a supplemental judgment in [2025] SGHC 15 (the “Second Judgment”). Facts 2 Muhammad Izwan bin Borhan (“Izwan”) and Ahmad Suhaimi bin Ismail (“Suhaimi”) were convicted of offences in relation to diamorphine (also known as heroin) and methamphetamine (also known as Ice). Izwan faced charges for possession for the purpose of trafficking 26.19g of diamorphine and 252.04g of methamphetamine (“Izwan’s Heroin Charge” and “Izwan’s Ice Charge”). Suhaimi faced conspiracy charges for the same quantities of drugs (“Suhaimi’s Heroin Charge” and (“Suhaimi’s Ice Charge”). They were sentenced to the mandatory death penalty. 3 Izwan and Suhaimi first met in 2008 and later reconnected in 2014 while attending prison school. During their time in prison, each of them met one Mohamed Yusof bin Kasim (“Yusof”) separately. After their release – Izwan in 2015 and Suhaimi in 2016 – they re-established contact with Yusof. They knew that Yusof dealt in drugs, including heroin sourced from Arun. Both appellants sourced their drugs from Arun but Suhaimi was the one who communicated with Arun. 4 On 29 September 2017, Izwan collected five packets (“biji”) of heroin and 500g of Ice from Arun’s runner near 31 Toh Guan East. When Izwan returned to his flat at Block 27 New Upper Changi Road (“Block 27”), he repackaged one “biji” of heroin into smaller portions and placed the remaining of the heroin from the one “biji” in an aluminium tray A3. The remaining four “biji” of heroin were left intact. He divided the Ice into four 125g packets as instructed by Suhaimi. He left one of these packets at an electrical box on the 11th floor of Block 27 for collection by one of Suhaimi’s customers. 5 Later that afternoon, Suhaimi arrived at the ground level of Block 27 in a black Subaru accompanied by Yusof and one Muhammad Zafar. Izwan handed Suhaimi a black plastic bag containing two packets of Ice, though Suhaimi later disputed that these were the items which Izwan handed to him. 6 Izwan was arrested at 4.10pm at the void deck of Block 27 and escorted to his flat, where Central Narcotics Bureau (“CNB”) officers seized various drug exhibits from his bedroom along with his mobile phone. His wife, mother and stepfather, who were present in the flat, were also arrested. 7 Around five minutes later, Suhaimi, Yusof, and Zafar were arrested at a petrol station, with their Subaru subsequently searched at a nearby multi-storey carpark. The search revealed packets of Ice. Yusof admitted that some of these packets belonged to him. The two packets of Ice which Suhaimi received from Izwan were also found in the Subaru. Suhaimi, Yusof and Zafar denied ownership of these items at the time of the arrest. Suhaimi’s handphone was seized during the arrest. 8 During investigations, officers from the CNB recorded ten statements each from both appellants and both underwent psychiatric evaluations at Changi Prison Complex Medical Centre, with their examining doctors providing detailed medical reports of their accounts. 9 The heroin exhibits seized from Izwan’s bedroom were found by the HSA to contain not less than 29.63g of diamorphine. The Ice exhibits were found by the HSA to contain not less than 252.04g of methamphetamine. The packet of 125g of Ice which Izwan left on the electrical box on the 11th floor of Block 27 was not recovered and was not included in the charges against the appellants. 10 Suhaimi’s Heroin Charge originally referred to one packet containing not less than 2270.95g of granular/powdery substance, found to contain not less than 29.63g of diamorphine. Izwan’s Heroin Charge originally referred to five packets containing these same quantities. On the fourth day of the trial, the Prosecution sought to amend Suhaimi’s Heroin Charge to refer to five packets instead of one, while maintaining the same weights for both the granular/powdery substance and the diamorphine. The trial Judge (“the Judge”) allowed the amendment. 11 Subsequently, the Judge decided to amend again both Izwan’s and Suhaimi’s Heroin Charges by excluding the drugs found in the aluminium tray A3 in Izwan’s home. This was because he held that there was a reasonable doubt whether the heroin found in the tray included heroin from a previous purchase. The amount of drugs in A3 (3.44g of diamorphine) was excluded accordingly and Izwan’s Heroin Charge and Suhaimi’s Heroin Charge therefore showed the present reduced amounts of not less than 1996.15g of granular/powdery substance and not less than 26.19g of diamorphine. 12 The Judge convicted the appellants on their amended charges and sentenced them to the mandatory death penalty. The appellants appealed against the Judge’s decision. Decision on appeal 13 The CA rejected the appellants’ arguments that the chain of custody for the seized drugs had been broken, as there was no reasonable doubt about either the identity or integrity of the drug exhibits: at [ 32] – [ 49] . 14 The CA rejected Izwan’s challenge to the admissibility of his statements to the CNB. Izwan claimed he was compelled by threat, inducement or promise to state untruths in those statements. These untruths were that he was Suhaimi’s worker and had ordered five “biji” of heroin, safe-keeping three “biji” for Suhaimi. The truth, according to Izwan, was that he was not Suhaimi’s worker and that he had changed his order of heroin from five “biji” to one “biji” during the early hours of 29 September 2017. However, the CA upheld the Judge’s finding that all of Izwan’s statements were made voluntarily. The evidence showed no threat, inducement or promise: at [ 50]–[86] . Izwan’s and Suhaimi’s Heroin Charges were proved beyond reasonable doubt 15 The evidence contradicted Izwan’s claim that he had reduced his order for heroin from five to one “biji”. After the alleged reduction, messages between Izwan and Suhaimi and Arun and Suhaimi continued to reference the original five “biji” order with no mention of any reduction or of excess drugs to be returned. Izwan’s conduct after collection was inconsistent with someone who had received excess drugs. He would have noticed immediately the significant weight difference of four extra “biji” but proceeded to repack the drugs instead of bringing the extra “biji” to Suhaimi’s attention. When Suhaimi asked Izwan to “[c]heck if everything is enough”, Izwan replied “[e]nough boss”. Finally, Izwan admitted in his Third and Sixth Statements that he ordered five “biji” of heroin and was supposed to safe-keep three “biji” for Suhaimi: at [87]–[111] . 16 The order for heroin was a joint order for Izwan and Suhaimi. Izwan’s admitted in his own statements to the CNB that three of the five “biji” were intended for Suhaimi and that he would hold them pending Suhaimi’s instructions. Additionally, Suhaimi’s message to Arun on 27 September 2017 stating that his heroin was “finishing” indicated his own involvement in heroin trafficking. Suhaimi’s claim that he was referring to Izwan’s supply was unconvincing. If Suhaimi meant Izwan’s heroin, he could have simply said so. Also, the messages showed that Suhaimi and Izwan had a working relationship where Suhaimi would instruct Izwan on how to repack and deliver heroin: at [112]–[117] . 17 Izwan possessed the five “biji” of heroin for the purposes of trafficking. The evidence, including Izwan’s Third Statement, established Izwan’s intention to traffic in the five “biji” of heroin by selling two of them and by delivering three of them according to Suhaimi’s instructions. These acts fell within the meaning of trafficking under s 2 of the MDA: at [122] . 18  Suhaimi knew of Izwan’s intention to traffic in heroin. The evidence showed that Izwan and Suhaimi were in a joint enterprise to distribute drugs and that Izwan was Suhaimi’s worker. This was clear from Izwan’s statements to the CNB and the fact that Izwan bore disproportionate risks by collecting, repacking and distributing drugs for both parties while Suhaimi maintained a safe distance and received his share of the drugs only after Izwan completed the high-risk activities. This indicated that Suhaimi was the managing partner directing the drug distribution operations. The Judge was thus correct to convict the appellants on their Heroin Charges: at [ 124]–[129] . 19 The CA agreed with the Judge that the additional evidence from a remittal hearing that was intended to support the appellants’ claim that the heroin order had been reduced from five to one “biji” did not raise any reasonable doubt. Two prisoner witnesses, Sumardi and Eddie, testified that their supplier (allegedly Arun) had asked them to find Suhaimi to recover four excess “batu” of heroin. However, it was implausible that Arun would ask them to locate Suhaimi without providing his contact details. The CA determined that the photographs of Suhaimi found on Sumardi’s phone, received just one day after Suhaimi’s arrest, were more likely sent by Arun seeking payment for the drugs rather than trying to recover excess heroin, The CA agreed with the Judge that although there was no direct evidence of collusion among the witnesses, the prisoners had opportunities to communicate in prison. Sumardi’s and Eddie’s testimony did not raise reasonable doubt about the appellants’ convictions: at [ 130] – [ 144] . Izwan’s and Suhaimi’s Ice Charges were proven beyond reasonable doubt 20 Izwan did not intend to consume part of his 125g portion of Ice. Izwan admitted in his Petition of Appeal that that his intention to keep some of the Ice for his own consumption only concretised after he collected the drugs. This means that when he took possession of the Ice, his intention was to traffic in all 500g of it. Any change in intention relating to the amount of drugs for trafficking that comes about after the point of possession cannot change the trafficking offence into a less serious one in relation to the quantity of drugs meant for trafficking, in particular, by reducing a capital charge into a non-capital one: at [148] –[156] . 21 In any event, the evidence showed that Izwan’s partial consumption allegation was an afterthought and could not be true. In Izwan’s Fourth Statement, he did not state that part of his 125g portion Ice was meant for personal consumption, even as he identified other packets of Ice meant for personal consumption (which were not part of the Ice Charges). On 24 September 2017, Izwan had messaged Suhaimi indicating he had a customer order for 125g of Ice. Subsequent messages revealed he was struggling to procure Ice from other sources. Subsequently, Suhaimi’s supplier confirmed the Ice would be delivered together with the heroin on 29 September 2017. This evidence demonstrated that Izwan’s 125g share was intended to fulfil the earlier order: at [ 157]–[159] . 22 Izwan was not a mere bailee for Suhaimi’s 250g share of Ice. The defence of “bailment” contemplates that the drugs in question are returned to a person who originally deposited those drugs with him. In this case, however, it was not Suhaimi who deposited the Ice with Izwan. By delivering 250g of Ice to Suhaimi, Izwan was moving the drugs towards their ultimate consumer, therefore trafficking in them: at [1 60]–[161] . 23 Suhaimi conspired with Izwan for Izwan to possess 375g of Ice. The CA upheld the Judge’s rejection of Suhaimi’s argument that he was not party to an agreement for Izwan to order 125g of Ice as Izwan made that order without consulting him. However, the testimony of both Suhaimi and Izwan revealed that, during a telephone conversation between Arun and Izwan (with Suhaimi present and listening through speaker mode), the arrangement was that Izwan would take 125g from the 500g of Ice which Suhaimi had already agreed to take from Arun. Suhaimi raised no objections. Hence, there was still a joint order for the Ice by both appellants and an agreement between them to take their respective shares: at [ 162]–[166] . 24 Suhaimi knew that Izwan intended to traffic in Izwan’s portion of 125g of Ice. As established above, the messages between Suhaimi and Izwan showed that Suhaimi knew that Izwan intended to sell the 125g of Ice to his customers, even if Suhaimi did not know who they were: at [16 7]–[170] . Miscellaneous issues 25 Izwan contended that the charges against him required the Prosecution to prove that his alleged offences took place on 29 September 2017 at 11.50am in the vicinity of Toh Guan East. Izwan contended that 11.50am, he was nowhere in the vicinity of Toh Guan East and there was no evidence that he was in possession of anything illicit then. Izwan actually arrived at Toh Guan East around 12.22pm and collected the drugs around 12.46pm on 29 September 2017. Nonetheless, the CA found that these actual timings fell reasonably within the meaning of “at about 11.50am” as stated in the charges: at [ 170]–[171] . 26 The CA rejected Izwan’s argument that his Ice charge was legally untenable due to containing two “distinct offences” – possessing his own 125g share for sale to his customers against possessing Suhaimi’s 250g share for delivery to Suhaimi. Whether Izwan was selling the drugs himself or delivering them to Suhaimi, the drugs were still for the purpose of trafficking, which was the only offence he was charged with: at [ 175]-[177]. 27 The CA rejected the appellants’ argument that the Judge erred in not impeaching ASP Bong’s credit. A witness who is unsure about many things or makes multiple mistakes in his testimony may be regarded as unreliable. This alone does not make the witness untruthful. However, even if a witness’ credit has been impeached, it does not necessarily entail a total rejection of all his evidence. The court must scrutinise the whole of the evidence to determine which aspect might be true and which aspect should be disregarded: at [ 178]–[185] . 28 Both appellants received a certificate of substantive assistance but they were obviously not mere couriers. The mandatory death penalty therefore applied. The CA dismissed the appeals against the appellants’ conviction and sentence: at [18 7]-[188] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.

court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 15 December 2025 Case Summary DPT v DPV [2025] SGHC(I) 29 SIC/OA 10/2025 --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Singapore International Commercial Court (delivered by Mohan J): Outcome: The SICC dismissed DPT’s application to set aside an arbitral award on the grounds of breach of natural justice. Background 1. DPX is a joint venture technology company started by the first and second respondents (collectively, “Founders”) and the second applicant, DPU. In 2017, DPU, the Founders, and DPX, entered into a shareholders’ agreement (“SHA”) and an investment agreement (“IA”) (collectively, “Agreements”): [6] –[9], [13] . 2. On 28 March 2019, DPU transferred its shareholding in DPX to the first applicant, DPT, a sister company: [20] . 3. Between August 2018 and August 2020, DPX and DPT (and previously, DPU) entered into a total of 12 convertible loan notes (“DPT CLNs”), which provided for certain circumstances pursuant to which DPX’s debts would be converted into equity for DPT: [ 19]–[21] . 4. The relationship between the Founders and the Applicants began to deteriorate sometime in early 2020. DPT purported to terminate the Agreements by way of termination notices sent on 28 December 2020 and 27 January 2021. The Founders were removed as directors of DPX on 10 February 2021: [23] –[25] . 5. On 21 May 2021, the DPT CLNs were converted into shares for DPT. This resulted in DPT becoming the 99.6% shareholder of DPX, and the Founders’ percentage shareholding being reduced from 10.71% to 0.4%: [28] . 6. The Founders commenced arbitration (“Arbitration”) against the Applicants and DPX for breaches of the Agreements and claimed against the Applicants for minority oppression under s 216(1) of the Companies Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed). In December 2024, the arbitral tribunal (“Tribunal”) issued a partial award (“Partial Award”) in which the Tribunal unanimously determined, inter alia, that DPT and / or DPX had variously breached the SHA and / or IA, and that a series of acts and breaches were individually and cumulatively oppressive. A majority of the Tribunal (“Majority”) also found, inter alia , that the issuance of shares to DPT on 21 May 2021 pursuant to the conversion of the DPT CLNs was null and void as regards the Founders. The Majority ordered the Applicants to buy out the Founders’ shares in DPX for a sum of US$14,736,000: [34] , [56]–[61] . OA 10 7. SIC/OA 10/2025 (“OA 10”) was an application by the Applicants to set aside (in whole or in part) the Partial Award on grounds that they were unable to present their case within the meaning of Art 34(2)( a )(ii) of the UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration (“Model Law”), and that there was a breach of natural justice under s 24( b ) of the International Arbitration Act 1994 (2020 Rev Ed) (the “IAA) : [1] – [ 2] . 8. The Applicants raised two main arguments: [ 44], [80] a. first, that the Tribunal had determined the buyout price for the Founders’ shares by going down a path which was not open to it and had done so without giving the parties an opportunity to be heard (“Buyout Issue”); and b. second, the Tribunal had accepted the evidence of Mr [X] without considering certain witness statements which had been filed in response to the evidence of Mr [X] and Ms [Y] (the “Responsive Evidence” and “Responsive Evidence Issue”). 9. Mr [X] was the CEO of DPX up to around February 2023. Ms [Y] was the former Head of Finance at a subsidiary of DPX: [27] , [40] . 10. On the Buyout Issue, the Applicants submitted that the Founders had taken the position in their opening statement that there were two ways of calculating the buyout price: (a) a buyout ordered on the basis that the DPT CLNs were not converted (“First Scenario”), and (b) a buyout ordered on the basis that the DPT CLNs were converted but that the Founders would have to pay a top-up to maintain their shareholding (“Second Scenario”). The Founders had ostensibly opted for the Second Scenario and had confirmed the same via their submissions and / or exchanges which their counsel had with the Tribunal. The Founders had only raised the prospect of a “Third Scenario” ( ie, a post-conversion valuation without a top-up) for the first time in their closing submissions. However, the Majority had adopted this Third Scenario as the basis for ordering the buyout: [94] –[95] . 11. Additionally, the Majority had justified adopting the Third Scenario by adopting a chain of reasoning which was allegedly unforeseeable and which the parties did not have reasonable notice of – the Majority had made two findings which allegedly bore no reasonable nexus to the parties’ cases. These were the findings that (a) the DPT CLNs were “worthless as debt”; and (b) that DPX’s pre-conversion value would have been the same as its post-conversion value: [96] – [97] . 12. On the Responsive Evidence Issue, the Applicants complained that the Tribunal had failed to consider the Responsive Evidence. The Responsive Evidence consisted of evidence contradicting Mr [X]’s and Ms [Y]’s account of events relevant to the issues in the Arbitration (“Substantive Evidence”); and (b) evidence going to the credibility of Mr [X] and / or Ms [Y] (“Credibility Evidence”): [18 8] . 13. Lastly, the Applicants submitted that the Tribunal’s breaches of natural justice in relation to both the Buyout Issue and the Responsive Evidence Issue were connected to the making of the Partial Award and had caused the Applicant’s prejudice: [98], [ 190]–[191] . Decision of the court The Buyout Issue 14. The Applicants’ argument that they had not been given the opportunity to submit on whether a top-up was required in a post-conversion scenario was time-barred as it was not raised in the Applicants’ supporting affidavit for OA 10: [104] – [109] . 15. The Third Scenario had been sufficiently pleaded by the Founders. There was no need to specifically mention that no top-up was required: [135], [137] . 16. The Third Scenario remained a live issue during the Arbitration, and there was no agreement and / or understanding between the parties that this would not be the Founders’ case. The Applicants had not provided sufficiently cogent evidence that some form of agreement or understanding had been reached that the Third Scenario was not in issue in the Arbitration. The exchanges which the Founders’ counsel had with the Tribunal were not so clear and unequivocal as to amount to a concession that the Third Scenario was not part of the Founders’ case. In view of the broad discretion conferred under Singapore law for the Tribunal to assess an appropriate valuation, cogent evidence was required to persuade the court that a party had given its consent to the Tribunal’s discretion being restricted in a manner which prevented that party from arguing, or the Tribunal from adopting, a position which was more advantageous to that party : [140] , [142], [145]–[146] . 17. If the Applicants truly believed and understood that the Founders had agreed not to rely on the Third Scenario as the basis for the buyout order and / or had dropped that case, they should have (but failed to) make the objection to the Tribunal that the Founders were acting in breach of an agreement and / or undertaking previously given to the Tribunal: [154] . 18. It was incongruent for the Applicants to have (a) provided their confirmation to the Tribunal that they were prepared for the Tribunal to adjudicate the matter based on the evidence already on record on the one hand; and (b) on the other, to now say that they were deprived of a chance to provide additional evidence in respect of the Third Scenario. Even if the Founders had (on the Applicants’ case) raised a new argument belatedly and in contravention of an alleged express agreement or undertaking not to, the Applicants had failed to take the opportunity to raise the objection in clear and unequivocal terms, and / or request for the chance to adduce further evidence: [157] . 19. In relation to the Majority’s finding that the DPT CLNs were “worthless as debt”, the Applicants’ core argument was that the finding was completely unsupported by the evidence. However, the Tribunal had, in a footnote of the Partial Award, referred to evidence in the form of statements from key witnesses as to the nature of the debt represented by the DPT CLNs. This was sufficient to insulate the Partial Award from challenge on this point : [161], [164] – [165] . 20. In relation to the Majority’s finding that DPX’s pre-conversion value was the same as its post-conversion value, the Applicants’ objection flowed from their case that the Founders had confirmed they would be seeking a buyout on the basis of a post-conversion scenario with a top-up. This alleged common ground meant that the parties did not argue the valuation of the Founders’ shareholding on a pre-conversion basis: [172] . 21. The Majority had not unduly taken into account the pre-conversion value of DPX. It was not strictly speaking correct to say that the Majority had valued DPX on a pre-conversion basis; the Majority had valued DPX based on DPX’s post-conversion value as at the agreed valuation date of 31 December 2021. The Tribunal’s consideration of DPX’s pre-conversion value had taken place at a separate stage of the analysis, where it had exercised its broad and flexible discretion to determine the appropriate deductions to be made to DPX’s value: [177 ]–[180] . 22. Additionally, when assessing DPX’s post-conversion value, the Majority needed to consider DPX’s pre-conversion value because it had taken the view that the conversion of the DPT CLNs did not have any effect on DPX’s value: [181] . 23. By deciding that no top-up was required and that the dilutive effect of the conversion of the DPT CLNs was to be ignored, the buyout order would necessarily be on the basis of DPX’s pre-conversion value and with no top-up . The Majority was entitled to come to the view that the pre-conversion value of DPX was relevant to its assessment of DPX’s post-conversion value, and by extension, to have regard to the available evidence in support of this: [183] , [185] . 24. The Buyout Issue was dismissed: [186] . The Responsive Evidence Issue 25. The mere fact that the Tribunal had omitted to specifically refer to the Responsive Evidence in the Partial Award was not particularly material to the court’s assessment: [197] . 26. The Tribunal had referred to the Responsive Evidence sufficiently. It had referred to receiving the Responsive Evidence in the “Procedural History” section of the Partial Award. The Tribunal had also referred to the Applicants’ closing submissions, where the Applicants had (albeit in a footnote) referred to some of the Responsive Evidence. While this was a somewhat tangential reference, it pointed away from a clear and virtually inescapable inference that the Tribunal completely failed to consider any of the Responsive Evidence: [199] –[206] . 27. The Tribunal was entitled to direct the flow of cross-examination away from non-essential issues in the interests of efficiency. At the time, the Applicants were content to proceed in the manner proposed by the Tribunal. It was uncharitable for the Applicants to now view the Tribunal’s comments in retrospect as suggesting that it had no interest in the Responsive Evidence: [209] . 28. In relation to the Substantive Evidence, the Applicants had placed particular emphasis on the evidence of [Witness 5]; the Applicants contended that it was surprising that it was not explained in the Partial Award why [Witness 5’s] evidence was disbelieved. [Witness 5] was, amongst others, the former Head of Legal and current Chief Legal & Compliance Officer at DPX. Tribunal had not failed to consider [Witness 5’s] third witness statement. The court noted that the Tribunal had referred to [Witness 5’s] third witness statement in order to rule that certain recordings were inadmissible. It was unlikely that the Tribunal had referred to only one aspect of [Witness 5’s] witness statement to decide whether said recordings were admissible, but ignored or failed to apply its mind to the rest of her witness statement in respect of other issues: [47] , [212], [215] . 29. In relation to the Credibility Evidence, the court could not rule out the possibility that by accepting Mr [X]’s evidence, the Tribunal was implicitly rejecting the Credibility Evidence: [219] . 30. The Applicants had failed to establish that a clear and virtually inescapable inference could and should be drawn in this case that the Tribunal failed to consider the Responsive Evidence and that a breach of natural justice had thereby been occasioned: [220] . Prejudice 31. Two observations were made on prejudice –one relating to the Responsive Evidence Issue and the other relating to both the Buyout Issue and the Responsive Evidence Issue: [221] . 32. First, even if the court’s conclusions on the Responsive Evidence Issue had been incorrect, it would have had difficulty finding any prejudice suffered by the Applicants as a result of the Tribunal’s failure to consider the Responsive Evidence. The Tribunal had requested counsel not to cross-examine the witnesses on issues relating to their credibility because such evidence was not particularly material to the dispute, given that it largely related to events occurring after the commencement of the Arbitration. As to the Substantive Evidence, it was not likely to have made a real difference to the Tribunal’s analysis because (a) much of the Substantive Evidence consisted of repeated evidence that had been adduced in earlier witness statements, and (b) many of the third round witness statements (comprising the Substantive Evidence) contained bare denials or qualifications as to the extent of the witness’ knowledge. Additionally, many of the Tribunal’s findings were largely founded upon contemporaneous documentary evidence: [222] –[223] . 33. Second, the court had difficulty identifying exactly what the prejudice suffered by the Applicants would have been. The Tribunal had found that a whole slew of acts, individually and cumulatively, amounted to oppression. Even if the court had found that the Tribunal had failed to consider the Responsive Evidence and that it would have potentially resulted in a different finding as to whether the conversion of the DPT CLNs was an act of oppression, this would not have made any difference to the overall outcome as the Applicants would still be found to have acted oppressively: [224] . 34. The Responsive Evidence only targeted the motivations behind the conversion of the DPT CLNs. However, the Tribunal had independently found the conversion of the DPT CLNs to be in breach of the SHA. The Tribunal would therefore still have been perfectly entitled to declare the issuance of the shares to the Applicants on 21 May 2021 null and void and to order the buyout pursuant to the other oppressive acts, even if the conversion was not found to be an act of oppression: [225] . 35. The Applicants’ real grievance with the Partial Award was against the terms of the buyout order but a calibrated adjustment to the buyout order also did not sit well with the Applicants’ request in OA 10 for the Partial Award to be set aside in full: [226] . 36. In respect of the Applicants’ alternative request to set aside the Partial Award in part, the Applicants’ counsel had significant difficulties identifying with clarity exactly what relief the Applicants required from the court in circumstances where setting aside the Partial Award entirely was plainly a non-starter. The Applicants’ request to set aside a subset of paragraphs from the Partial Award could only be interpreted as (a) a request to vary the Partial Award – which the court did not have the power to do, (b) a request to reverse the findings in the Partial Award that the conversion of the DPT CLNs was illegitimate and in breach of the SHA, which was a disguised challenge against the merits, or (c) a request in substance to set aside the Partial Award in its entirety, which would not be appropriate for the reasons given above: [227] –[229]. Conclusion 37. The court dismissed OA 10 in its entirety: [2 30]. This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s judgment. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s judgment.

court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 28 November 2025 Case Summary Law Society of Singapore v Yeo Yao Hui Charles (Yang Yaohui) and other matters [ 2025] SGHC 234 Court of 3 Supreme Court Judges Originating Applications Nos 16 of 2023 and 6, 7, 12 and 14 of 2024 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of Sundaresh Menon CJ, Tay Yong Kwang JCA and Steven Chong JCA (judgment of the court delivered by Steven Chong JCA): Outcome: the Court of 3 Supreme Court Judges ( “C3J” ) affirmed the disciplinary tribunals’ convictions of the respondent advocate and solicitor on an array of disciplinary charges , in five originating applications seeking that the respondent be sanctioned under ss 83(1) r/w 98(1) of the Legal Profession Act (Cap 161, 2009 Rev Ed) or Legal Profession Act 1966 (2020 Rev Ed) (as the case may be) (the “LPA” ). The C3J ordered that the respondent be struck off the roll of advocates and solicitors of the Supreme Court of Singapore. Factual Background 1 The respondent was admitted to the roll of advocates and solicitors on 27 August 2016. He held practising certificates from 20 April 2020 to 31 March 2023, save for the period spanning 1 April 2022 to 13 June 2022, during which he did not hold a valid practising certificate. He was convicted by a separate disciplinary tribunal of related charges on 30 November 2023, for which a fine of $10,000 was imposed. 2 The Law Society brought five originating applications seeking that the respondent be made to suffer punishment as due cause had been shown pursuant to ss 83(1) r/w 98(1) of the LPA. Three of them – C3J/OA 16/2023, C3J/OA 6/2024, C3J/OA 7/2024 – concerned alleged misconduct in relation to three migrant worker clients (collectively, the “Complainants” ) whilst the respondent was a director at Whitefield Law Corporation ( “Whitefield” ). The charges concerned his failures to ascertain the instructions of the Complainants in relation to their workplace injury-related legal matters, having acted upon their purported instructions as conveyed to him by one Mr Saha Ranjit Chandra ( “Mr Ranjit” ). In each case, the respondent purported to act for the Complainants, to have authority to represent them in their personal injury lawsuits, settled those lawsuits on their behalf with insurers, received compensation from the insurers on their behalf, and authorised disbursements of their moneys to Mr Ranjit. 3 The application in C3J/OA 14/2024 arose from an investigation that the Law Society ordered into the financial accounts of Whitefield. Foo Kon Tan LLP, an accountancy practice ( “FKT” ), was appointed in February 2022 to review the books of account of Whitefield from 1 November 2020 to 31 August 2021 ( “Relevant Period” ), during which time the respondent had charge of Whitefield’s Roberts Lane office. The accounting report prepared by FKT dated 7 September 2022 (the “FKT Report” ) identified no fewer than 185 breaches of the Legal Profession (Solicitors’ Accounts) Rules (the “SAR” ) within the Relevant Period. These breaches were organised into four charges (the “SAR Charges” ) based on the subject-matter of the violation. 4 The final application – C3J/OA 12/2024 ( “OA 12” ) – contained eight charges in total, which may be sub-divided into two categories of four charges each. The first four charges concerned the respondent’s conduct of a judicial review application with respect to the legality of the death sentences imposed on two convicted persons then on death row (the “Prisoners” ). The respondent filed th e “Judicial Review Application” on 15 February 2022, the day before the Prisoners were due to be executed on 16 February 2022, and despite the fact that its previous criminal motion for permission to review the Prisoners’ death sentences (the “Criminal Review Application” ) had been dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 15 February 2022. The grounds for the Judicial Review Application were substantially similar to the Criminal Review Application, thereby amounting to an abuse of process. In addition, when the Judicial Review Application was heard before the then-Judge of the High Court (the “Judge” ), the respondent made three material misrepresentations of fact to the Judge, to the effect that: (a) the two applications covered distinct subject-matters; (b) it was undisputed by the Institute of Mental Health psychiatrists that one of the Prisoners had an IQ of 67; and (c) the Singapore Prison Service had an internal policy against the execution of mentally disabled prisoners (the “Court Conduct Charges” ). 5 The last four charges in OA 12 concerned social media publications published by the respondent over his social media account on the Instagram application ( “Instagram Account” ) from 28 January 2022 to 25 April 2022. These publications involved attacks and aspersions concerning: (a) the Singaporean Judiciary; (b) the Attorney-General (acting by way of his Chambers) ( “AGC” ); ( c) three pending applications by the AGC for personal costs orders against the respondent in the Criminal Review Application and Judicial Review Application, which were pending before the court at the time of the respondent’s publications over the Instagram Account; and (d) personal attacks upon fellow members of the Bar (the “Social Media Charges” ). One set of publications falling into the last of the four sub-categories took place on or around 25 April 2022 (the “Affected Publications” ), ie , when the respondent did not have a valid practising certificate in force during the period at [1] above. 6 The respondent was convicted of the charges against him by five disciplinary tribunals in the five applications, all five of which found that cause of sufficient gravity was made out under s 93(1) of the LPA. The respondent did not participate in any of the proceedings before the disciplinary tribunals (the “DT Proceedings” ), despite notices of the DT Proceedings having been served at the respondent’s last-known residential address and office address in Singapore. The respondent’s awareness of the DT Proceedings was demonstrated by his replies via his personal email account ( “Personal Email Account” ) to lawyers for the Law Society when they informed him of various developments in the DT Proceedings. 7 With leave of the C3J, substituted service of the cause papers for the C3J proceedings was effected on the respondent by way of service to the Personal Email Account. In addition, correspondence from the court was sent by way of email to the Personal Email Account to update the respondent of developments in the C3J proceedings, including the date on which the applications would be heard, and the Zoom details for the respondent to participate remotely in the “hybrid” hearing, if he chose to do so. However, the respondent did not attend the “hybrid” hearing on 11 September 2025. The Court’s judgment The SAR Charges 8 The C3J was satisfied of the accuracy of the FKT Report, which cohered with the objective financial documentation that was available (at [87]–[88] ). Based on the FKT Report, the following breaches of the SAR were proven beyond reasonable doubt – (a) 61 breaches of r 8(4) whereby moneys were withdrawn from Whitefield’s Roberts Lane client account ( “Client Account” ) on 61 occasions from 5 November 2020 to 30 August 2021 via cash cheque without permission of the General Division of the High Court; ( b) 51 breaches of r 8(5) whereby moneys exceeding $5,000 were withdrawn from the Client Account via cash cheque with only one signatory instead of the required two from 5 November 2020 to 30 August 2021; (c) 16 breaches of r 3(1) from 28 December 2020 to 26 February 2021 where client moneys were not deposited into the Client Account as required; and (d) 57 breaches of r 11 in which the respondent failed to maintain accurate profit and loss statements and balance sheets, failed to properly maintain the firm’s account ledger, failed to keep and maintain financial documentation such as vouchers of payment from the Client Account (among others), failed to record transfers for legal fees agreed upon with clients in the cash book and sales ledger, failed to reconcile the Client Account bank statement and cash book, and failed to keep a record of all bills of costs and written intimations of solicitor’s costs incurred (among other things) (at [19] , [80]–[81] , and [88]–[90] ). 9 The SAR Charges were made out beyond reasonable doubt and, given the repeated and systemic nature of the breaches and the quantitative scale of the moneys that had been compromised, due cause of sufficient gravity was made out (at [91]–[92] ). The Workplace Injury Charges 10 The C3J was satisfied that the Workplace Injury Charges did not require any implied retainer between the respondent and the Complainants. The wording of the rules concerned, and the spirit and rationale behind them, supported the interpretation that the rules applied even in the absence of a retainer, prior to the formation of a solicitor-client relationship or in cases where such a relationship is prospective in nature but not concluded (at [107]–[121] ). 11 The Complainants’ evidence was clear that they never communicated directly with the respondent or spoke with him before their personal injury suits were settled. There was no contemporaneous evidence of attendance notes or other correspondence to prove that the respondent performed any requisite customer due diligence measures in respect of the Complainants, including verifying their identities with objective documentation (at [122]–[127] ). 12 The respondent did not have authority to act, and the documents purporting to confer such authority on the respondent – such as warrants to act and powers of attorney – were forgeries which the Complainants did not execute. The respondent failed to verify Mr Ranjit’s authority to convey the Complainants’ alleged instructions, despite the suspicious circumstances which ought to have raised red flags as to whether Mr Ranjit was accurately conveying their instructions, such as the fact that Mr Ranjit himself would benefit from the purported instructions by his receiving a huge cut of the Complainants’ settlement moneys. Further, the respondent failed to directly verify the instructions with the Complainants. In fact, the respondent had delegated almost all responsibilities vis-à-vis the Complainants to Mr Ranjit. Such substantial or total abdication of a solicitor’s responsibility to a client was not permissible, particularly in the present case where the Complainants were not only referred clients but also migrant workers who were no longer physically in Singapore. It was irrelevant that the respondent was not involved in the forgeries and genuinely believed in the authenticity of these documents as he was still grossly negligent in failing to take any measures to verify that those documents were indeed signed by the Complainants (at [128]–[138] ). 13 It followed that the respondent was unauthorised in taking over conduct of their suits, settling them with the insurers, receiving settlement moneys on their behalf, and then authorising disbursements of their moneys to Mr Ranjit (at [139]–[144] ). 14 The respondent also failed to properly supervise Mr Ranjit, as he failed to ensure that Mr Ranjit obtained authorisation for Whitefield to act for one of the Complainants, failed to ensure that he had obtained authorisation to enter into a settlement agreement, and failed to ensure that Mr Ranjit obtained authorisation in relation to the settlement sum (at [145]–[14 7] ). The Court Conduct Charges 15 First, the C3J agreed with the disciplinary tribunal in OA 12 that the filing of the Judicial Review Application following the earlier dismissal of the Criminal Review Application was an abuse of process. Given that they were based on substantially similar grounds, after the Court of Appeal had already dismissed the Criminal Review Application, the respondent would have known that there was no merit in the Judicial Review Application. He filed it nonetheless not to resolve any legitimate dispute as to the legality of the Prisoners’ sentences but to re-litigate the Criminal Review Application’s dismissal without basis and frustrate or delay the carrying out of the Prisoners’ executions which were scheduled for the next day. That constituted an abuse of the court’s machinery for an improper purpose (at [157]–[159] ). 16 Furthermore, the three material misrepresentations of fact to the Judge in the Judicial Review Application were shown to have been dishonest. The first representation that the two applications concerned distinct subject-matter must have been deliberately dishonest, given that the respondent was the Prisoners’ lawyer for both applications and he would have known that they canvassed the same ground; thus, he intentionally lied to the Judge so that the dismissal of the Criminal Review Application would not jeopardise the Judicial Review Application (at [161]–[162] ). The latter two representations were recklessly dishonest, viz , at the least, the respondent had no basis to believe that either of them were true , and the inference to be drawn is that, at a minimum, the respondent did not care either way whether they were true or false when he represented them to be true to the Judge (at [163]–[167] ). The Social Media Charges 17 The Law Society was permitted to withdraw the Affected Publications from the scope of the last of the Social Media Charges as the respondent did not hold a valid practising certificate at the time (at [173]– [174] ). 18 The C3J was satisfied that the impugned publications over the Instagram Account had been proved to have been made (at [176] ), and accepted the meanings attributed to the publications by the disciplinary tribunal in OA 12. Considering their wordings when situated in their overall contexts, those impugned publications conveyed the following four meanings, corresponding with the four Social Media Charges – (a) the Singapore judiciary did not impartially dispense justice but accorded preferential treatment based on factors such as wealth or political party affiliation, thus scandalising the judiciary; (b) AGC’s officers lacked integrity in the discharge of their responsibilities by serving corporate interests or persecuting innocent people or critics of the government; (c) AGC took out the pending applications for personal costs orders against the respondent for improper reasons, thereby amounting to sub judice contempt of court; and ( d) personal attacks against officers in AGC which alleged that they were guilty of various professional improprieties (at [56]–[61] , [171] , and [177]–[189] ). The appropriate sanction 19 The only appropriate sanction was a striking-off order (at [208] ) . The totality of the charges proven against the respondent disclosed four major character defects which were incompatible with the discharge of a legal practitioner’s professional duties – (a) total disregard for the SAR regime as a prophylactic safeguard for the proper safeguarding of client moneys (at [196]–[197] ); ( b) callous absence of due diligence in verifying who his actual clients were and what their actual instructions were, in breach of a lawyer’s role to safeguard their best interests (at [198]–[200] ); ( c) dishonesty to the court impairing the fair administration of justice and in violation of a lawyer’s overriding duty to assist the court (at [201]–[202] ); and ( d) conducted himself over the public platform of his Instagram Account in a disreputable manner that would be perceived as disgraceful by the average right-thinking member of the public, bringing shame and discredit to the honourable profession that he was a member of (at [203]–[204] ). There were no mitigating circumstances militating against the presumptive sanction of a striking-off order (at [205]–[207] ). Conclusion 20 Accordingly, the C3J affirmed the respondent’s convictions on the charges in all five originating applications and rendered an order striking him off the roll of advocates and solicitors of the Supreme Court of Singapore (at [209] ). This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s judgment. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s judgment.
