court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 26 November 2025 Case Summary da Silveira, Virgilio Tarrago and another v Hashstacs Pte Ltd and another [ 2025] SGCA(I) 3 Court of Appeal Civil Appeal from the Singapore International Commercial Court No 1 of 2025 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of Steven Chong JCA, Belinda Ang Saw Ean JCA and Arjan Kumar Sikri IJ (grounds of decision delivered by Belinda Ang Saw Ean JCA): Outcome: the Court of Appeal (the “Court” ) dismissed an appeal against the decision of the International Judge (the “Judge” ) sitting in the Singapore International Commercial Court and in doing so affirmed the Judge’s dismissal of the appellants’ claims in fraudulent and/or negligent misrepresentation against the first respondent. The Court also ordered default indemnity costs against the appellants in respect of their appeal. Factual Background 1 The appellants were the claimants in a misrepresentation claim before the Judge below, instituted against the first respondent alone. The first appellant ( “Mr da Silveira” ) was a British citizen residing in Cyprus and the sole director and shareholder of the second appellant which he incorporated as a special purpose vehicle in Cyprus ( “Munchetty” ). 2 The first respondent was a Singapore-incorporated company named Hashstacs Pte Ltd. It was the wholly-owned subsidiary of a British Virgin Islander (BVI) entity named Hashstacs Inc. The former is referred to in the Court’s grounds of decision as “Hashstacs (SG)” and the latter as “Hashstacs (BVI)” to distinguish them. The second respondent ( “Mr Soh” ) was the director of Hashstacs (SG), a material witness in the trial below, and a defendant in the appellants’ actions in unjust enrichment and conspiracy, which were dismissed by the Judge below and not appealed against. Another material witness for the respondents in the trial below ( “Mr Cowan” ) was the founder and the Group Chief Executive Officer of a Gibraltarian entity ( “GSX” ) . GSX was the majority shareholder in Hashstacs (BVI). 3 The misrepresentation claims stemmed from a number of statements drawn from two sources – first, the third whitepaper published in relation to a blockchain technology project known as the “STACS Protocol” on or around 18 March 2019 (the “Third Whitepaper” ) (the “Whitepaper Representations” ); second, a website which was a product launching page of the STACS Protocol (the “STACS Website” ) (the “Website Representations ) . The representations related inter alia to statements that, when the hybridised STACS Protocol project was implemented and began to earn transaction fees on a private permissioned blockchain mechanism for verified partners ( “Native STACS” ) and an open publicly accessible blockchain system for the clearing of trades in digital securities and assets worldwide (the “Global STACS” ) , the receipts would be distributed in a given manner, including by using 80% of those receipts to purchase the STACS Protocol’s utility token ( “STACS Token s” ) from the open market , which had a limited quantity of 900 million STACS Tokens. 4 Mr da Silveira’s evidence below was that he saw the representations sometime in or around March–April 2019. Induced by those representations, he decided to purchase STACS Tokens from 15 August 2019 to 5 December 2019 (the “Transacted STACS Tokens” ). In September 2020, he transferred his legal title to the Transacted STACS Tokens to Munchetty, but he asserted that he retained the beneficial interest in them. 5 In the first quarter of 2019, the Native STACS was implemented in a limited fashion. The Global STACS was never implemented. According to Mr Cowan’s unchallenged evidence below, that was on account of regulatory issues arising from GSX’s unsuccessful talks with the Gibraltarian financial services regulator. Thereafter, Mr Cowan decided to change GSX’s business model by inter alia replacing the STACS Protocol project with a new project known as “GATENet” which was said to overcome a number of regulatory and other obstacles in the STACS Protocol model. As part of that shift, a one-to-one swap was effected between the old STACS Tokens and the new “Gate Tokens” , with new Gate Tokens being air-dropped to the private wallets of existing STACS Tokens holders around January 2021 ( “Token Swap” ), and with the old STACS Tokens ceasing to have any further utility thereafter. 6 The appellants’ case below was based on various causes of action. On the torts of deceit and negligent misrepresentation, the appellants pleaded that Hashstacs (SG) made fraudulent or negligent misrepresentations that led to Mr da Silveira’s purchase of the STACS Tokens. The Token Swap allegedly showed that the appellants’ pleaded representations were false and fraudulently or negligently made. The appellants had suffered consequential economic loss as a result of the Token Swap. The first respondent’s defence below was that inter alia it did not make the pleaded representations, which had been made by Hashstacs (BVI) and/or GSX instead. 7 Following the trial below, the Judge dismissed the appellants’ claims in toto in misrepresentation against the first respondent and unjust enrichment and conspiracy against both respondents. Among other findings, the Judge held that – (1) Hashstacs (SG) could not be regarded as the maker of the Whitepaper Representations, because he accepted the evidence of Mr Soh and Mr Cowan that employees of Hashstacs (SG) had edited the Third Whitepaper and made them available on the STACS Website on the instructions of Mr Cowan and solely for the benefit of Hashstacs (BVI) and GSX, and there was no need to go on to separately consider the Website Representations; and (2) in the alternative, if Hashstacs (SG) had been the maker of the Whitepaper Representations, he would have found one aspect of them to be actionable in tort, viz , the undertaking as to how transaction fees received from the STACS Protocol would come to be distributed, subject to the caveat that it was viable to implement the STACS Protocol and the project proved to be commercially successful. He awarded costs to the respondents jointly payable by the appellants in instalments. 8 The appellants did not appeal against the Judge’s dismissal of their claims in unjust enrichment and conspiracy, but they did appeal against the dismissal of their claims in fraudulent and negligent misrepresentation. The Court’s grounds of decision The appellants failed to prove that the first respondent was either the representor of the pleaded representations or had adopted and ratified their contents as its own 9 The Court agreed with the Judge’s exposition on the law on the tort of deceit, the first ingredient being that there must be a representation of fact made by words or conduct by the defendant, or alternatively, the defendant manifestly approved and adopted the representation of a third party (at [7 3]–[74] ). The applicable legal test was whether, on an objective assessment of the totality of Hashstacs (SG)’s words or conduct, in all the circumstances, a reasonable person would have considered that Hashstacs (SG) was a maker of the pleaded representations or, alternatively, it approved and adopted those representations which had been made by another person (at [78]–[80] ). 10 Applying that legal test to the facts concerned, the Judge was correct in accepting the consistent evidence of Mr Soh and Mr Cowan that everything done by employees of Hashstacs (SG) in relation to the Third Whitepaper, viz , editing the Third Whitepaper and making it available to the public on the STACS Website in March 2019, was done on the instructions of Mr Cowan and performed for the benefit of Hashstacs (BVI) and GSX. The appellants had not put to either witness in the trial below that this evidence was false and hence they were precluded by the rule in Browne v Dunn from submitting that their evidence should not be believed (at [ 81]–[89] ). 11 On the question whether the acts of the employees of Hashstacs (SG) as described above would objectively constitute it a maker of the Whitepaper Representations (at [90] ) , the Court agreed with the Judge that Hashstacs (SG) was not the maker. Having regard to the facts and considerations of authorial and editorial control and control over the process of publication, a reasonable person in the position of the representee would come to the view inter alia that all acts of Hashstacs (SG)’s employees in editing and uploading the Third Whitepaper were not performed for its own ends but only for Hashstacs (BVI), and that Hashstacs (BVI) had control of the STACS Website in the substantive sense of controlling the contents uploaded thereupon. The Judge correctly accorded weight to the facts that the Third Whitepaper made no mention of Hashstacs (SG), named Hashstacs (BVI) on the cover page as its publisher, was written from the perspective of GSX as the persona, and expressly identified GSX and Hashstacs (BVI) as the service-providers in relation to the STACS Protocol which were capable of fulfilling the Whitepaper Representations, a fact confirmed by the commercial background surrounding the STACS Protocol that evidenced that it was GSX which owned and controlled the STACS Protocol and not Hashstacs (SG). The Court, in rejecting the appellants’ argument, concluded from Hashstacs (SG)’s words or conduct that it never made the Whitepaper Representations and had not adopted its contents as its own (at [91]–[98] ). 12 On the Website Representations, the appellants failed to discharge their burden of proof that Hashstacs (SG) was the maker of the Website Representations. The only evidential basis adduced therefor was a screenshot in Mr da Silveira’s witness statement. On his oral evidence, he had never seen the original source of that screenshot and he could not provide the full context in which the Website Representations had originally been found. That context was critical in determining the identity of the maker of the Website Representations, having regard to the words or conduct of Hashstacs (SG) in the totality of their circumstances. That evidential gap was resolved against the appellants (at [ 100]–[104] ). 13 As the appellants failed to show that Hashstacs (SG), by its words or conduct, made or adopted the pleaded representations, the Court dismissed the appellants’ appeal on that ground (at [104]– [105] ). The pleaded representations were either not proven to have been made or did not amount to actionable representations of past or present fact 14 Additionally, the Court found the appellants were not entitled to succeed in their claim in misrepresentation for a second reason, viz , the first ingredient of the tort of deceit at [ 9] above was not met because the pleaded representations were not representations of fact. In particular, a representation of fact requires that the representation be one of past or present fact, capable of being true or false at the time it was made. In contrast, where the representation concerns only future facts or the representor’s future conduct, it is not capable of being true or false at the time, reflecting either a belief or opinion as to the future, an aspiration to make it come true, or a promise to perform as stated in the future. While a promise as to the future may give rise to liability in contract law, it is not actionable in the tort of deceit (at [10 6] and [108] –[110] ). 15 To determine whether the pleaded representations were representations of fact, the Court first assessed which representations were objectively shown to have been made in the first place, applying the reasonable person test as at [9] above (at [ 111] ). Based on that legal test, the Court found that two of the Whitepaper Representations had not been made, as their pleaded contents did not cohere with the contents of the Third Whitepaper looked at in the full context of that document (at [112]–[ 118] ). In contrast, three of the Whitepaper Representations cohered with an objective reading of the Third Whitepaper’s contents, viz , that the STACS Tokens would be the utility token powering the ecosystem of the STACS Protocol, that verified partners would be required to “stake” a minimum number of STACS Tokens to enjoy such rights as access to the Native STACS, and transaction fees earned on the STACS Protocol would be distributed in a promised fashion, with 80% being used to purchase STACS Tokens from the open market (the “Representations” ) (at [ 119]–[120] ). 16 None of the three Representations were representations of fact. They did not concern any past or present facts but were representations of the future conduct of the maker in relation to the prospective operation of the STACS Protocol. That was shown upon reading the Representations in the full context of the Third Whitepaper, with the totality of its contents evidencing that it was describing a future project that had yet to be fully implemented, representing an aspirational vision of the maker(s) that they envisaged to be brought to fruition in the ideal state of affairs. The Representations were therefore not representations of fact and were not actionable in tort as misrepresentations (at [122]–[ 126] ). The Court was, with respect, not able to concur with the Judge’s views, expressed in the alternative at [ 7] above, that the Representations were capable of being false if the undertaking as to the distribution of the transaction receipts was not implemented as promised in the event the STACS Protocol proved viable to implement and a success. Such a caveated undertaking was not reconcilable with the proper analysis that the Representations were actionable only to the limited extent it impliedly represented a then-present fact as to the state of mind of the maker(s) and their genuine intent to implement the STACS Protocol project as described, being restricted to their state of mind solely at the time of their making. The Representations remained true even if there was a genuine change of heart thereafter (at [ 127]–[136] ). 17 As for the Website Representations, the appellants failed to discharge their burden of proof based on Mr da Silveira’s screenshot at [12] above. That screenshot did not show the context in which the Website Representations were made to shed light on how they would reasonably have been understood. The appellants failed to prove their objective meaning. In any event, the Website Representations clearly pertained only to the future (at [121] ). Conclusion 18 The appellants’ civil appeal was dismissed with default indemnity costs being ordered against them. The usual consequential orders applied (at [ 137]–[138] and [140] ). This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s judgment. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s judgment.

court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 26 November 2025 Case summary Saminathan a/l Selvaraju v Attorney-General [2025] SGCA 54 Court of Appeal – Originating Application (OAC) No 3 of 2025 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Court of Appeal (delivered by Justice Tay Yong Kwang): Outcome: The Court of Appeal dismissed an application for a stay of execution by a PACP. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment • Where a person awaiting capital punishment seeks a stay of execution or files an application for permission to file a post-appeal application in a capital case (“PACC application”) on the basis of a pending proceeding, the court will consider whether the PACC application has reasonable prospects of success, which hinges on whether the underlying pending proceeding has reasonable prospects of success: at [38]. Introduction 1 The applicant Mr Saminathan a/l Selvaraju (“Mr Saminathan”) is a prisoner awaiting capital punishment (“PACP”) who was scheduled for execution on Thursday 27 November 2025. He filed an application under s 60G(1) of the Supreme Court of Judicature Act 1969 (2020 Rev Ed) (“SCJA”) for permission to file PACC application to seek a prohibiting order against his execution scheduled for Thursday 27 November 2025, a quashing order for the notice of execution dated 20 November 2025 and a stay of his execution pending the conclusion of this application for permission and the PACC application. 2 In this application, Mr Saminathan relies on an action HC/OA 1213/2025 (“OA 1213”) filed by members of an unincorporated body called the Transformative Justice Collective, a non-governmental organisation, to challenge the constitutionality of the mandatory death penalty under s 33(1) of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1973 (2020 Rev Ed) read with its Second Schedule. OA 1213 is scheduled for hearing before the General Division of the High Court on 3 December 2025. 3 Mr Saminathan claims that the outcome of OA 1213 may may have an effect on his conviction and sentence and his execution should therefore be stayed pending that outcome. 4 On Wednesday 26 November 2025, in the morning, Mr Saminathan filed further submissions alleging that new evidence pertaining to his case had surfaced. Decision 5 One of the factors that Parliament requires the Court to consider is whether the PACC application to be made has reasonable prospects of success (s 60G(7)( d ) of the SCJA) . In the context of the present application, since the pending OA 1213 formed the very substratum of Mr Saminathan’s arguments for a stay of execution, the issue whether the PACC application had reasonable prospects of success hinged entirely on the question whether OA 1213 has reasonable prospects of success: at [38]. 6 In considering whether OA 1213 has reasonable prospects of success, the Court looked only at the legal issue of the constitutionality of the mandatory death penalty in the MDA and expressed no views on the legal standing of the seven applicants or the reliefs sought: at [39] . 7 The applicants in OA 1213 averred on affidavit that they were relying on the grounds that the mandatory death penalty contravenes both Arts 9(1) and 12(1) of the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (2020 Rev Ed) (“Constitution”): at [39] . 8 The grounds relied on in OA 1213 were substantively similar to those raised and decided in other cases by the highest courts in Singapore. OA 1213 was merely a challenge to clear established law and there were no reasonable prospects of success where the constitutional questions were concerned: at [40] to [42] . 9 The applicant’s further submissions were an abuse of the process of the Court because he was trying to re-argue factual issues decided by the Court of Appeal in his appeal against conviction and sentence, or he was trying to introduce new evidence without complying with the law: at [43] to [45] . 10 The Court therefore refused to grant a stay of execution: at [46]. This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.

subject_tags: ["Criminal Procedure and Sentencing — Extradition — Bail"]
court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 21 November 2025 Case summary Paulus Tannos v The State [20 25] SGHC 229 General Division of the High Court/Criminal Motion No. 41 of 2025 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the General Division of the High Court (delivered by Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon): Outcome: The General Division of the High Court (“High Court”) dismissed Criminal Motion No 41 of 2025 (“CM 41”) brought by the applicant (“Applicant”) seeking the High Court’s exercise of its revisionary jurisdiction to release him on bail. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment • CM 41 was dismissed because the High Court was amply satisfied that the District Judge below (“DJ”) made no error in refusing to grant bail to the Applicant: at [67] . • The Applicant was not “sick or infirm” within the meaning of r 6(1)( b ) of the Criminal Procedure Rules 2018 (“CPR”). The words “sick or infirm” referred to the exceptional situation of a fugitive suffering from a sickness or infirmity that could not reasonably be managed by the Singapore Prison Service (“SPS”) safely. This was precisely how the DJ interpreted the words “sick or infirm”: at [ 50]–[51] . • The Applicant did not suffer from any sickness or infirmity that could not reasonably be managed by the SPS safely: at [5 5] . • If a fugitive was able to demonstrate that he was “sick or infirm” within the meaning of r 6(1)( b ) of the CPR, bail should ordinarily be granted to the fugitive prior to his committal hearing provided the fugitive did not pose a real risk of flight that could adequately be managed: at [60] and [64] . • Even if the Applicant was “sick or infirm” within the meaning of r 6(1)( b ) of the CPR, which the High Court held he was not, the DJ did not err in refusing to grant bail to the Applicant because she correctly concluded that he posed a real flight risk: at [61] . Background 1 After a District Judge (the “DJ”) refused to grant bail to the applicant, Mr Paulus Tannos (the “Applicant”), the Applicant brought Criminal Motion No 41 of 2025 (“CM 41”) seeking that the General Division of the High Court (“High Court”) exercise its revisionary jurisdiction and release him on bail. The material facts 2 In January 2025, the Applicant was arrested by officers from the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau. The warrant of apprehension for the Applicant’s arrest was issued pursuant to s 12(1) of the Extradition Act 1968 (2020 Rev Ed) (“Extradition Act”). The Applicant was informed that the Republic of Indonesia (“ROI”) had intimated its intention to apply for his extradition there. The Applicant has been remanded in Changi Prison since then. 3 In February 2025, the ROI issued a formal extradition request in respect of the Applicant. The extradition request was for the Applicant to be produced in the ROI to answer a charge in respect of an alleged corruption offence that related to the procurement of goods and services for the National Resident’s Identity Number-based Electronic Card project (otherwise known as the Kartu Tanda Penduduk Elektronik Berbasis Nomor Induk Kependudukan project) between 2011 and 2013. 4 In March 2025, the Applicant applied to be released on bail on the basis that he was sick or infirm. The DJ dismissed the application for bail, holding that the Applicant had failed to show why bail should be granted. First, the Applicant was not “sick” or “infirm” within the meaning of r 6(1)( b ) of the Criminal Procedure Rules 2018 (“CPR”), which might have provided an exception to the default rule that bail was not generally available to persons like the Applicant who were apprehended under the Extradition Act. The DJ construed the words “sick or infirm” to refer to a sufficiently serious illness or physical weakness that could not reasonably be managed in prison. Based on the affidavits and medical reports filed, the DJ concluded that the Applicant did not suffer from any medical conditions of such gravity that the Singapore Prison Service (“SPS”) could not reasonably manage them. Second, the DJ would not have exercised her discretion to grant the Applicant bail even if he was sick or infirm as she took the view that the Applicant was a high flight risk. 5 The Applicant brought CM 41 seeking to be released on bail. Decision in the Criminal Motion 6 The High Court would exercise its revisionary jurisdiction sparingly. It was typically invoked in circumstances where an appeal did not lie, and two conditions must be satisfied before a court would exercise such jurisdiction. The first was that the decision or order made by the judge below must contain some error, absent which there would be no room for invoking the court’s revisionary jurisdiction. Showing the presence of an error was necessary but insufficient to warrant invoking the court’s revisionary jurisdiction. This led to the second condition, which was that material and serious injustice must be shown to follow from the error. Put another way, the applicant must show that there was something so clearly wrong with the lower court’s decision that it cast doubt on that court’s exercise of judicial power. This was plainly a high threshold, which was unsurprising where, as was the case here, the court was dealing with the review of a decision against which there was no provision for appeal: at [12] . 7 Where a fugitive apprehended under the Extradition Act applied to be released on bail, the starting point was that the fugitive was not to be released on bail. A two-step framework would assist the court to determine whether it should nevertheless extend bail to the fugitive. First, the court should consider whether the fugitive fell within the letter of any of the exceptions set out in r 6(1) of the CPR. Only if one or more exceptions were applicable would the court turn to the second step of the framework. At the second step, even if the fugitive fell within an exception, the court retained a residual discretion to determine whether bail ought to be granted having balanced all the relevant considerations: at [19] . 8 When the Applicant applied to be released on bail, the burden of proof was on him to show that he could bring himself within one or more of the exceptions found in r 6(1) of the CPR: at [36] . 9 Applying a purposive interpretation in respect of the words “sick or infirm” under r 6(1)( b ) of the CPR , these words referred to the exceptional situation of a fugitive suffering from a sickness or infirmity that could not reasonably be managed by the SPS safely. It followed that the DJ made no error of law in her judgment because this was precisely how she interpreted the words “sick or infirm”: at [37], [47] and [50]–[51] . 10 The DJ accepted the assertion by the SPS that it could adequately manage the Applicant’s medical conditions, and there was no reason to come to a different view. The SPS had ensured that the Applicant was prescribed the relevant medications to manage his medical conditions. The SPS was also prepared to handle any medical emergencies and make the necessary arrangements if the Applicant required specialist medical care: at [52] . 11 The Applicant also contended that in considering the adequacy of the care afforded by the SPS, the High Court had to consider the fact that the Applicant applied for – but was unsuccessful in seeking – the assistance of his private physician to assess his condition and to respond to the State’s assertion of the adequacy of the care facilities that had been provided. But the Applicant’s medical conditions were pre-existing conditions that manifested a degree of stability. There was no suggestion of some new important medical development, and it was open to the Applicant’s private physicians to consider and opine on the adequacy of the care that had been extended to the Applicant. Nothing, however, was forthcoming in this respect. In the circumstances, there was nothing to show that the SPS could not reasonably manage the Applicant’s medical conditions safely: at [53] . 12 There was also nothing else to suggest that the Applicant suffered from any specific infirmity that could not reasonably be handled by the SPS safely. In this regard, the Applicant was currently housed at the lower level of the correctional unit such that he did not have to use the stairs to reach his cell. Moreover, the Applicant had been offered the use of a commode in the cell instead of a squatting toilet to accommodate his age. Nonetheless, the Applicant had declined the offer, stating that he was able to manage using the squatting toilets. In all the circumstances, the High Court found that the Applicant had failed to establish that the SPS could not reasonably manage his alleged infirmities safely: at [54] . 13 The High Court therefore affirmed the DJ’s conclusion that the Applicant was not “sick or infirm” within the meaning of r 6(1)( b ) of the CPR: at [55] . 14 Notwithstanding that a fugitive was able to demonstrate that he was “sick or infirm” within the meaning of r 6(1)( b ) of the CPR, bail would ordinarily only be granted to the fugitive prior to the committal hearing if the fugitive did not pose a real risk of flight. This called for a balancing exercise of all the relevant considerations, including the nature of the illness, the imminence and likelihood of serious harm to the fugitive owing to the inability of the SPS to safely manage the illness, and the possibility of medical treatment being made available subject to measures being put in place to prevent the risk of flight materialising: at [60] . 15 Even if the Applicant was “sick or infirm” within the meaning of r 6(1)( b ) of the CPR, which the High Court held he was not, the DJ did not err in refusing to grant bail to the Applicant because she correctly concluded that he posed a real flight risk. The Applicant held multiple passports from the Republic of Guinea-Bissau (“Guinea-Bissau”) and the Republic of Vanuatu. On the Applicant’s own account, these passports were acquired for the purpose of facilitating travel, and it was clear from his travel records that he had indeed used them for this purpose. The Applicant was not a citizen of Singapore, and both his children resided abroad in Hong Kong and the United States of America respectively: at [61] . 16 Further, the Applicant’s passports included a diplomatic passport issued by Guinea-Bissau under the name “Joao Paulo Gomes”. The High Court found the inconsistent accounts furnished by the Applicant as to how he came to procure this diplomatic passport to be troubling. No explanation was advanced for the inconsistent accounts. And in any event, regardless of why there were these inconsistencies, it was clear that the Applicant had the means of obtaining a foreign passport and of travelling inconspicuously under a completely different identity, which escalated the risk of flight: at [62] . 17 Finally, the nature of the underlying offence was relevant in assessing the Applicant’s flight risk. The Applicant was accused of committing a serious corruption offence which carried a maximum penalty of life imprisonment: at [63] . 18 In all the circumstances, there was a real risk that the Applicant would abscond if he was released on bail. There was, in the High Court’s view, a real risk of flight in this case that could not adequately be managed. The DJ’s view that bail should not be extended to the Applicant even if he was “sick or infirm” was entirely justified: at [64] . 19 There was no basis for the Applicant’s assertion that the court should exercise its inherent power to nonetheless release the Applicant on bail: at [65]–[66] . 20 The High Court was amply satisfied that the DJ made no error in refusing to grant bail to the Applicant. Accordingly, the High Court dismissed CM 41: at [67] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.

subject_tags: ["Family Law — Matrimonial assets — Division — Consideration of rent-free occupation of matrimonial home — Section 112(2)(f) Women’s Charter 1961 (2020 Rev Ed)", "Family Law — Maintenance — Wife — Application of rationale of financial preservation to award of final spousal maintenance — Section 113(1)(b) Women’s Charter 1961 (2020 Rev Ed)", "Family Law — Maintenance — Child — Application of issue estoppel doctrine where prior interim maintenance summons was rejected — Section 127(2) Women’s Charter 1961 (2020 Rev Ed)"]
court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 18 November 2025 Case Summary XHG v XHH [ 2025] SGHC(A) 24 Appellate Division of the High Court Civil Appeal No 6 of 2025 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Debbie Ong Siew Ling JAD (delivering the judgment of the court): Outcome: the Appellate Division of the High Court (the “A ppellate Division” ) dismissed all issues appealed against on the ancillary matters following divorce, save for one issue – that of the order of the Judge in the Family Division of the High Court (the “Judge” ) for an award of lump sum backdated spousal maintenance for the wife. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment • A final maintenance order made under s 113(1)( b ) of the Women’s Charter 1961 (2020 Rev Ed) (the “Charter” ) has a different purpose from that for ss 69(1) and 113(1)( a ) of the Charter. The former concerns a broader remedy to even out the economic disadvantages arising from the role the spouse undertook in the marriage in order to achieve financial preservation in post-divorce life. The latter concerns an enforcement of a spouse’s duty to provide for the other spouse’s immediate financial needs during the subsistence of their marriage. These purposes should not be conflated such that an order under s 113(1)( b ) is used to provide for a former wife’s past financial needs during the marriage (at [70] –[75] ). • Where there is no basis for a final order of spousal maintenance under s 113(1)( b ) of the Charter, there is simply no maintenance order to be “backdated” – in the absence of an order for spousal maintenance under s 113(1)(b), the court has no power under s 113(1)( b ) to make only an award of spousal maintenance covering earlier periods (at [79]–[80] ). • While not necessary to resolve the dispute before it, the Appellate Division made provisional observations that the legislative history of s 127(2) of the Charter informs that this provision was never intended to impose the requirement of proof of neglect or refusal to maintain (contained in s 69(2)) on child maintenance orders made in ancillary matters proceedings. The court has matrimonial jurisdiction over the parties in divorce proceedings, with the ancillary powers to make orders for the family where the marriage has broken down – its task is to ensure that family obligations continue to be discharged after the drastic event of a divorce and is independent of whether a parent has neglected or refused to maintain the child in the past (at [45]–[59] ). Factual Background 1 The appellant (the “Husband” ) and respondent (the “Wife” ) were married in 2013. They had two children (the “Children” ). The Husband left the “Matrimonial Home” in May 2022, which the family had lived in since December 2014. The Husband commenced divorce proceedings in February 2022. An Interim Judgment of divorce was granted in October 2022. 2 During the marriage, the Husband worked for a financial services group since April 2015, earning around $58,800 a month (including bonuses). The Wife earned around $26,500 a month (excluding bonuses) from her job at a bank – this employment ended in April 2021. She remained unemployed until she received an offer to work for a bank with a base monthly salary of $18,000 in October 2024 and resumed work in November 2024. 3 The Wife had taken out a summons against the Husband for interim maintenance in the Family Court on 21 September 2022 ( “Interim Maintenance Summons” ) for both herself and the Children. A district judge ( “DJ” ) found that the Husband had not neglected or refused to maintain the Wife and Children. Nevertheless, she made orders for spousal and child maintenance to assist the parties ( “Family Court Orders” ) but declined to backdate the orders to January 2022. The Husband appealed against the Family Court Orders, and the Family Division of the High Court ( “HCFD” ) found that since the Husband had not neglected or refused to maintain the Wife and Children, there was no basis for the Interim Maintenance Summons to be granted below. The HCFD set aside the Family Court Orders on 27 July 2023. 4 The ancillary matters were heard by the Judge in November 2024. The Judge ordered the matrimonial assets to be divided in the ratio of 53:47 in the Husband’s favour, being the average of their direct contributions ratio (56:44 in the Husband’s favour) and their indirect contributions ratio (50:50). He declined to accord a 3.5% uplift to the Husband’s share which the Husband sought on the basis that the Wife enjoyed exclusive rent-free occupation of the Matrimonial Home. He ordered the Husband to pay $4,819 per month for the Children’s maintenance, being 72.5% of the Children’s reasonable monthly expenses of $6,647. That sum of $6,647 included the figure of $2,386 per month for the Children’s enrichment classes. He also ordered the Husband to pay $17,000 in backdated maintenance for the Children for the period of August 2023 to December 2024. The Judge awarded $144,000 in backdated spousal maintenance to the Wife for the period of December 2021 to December 2023, during which the Wife was unemployed. He also found that the Husband breached his duty of full and frank disclosure, and that he only belatedly disclosed bank statements in his “SCB Account” in his “ 5th Affidavit” , which warranted adverse costs orders against the Husband. He fixed costs against the Husband in the quantum of $5,000 on a standard costs basis for the ancillary matters proceedings and $2,000 on an indemnity basis for the Wife’s thrown-away costs for having to prepare her response to the 5th Affidavit. The Court’s judgment Enrichment Class Payments 5 There was no merit to the Husband’s argument that the child maintenance sum payable should be lower on the basis that he was already paying a certain sum directly to the enrichment class service-providers. The Judge did not make any orders relating to the Children’s specific enrichment classes and he only estimated a reasonable sum for their enrichment classes more generally. He did not order that the Husband had to continue paying a sum directly to the specific service providers in addition to paying 72.5% of $6,647 as monthly child maintenance, and thus there was no double counting. In assessing a reasonable sum for the Children’s enrichment, the Judge adopted the Husband’s own proposed figure. There was therefore no basis to interfere with the Judge’s award of monthly child maintenance (at [22] –[26] ). Backdated Child Maintenance 6 The Husband’s invocation of the issue estoppel doctrine was misplaced. There was no identity of subject-matter between the refusal of the Interim Maintenance Summons by the HCFD on the one hand, and the Judge’s award of Backdated Child Maintenance on the other. The HCFD affirmed the DJ’s finding that the Husband had not neglected or refused to maintain the Wife and Children as at 21 September 2022 (when the Interim Maintenance Summons was filed). That finding had no bearing on whether the Husband neglected or refused to maintain the Children in the different period of August 2023 to December 2024 (at [33] –[37] ). 7 The Husband’s reliance on AXM v AXO [2014] 2 SLR 705 ( “ AXM v AXO ” ) was also misplaced. AXM v AXO precluded the court from backdating a final maintenance order to include a period that overlapped with a subsisting interim maintenance order, giving rise to two different but equally binding payment obligations. As the HCFD had dismissed the Interim Maintenance Summons, there was no interim maintenance order capable of overlapping with the award of Backdated Child Maintenance (at [39] ). 8 There was no merit to the Husband’s argument that the Judge ought not to have made the order for Backdated Child Maintenance on the basis that the Wife was capable of providing for the Children’s reasonable needs on her own in the period concerned. Parents have a shared duty to maintain their child based on their respective means and capabilities. Even if the Wife were capable of maintaining the Children by herself, it did not change the fact that the Husband was not contributing his fair share towards their maintenance in the period concerned (at [40] –[43] ). 9 While not necessary to resolve the dispute before it, the Appellate Division made provisional observations that the legislative history of s 127(2) of the Charter informs that this provision was never intended to impose the requirement of proof of neglect or refusal to maintain (contained in s 69(2)) on child maintenance orders made in ancillary matters proceedings. The court has matrimonial jurisdiction over the parties in divorce proceedings, with the ancillary powers to make orders for the family where the marriage has broken down – its task is to ensure that family obligations continue to be discharged after the drastic event of a divorce and is independent of whether a parent has neglected or refused to maintain the child in the past (at [45]–[59] ). Backdated Spousal Maintenance 10 The Husband’s invocation of the rule in AXM v AXO to impugn the award of Backdated Spousal Maintenance was rejected for the same reasons at [ 7] above (at [63] ). 11 The Husband’s invocation of the issue estoppel doctrine was misplaced. There was no identity of subject-matter between the HCFD’s refusal of the Interim Maintenance Summons on one hand, and the Judge’s award of Backdated Spousal Maintenance on the other. The HCFD found that the pre-requisite that the Husband had neglected or refused to maintain was not met for the Interim Maintenance Summons. No such requirement governs the making of a final spousal maintenance order, which is undergirded by the principle of financial preservation to enable the former wife to continue to live at the level she did immediately prior to the breakdown of the marriage so far as is practicable (at [64] –[67] ). 12 However, the Judge ought not to have awarded Backdated Spousal Maintenance to the Wife. The mere fact that the Wife was unemployed in the relevant period was insufficient and was only one of the factors to consider. The Judge ought to have had regard to other factors such as the Wife’s financial resources including her share of the matrimonial assets after division (she stood to receive 47% of a matrimonial pool valued at about $8.1 million). Significantly, she was gainfully employed and earning a substantial income by the time of the AM hearing. The exercise of the power in s 113(1)( b ) of the Charter is undergirded by the principle of financial preservation. The discretion to backdate a final maintenance order only arises where there is such an order made under s 113(1)( b ) of the Charter. Since there was no basis to make a final maintenance order here (and indeed the Wife did not seek such prospective maintenance), there was no order under s 113(1)( b ) of the Charter that could be backdated. The Judge’s award of $144,000 in Backdated Spousal Maintenance was set aside (at [69] –[84] ). Indirect Contributions Ratio 13 The court focuses on broad factual indicators and not the minutiae of family life when determining the ratio of the parties’ indirect contributions. The broad factual indicators here point to a marriage where the Husband made greater indirect financial contributions to the well-being of the family, while the Wife made greater indirect non-financial contributions. There is no merit in the Husband’s contention that the indirect contributions ratio had to be adjusted in his favour because he played an active role in the Children’s lives. The Judge did not downplay his contributions and had found him to be an active father who made substantial contributions in the Children’s lives. The Wife was a stay-at-home mother from May 2021 and was the Children’s primary caregiver even before she was unemployed. There was no basis to disturb the indirect contributions ratio of 50:50 (at [87] –[92] ). Rent-Free Occupation 14 The Husband’s expenses on alternative accommodation are not an appropriate proxy for his requested 3.5% uplift to his share in the matrimonial pool to account for the alleged rent-free occupation or other benefit enjoyed by the Wife in the Matrimonial Home. The text of s 112(2)( f ) suggests that that factor is focused not on compensating the excluded spouse for the consequential losses flowing from their exclusion from the matrimonial home, but on considering the benefit received by the occupying spouse. In any event, the factor in s 112(2)( f ) should be considered in the balance together with all other relevant factors in this case, including, in particular, another factor expressly stated in s 112(2)( c ) – the needs of the children of the marriage. When it became impracticable for the parties to live together in the Matrimonial Home, it was reasonable for the Wife to remain in the Matrimonial Home with the Children, having been their primary caregiver at that time. There was no reason to disturb the final ratio of division reached by the Judge (at [95] –[106] ). Adverse Costs Orders 15 The Judge was fully entitled to exercise his discretion to make the Adverse Costs Orders. There was no basis for the Husband’s argument that he was not required to disclose the SCB Account’s bank statements in the absence of a specific order from an assistant registrar to disclose them. The duty of full and frank disclosure existed independently of any discovery orders. The onus was on the Husband to produce any documents relevant to the exercise of the court’s power under s 112(1) of the Charter. This he did not do, and his belated disclosure in the 5th Affidavit added to the time and costs of the proceedings below. There was no basis to interfere with the Adverse Costs Orders below (at [109] –[116] ). Conclusion 16 The Appellate Division set aside the order that the Husband pay backdated spousal maintenance of $144,000 to the Wife, and dismissed all other points on appeal (at [117] ) . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s judgment. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s judgment.

court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 17 November 2025 Case summary Public Prosecutor v ZH Builders and another appeal [20 25] SGHC 227 General Division of the High Court/ Magistrate’s Appeals No. 9195 of 2024/01 and 9198 of 2024/01 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the General Division of the High Court (comprising Sundaresh Menon CJ, Tay Yong Kwang JCA and Vincent Hoong Judge) (delivered by Tay Yong Kwang JCA): Outcome: The General Division of the High Court (“High Court”) comprising three Judges set out a sentencing framework for corporate offenders charged with offences under s 11(1)( a ) and punishable under s 11(6) (the “s 11(1)( a ) Offence”) and s 20(1)( a ) and punishable under s 20(1)(i) (the “s 20(1)( a ) Offence”) of the Building Control Act (Cap 29, 1999 Rev Ed), and enhanced the fines imposed on the builder (“ZH Builders”) and the developer (“457 Balestier”) of a project involving an existing shophouse at Balestier Road. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment • There was no need for separate sentencing frameworks for the s 11(1)( a ) Offence and the s 20(1)( a ) Offence. The sentencing framework for the offences here could be adapted from the sentencing framework developed for offences under the Workplace Safety and Health Act (Cap 354A, 2009 Rev Ed) (“WSHA”). In this regard, the sentencing matrix adopted by the DJ in respect of corporate offenders utilised the appropriate indicative starting ranges. Furthermore, the High Court agreed that the relevant factors in ascertaining harm and culpability for offences under the Act would be broadly similar to those for offences under the WSHA. Where culpability was concerned, it was important to consider whether the offender acted intentionally or negligently in failing to comply with his statutory duties. Deliberate concealment of non-compliance would increase the offender’s culpability: at [30], [32] , [36]–[37] and [39] . • The High Court allowed the Prosecution’s appeals and enhanced the sentences imposed by the DJ. Having regard to the sentencing matrix and considering that the culpability of ZH Builders and 457 Balestier was high (with 457 Balestier’s culpability being higher than ZH Builders’) and the potential harm was medium, the High Court was of the view that the appropriate starting sentence for ZH Builders was a fine of $100,000 for each charge and that for 457 Balestier was $120,000. As both companies pleaded guilty at the earliest opportunity, they were given a discount in sentence ranging from 25% to 30%. This resulted in a fine of $70,000 for each of ZH Builders’ two charges and a fine of $90,000 for 457 Balestier’s sole charge: at [5]–[6] and [56] . Background 1 These were two appeals brought by the Prosecution against the sentences imposed by a Magistrate’s Court, presided over by a District Judge (the “DJ”). The respondents in HC/MA 9195/2024/01 and HC/MA 9198/2024/01 were two companies (“ZH Builders” and “457 Balester” respectively). They were charged with offences under the Building Control Act (Cap 29, 1999 Rev Ed) (“Act”) pertaining to building works in a project (the “Project”) involving an existing shophouse at Balestier Road. The relevant offences here were under s 11(1)( a ) and punishable under s 11(6) of the Act (the “s 11(1)( a ) Offence”) and s 20(1)( a ) and punishable under s 20(1)(i) of the Act (the “s 20(1)( a ) Offence”). The material facts 2 ZH Builders was the builder of the Project while 457 Balestier was the developer of the Project. The Project involved, among other things, the construction of an additional floor to the existing two-storey structure (the “Front Building”) as well as a rear extension comprising six storeys of residential units. 3 On 25 May 2021, the Commissioner of Building Control (“Commissioner”) received feedback that the Project involved building works that contravened the Act. A stop work order was issued on 16 June 2021. The stop work order was lifted on 5 July 2021. 4 Both ZH Builders and 457 Balestier pleaded guilty to the two charges and the sole charge brought against them respectively. 5 The DJ agreed that the sentencing framework for the offences here could be developed with reference to the sentencing framework for offences under the Workplace Safety and Health Act (Cap 354A, 2009 Rev Ed) (“WSHA”). Applying her proposed sentencing matrix, the DJ agreed with the parties that the level of harm caused by the offences both on the part of ZH Builders and 457 Balestier was low. The DJ assessed the culpabilities of ZH Builders and 457 Balestier for the offences to be medium. The DJ imposed fines of $38,000 and $28,000 on ZH Builders for each of the two charges brought against it and a fine of $38,000 on 457 Balestier for the sole charge brought against it. Dissatisfied with the DJ’s decision on sentence, the Prosecution appealed. Decision on appeal The applicable sentencing framework for the offences in the present case 6 There was no need for separate sentencing frameworks for the s 11(1)( a ) Offence and the s 20(1)( a ) Offence. The sentencing framework for the offences here could be adapted from the sentencing framework developed for offences under the WSHA. In this regard, the sentencing matrix adopted by the DJ in respect of corporate offenders utilised the appropriate indicative starting ranges. Further, the High Court agreed that the relevant factors in ascertaining harm and culpability for offences under the Act would be broadly similar to those for offences under the WSHA. Where culpability was concerned, it was important to consider whether the offender acted intentionally or negligently in failing to comply with his statutory duties. Deliberate concealment of non-compliance would increase the offender’s culpability: at [30], [32], [36] –[37] and [39] . 7 Once the Court assessed the level of harm and culpability, the indicative starting point was determined according to the following sentencing matrix, with the starting points reflecting first-time offenders who claimed trial: at [42(a)] Culpability Low Medium High Harm Low Fine of up to $30,000 $30,000 to $60,000 $60,000 to $90,000 Medium $30,000 to $60,000 $60,000 to $90,000 $90,000 to $120,000 High $60,000 to $90,000 $90,000 to $120,000 $120,000 to $200,000 8 The Court next adjusted the starting point, having regard to offender-specific aggravating and mitigating factors. Finally, in a case involving a plea of guilt, the Court factored in the appropriate discount in sentence using the Sentencing Advisory Panel’s Guidelines on Reduction in Sentences for Guilty Pleas: at [42(b)] . The High Court enhanced the sentences imposed by the DJ on ZH Builders and 457 Balestier 9 The High Court allowed the Prosecution’s appeals and enhanced the sentences imposed by the DJ. Having regard to the sentencing matrix and considering that the culpability of ZH Builders and 457 Balestier was high (with 457 Balestier’s culpability being higher than ZH Builders’) and the potential harm was medium, the High Court was of the view that the appropriate starting sentence for ZH Builders was a fine of $100,000 for each charge and that for 457 Balestier was $120,000. As both companies pleaded guilty at the earliest opportunity, they were given a discount in sentence ranging from 25% to 30%. This resulted in a fine of $70,000 for each of ZH Builders’s two charges and a fine of $90,000 for 457 Balestier’s sole charge: at [5]–[6] and [56] . 10 Prior to the hearing of the appeal, ZH Builders paid the total of $66,000 in respect of the fines imposed by the DJ while 457 Balestier paid its fine of $38,000. At the conclusion of the appeals, ZH Builders and 457 Balestier asked to pay the balance of the fines imposed on appeal ($74,000 for ZH Builders and $52,000 for 457 Balestier) by way of instalments. The High Court allowed their applications and ordered that payment of the remaining fines be made by way of four equal monthly instalments, with the first instalment to be paid on or before 26 August 2025: at [58] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. case_name: DMZ v DNA
subject_tags: ["Arbitration — Conduct of arbitration — UNCITRAL Model Law — Article 5 — Whether party permitted to apply to court while the arbitration is ongoing to challenge a decision of the arbitral institution", "Arbitration — Conduct of arbitration — Rules — Arbitration Rules of the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (6th Ed, 1 August 2016) — Rules 40.1 and 40.2 — Whether tribunal or court permitted to review a decision of the arbitral institution"]
court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 14 November 2025 Case summary DMZ v DNA [2025] SGCA 52 Civil Appeal No 5 of 2025 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Judgment of the Court of Appeal (comprising Sundaresh Menon CJ, Steven Chong JCA, Ang Cheng Hock JCA) (delivered by Sundaresh Menon CJ): Outcome: The Court of Appeal (the “CA”) dismissed an appeal against a decision of a judge (the “Judge”) of the General Division of the High Court (the “GDHC”) to deny permission to proceed with an application for declaratory relief in respect of an ongoing arbitration (the “Arbitration”). Pertinent and significant points of the judgment •  A two-step inquiry applies to determine whether Art 5 of the UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration (“Art 5” and the “Model Law”) prohibits court intervention in a given case. At the first step, the court will consider whether the application for the court’s intervention concerns a “matter” governed by the Model Law. At the second step, the court is concerned with whether the intended intervention is permitted, either because the legislation does make express provision for such intervention, or, if the “matter” is not governed by the relevant legislation, then because the grant of relief is warranted: at [28] . •  In applying this two-step inquiry, it is critical to frame the relevant “matter” in broad rather than narrow terms. In this case, the appropriate level of abstraction for framing the “matter” should be one that encompasses challenges against a procedural determination which would affect the progress or conduct of an ongoing arbitration. It would be most exceptional that the court would countenance intervention in an ongoing arbitration by seeking to second-guess a procedural determination, absent express empowerment to do so under the Model Law or International Arbitration Act 1994 (2020 Rev Ed) (the “IAA”): at [ 37] and [ 43] . Facts 1 The respondent entered into five contracts for the sale of oil products to the appellant (the “Five Contracts”), each of which provided for arbitration under the auspices of the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (respectively the “SIAC” and the “Five Arbitration Clauses”). 2 On 24 June 2024, the respondent filed a notice of arbitration (the “NOA”) against the appellant to seek repayment of sums that were allegedly due under the Five Contracts, by various dates on or before 1 July 2018. The NOA was thus filed just a week before the respondent’s claims might have become time-barred on 1 July 2024. 3 After confirming with the respondent on 3 July 2024 that it was relying on all Five Arbitration Clauses, the Registrar of the SIAC (the “Registrar”) issued a decision stating that the arbitration (the “Arbitration”) was deemed to have commenced on 3 July 2024 (the “Initial Decision”). 4 In its response to the NOA, the appellant argued that the respondent’s claims were time-barred, given that the Arbitration was deemed to have commenced several days after 1 July 2024 (see [3] above). The next day, the respondent wrote to the SIAC to request that the commencement date of the arbitration be amended to 24 June 2024, ie , the date on which the NOA was filed (see [3] above), and the appellant wrote to the SIAC to object to this request. 5 Having heard from both parties, the Registrar issued a letter to the parties stating that he had considered the parties’ submissions and was satisfied that the date of commencement of the Arbitration should be amended to 24 June 2024 (the “Amended Decision”). 6 Dissatisfied with the Amended Decision, the appellant filed an application in the GDHC seeking a declaration that (a) the Amended Decision was unlawful on various grounds; and (b) the commencement date of the Arbitration was 3 July 2024. The appellant also sought an order setting aside the Amended Decision (the “Main Application”). 7 At the time that the Main Application was filed, the respondent was subject to insolvency proceedings in the Hong Kong court. The appellant thus filed an application for permission to proceed with the Main Application against the respondent pursuant to s 133(1) of the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act 2018 (2020 Rev Ed) (the “Permission Application”). 8 The Judge dismissed the Permission Application on grounds that the Main Application was legally unsustainable. Pertinently, the Judge found that the GDHC did not have the power to review the Amended Decision, because r 40.2 of the SIAC Rules stated that the parties waived any right of appeal or review in respect of any decision by the SIAC Registrar to any judicial authority. In any event, the Judge was of the view that the Registrar was plainly entitled to issue the Amended Decision; and there was no merit to the submissions made in the Main Application. Decision on appeal Prohibition of court intervention in an ongoing arbitration under Art 5 of the Model Law The two-step interpretation of Art 5 9 Article 5 of the Model Law prescribes that “[i]n matters governed by this Law, no court shall intervene except where so provided in this Law”. In other words, in matters governed by the Model Law, the court must not act in any way to impede or alter the progress or conduct of a pending arbitration, save to the extent that express provision is made in either the Model Law or the implementing legislation (in our case, the International Arbitration Act 1994 (2020 Rev Ed) (the “IAA”)) that permits this. This applies both at the pre-award and post-award stage: at [25] –[26] . 10 To determine whether Art 5 applies to circumscribe the court’s power in a particular case, a two-step inquiry applies. At the first step, the court will consider whether the application for the court’s intervention concerns a “matter” governed by the Model Law. At the second step, the court is concerned with whether the intended intervention is permitted, either because the legislation does make express provision for such intervention, or, if the “matter” is not governed by the relevant legislation, then because the grant of relief is warranted: at [28] . 11 The court adopted this two-step interpretation of Art 5 for three reasons: a. First, Art 5 is itself limited by the opening words “[i]n matters governed by this Law”, which makes clear that Art 5 does not apply to every instance where court intervention is sought in a matter that may be connected to an arbitration governed by the Model Law: at [29] . b. Second, the ancillary material covering the discussions that led to the adoption of the Model Law demonstrates that there would be certain types of intervention that fell outside the scope of the Model Law: at [30] . c. Third, previous jurisprudence of the court adopted a similar interpretation of Art 5. In LW Infrastructure Pte Ltd v Lim Chin San Contractors Pte Ltd [2013] 1 SLR 125, the court declined to grant a declaration that an arbitral award was a nullity, because that pertained to a matter, viz , the recognition and enforcement of awards, that was governed by the legislation in question: at [31] . The framing of a “matter” governed by the Model Law 12 It was critical to determine how the “matter” raised in the Main Application should be framed, as this would directly impact the applicability of Art 5: at [32] . In this regard, the appellant sought to circumvent the application of Art 5 by characterising the “matter” raised in the Main Application in narrow terms; as an application for judicial recourse against the decision of an arbitral institution , which it argued was not an issue governed by the Model Law or the IAA: at [27] . 13 The word “matters” in Art 5 should be construed more broadly rather than narrowly, as a result of the confluence of: a. the underlying purpose of Art 5 which is to provide the greatest degree of certainty by having the Model Law set out the circumstances in which court intervention is permissible as completely as possible; and b. the overall policy of the IAA and the Model Law which is to minimise judicial intervention in arbitral proceedings: at [35] –[36] . A broad interpretation of the word “matters” in Art 5 would further these two objectives as it would (a) widen the range of matters that are governed by the Model Law; (b) limit the opportunities for a court to intervene; and (c) in this way, advance certainty as to when the court may intervene. In line with this, when determining what is governed by the Model Law, the inquiry extends to both the express and the implied reach of the legislation: at [37] –[38] . 14 Applying this broad interpretation, the appropriate level of abstraction for framing the “matter” in this case should be one that encompasses challenges against a procedural determination which would affect the progress or conduct of an ongoing arbitration. It would be most exceptional that the court would countenance intervention in an ongoing arbitration by seeking to second-guess a procedural determination, absent express empowerment to do so under the Model law or IAA: at [43] . 15 This broad framing of the “matter” is entirely in line with the nature of arbitration, which is a mode of dispute resolution that is rooted in the agreement of the parties, and which places a high degree of procedural autonomy in the hands of the parties and their chosen arbitrators. The obligation of the parties in this respect should be understood as one to arbitrate in accordance with their agreed rules; and absent agreement on any given point of procedure, the obligation is to arbitrate in accordance with the procedural determinations of the tribunal. Once this is understood, it becomes apparent why Mitsui Engineering & Shipbuilding Co Ltd v Easton Graham Rush and another [2004] 2 SLR(R) 14 , Republic of India v Vedanta Resources plc [2021] 2 SLR 354 , and the present case were all decided in the way that they were. In each of these cases, a procedural issue affecting the progress and conduct of the arbitration was determined, and there was no basis for the court to second-guess that determination or intervene in any other way: at [44] –[46] . 16 Specifically, in the present case, the Registrar made a decision on the commencement date of the Arbitration, as he was empowered to do under the SIAC Rules. While it is true that the Registrar was not part of the tribunal charged with deciding the substantive dispute between the parties, that had nothing to do with the procedural nature of his decision, or with the court’s lack of power to intervene at this stage. Where the rules, which the parties have agreed to, provide that certain decisions may be made by a particular decision-maker, that is as much a part of the agreement of the parties as to how their arbitration is to be conducted; and hence, as much a part of the process that is beyond the intervention of the court at this stage of the proceedings. Given the absence of an express enabling provision to support the appellant’s Main Application, there was simply no room for the court to intervene in the Registrar’s determination of the commencement date of the arbitration: at [47] –[48] . Waiver of the right of appeal under r 40.2 of the SIAC Rules 17 Pursuant to r 40.2 of the SIAC Rules, the parties agree to “waive any right of appeal or review in respect of any decisions of the President, the Court and the Registrar to any State court or other judicial authority” “save in respect of Rule 16.1 and Rule 28.1”. As the Amended Decision did not fall within either of the prescribed exceptions, r 40.2 posed an additional bar to the Main and Permission Applications: at [52] –[53] . 18 Rule 40.2 of the SIAC Rules was not an unenforceable ouster clause as it did not completely exclude all recourse to the court’s jurisdiction. While r 40.2 might preclude the parties from seeking a direct review of decisions rendered by various organs of the SIAC, it certainly does not preclude the parties from taking the position that the tribunal had wrongly accepted or incorporated such a decision into the final award, and on this basis, that the award should be set aside : at [57] . Observations on r 40.1 of the SIAC Rules 19 Rule 40.1 of the SIAC Rules states that decisions of the Registrar shall be “conclusive and binding on the parties and the Tribunal”. It was evident to that much energy was expended on the Main and Permission Applications because the appellant was concerned that, by application of r 40.1, the Amended Decision would bind the Tribunal in respect of an issue that was material to its time-bar defence. However, the question of whether it was possible and appropriate to review the Amended Decision should have been raised to the Tribunal rather than to the court: at [58] –[61] . 20 The CA dismissed the appeal and awarded indemnity costs in favour of the respondent: at [ 62] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.

court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 12 November 2025 Case summary Singapore International Commercial Court – Originating Application No 10 of 2024 (Summons No 1133 of 2024) DKB v DKC [202 5] SGHC(I) 26 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Judgment of the Singapore International Commercial Court (delivered by International Judge Thomas Bathurst): Outcome: The SICC declined to order that questions as to the ownership of the claimant be determined separately on a preliminary basis as the proposed questions were based on assumptions rather than admitted facts. Background 1 The Claimant sought to enforce an arbitral award (the “Award”) against the Defendant in Singapore. The Claimant obtained leave to do so, and the Defendant sought in HC/SUM 1133/2024 (“SUM 1133”) to set aside the order granting leave. 2 The basis for SUM 1133 was that: (a) one Mr [H] is subject to sanctions imposed by the US and other countries; (b) the Claimant is allegedly owned and controlled by Mr [H]; (c) allowing the Claimant to enforce the Award against the Defendant in Singapore would result in the Defendant violating those sanctions; and (d) therefore, allowing the enforcement of the Award would be contrary to Singapore public policy. 3 The Claimant suggested three separate questions which were intended to avoid the necessity of a factual inquiry into whether the Claimant was owned and controlled by Mr [H]. Broadly, these questions concerned whether, assuming that the Claimant was subject to the relevant sanctions, (a) enforcement of the Award or any judgment entered in its terms would amount to breaches of those sanctions; (b) s 29 of the International Arbitration Act 1994 (2020 Rev Ed) (“IAA”) read with s 19 of the IAA permits the enforcement of a foreign arbitral award by entry of a judgment in Singapore dollars notwithstanding that the currency of the award is expressed in United States dollars (“USD”); and (c) whether the debt under the Award could be satisfied by the Defendant in USD without breaching sanctions in any event. Prior to a Case Management Conference, the Claimant requested for these questions to be determined separately from the hearing or trial, pursuant to O 16 r 11 of the Singapore International Commercial Court Rules 2021 (2020 Rev Ed). The court’s decision 4 On 12 November 2025, the Court rejected the Claimant’s request. 5 First, any answers to the proposed questions would be based on assumptions rather than facts found or admitted: [7] . 6 Second, the underlying facts were uncertain and there was a degree of novelty in the questions of law involved: [7] . 7 Third, it was uncertain as to whether the proposed questions, even if answered in favour of the Claimant, would lead to finality of the litigation: [8] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court.
