court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 11 November 2025 Case summary [Neo Tiam Ting v Singapore Vehicle Traders Association [ 2025] SGHC(A) 23 Civil Appeal No 96 of 2024] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Appellate Division of the High Court (delivered by Justice See Kee Oon): Outcome: The Appellate Division of the High Court dismisses the appeal against the decision of a Judge of the High Court to grant a declaration sought by the Singapore Vehicle Traders Association, declaring that the election of candidates for the Association’s 27th Term Executive Committee held on 6 June 2024 had no legal effect and was therefore null and void. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment • In the absence of an explicit article in an unincorporated association’s constitution permitting or authorising a meeting’s presiding officer to unilaterally adjourn a meeting without the consent of the majority of attendees, no such power exists simply by virtue of the presiding officer’s role. The narrow exception would be when exigent circumstances enable the residual common law power to be invoked. • To show that it was impossible for a presiding officer to ascertain the wishes of the meeting, it would be insufficient to show that there were risks in proceeding with a vote on adjournment. Generally, the presiding officer would need to show that there were practical or physical restrictions which made it impossible for those present to participate in any debate or discussion or to vote on an adjournment. • The appeal was dismissed as the appellant was unable to show that exigent circumstances existed such that he was entitled to adjourn the Singapore Vehicle Traders Association’s 51st Annual General Meeting, during the meeting held in May 2024. It followed that he could not reconvene the aforementioned meeting in June 2024, and thus any election conducted during that meeting was invalid. 1 This was an appeal by Mr Neo Tiam Ting (“Mr Neo”) against the decision of a Judge of the High Court (the “Judge”) to grant a declaration sought by the Singapore Vehicle Traders Association (the “SVTA”). The declaration stated that the alleged election of the SVTA’s Executive Committee (the “Exco”) for its 27th Term of office during a meeting on 6 June 2024 was not held in accordance with the SVTA’s constitution (the “Constitution”), and was null and void. 2 The declaration did not affect Mr Neo’s election as the President for the SVTA’s 26th term of office. He was re-elected, unopposed, as its President for its 27th term of office. The material facts 3 On 27 February 2024, the SVTA’s Exco holding office for the SVTA’s 26th term (the “26th Term Exco”) commenced arrangements for the 51st Annual General Meeting (the “51st AGM”). These arrangements included the formation of a subcommittee called the Elections Committee (“EC”) and the appointment of its members to oversee the SVTA’s upcoming election of a President and 20 members to form the Exco for the 27th term of office (the “27th Term Exco”). 4 On 4 April 2024, the 26th Term Exco gave notice to the SVTA’s members that the 51st AGM would be held at 4.30pm on 6 May 2024. The key issues on the agenda were the election of the 27th term President and the 27th Term Exco. This notice stipulated that proxies ( ie , any representative who is not a partner or director of the member firm or company that appointed them) would be prohibited from voting on behalf of a firm or company and that each member cannot represent more than one vote (“the narrow view”). Conversely, Mr Neo argued that the representative can be any person, regardless of whether that person is a partner or a director of the member, and that the representative should be allowed to vote on behalf of more than one member (“the wide view”). 5 On 6 May 2024, the 51st AGM took place (the “May Meeting”). At this meeting, Mr Neo maintained that the wide view should apply, whilst the EC took the opposing view. The issue of which view to adopt was put to a vote, upon which a majority of those present voted in favour of applying the narrow view. The EC then invited members to begin voting on the basis of the narrow view. Mr Neo opposed this and tried to declare an adjournment of the 51st AGM and the election twice. The EC disregarded his attempts and directed members to continue to vote, prompting Mr Neo to leave the meeting premises. The voting for this election (the “May Election”) concluded soon thereafter, with the 19 candidates who had received the most votes forming the 27th Term Exco (the “May Exco”). 6 On 7 May 2024, the EC informed the SVTA’s members that the May Exco had been elected as the 27th Term Exco. In response, Mr Neo informed members that the results of the May Election were void and stated that he would be reconvening the 51st AGM to resolve uncompleted items on the agenda, namely the proposed amendments to the Constitution and the election of the 27th Term Exco. On 6 June 2024, Mr Neo purported to reconvene the 51st AGM. Mr Neo conducted a vote with the members present in accordance with the wide view (the “June Election”). Mr Neo then informed members and the Registry of Societies that the SVTA’s 27th Term Exco had been duly elected at the June Meeting (the “June Exco”). 7 On 25 June 2024, the law firm of Messrs R. S. Solomon LLC (“RSS”) was instructed by the May Exco to commence HC/OA 611/2024 (“OA 611”) seeking a declaration that the purported election of the June Exco was not properly held and that the results of the election be declared null and void. On 17 July 2024, Mr Neo applied to strike out OA 611 in its entirety. On 16 August 2024, an Assistant Registrar heard and dismissed Mr Neo’s striking out application. Dissatisfied with the Assistant Registrar’s decision, Mr Neo appealed in HC/RA 159/2024 (“RA 159”) against that decision. On 1 November 2024, the Judge dismissed RA 159. The Judge heard substantive arguments in relation to OA 611 on 21 and 25 November 2024. On 25 November, the Judge delivered his decision on OA 611 and granted the declaration sought by the SVTA. 8 The Judge determined that the wide view ought to be preferred and consequently found that Neo had correctly exercised his power to adjourn the 51st AGM at the May Meeting. It followed that the events which took place at the May Meeting after Mr Neo’s departure, ie , the May Election, ha d no legal effect and the results of the May Election were thus null and void. That said, although Mr Neo had validly adjourned the 51st AGM during the May Meeting, he had no power to reconvene the 51st AGM after the May Meeting had ended. The Judge thus granted the declaration sought in OA 611 and ordered Mr Neo to bear the costs of OA 611 fixed at $13,000. This included the costs of RA 159, which the Judge had reserved to the hearing of OA 611. Disbursements were to be agreed or fixed by the court, but this remained unresolved at the date of the hearing of this appeal. 9 In light of the foregoing, the court identified the following issues for determination on appeal: (a) whether the Judge was right to find that the May election was null and void; (b) whether Mr Neo had the power to adjourn the 51st AGM at the May Meeting, and had validly exercised that power; and (c) whether Mr Neo lacked the power to reconvene the 51st AGM after he had adjourned the 51st AGM. Decision The validity of the May Election 10 On appeal, it was common ground between Mr Neo and the SVTA that the wide view was in line with the Constitution and was the correct approach. Accordingly, the May Election was invalid as it was conducted in accordance with the narrow view, in breach of the Constitution. This engaged the related preliminary point on whether the SVTA was properly authorised to instruct RSS to act in OA 611: [27] . 11 It was incongruous for the Judge to remark that the validity of the May Election was “an intermediate issue that [he] must consider in dealing with the Association’s sole substantive prayer for relief”, and yet state that his determination on its validity was simply an “intermediate finding” that “does not, in itself, lead to the grant of any final relief” and it “will be for any future court … to determine the effect of [his] finding”. The ordinary principles of res judicata applied to the Judge’s finding on the May Election , as such a finding was a necessary precursor to his determination on the declaration sought by the SVTA: [28] . 12 On the facts, it was undisputed that a majority of the May Exco, which authorised the appointment of RSS, also formed part of the 26th Term Exco. Article 21(i) of the Constitution provided that “[t]he outgoing Executive Committee shall not relinquish its duties until the Executive Committee-elect have taken office”. In light of the court’s determination that both the May Election and June Election were invalid, this meant that a 27th Term Exco had not been properly elected. As such, pursuant to Art 21(i) of the Constitution, the 26th Term Exco, as the outgoing Exco, had not relinquished its duties. Given the significant overlap between the members of the 26th Term Exco and the May Exco, the fact that the resolution was ultimately passed by the May Exco suggested that it would have been similarly passed by the 26th Term Exco (as the body with the requisite authority). Thus, RSS was validly authorised to commence OA 611 on behalf of SVTA and possessed the required standing to represent the SVTA in the present proceedings: [ 32]–[34] . Mr Neo’s exercise of his power to adjourn the May Meeting 13 It is well established that in the absence of an authorising rule or statute, the chairperson of a meeting ( ie , the individual presiding over the meeting ) has no power to unilaterally adjourn a meeting without the consent of the majority of the attendees. The only exception to this rule is that under certain circumstances, the chairperson of a meeting has a common law power to adjourn on an exceptional and residual basis. Here, it was undisputed that there was no specific rule in the Constitution which empowered Mr Neo to unilaterally adjourn the May Meeting. The key question was whether Mr Neo was able to show that, as the presiding officer of the 51st AGM, he was entitled to avail himself of the residual common law power to adjourn a meeting: [37] –[38] . 14 The court disagreed with the Judge’s finding that Mr Neo’s common law power to adjourn arose in the present case. It was not impossible for Mr Neo to ascertain the wishes of those present at the May Meeting. First, the Judge appeared to have presumed the outcome of a potential vote on a resolution to adjourn. It was possible that had a vote on a resolution to adjourn actually taken place, the same result might have been obtained regardless of whether the wide view or narrow view was taken. Second, and more importantly, even if the vote on an adjournment proceeded on the basis of the “incorrect” narrow view, it did not follow that the wishes of those at the meeting could not be ascertained. If the meeting’s wishes can be ascertained through a vote, and even if the vote may have wrongly infringed on certain members’ voting rights, if the members do not consent to an adjournment, the meeting must proceed, even though there may be risks of whatever nature in proceeding: [39], [43]–[44] . 15 No practical or physical restrictions existed in the present case which made it impossible for those present at the May Meeting to participate in any debate or discussion or vote on an adjournment. This clearly showed that it was possible for Mr Neo to have sought a resolution to adjourn the 51st AGM: [45]–[46] . . 16 Accordingly, Mr Neo should have put the question of adjourning the May Meeting to a vote. If the members voted, based on the narrow view, not to adjourn and proceeded to elect the 27th Term Exco, Mr Neo could have then sought a court order or declaration that that election was invalid on the basis that the votes ought to have been cast in accordance with the wide view. However, he elected to take the unilateral step to adjourn the 51st AGM: [51] . Mr Neo’s power to reconvene the May Meeting 17 The court made provisional observations on the Judge’s determination that Mr Neo lacked the power to reconvene the 51st AGM after the May Meeting. It was arguably permissible for Mr Neo to adjourn the May Meeting without stipulating the date for when the reconvened meeting would be held. This would have been akin to an adjournment indefinitely. Mr Neo would need to simply issue a subsequent notice advising members of the SVTA on the date and place of the reconvened meeting. That said, it was arguable that only the Honorary Secretary, and not Mr Neo, had the power to fix the date to reconvene the 51st AGM via such a subsequent notice: [53] –[56] . Costs and observations 18 The court was of the view that the parties had maintained an overly narrow focus on the validity of the June Election and the appointment of the June Exco, and thereby failed to address other crucial issues before the Judge, such as the validity of the May Election. This was despite clear prompting by the Judge to put all of the issues before him. The court noted the parties’ agreement that the wide view should be adopted and that the Judge’s finding that the May Meeting was invalid was binding. It was also only revealed during the course of the hearing of the appeal that there were subsequent attempts to conduct fresh elections in light of the aforementioned consensus, though it appeared that such attempts were unsuccessful: [57] –[59] . 19 The court thus took the position that the parties’ respective responsibility for the present state of affairs be borne out in appropriate costs orders. Given the unsatisfactory manner in which this case was managed by the parties, and their respective actions which contributed to the ongoing impasse, each party was ordered to bear their own costs and disbursements, both in the proceedings below and on appeal: [ 60]–[61] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.

court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 5 November 2025 Case summary XLK v XLJ [2025] SGHC(A) 22 Appellate Division of the High Court — Originating Application No 33 of 2025 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Appellate Division of the High Court (delivered by Debbie Ong Siew Ling JAD): Outcome: the court dismissed the applicant-father’s application for permission to appeal against the decision of a Judge in the Family Division of the High Court (the “Judge”) which affirmed the Family Court’s order granting custody, and care and control of the parties’ child to the respondent-mother. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment • There was no merit to the father’s argument that the Judge failed to apply the welfare principle. The Judge had considered that the crucial point was that it would be in the best interests of the child to be with his mother. He had considered various factors including those which pointed to the family’s apparent lack of connection to Singapore and the absence of any secure basis for the child’s parents to remain in Singapore in the longer term, which would have a negative impact on the long-term stability of the child: at [ 23 ] . • The Judge was not correct in saying that the appeal could be dismissed on the basis of comity alone. The court must instead apply the welfare principle as the paramount consideration in cross-border custody disputes which are not brought under the International Child Abduction Act 2010 (2020 Rev Ed) (the “ICAA”). However, this error had no impact on the outcome of the appeal because the Judge had in fact considered the welfare of the child in coming to his decision, and thus permission to appeal was not granted: at [ 31 ], [ 3 4 ] and [ 37 ]. 1 This was an application for permission to appeal against the decision of the Judge which affirmed the Family Court’s order granting custody, and care and control of the parties’ child to the respondent. Background to the application 2 The applicant (“Father”) and respondent (“Mother”) were married in the People’s Republic of China (“China”) in March 2016. Both were Chinese citizens who did not have any long-term immigration status in Singapore. They had a son (the “Child”) who was born in January 2019. He was also a Chinese citizen and had spent almost the first five years of his young life in China. Prior to the breakdown of the marriage, the family resided in China. 3 On 28 February 2023, the Mother filed for divorce in China. A court in China granted a divorce and ordered that the Child “shall be raised and educated” by the Mother. The Father filed an appeal in China, but this appeal was dismissed on 23 November 2023. 4 Subsequently, on 11 December 2023, the Father brought the Child to Singapore and enrolled him in an international school here. Although he claimed to have moved to Singapore with the Child, he did not have any long-term immigration status to reside in Singapore. The Mother later commenced proceedings in Singapore, seeking an order for sole custody, and care and control of the Child, and for the Father to take all required steps to hand over the Child and the Child’s passport to her. 5 A district judge in the Family Court (the “DJ”) granted sole custody, and care and control of the Child, to the Mother. The Father’s appeal against the DJ’s decision was dismissed by the Judge. 6 The Father filed the present application for permission to appeal against the Judge’s decision, on the following grounds: a. the Judge made a prima facie error of law when he failed to apply the welfare principle in coming to his decision and instead treated international comity and the label of “child abduction” as decisive factors. b. to address a question of general principle, namely, “whether, and to what extent, considerations of comity may override and/or displace a full welfare inquiry under s 3 of the GIA in cross-border custody disputes”. Decision No prima facie error 7 The Judge did not dismiss the appeal on the sole basis of comity but instead considered various factors which pointed to the family’s apparent lack of connection to Singapore and the absence of any secure basis for the Child’s parents to remain here in the longer term, which would have a negative impact on the long-term stability of the Child: at [ 23 ]. 8 There was no merit to the argument that the Judge failed to properly consider the various factors affecting the Child’s welfare, such as his integration in Singapore, schooling and stability. The DJ had already undertaken a comprehensive analysis of the relevant factors, including the factors raised by the Father, and determined that it would be in the best interests of the Child for him to be with his mother. The Judge agreed with the DJ and concluded that these factors were insufficient to overcome the significant countervailing factors weighing against the Father in the present case: at [ 27 ] –[ 29 ] . 9 The fact that the Judge did not obtain a welfare report or conduct a child interview also did not disclose any error of law. It could not be said that the DJ or the Judge exercised their discretion wrongly: at [ 30 ]. The relevance of the doctrine of comity of nations 10 The Judge was not correct in saying that the appeal could be dismissed on the basis of comity alone. The court must instead apply the welfare principle as the paramount consideration in cross-border custody disputes which are not brought under the ICAA. However, this error had no impact on the outcome of the appeal because the Judge had in fact considered the welfare of the Child in coming to his decision, and thus permission to appeal was not granted: at [ 31 ] , [ 34 ] and [ 37 ] . 11 That said, in appropriate circumstances, the court may, pursuant to the welfare principle, order the immediate return of a child to a foreign jurisdiction without conducting a full investigation of the merits. For instance, if a child habitually resident in a foreign jurisdiction is unilaterally brought to this country where he is unaccustomed to its language, culture and contacts, a court may find that it is in the child’s best interests to ensure his swift and immediate return to minimise the disruption in his circumstances. In doing so, the court gives due consideration to the foreign court orders and the fact that the child was removed from his habitual residence because these have material bearing on the welfare of the child and not because of the interests of comity: at [ 35 ]. No question of law of importance 12 There were no questions of general importance which would justify granting permission to appeal in the present case. It was clear that considerations of comity did not override the welfare principle in guardianship and custody applications outside of proceedings under the ICAA. As for the weight to be accorded to foreign court orders in the analysis of what would be in the interests of a child, this was not a question of law but instead involved a fact-sensitive value judgment: at [ 39 ] –[ 40 ]. This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 31 October 2025 Case summary Sun Weiyeh v Public Prosecutor [2025] SGHC 216 Magistrate’s Appeal No. 9126 of 2024 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the General Division of the High Court comprising Tay Yong Kwang JCA: Outcome: the court dismissed the appellant’s appeal against his conviction and sentence in respect of two charges under s 201( b ) of the Securities and Futures Act (Cap 289, 2006 Rev Ed) (“SFA”) , for engaging in acts in connection with the sale of securities which were likely to operate as a fraud. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment • Section 201( b ) of the SFA is a catch-all provision intended to cover a wide range of securities fraud. One of the key legislative objectives is the protection of investors : at [ 39 ], [ 40 ] and [ 61(a) ] . • While there would inevitably be overlap between the “fraud” and “deception” limbs of s 201( b ), the scope of “fraud” was not confined exclusively to cases also involving “deception”. Given that s 201( b ) was intended to be broad in scope, “fraud” in this context can take many forms : at [ 41 ], [ 42 ], [ 46 ] and [ 61(b) ]. • Where a person (A) is placed in a position where A is expected to safeguard, or not to act against, the financial interests of another person (B), the abuse of such a position which results in detriment to the financial interests of B would fall within the types of acts envisaged in s 201( b ) of the SFA: at [ 47 ] and [ 61(c) ]. • There is no requirement that the offender must have a specific intent to deceive, manipulate or defraud for an offence under s 201( b ) of the SFA to be made out. The touchstone of fraud is dishonesty and an offence would be made out upon proof that the offender acted with an objectively dishonest state of mind: at [ 60 ] and [ 61(d) ]. 1 This was an appeal against the decision of a District Judge (the “DJ”), who found the appellant guilty of two charges under s 201( b ) of the SFA for engaging in acts in connection with the sale of securities which were likely to operate as a fraud. Background to the appeal 2 The appellant was a portfolio manager at One Asia Investment Partners (“OAIP”), which in turn managed several investment funds. Two of these funds were material to the appeal, namely SP1 and SP5. 3 Stafford Capital Ltd (“Stafford”) invested US$10m in SP1 on 14 October 2014 and was the majority shareholder of SP1 (owning 86.85% of the fund) at the material time. SP1 held various bonds, including 2.5m units of MIE18, 1.5m units of MIE19, and 3m units of INDIKA23. 4 Sometime in December 2015, Stafford’s representative informed the appellant of Stafford’s intention to redeem its investment in SP1 because the fund was not performing well. Pursuant to a redemption notice, Stafford’s shares in SP1 were to be redeemed on 1 February 2016 based on the net asset value of the fund on 29 January 2016. Owing to the size of Stafford’s investment in SP1, the majority of SP1’s assets (including the MIE bonds) had to be sold to meet Stafford’s redemption request. Some of SP1’s positions were sold on 4 and 15 January 2016, including 1m units of INDIKA23. 5 On 18 January 2016, the appellant reached out to his contacts at Goldman Sachs to ask for indicative bid prices for 1m units each of MIE18 and of MIE19. Goldman Sachs responded with an offer of US$34 for MIE18 and US$31 for MIE19. The appellant did not accept this offer. Later that day, the appellant invested US$3m in SP5, thereby owning a majority share (94.1%) of the fund. 6 At around 10am the next day, on 19 January 2016, the appellant sent a mass message to at least 11 counterparties, using the Bloomberg chat terminal, seeking bids for the entire block of MIE18, MIE19 and INDIKA23 bonds held by SP1. He received bids from four separate counterparties in the hour that followed. These were as follows: a. Morgan Stanley Asia (“Morgan Stanley”), bidding US$33/unit for 2.5m units of MIE18 and US$32/unit for 1.5m units of MIE19. b. Haitong International Securities (Singapore) Pte Ltd (“Haitong”), bidding US$25/unit for 2.5m units of MIE18 and US$20/unit for 1.5m units of MIE19. c. BNP Paribas (“BNP”), bidding US$34/unit for MIE18, US$31.50/unit for MIE19 and US$36/unit for INDIKA23. d. SC Lowy Financial (“SC Lowy”), bidding US$28.50/unit for 1.5m units of MIE19. 7 The appellant did not accept any of these bids. Instead, from around 10.30am, he began communicating with Mr Reshad Sabed (“Mr Reshad”) of Pareto Securities Pte Ltd (“Pareto”) to carry out a “pass through trade”. This involved the sale of MIE18 and MIE19 (collectively, the “MIE bonds”) from SP1 to SP5 through Pareto as intermediary. The following trades took place as a result of the pass through trade: a. SP1 sold to Pareto: 2.5m units of MIE18 at a price of US$25.375/unit; and 1.5m units of MIE19 at a price of US$21.875/unit. b. Pareto sold to SP5: 2.5m units of MIE18 at a price of US$25.50/unit; and 1.5m units of MIE19 at a price of US$22/unit. 8 The remainder of SP1’s assets were sold between 20 and 25 January 2016 in order to fulfil Stafford’s redemption and to effect the liquidation of SP1. Stafford’s redemption was confirmed on 5 February 2016, with a redemption amount of US$6.5m. 9 The two charges against the appellant were brought on the basis that he had engaged in an act which was “likely to operate as a fraud” upon the investors of SP1, namely, by carrying out the pass through trade of the MIE bonds when he knew that there was an earlier bid for MIE18 and MIE19 at a price of US$33/unit and US$32/unit, respectively. The DJ convicted him on both charges and sentenced him to 6 months’ imprisonment on each charge, with both sentences running concurrently. The appellant appealed against his conviction and sentence. Decision The elements of s 201(b) of the SFA 10 Section 201( b ) of the SFA is a catch-all provision intended to cover a wide range of securities fraud. One of the key legislative objectives is the protection of investor s (at [ 39 ] , [ 40 ] and [ 61(a) ] ). 11 While there would inevitably be overlap between the “fraud” and “deception” limbs of s 201( b ), the scope of “fraud” was not confined exclusively to cases also involving “deception”. Given that s 201( b ) was intended to be broad in scope, “fraud” in this context can take many forms (at [ 41 ], [ 42 ] , [ 46 ] and [ 61(b) ] ). 12 Where a person (A) is placed in a position where A is expected to safeguard, or not to act against, the financial interests of another person (B), the abuse of such a position which results in detriment to the financial interests of B would fall within the types of acts envisaged in s 201( b ) of the SFA (at [ 47 ] and [ 61(c) ] ). 13 There is no requirement that the offender must have a specific intent to deceive, manipulate or defraud for an offence under s 201( b ) of the SFA to be made out. The touchstone of fraud is dishonesty and an offence would be made out upon proof that the offender acted with an objectively dishonest state of mind (at [ 60 ] and [ 61(d) ]). The convictions were upheld 14 The appellant accepted that he had a duty to act honestly. It would be futile to argue that such duty did not exist. As the portfolio manager of SP1, the appellant was working in a position in which he was dealing with assets which belonged to the investors. He had therefore assumed a position where he was expected to deal with those assets honestly and was also expected not to act against the financial interests of the investors of SP1 (at [ 62 ]) . 15 The appellant was aware of Ms Goyal’s interest in the MIE bonds at the latest by 10.15am. That was when he sought clarification on whether Ms Goyal’s bids were for the entire block of MIE bonds which he was selling. It was hard to believe his claim that he did not see Ms Goyal’s affirmative response which was sent a mere 13 seconds after he sought clarification. This message was posted on the same chatroom where the appellant had asked Ms Goyal to repost her bids. He would surely have been monitoring this chatroom with keen interest (at [ 68 ]). 16 The evidence showed that the appellant acted dishonestly. The appellant was aware that Morgan Stanley had expressed a keen interest in the MIE bonds, yet he did not follow up with Ms Goyal on her bids. He instead gave a false reason to Ms Goyal to explain why he did not sell the MIE bonds to her. He eventually sold the MIE bonds to himself using the Haitong bid prices as market context because he was clearly aware of their high potential value. Viewed in totality, the irresistible inference to be drawn was that the appellant’s conduct was calculated to enrich himself at the expense of the investors of SP1 (at [ 71 ] to [ 75 ]) . 17 The appellant was conducting price discovery not for the honest purpose of obtaining the best price for SP1 but for the dishonest purpose of obtaining the lowest possible price at which he could sell the MIE bonds to himself without attracting allegations of undervalue sales. This was made even clearer from the fact that he received higher bids from two other counterparties at the material time (at [ 76 ] to [ 79 ]). 18 The appellant’s contention that he thought that Pareto would conduct independent price discovery was not supported by the evidence (at [ 80 ]). The sentences were upheld 19 There were various aggravating factors in the present case. In particular, the offences were committed for personal gain; the investors of SP1 were at the appellant’s mercy; the offences were hard to detect; and there was a degree of premeditation involved (at [ 84 ]). 20 The custodial threshold was crossed. A review of the relevant precedent cases showed that cases involving an abuse of position, coupled with other aggravating factors, would generally warrant the imposition of a custodial sentence. The imprisonment terms for cases which involved an abuse of a position of fidelity tended to range from four to six months for each charge (at [ 85 ] , [ 87 ] and [ 89 ] ). 21 The appellant also failed to demonstrate any remorse for his actions. He continued to maintain his innocence at the trial and on appeal despite being unable to provide any reason to justify his actions. He also made no offer of restitution to the investors of SP1 despite having made profits exceeding US$1m when he eventually sold the MIE bonds to the market. The circumstances of this case clearly justified the aggregate sentence of six months’ imprisonment imposed by the DJ (at [ 90 ]). This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.

court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 16 October 2025 Case summary POP Holdings Pte Ltd v Teo Ban Lim and others [2025] SGCA 51 Court of Appeal – Originating Application No 13 of 2025 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Court of Appeal (delivered by Justice Steven Chong): Outcome: The Court of Appeal dismissed an application for permission to appeal against a decision of the Appellate Division of the High Court. For different reasons, the Court agreed with the Appellate Division’s ultimate conclusion that the applicant had failed to prove its loss and was thus only entitled to nominal damages. The Court clarified (a) the importance of a claimant seeking an award of damages establishing its loss by pleading and proving the position it would have been in but for the defendant’s wrongdoing; and (b) the circumstances in which it would be appropriate to assess damages as at the date of the transaction in a case of deceit inducing the claimant’s entry into a transaction to acquire property. Pertinent and significant points of the grounds of decision • The purpose of an award of damages for a private law wrong was to put the claimant, as far as money could do it, in the same position that it would have been in had the wrong not been committed. In practice, this called for a comparison between two positions: (a) the position that the claimant was currently in as a result of the defendant’s breach or wrongdoing (the “breach position”); and (b) the position that the claimant would have been in if the defendant’s breach or wrongdoing had not occurred (the “non-breach position”). The difference between these two positions constituted the claimant’s loss: at [28] . • In a case where the claimant had been induced by the defendant’s deceit to enter into a transaction to purchase property, and the claimant’s non-breach position is that it would not have entered into the transaction, the date of the transaction would typically not be the appropriate date for assessment of damages as the causal influence of the defendant’s deceit on the claimant’s retention of the asset continued to subsist past that date. Instead, the relevant date would be the date when the claimant discovered the fraud, as it is on that date when the claimant is able to exercise a free choice to retain the asset, such that any losses incurred thereafter are caused by the claimant’s choice to retain the property rather than the defendant’s wrongdoing: at [57] –[65] . Background to the application 1 In 2015, the applicant, POP Holdings Pte Ltd (“POP”), entered into a sale and purchase agreement (“SPA”) to acquire 70% of the shares in RIC Dormitory (SG) Pte Ltd (“RIC Dormitory”), a company that owned a dormitory at 34 Kaki Bukit Place (“34KB”). The purchase price under the SPA was derived (in part) from a valuation of 34KB at $14m in 2014, based on 34KB having an accommodation capacity of 360 workers (the “2014 Valuation Report”). The true legally approved capacity of 34KB was, however, only for 130 workers. 2 In HC/S 27/2022, POP brought claims against the respondents seeking, among other things, damages for the tort of deceit. In essence, POP argued that it had been induced by false representations made by the respondents as to 34KB’s capacity to enter into the SPA. 3 At first instance, a Judicial Commissioner of the General Division of the High Court (the “Judge”) allowed POP’s claim in deceit and found that the respondents had indeed made false representations as to 34KB’s legally approved accommodation capacity to induce POP to enter into the SPA. 4 As for the damages to be awarded to POP, the Judge considered the applicable principles to be that (a) POP was entitled to damages assessed as the difference between the price POP had paid for 34KB and the real value of 34KB (the “Valuation Method”); and (b) damages were to be assessed at the date of the transaction unless there was some reason why damages should be assessed at a different date (the “Transaction Date Rule”). The Judge held that, in a case of deceit inducing the claimant to enter into a transaction, the Transaction Date Rule should be departed from if the claimant could not have discovered the falsity of the representations made to it. In this case, POP only discovered the truth in April or November 2018. 5 Applying these principles, the Judge awarded POP damages in the sum of $3.5m. This figure represented 70% of the difference between (a) the component of the purchase price under the SPA made up by the value of 34KB ( ie , $14m) ; and (b) the value of 34KB in April or November 2018 when POP discovered the fraud ( ie , $9m). 6 Subsequently, the respondents appealed to the Appellate Division of the High Court (the “Appellate Division”) on the issue of damages. The Appellate Division allowed the appeal. Although the Appellate Division agreed with the Judge that damages should be assessed based on the Valuation Method, it held that the Judge was wrong to disapply the Transaction Date Rule based on POP having only discovered the falsity of the representations after the date of the transaction as this would render the Transaction Date Rule otiose in cases of deceit. Applying the Transaction Date Rule, the Appellate Division found that POP had failed to prove its loss as there was no evidence of the value of 34KB at the date of the transaction in 2015. The Judge’s award of damages was thus set aside and substituted with an award of nominal damages. 7 In this application, POP sought permission to appeal against the Appellate Division’s decision on the ground that the Appellate Division had erred in law in its understanding of the Transaction Date Rule. The Court of Appeal’s decision The Valuation Method and the Transaction Date Rule were irrelevant 8 The purpose of an award of damages for a private law wrong was to put the claimant, as far as money could do it, in the same position that it would have been in had the wrong not been committed. In practice, this called for a comparison between two positions: (a) the position that the claimant was currently in as a result of the defendant’s breach or wrongdoing (the “breach position”); and (b) the position that the claimant would have been in if the defendant’s breach or wrongdoing had not occurred (the “non-breach position”). The difference between these two positions constituted the claimant’s loss: at [28] . 9 POP had initially pleaded three non-breach positions: (a) first, that it would not have purchased any shareholding in RIC Dormitory (“the No Transaction Counterfactual”); (b) second, that it would have acquired less shares in RIC Dormitory than the 70% stake that it did (the “Less Shares Counterfactual”); and (c) third, that it would have acquired the same 70% shareholding in RIC Dormitory that it did, albeit at a lower price than what it paid (the “Lower Price Counterfactual”). But at the trial before the Judge, POP did not lead any evidence to prove any of these non-breach positions, and simply elected to compute its claim for damages based on the Lower Price Counterfactual. This was unsatisfactory as a non-breach position was a factual premise of a claim that not only had to be pleaded but proven by evidence. It was questionable if POP had even proved its non-breach position and, in turn, the fact of loss: at [29] –[34] 10 The Valuation Method was irrelevant to POP’s claim for damages based on the Lower Price Counterfactual. The Valuation Method gave form to the logic that, to extricate the claimant from the transaction and to restore it to a non-breach position of the status quo ante the transaction, the damages awarded would be the difference between what the claimant paid and the value of the benefits it received from the transaction. It would have thus been applicable if POP had claimed damages based on the No Transaction Counterfactual. But in a claim founded on the Lower Price Counterfactual, POP would have entered into the same transaction and acquired the same shares in RIC Dormitory save for paying a lower price. The loss that POP had suffered under the Lower Price Counterfactual was the difference between the price it paid under the SPA and the lower price that it would have paid if the respondents’ misrepresentations as to the capacity of 34KB had not been made: at [37] –[42] . 11 The Transaction Date Rule was similarly irrelevant to POP’s claim for damages based on the Lower Price Counterfactual. As the Valuation Method assessed the claimant’s loss by setting off the benefits received by the claimant under the transaction from the price paid, its adoption required the selection of a date for valuing the said benefits, and for this purpose, the Transaction Date Rule was a default rule. If the Valuation Method was not applicable, the Transaction Date Rule would also not relevant: at [44] . 12 As the Valuation Method and Transaction Date Rule were irrelevant, any error in the Appellate Division’s approach to the Transaction Date Rule was academic and did not provide a basis for POP to be given permission to appeal. The application was accordingly dismissed on this basis: at [45] . POP had failed to prove its loss 13 There was no reasonable prospect that POP could have succeeded in establishing the quantum of its loss under the Lower Price Counterfactual based on the evidence before the court. The purchase price under the SPA was based on a valuation of 34KB undertaken in 2014 in the 2014 Valuation Report. The 2014 Valuation Report valued 34KB based on it having a capacity of 360 workers. Assuming that the parties would have agreed to transact at a lower price if the misrepresentations as to 34KB’s capacity had not been made, the parties would have agreed to a purchase price based on a valuation of 34KB in 2014 based on its actual capacity of 130 workers. POP’s loss under the Lower Price Counterfactual was thus the difference between the price it had paid and this lower purchase price that the parties would have agreed to. To prove the quantum of this loss, POP would have had to establish the value of 34KB in 2014. However, there was no evidence before the court of this and POP accordingly failed to prove the quantum of its loss: at [47 ] . The proper understanding of the Transaction Date Rule 14 Based on a principled understanding of the Transaction Date Rule, it would generally be disapplied in cases of deceit where the claimant only discovered the fraud at a time after the transaction. The Appellate Division was incorrect to doubt this conclusion on the basis that the Transaction Date Rule would be rendered otiose in deceit claims: at [57] , [58] and [65] . 15 If the claimant could exercise a free choice to hold on to the acquired asset at the date of the transaction and thereby extricate itself from the consequences of the defendant’s wrongdoing at that date, the Transaction Date Rule would be applicable as the date of the transaction would be an appropriate cut-off point for the defendant’s liability for the claimant’s losses as subsequent losses after the date of the transaction was not caused by the defendant’s wrongdoing but the claimant’s free choice to retain the property. But if the claimant was unable to exercise a free choice to retain the asset at the date of the transaction because it continued to labour under the misimpression created by the defendant’s wrong, the Transaction Date Rule would not apply as the causal influence of the defendant’s wrong on the claimant’s retention of the asset continued to subsist past that date, and it was thus fair for the defendant to remain liable for the claimant’s losses: at [ 59]–[60] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s judgment. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s judgment.

case_name: PUBLIC PROSECUTOR v Mark Kalaivanan s/o Tamilarasan
subject_tags: ["Criminal Procedure and Sentencing — Sentencing — Principles — Discretion to impose imprisonment in lieu of caning"]
court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 13 October 2025 Case summary Public Prosecutor v Mark Kalaivanan s/o Tamilarasan [2025] SGCA 48 Criminal Appeal No. 21 of 2024 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Court of Appeal (delivered by Tay Yong Kwang JCA): Outcome: the Court of Appeal dismissed the Prosecution’s appeal for an additional imprisonment term of six months to be imposed in place of caning. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment • The court did not have the power to impose an additional term of imprisonment in place of caning where an offender who is sentenced to preventive detention (“PD”) and caning cannot be caned for any of the reasons provided by law: at [ 29 ] . • Even if additional imprisonment could be imposed in place of caning for PD cases, such additional imprisonment cannot result in the PD effectively exceeding the statutory maximum of 20 years: at [ 33 ] . • In any event, even if the court had the power to impose additional imprisonment in place of caning, it was not necessary to do so on the facts of this appeal: at [ 45 ] . 1 This was an appeal against the decision of a Judge of the High Court (the “Judge”), who declined to impose an additional term of imprisonment in place of caning on the respondent. Background to the appeal 2 The respondent was convicted of a charge of aggravated sexual assault by penetration and three other related charges. He was originally sentenced to preventive detention (“PD”) for 18 years and to the mandatory minimum of 12 strokes of the cane. The PD was not backdated but took effect on the date of sentence on 7 August 2023. 3 The respondent appealed against his sentence. On 9 September 2024, the Court of Appeal varied the sentence by increasing the PD from 18 years to the maximum 20 years. However, the Court of Appeal also backdated the PD to commence from the date of arrest on 15 July 2017. The sentence of 12 strokes of the cane was upheld. 4 After the appeal, it transpired that the respondent had been certified to be medically unfit for caning before the appeal was heard. Pursuant to s 332 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cap 68, 2012 Rev Ed) (“CPC”), a further hearing was fixed before the Judge for him to decide whether to remit the caning fully or to impose a term of imprisonment in place of the caning. 5 At the further hearing, the Prosecution asked that an additional imprisonment term of six months be imposed by the court in place of the caning. The Judge declined to do so. Instead, he remitted the sentence of caning in full. The Prosecution appealed against this decision. Decision 6 The court did not have the power to impose an additional term of imprisonment in place of caning where an offender who is sentenced to PD and caning cannot be caned for any of the reasons provided by law. Section 304(2) of the CPC provides that PD is “in lieu of any sentence of imprisonment”, which makes it clear that all sentences of imprisonment would be subsumed in a sentence of PD (at [ 29 ]) . 7 Although s 332(2)( b ) of the CPC provided that imprisonment in lieu of caning may be “in addition to any other punishment”, this power was constrained by “any other written law”. Section 304(2) constrained the meaning of the words “any other punishment” in s 332(2)( b ) by excluding additional imprisonment in place of caning for an offender who is sentenced to undergo PD (at [ 30 ]) . 8 Rule 31(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Corrective Training and Preventive Detention) Regulations 2010 provides that all sentences of imprisonment imposed at a subsequent trial shall run concurrently with the remainder of a PD sentence originally imposed. If a person’s imprisonment for subsequent offences must be concurrent with his existing PD, it seemed logical that any additional imprisonment term in place of caning arising from the charges which were the subject of the PD should also count as part of the PD period (at [ 31 ]) . 9 As a practical observation, it seemed odd that an offender who may be released on licence would thereafter be required to serve imprisonment upon the completion of PD. (at [ 32 ]). 10 Even if additional imprisonment could be imposed in place of caning for PD cases, such additional imprisonment cannot result in the PD effectively exceeding the statutory maximum of 20 years. Section 332(3) of the CPC only permitted the court to impose an additional imprisonment term which would exceed the maximum term of imprisonment prescribed for an offence. It did not authorise the same for the maximum term of PD (at [ 3 3 ], [ 3 7 ] and [ 39] ). 11 In any event, the additional six months’ imprisonment sought by the Prosecution would not have a significant retributive or deterrent effect on the respondent. This was because the sentence of 20 years’ PD was a lengthy one and was sufficiently retributive and deterrent. Accordingly, even if the court had the power to impose an additional term of imprisonment in place of caning, it was unnecessary on the facts in this appeal (at [ 4 2 ] and [ 4 5 ]). This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.
