case_name: Soh Chee Wen v PUBLIC PROSECUTOR
subject_tags: ["Criminal Law — Appeal", "Criminal Law — Statutory offences — Penal Code", "Criminal Law — Statutory offences — Securities and Futures Act"]
court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 10 October 2025 Case summary Soh Chee Wen and another v Public Prosecutor [2025 ] SGCA 49 Criminal Appeal s No. 40 & 41 of 2022 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Court of Appeal (delivered by Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon): Outcome: In Soh Chee Wen and another v Public Prosecutor [2025] SGCA 49, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appellants' appeals against their conviction. In the main, this was because the appellants had failed to demonstrate any error in the trial judge's findings of fact. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment • A high threshold must be met before findings of fact will be overturned on appeal. Whenever a factual finding is challenged on appeal, it is incumbent on the appellant to identify precisely where the trial judge is said to have erred and to demonstrate that the high threshold for appellate intervention has indeed been crossed: at [1] and [64] –[65] . • Criminal liability under s 120B of the Penal Code (Cap 224, Rev Ed 2008) (the “Penal Code”) is predicated upon a person being a party to a criminal conspiracy and not by the specific act of entering into that criminal conspiracy. It necessarily follows that the offence under s 120B continues for such time as the offender remains a party to the criminal conspiracy: at [17] –[18] . • The required particulars in a charge concern facts giving rise to criminal liability and not those affecting punishment: at [34] –[36] . • Section 120B of the Penal Code (which is the punishment provision for a criminal conspiracy offence) provides that an offender will be punished “as if” he had abetted the offence. The applicable punishment for the abetment of an offence, in turn, is set out in various other provisions in the Penal Code and the choice of the applicable provision depends on what the Prosecution is able to establish: at [46] . • Where accused persons are alleged to have agreed to commit multiple offences, they could have entered into an overarching agreement to commit all the offences , as well as separate additional agreements to commit each of the offences. In this scenario, the Prosecution has the discretion to determine how broadly or narrowly it wishes to frame the charge(s) for criminal conspiracy. It might choose to bring a single charge in relation to the overarching agreement, or it may bring separate charges in relation to each separate agreement to commit each offence: at [217] –[218] . • The court upheld the Appellants’ convictions on 153 charges of being a party to conspiracies to engage in manipulative or deceptive devices in connection with the subscription, purchase, or sale of securities under s 201( b ) of the Securities and Futures Act (Cap 289, 2006 Rev Ed) . It was no defence for the Appellants to show that the persons authorised to operate the relevant accounts were aware of the Appellants’ involvement because those persons were not the victims of the aforementioned deceptive practices. Rather the financial institutions were the victims of the deception. It was also no defence for the Appellants to show that the trading representatives of the deceived financial institutions, were aware of their involvement since the former’s knowledge could not be attributed to the latter: at [232] –[243] . • The court upheld the Appellants’ convictions on six charges of being a party to conspiracies to commit the offences of cheating and dishonestly inducing property to be delivered, under s 420 of the Penal Code. The court did not accept the premise that the Appellants were guilty only of omitting to disclose certain facts. The Appellants had held out the securities as collateral for margin financing . This could only have been understood as a positive representation that these securities were legitimate collateral for the facilities they were to secure: at [ 244]–[247] . Background 1 Mr Soh Chee Wen (the “First Appellant”) and Ms Quah Su-Ling (the “Second Appellant”) (collectively, the “Appellants”) were jointly tried in the General Division of the High Court for various offences arising out of an alleged scheme to manipulate the markets for and prices of three counters that were being traded on the Mainboard of the Singapore Exchange (“SGX”), namely Blumont Group Limited (“Blumont”), Asiasons Capital Ltd (“Asiasons”) and LionGold Corp Ltd (“LionGold”) (collectively, “BAL”). It was the Prosecution’s case that, between 1 August 2012 and 3 October 2013 (the “Relevant Period”), the Appellants masterminded a scheme to artificially inflate the markets for, and so manipulate the prices of, BAL shares (the “Scheme”). The Appellants were alleged to have carried out the Scheme by controlling, coordinating their use of, obtaining financing for, and conducting illegitimate trading activity using an extensive web of 189 trading accounts (the “Relevant Accounts”) held with 20 financial institutions (“FIs”) in the names of 60 individuals and companies (the “Relevant Accountholders”). 2 The Judge convicted the Appellants of: a. Ten charges of being a party to conspiracies to commit offences under s 197(1)( b ) of the Securities and Futures Act (Cap 289, 2006 Rev Ed) (the “SFA”), which prohibited “ [f]alse trading and market rigging transactions”. Six of these ten charges concerned the markets for BAL shares (the “False Trading Charges”) while the remaining four concerned the prices of BAL shares (the “Price Manipulation Charges”). b. 153 charges of being a party to conspiracies to commit offences under s 201(b) of the SFA, which prohibited the use of manipulative or deceptive devices in connection with the subscription, purchase or sale of securities (the “Deception Charges”). c. Six charges of being a party to conspiracies to commit the offences of cheating and dishonestly inducing property to be delivered, under s 420 of the Penal Code (the “Cheating Charges”). These 169 charges will be referred to collectively as the “Conspiracy Charges”. 3 The Judge also convicted the First Appellant of: a. Three charges of being concerned in the management of Blumont, Asiasons and LionGold while being an undischarged bankrupt, contrary to s 148(1) of the Companies Act (Cap 50, 2006 Rev Ed) (the “Company Management Charges”). b. Five charges of perverting the course of justice contrary to s 204A of the Penal Code, and a further three charges of attempting to pervert the course of justice contrary to s 204A read with s 511 of the Penal Code (collectively, the “Witness Tampering Charges”). 4 The Judge sentenced the First Appellant to an aggregate of 36 years’ imprisonment and the Second Appellant to an aggregate of 20 years’ imprisonment. 5 CA/CCA 40/2022 and CA/CCA 41/2022 (collectively, “the Appeals”) were the respective appeals of the First and Second Appellants against their convictions and sentences. The Appellants challenged their convictions and sentences in their entirety, save that the First Appellant did not challenge his convictions or the related individual sentences for the Company Management Charges. 6 Given the scale of the materials and the nature of the issues before the court, the court decided to hear the Appeals over three tranches, dealing respectively with the following broad heads of issues: (a) preliminary issues raised by the Appellants; (b) substantive issues relating to the Appellants’ convictions; and (c) if the appellants’ convictions were affirmed in whole or in part, issues relating to their sentences. The first two tranches of the hearing having now been concluded, the court dismissed the Appellants’ appeals against their convictions. Decision Whether the Conspiracy Charges were legally defective Whether the Conspiracy Charges were sufficiently particularised 7 The Conspiracy Charges were adequately particularised. The charges did not have to specify when or where the Appellants were said to have entered into each conspiracy as criminal liability under s 120B of the Penal Code was predicated upon a person being a party to a criminal conspiracy and not the specific act of entering into that conspiracy. Furthermore, the Prosecution’s case for some of the Deception Charges was that the criminal conspiracies which formed the subject of those charges crystallised on or about the account opening date. In any event, the omission to state the circumstances under which the conspiracies were entered into could not have been said to have misled or prejudiced the Appellants: [ 16]–[24]. 8 The mere fact that the Conspiracy Charges did not specify the precise trades or transactions that the Appellants had purportedly conducted in furtherance of each conspiracy did not render those charges defective. All that was required to establish criminal liability under s 120B of the Penal Code was an agreement between the Appellants to commit an offence. There was no need for them to have taken steps to carry out that arrangement. Furthermore, the Conspiracy Charges contained sufficient particulars that would have allowed the Appellants to understand the nature of the allegations levelled against them. It was not necessary for the Conspiracy Charges to particularise the specific manner in which the underlying offences in the Conspiracy Charges were purportedly completed or the specific transactions that were carried out as a result; it was sufficient for the Conspiracy Charges to assert that the underlying offences were completed: at [25] –[37] . 9 The time periods stated in the Conspiracy Charges were not overly broad. They did not purport to state a range of dates on which the Appellants carried out the underlying offences. Instead, they alleged that the conspiracies subsisted throughout the range of dates as stated in the charges: at [39] . Whether the Conspiracy Charges were duplicitous 10 It was permissible for the Conspiracy Charges to refer both to ss 120 and 109 of the Penal Code, and for the Appellants to be so charged. Section 120B of the Penal Code requires that a criminal conspirator be punished “as if” he is an abettor. Sections 109 and 116 of the Penal Code provide for different penalties depending on whether the abetted offence is committed as a consequence or not. The plain language of s 120B of the Penal Code provides that the punishment to be imposed on a criminal conspirator would similarly depend on whether the substantive offence underlying the conspiracy had actually been committed. Such a view is not only supported by the plain language of the statute but also finds support in the case law. Therefore, it was entirely acceptable for an individual, charged for criminal conspiracy, to be punished under s 109 of the Penal Code: [42] –[47]. 11 In any event, the framing of the Conspiracy Charges did not cause the Appellants to be misled as to the case against them, nor were they prejudiced. The purpose of a charge is to ensure that an accused person knows the offence of which they are accused and thus be able to meet the case against them. The Second Appellant could not claim that she was unable to know the case that she had to meet as a result of how the Conspiracy Charges were framed. It would have been clear to the Second Appellant, from the words of the Conspiracy Charges, that she was being charged with being a party to a criminal conspiracy and punished as if she abetted an offence that was committed. Moreover, there was even a letter from the court to the Second Appellant explaining as much. Even assuming there was anything legally impermissible in the framing of the charges – the court could have simply rectified it, under s 390(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (2020 Rev Ed), and there would be no prejudice to the Appellants: [48] –[55]. The allegation of bias 12 Finally, it was wholly improper for the Second Appellants’ counsel , Mr Sivananthan Nithyanantham (“Mr Sivananthan”), to raise baseless allegations of bias against the Judge. Mr Sivananthan alleged that the Prosecution had only ever intended to prove, in relation to the Conspiracy Charges, that the Appellants were parties to the alleged criminal conspiracies and that the Prosecution did not originally intend to also show that they committed the substantive offences underlying those criminal offences until the Judge prompted the Prosecution to reconsider its position in this respect. Mr Sivananthan initially accused the Judge of actual bias, apparent bias and excessive inference, then withdrew those allegations before inexplicably repeating his allegations. These allegations of bias were premised on a clear and blatant mischaracterisation of the proceedings before the Judge, as it is clear from the record that the Prosecution always took the position that the underlying offences were committed in furtherance of the conspiracy, and the Judge only sought to make that position clear in the charges. It was wholly unsatisfactory and improper for Mr Sivananthan to make the allegations that he did: [56] –[62] . Review of the Judge’s main findings of fact 13 In factually intensive cases that involved appeals on points of fact, like the present, an appellate court would generally be slow to overturn the trial judge’s findings of fact, especially where they hinged on the trial judge’s assessment of the credibility and veracity of witnesses, unless they could be shown to be plainly wrong or against the weight of the evidence. The factual findings of a trial judge would not lightly be disturbed in the absence of good reasons: [64] –[65]. 14 The thrust of the First Appellant’s case on appeal was that the bulk of the trading activity in the Relevant Accounts during the Relevant Period was conducted by a group of individuals acting on their own or collectively, but not at the Appellants’ behest or with their knowledge. These individuals were Mr Dick Gwee (“Mr Gwee”), Mr Ken Tai (“Mr Tai”), Mr Henry Tjoa (“Mr Tjoa”) and Mr Gabriel Gan (“Mr Gan”), who belonged to a group which the parties and the Judge referred to as the “Manhattan House Group” (“MHG”), as well as one Mr Leroy Lau (“Mr Lau”). These individuals allegedly operated as a separate entity beyond the control of the Appellants and had conducted their trades without the Appellants’ knowledge or consent . In support of his case, the First Appellant focused largely on attacking the Judge’s treatment of the oral evidence of the members of the MHG and Mr Lau and, in particular, her assessment of their credibility and the inferences that she drew from their evidence. In sum, he submitted that the Judge ought not to have accepted or relied upon the evidence of these individuals. The First Appellant also challenged the Judge’s reliance on certain pieces of objective evidence: [66] –[68] . 15 The Judge was cognisant of the fact that a key aspect of the Appellants’ case at trial was that the trading activity in all of the Relevant Accounts had been conducted without their knowledge or involvement and that their primary strategy was to challenge the cogency and credibility of the evidence of the alleged rogue traders who testified on behalf of the Prosecution. She thus took an assiduous approach in reviewing the evidence before her in order to determine which of the 189 Relevant Accounts were controlled by the Appellant. The Judge first categorised the Relevant Accounts into four main categories, and she further subdivided the accounts based on the identity of either the TR or the Relevant Accountholder associated with those accounts. In analysing each of these sub-groups, the Judge broadly adopted the following approach: (a) first, she reviewed the testimony of various witnesses regarding the role they played in the Scheme, having regard to factors that weighed upon the reliability of their evidence; (b) second, she considered the available corroborating evidence which supported the witnesses’ evidence; and (c) third, she evaluated the combined weight of the witnesses’ testimony and corroborating evidence against the Appellants’ counter-narrative and determined which of the two she ultimately found to be the true version of events. While the Judge relied upon certain pieces of objective evidence in her analysis and found them to be highly probative, she remained cognisant of their limitations and certainly did not regard them as being conclusive of the Appellants’ guilt. Instead, she relied on them chiefly for their corroborative value. It was only upon a careful and holistic consideration of various interlocking strands of evidence that the Judge came to a conclusion as to whether the Appellants had been in control of each of the Relevant Accounts: [70] –[83]. 16 The Appellants failed to show that the Judge was plainly wrong in her analysis of the available evidence or that the findings she made were clearly against the weight of the evidence. As such, the threshold for appellate intervention in relation to the Judge’s factual findings was not met: [85] and [193]–[194]. 17 As regards the First Appellant’s contentions regarding the witness testimonies, he failed to show that the Judge was plainly wrong in her analysis of the available evidence or that the findings she made were clearly against the weight of the evidence. Many of the purported inconsistencies raised by the Appellant were either not actually inconsistencies when properly understood or material inconsistencies. Where there were material inconsistencies, the Judge rightly evaluated the witnesses’ explanations for these inconsistencies in deciding not to impeach their credibility. The First Appellant also largely failed to engage with the other strands of evidence, in particular the objective evidence that further bolstered the Judge’s decision: [86] –[119]. 18 Turning to the available objective evidence, the Judge relied on various incriminating communications (typically text messages and e-mails) between the Appellants and others involved in the Scheme, which clearly showed that the Appellants conveyed trading instructions to the various TRs and Relevant Accountholders. Before the Judge, and even on appeal, no satisfactory explanation was proffered by either Appellant for such incriminating correspondence. The Judge further took into account other pieces of evidence (such as the analysis done by the Government Technology Agency and expert evidence). Although such evidence had limitations of its own, the Judge remained cognisant of these limitations and relied on them for their corroborative value. She did not regard them as being dispositive of the Appellants’ guilt: [120] –[164]. 19 Finally, the court considered the various witnesses’ testimonies in tandem with the corroborating pieces of evidence and weighed that against the Appellants’ counter-narrative to determine whether the Judge’s decision to prefer the former was plainly wrong or against the weight of the evidence. Ultimately, on a holistic consideration of the various trading activities as well as the testimonies of the MHG and Mr Lau, it was clear that there was no basis to interfere with the Judge’s decision to reject the Appellants’ claims that the MHG and Mr Lau were rogue traders acting beyond the Appellants’ instructions and knowledge: [164] –[192]. Framing of the Conspiracy Charges 20 The overarching Scheme to manipulate the markets for and prices of the BAL shares during the Relevant Period did not form the subject of any specific charge. Instead, the Prosecution’s case was that the overarching scheme only formed the factual background to the Conspiracy Charges and that the Conspiracy Charges were concerned with narrower aspects of the Scheme. On the Prosecution’s case, the overarching Scheme co-existed alongside multiple other conspiracies in furtherance of the Scheme. Those other conspiracies, rather than the Scheme, were the subject of the Conspiracy Charges: at [208] . 21 Where accused persons were alleged to have agreed to commit multiple offences, the nature of their agreement(s) might fall into three possible categories: (a) they may have entered into multiple separate agreements to commit each of the offences; (b) they may have entered into a single agreement to commit all the offences; or (c) they could have entered into an overarching agreement to commit all the offences as well as separate additional agreements to commit each of the offences. The precise nature of the accused persons’ agreement(s) was a question of fact, which was to be determined in all the circumstances of the case. In the first scenario, the Prosecution could only proceed with separate charges for criminal conspiracy. In the second scenario, the court was of the tentative view that the Prosecution could ordinarily only bring a single charge in relation to the single agreement to commit all the offences. In the third scenario, the Prosecution had the discretion to determine how broadly or narrowly it wished to frame the charge(s) for criminal conspiracy: at [217] –[218] . 22 The Prosecution could bring separate charges for the Deception, Cheating and Price Manipulation Charges as its case was that each charge related to a separate and distinct conspiracy: at [220] . 23 The Prosecution could not be faulted for having categorised the False Trading Charges according to each of the relevant BAL counters. It was not the Appellants’ case that there was only a single agreement to undertake all of the conduct involving all three BAL counters. Furthermore, in the absence of specific evidence to the contrary, it logically followed that each False Trading Charge which related to a different BAL counter related to an agreement to carry out a distinct offence and was thus capable of forming the subject of a separate charge: at [222] . 24 Even where the False Trading Charges concerned the same BAL counters, they related to different offences under s 197(1)( b ) of the SFA by virtue of the different time periods prescribed in the charges. Material amendments had been made to this provision, which had come into effect on 18 March 2023. As such, even if the Appellants had a single conspiracy to create a false or misleading appearance as to the market for the shares of a single company, this conspiracy would have concerned two distinct offences under s 197(1)( b ) of the SFA . Such offences were distinct in so far as they comprised separate elements. Thus, on the facts of the case , t he Prosecution was entitled to bring separate charges in relation to the pre-amendment and post-amendment versions of s 197(1)( b ) of the SFA . Where there was a relevant change in the law, the consideration of whether there was an agreement to commit an act punishable under the SFA had to be assessed independently and it could not be the case that it would necessarily constitute one and the same offence of conspiracy. Further, to mandate that a single charge be brought would likely create confusion in the mind of the Appellants as to the case they had to meet, given that the pre-amendment and post-amendment versions of s 197(1)( b ) of the SFA had different mens rea requirements : at [223] –[224] . 25 The Appellants’ reliance on certain Indian cases which were cited in Ratanlal & Dhirajlal’s the Indian Penal Code vol 1 (Anjana Prakash Ed) (LexisNexis, 35th Ed, 2021) did not assist them. Those cases were concerned with the opposite scenario, where the accused persons alleged that a single s 120B charge was defective because it related to multiple distinct conspiracies. Furthermore, those cases were merely concerned with whether it was permissible for the Prosecution to prefer a single conspiracy charge : at [225] . 26 The Judge did not assume the existence of the individual conspiracies from the existence of the overarching Scheme. Instead, she cautioned herself against doing so before finding that the individual conspiracies were established. For instance, the Judge was alive to the Prosecution’s burden to separately establish the individual conspiracies underlying the False Trading Charges and Deception Charges and carefully considered the factual nuances specific to each of the individual conspiracies: at [226] –[230] . The proceeded categories of charges The Witness Tampering Charges 27 The First Appellant’s alleged acts went well beyond a discussion of potential lines of defence. On the Prosecution’s case, the First Appellant had caused or attempted to cause Mr Tai, Mr Gan, Mr Wong Xue Yu (“Mr XY Wong”) and Mr Peter Chen Hing Woon (“Mr Chen”) to lie to the investigating authorities. This would clearly have amounted to an offence regardless of whether the witness in question was a Prosecution witness or a potential co-accused person: at [196] . 28 The Judge had carefully considered the meaning of the First Appellant’s statements in context before concluding that, properly understood, they amounted to requests to conceal the truth from the investigating authorities. The court saw no reason to depart from her conclusions as to the proper meaning, when read in context, of the First Appellant’s communications with the various witnesses: at [197] –[199] . 29 The court did not see any circularity in the Judge’s reasoning. The Judge did not generally rely on the Witness Tampering Charges to explain why she accepted the evidence of Mr Tai, Mr Gan, Mr XY Wong and Mr Chen in relation to the Conspiracy Charges. Rather, the Judge saw the primary relevance of the Witness Tampering Charges to the Conspiracy Charges as being that the Witness Tampering Charges all involved various attempts by the First Appellant to minimise the Appellants’ involvement in the Scheme and/or to redirect suspicion to other persons. This raised the question of why the First Appellant had thought such conduct to be necessary if the Appellants were truly innocent of the Conspiracy Charges: at [201] . 30 The court therefore affirmed the First Appellant’s convictions on the Witness Tampering Charges: at [205] . The False Trading and Price Manipulation Charges 31 There was no reason for the court to disturb the Appellants’ convictions on the False Trading and Price Manipulation Charges. This was because the Appellants’ arguments revolved around the Judge’s factual findings, and these arguments had been rejected in the preceding portions of the judgment: at [231] . The Deception Charges 32 The Deception Charges alleged that the Appellants were parties to a criminal conspiracy to engage in a practice which was likely to operate as a deception upon various FIs, in connection with the purchase or sale of shares in BAL. The practice in question was the concealment of the Appellants’ involvement in the orders and trades of the BAL shares. The Judge ultimately convicted the Appellants of 153 of the 161 charges brought by the Prosecution and found that the underlying offence of deception was committed in respect of all 153 charges. To refute the Judge’s findings, the First Appellant raised two arguments on appeal to show why there was no deception: first, the Appellants had been permitted by the Relevant Accountholders to use their accounts; and second, the TRs of the relevant FIs were aware of the Appellants’ involvement. The court rejected both of these arguments: [232] –[233] and [243] 33 First, it was not a defence for the Appellants to show that they had relayed their instructions through the Relevant Accountholder or authorised person. The Deception Charges made clear that the victims of the deception were not the authorised persons but the FIs. It was therefore entirely irrelevant that the authorised persons may have been aware of or permitted the Appellants’ use of their accounts. Representatives of the FIs also gave evidence that even if the individual giving instructions was the accountholder or an authorised representative, concerns would remain about the possibility of third parties engaging in nominee trading or other illicit trading activities. Second, the fact that TRs were aware was immaterial since the TRs’ knowledge could not be attributed to their respective FIs. The TRs, by accepting instructions from the Appellants without proper formal authorisation, and in breach of the Singapore Exchange Securities Trading Limited Rules, had clearly acted beyond the scope of their actual and ostensible authority. The individuals seeking to rely on the principles of Attribution were also not innocent third parties but rather individuals who were complicit in the breaches of duty by those agents. Hence, no principle of attribution could apply such that the TRs’ awareness of the Appellants’ involvement could be attributed to the FIs: [234] –[242] . The Cheating Charges 34 The First Appellant’s primary submission on appeal was that an omission could only amount to deception if certain conditions were satisfied. However, the court did not accept the premise that the Appellants were guilty only of omitting to disclose certain facts to Goldman Sachs International (“Goldman Sachs”) and Interactive Brokers LLC (“IB”). The Appellants had held out the BAL securities to Goldman Sachs and IB as collateral for margin financing . This could only have been understood as a positive representation that these BAL securities were legitimate collateral for the facilities they were to secure: at [245] –[248] . 35 The First Appellant also submitted that even if the Appellants had practised a deception on Goldman Sachs and IB, those FIs could not be said to have been deceived or induced to provide margin financing because they had conducted their due diligence and had satisfied themselves that all desired conditions were met before extending financing. However, the Judge had accepted the evidence of Goldman Sachs and IB through their representatives that they would not have provided margin financing to the Relevant Accounts had they known that BAL shares were the subject of manipulative trading practices. It was entirely irrelevant that without such deception and on an entirely different set of factual premises, Goldman Sachs and IB might have arrived at such a decision: at [249] –[250] . 36 The court therefore upheld the Appellants’ convictions on the Cheating Charges: at [251] . Further arguments and some observations specific to the Second Appellant 37 The Judge was entitled to reject the Second Appellant’s explanation for her election not to give evidence. She was also entitled to draw an adverse inference from that election where the facts were such as to call for an explanation from the Second Appellant. In doing so, the Judge adopted a careful approach, which the court saw no basis to fault: at [259] . 38 No objection was taken during the proceedings below to the joint trial of the Witness Tampering Charges. On the contrary, the Second Appellant’s counsel had expressly confirmed at the commencement of the proceedings below that the Second Appellant had no objection to a joint trial with the First Appellant, which would necessarily have entailed a joint trial of the Witness Tampering Charges. It was much too late for the Second Appellant to raise this issue now: at [262] . 39 The Judge was entitled to draw inferences against both Appellants from the Witness Tampering Charges. Although the Witness Tampering Charges were brought against the First Appellant alone, it was significant that he had also attempted to minimise the Second Appellant’s involvement in the Scheme: at [264] . 40 Mr Sivananthan eventually informed the court that the Second Appellant was “not arguing against the actus reus of whatever took place ”. However, the obvious difficulty with such an argument was that the Second Appellant had elected not to give evidence during the trial below. She was therefore in no position to offer an alternative explanation for the objective evidence which, to put it at its lowest, strongly pointed to the conclusion that she was possessed of the requisite mens rea : at [266] –[268] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s judgment. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s judgment.

case_name: VIETNAM OIL AND GAS GROUP v JOINT STOCK COMPANY (POWER MACHINES – ZTL, LMZ, ELECTROSILA ENERGOMACHEXPORT)
subject_tags: ["Arbitration — Award — Remission", "Arbitration — Award — Recourse against award — Setting aside"]
court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 10 October 2025 Case summary Vietnam Oil and Gas Group v Joint Stock Company (Power Machines – ZTL, LMZ Electrosila Energomachexport) and another appeal [2025] SGCA 50 Court of Appeal – Civil Appeals Nos 48 and 49 of 2024 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Court of Appeal (delivered by Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon): Outcome: The Court of Appeal held that remission was not an appropriate remedy in respect of an arbitral award which was made in breach of the fair hearing rule. The Court therefore set aside the arbitral award and also set aside an order by the General Division of the High Court for certain matters to be remitted to the arbitral tribunal. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment • A request for remission under Art 34(4) of the UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration (“Model Law”) did not need to be made by way of a summons accompanied by supporting affidavit under the Rules of Court 2021 (“ROC 2021”): at [ 109] . • In deciding whether remission would be an appropriate remedy to cure certain defects in an arbitral award, a court would consider whether remittance was appropriate in all the circumstances, having regard to whether it was to address a defect capable of being rectified, as well as (a) whether the defect would cause the fair-minded observer to reasonably apprehend that the tribunal may not be able to afford the parties a fair process in its consideration on the remitted issue(s); (b) the centrality of the affected issue to the arbitral award; (c) the need for a party to amend its pleadings if remission was granted; and (d) any time and costs savings if the award were to be remitted: at [ 113]–[130] . Background 1 In or around 2013, Joint Stock Company (Power Machines – ZTL, LMZ, Electrosila Energomachexport) (“PM”) entered into a contract (the “EPC Contract”) with Vietnam Oil and Gas Group (“PVN”) to serve as a contractor to construct a thermal power plant in Vietnam (the “Project”). The EPC Contract included a contractual document (the “Conditions”), which provided that the EPC Contract was governed by Vietnamese law. The Conditions also contained an arbitration agreement providing that any dispute arising out of or in connection with the EPC Contract was to be referred to arbitration in Singapore. 2 Two sub-clauses of the Conditions provided for the parties’ rights of termination. Clause 19.6 of the Conditions permitted any party to the EPC Contract to terminate the contract if, among other things, execution of substantially all the works in progress was prevented for a continuous period of 84 days by reason of force majeure . Clause 16.2(b) permitted PM to terminate the EPC Contract if payments due were not received within 150 days of the contractually specified time. 3 The Project commenced in 2015. A few years later, in January 2018, PM was designated on the list of Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons by the United States Office of Foreign Assets Control (the “US Sanctions”). Consequently, many of PM’s subcontractors suspended the performance of their obligations under their subcontracts with PM. 4 PM and PVN subsequently engaged in negotiations on, among other things, the possibility of arranging direct payment between PVN and PM’s subcontractors, and on ways to arrange payments between PVN and PM without breaching the US Sanctions. Around the same time, PM made several applications for payments due under the EPC Contract. 5 Eventually, PM issued two notices of termination. On 28 January 2019, PM issued its first notice of termination of the EPC Contract pursuant to cl 19.6 of the Conditions, on the ground that the imposition of the US Sanctions constituted a force majeure event (the “First Notice”). The First Notice provided that the EPC Contract would terminate on 18 February 2019. 6 On 8 February 2019, PM issued a second notice of termination pursuant to cl 16.2(b) of the Conditions, on the ground that various payments had been outstanding for more than 150 days (the “Second Notice”) The Second Notice stated that the EPC Contract would terminate on 22 February 2019. 7 The parties referred their dispute to arbitration. PM’s primary case was that the EPC Contract was deemed to have been terminated on 18 February 2019 pursuant to cl 19.6 of the Conditions, by reason of force majeure . PM’s alternative case was that the EPC Contract was deemed to have been terminated on 22 February 2019 pursuant to cl 16.2(b) of the Conditions, by reason of PVN’s non-payment. A facet of PM’s alternative case was that, if the First Notice was found to be without legal basis, it would not in and of itself result in termination of the EPC Contract. Unless PVN exercised its corresponding right to terminate the EPC Contract for wrongful issuance of a termination notice, the EPC Contract would remain effective and instead be terminated by the Second Notice. 8 In November 2023, the arbitral tribunal (the “Tribunal”) issued an award (the “Final Award”). The Tribunal found that the First Notice was issued without basis as PM had failed to establish that the US Sanctions constituted a force majeure event. The Tribunal also found, in contrast to PM’s submission, that a notice of termination issued without basis was sufficient, without more, to terminate the contract. Therefore, the First Notice, without more, was sufficient to terminate the EPC Contract. 9 However, the Tribunal went on to hold at para 548 of the Final Award that the Second Notice, having been issued while the EPC Contract remained afoot, would override and supersede the ineffective First Notice. In the Tribunal’s view, by issuing a Second Notice prior to the First Notice taking effect, PM must be taken to have intended the Second Notice to replace or supplement the First Notice. The Tribunal further acknowledged at para 549 that the Vietnamese law experts had not specifically dealt with the present scenario involving an unlawful First Notice and a lawful Second Notice. 10 Dissatisfied with the Final Award, PVN applied to the General Division of the High Court to set aside the Final Award in HC/OA 346/2024 (“OA 346”), and also applied to set aside an order granting PM leave to enforce the Final Award in Singapore. The Judge held that the Tribunal’s reasoning at para 548 had no nexus to the parties’ cases. Accordingly, the Tribunal had breached the fair hearing rule and acted in excess of jurisdiction. However, instead of setting aside the Final Award, the Judge considered it appropriate to remit certain relevant matters to the Tribunal, to give the Tribunal an opportunity to eliminate the grounds for setting aside. 11 The Judge’s decision is the subject of cross-appeals in CA/CA 48/2024 (“CA 48”) brought by PVN and CA/CA 49/2024 (“CA 49”) brought by PM. In CA 49, PM asserts that the Judge erred in finding that the Tribunal acted in breach of the fair hearing rule and in excess of jurisdiction. In CA 48, PVN argues that PM had failed to make any valid request for remission as required under Art 34(4) of the Model Law and the ROC 2021, and that the Judge erred in ordering remission in any event. Decision Breach of natural justice 12 Paragraph 548 of the Final Award comprised separate findings of law and fact. As a matter of law, the Tribunal had found that a Second Notice issued while the EPC Contract remained on foot could override and supersede the invalid First Notice. As a matter of fact, the Tribunal found that PM must be taken to have intended the Second Notice to replace or supplement the First Notice when it issued the Second Notice prior to the First Notice taking effect: at [5 4] . 13 A party in PVN’s shoes could not reasonably have anticipated the Tribunal’s conclusion at para 548 of the Final Award. On the issue of law, it was neither party’s case that the Second Notice was capable of overriding or superseding the First Notice in such a scenario, and no reasonable party in PVN’s shoes would have foreseen the possibility of the Tribunal making that finding of law. On the issue of fact, PM had not led any evidence to show that it intended to replace or supplement the First Notice, and it instead expressly pleaded that the issuance of the Second Notice was not intended to withdraw the First Notice : at [ 55]–[65] . 14 The Tribunal’s failure to bring its contemplated chain of reasoning to the notice of the parties did cause prejudice to PVN. If PVN had been given notice, it would have been reasonable for it to have adduced relevant expert evidence and make submissions on the Tribunal’s view of the factual position pertaining to PM’s putative intention in issuing the Second Notice and this could have had a material impact on the outcome of the dispute: at [68]. 15 Accordingly, the Judge’s holding that there had been a breach of the fair hearing rule was affirmed: at [69] . Excess of jurisdiction 16 The Judge might have erred in holding that the Final Award offended Art 34(2)( a )(iii) of the Model Law due to the Tribunal’s departure from the parties’ cases. The issue of whether the Second Notice overrode, superseded, replaced or supplemented the First Notice was a logically anterior issue to the validity of the Second Notice, and was well within the scope of the parties’ submission to arbitration : at [ 76] . 17 A question remained as to whether the Tribunal exceeded its jurisdiction in reaching a conclusion that was diametrically opposite to the specific position taken by PM in its pleadings. The court’s provisional views were that while a tribunal has the ability to come to an independent conclusion or inference and is not bound to adopt either of the parties’ positions, the position may be different where one party takes a position in respect of a factual point concerning its own acts and the other party either accepts or does not dispute that factual position. However, given the findings on PVN’s complaint concerning the breach of natural justice, the Court declined to express a conclusive view on the issue: at [85] –[87] and [90]. Procedural requirements for a request for remission 18 Nothing in the ROC 2021 set down a mandatory requirement as to the form of a valid request for remission under Art 34(4) of the Model Law. Order 48 r 3 of the ROC 2021 specified certain applications or requests under the International Arbitration Act 1994 (2020 Rev Ed) (“IAA”) which had to be commenced by way of summons or an originating application, which did not include a request for remission under Art 34(4) of the Model Law. PVN’s proposed position would have denuded O 48 r 3 of its significance: at [ 98], [99] and [101] . 19 Order 9 r 9(8) and O 2 r 9(9) of the ROC 2021 did not impose a requirement that a party seeking to make a request for remission had to obtain the prior approval of the court to make an application for a remission order. Order 9 r 9 was intended to be invoked primarily in respect of trials pursuant to originating claims, rather than hearings pursuant to originating applications. Meanwhile, O 2 r 9 was part of an overview of how an originating claim or an originating application under Part 1 of the ROC 2021 proceeds, and O 2 r 1 expressly highlighted that an action need not proceed in precisely the same way as set out in O 2. Furthermore, if O 2 r 9 and O 9 r 9(7) were to be unthinkingly applied to all applications made under the IAA, that could result in the absurd outcome that a party seeking permission to enforce interim orders on an urgent and ex parte basis would need to write to court for approval to file the application: at [103]. 20 It did not make sense to require a party to pre-emptively file a summons for a remission order, when that same party would first be concerned with resisting the grounds of the setting aside application. Requests for remission were typically advanced as a fallback case: at [1 05] . Whether remission was an appropriate remedy 21 Remission of an award would only be appropriate when the identified defect in the arbitral process was capable of being cured. In assessing whether to order remission, the court would assess several factors including: (a) whether the defect would cause the fair-minded observer to reasonably apprehend that the tribunal might not be able to afford the parties a fair process in its consideration on the remitted issues; (b) the centrality of the affected issue to the arbitral award; (c) the need for a party to amend its pleadings if remission is granted; and (d) any time and costs savings if the award were to be remitted: at [ 111], [113], [125], [128] and [1 30]. 22 In assessing whether a fair-minded observer would continue to have confidence in the tribunal’s ability to afford the parties a fair process in its consideration on the remitted issue, exacting scrutiny would typically be applied where a tribunal had already come to a decision on an issue in breach of the chain of reasoning rule. A fair-minded observer might be concerned about the prospect of the tribunal being improperly influenced by the anchoring and confirmation biases if a matter was remitted to them for reconsideration. Much would turn on the significance and materiality of the breach: at [11 3]–[124] . 23 In considering whether the impugned point was central to the award, one had to examine the centrality of the point in the context of the entire award. The court ought to consider whether the issue in question can fairly be described as affecting a substantial part of the award, or even as being pivotal to the case as a whole: at [12 6] . 24 Applying the foregoing factors, remission was not an appropriate remedy. The Tribunal’s breach of the fair hearing rule was serious and in respect of a pivotal decision that went to the heart of the dispute on liability. The Tribunal had also come to its decision despite knowing that neither party’s expert evidence had addressed the issue, which gave rise to the concern of prejudgment if the matter was remitted. Lastly, it would likely have been necessary for PM to change its case as stated in its pleadings if an order of remission was made. Accordingly, the matter could not fairly be remitted: at [1 31]. This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.

case_name: CHANGI AIRPORT GROUP (SINGAPORE) PTE LTD v COMPTROLLER OF INCOME TAX
subject_tags: ["Revenue Law — Income taxation — Appeals — Whether expenditure eligible for capital allowance — Whether asset considered “plant” or structure"]
court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 25 September 2025 Case summary Changi Airport Group (Singapore) Pte Ltd v Comptroller of Income Tax [2025] SGHC(A) 20 Appellate Division of the High Court — Civil Appeal No 93 of 2024 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Appellate Division of the High Court (delivered by Justice See Kee Oon): Outcome: The Appellate Division of the High Court dismissed the taxpayer’s appeal seeking to qualify the runways, taxiways and aprons located at Changi Airport as “plant” for the purposes of s 19A of the Income Tax Act, in order to write down capital expenditure incurred on those assets over a period of two or three years. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment: • The runways, taxiways and aprons should be evaluated separately and not as a single integrated asset together with the airport’s aerodrome equipment, because they serve distinct purposes and can function independently of each other. • The Income Tax Board of Review and the Judge of the High Court who presided over the proceedings in the General Division below both found that the assets in question were not “plant” but structures. They had reached reasonable conclusions after applying the applicable legal principles to the facts of the case. This was consistent with the legislative intent, which preserves a clear and mutually exclusive distinction between plant and machinery on the one hand and buildings and structures on the other. Background to the appeal and material facts 1 This appeal centred on the following question: can an airport operator claim capital allowances for expenditure incurred in respect of its runways, taxiways and aprons ? 2 The appellant, Changi Airport Group (Singapore) Pte Ltd, owned and operated the certified aerodrome in Changi Airport, which facilitated the arrival, departure and surface movement of aircraft operated by air transportation carriers. The assets forming part of the aerodrome relevant to this appeal were (a) the runways, taxiways and aprons (collectively, the “RTA”); and (b) specialised systems and sub-systems equipment including the airfield lighting system, the instrument landing system, signs, the aircraft docking guidance system, ground movement detectors and radars, and the foreign object detection system (collectively, the “Aerodrome Equipment”). The parties agreed that the RTA were “designed to facilitate and ensure the safe landing, taxi-ing, and take-off of aircraft at Terminals 1, 2, 3 and 4 of Changi Airport”. 3 The appellant asserted that the RTA, which were essential to its business and purposefully designed to accommodate the complex demands of modern aviation, qualified as “plant” under s 19A of the Income Tax Act (Cap 134, 2008 Rev Ed) (the “ITA”). This would have allowed it to write down capital expenditure incurred on the RTA across three years of assessment (“YAs”) and amounting to over $272m over a period of two or three years. The respondent, the Comptroller of Income Tax (the “Comptroller”), in turn contended that the RTA were simply structures, and as such, were ineligible for the capital allowances claimed under s 19A of the ITA. The Comptroller regarded the expenditure on the RTA claimed by the appellant as eligible to be written down at a slower rate of 3% annually under the industrial building allowances (“IBA”) scheme under s 16 read with s 18(1)( b ) of the ITA. 4 The appellant appealed the Comptroller’s determination in relation to the RTA. In ITBR Appeal Nos 21 to 23 of 2016 (the “ITBR Proceedings”), the Income Tax Board of Review (the “Board”) found the RTA to be structures rather than “plant”, on an application of the factors set out in ZF v Comptroller of Income Tax [2011] 1 SLR 1044 (“ ZF ”). Its decision was based on the following factors: (a) the physical nature and characteristics of the RTA; (b) the fact that the RTA were made of very durable materials; and (c) the fact that a runway would not be relocated very frequently. The Board found the RTA to have been “structures” on which the appellant’s business was carried on and accordingly did not qualify for capital allowances under s 19A of the ITA. 5 The appellant lodged a further appeal. A Judge of the High Court (the “Judge”) affirmed the finding of the Board and dismissed the appeal. The Judge held that the RTA and the Aerodrome Equipment were not considered a single asset and were divisible for income tax purposes. Accordingly, focusing on the RTA alone, the RTA were structures which allowed aircraft to traverse and rest, and thus were the premises on which the appellant’s trade occurred as opposed to an apparatus used for the trade. On this basis, the RTA were more akin to structures than “plant”. The appellant appealed the Judge’s determination, leading to the present appeal. 6 The central contention in this appeal related to whether the RTA should be classified as “plant” or as structures for the purposes of the appellant’s claim for capital allowances under the ITA. Aside from the appellant’s ancillary argument on policy grounds, the two main issues which arose for determination in the appeal were as follows: a. Divisibility Issue: Whether the RTA should be assessed in isolation or whether they should be considered together with the Aerodrome Equipment such that both groups of assets formed a single, integrated unit (which the appellant referred to as the “Integrated RTA”) for the purposes of the inquiry to follow; and b. Plant Issue: Whether the RTA (or the Integrated RTA) were or were not “plant”. The court’s grounds of decision 7 In an appeal from the Board’s decision, the role of the courts was not to conduct a fresh and wholly unconstrained review of the merits of the Comptroller’s decision. Instead, a more limited degree of review was inherent in the appellate review process in such a context: the court extended deference to the Board where findings of fact were concerned, notwithstanding the availability of an appeal, by asking whether no reasonable body of members constituting an Income Tax Review Board could have reached the findings reached by the Board. The appellant thus had to show that the Board reached an “unreasonable conclusion on the facts” that the RTA were not “plant”. The focus was not on the Judge’s decision, but on that of the Board: at [26] and [29] . 8 Specifically, in the context of tax cases of the type in this appeal, the question of whether a relevant asset was “plant” was one of fact and degree and the answer given by the Board should be treated as decisive unless it was an unreasonable conclusion on the facts. In cases falling on the borderline, where it was reasonable to conclude that an asset can be either “plant” or a building, an appellate court should not interfere with the decision rendered at first instance. This approach could be explained by the fact that the Board was the primary trier of fact. It had the benefit of hearing witness testimony and visiting the relevant sites, and was a specialist tribunal constituted by the legislature with the subject-matter expertise to adjudicate upon these disputes: at [27] to [28] . 9 The primary authority on determining whether an asset was a “plant” or a “building or structure” was ZF . “Plant” and “buildings and structures” were mutually exclusive categories; a n asset might be considered “plant” in some respects and a building in others but, ultimately, for the purposes of income tax, it could only be depreciated either purely as “plant” or purely as a “building or structure”. Since the two categories were mutually exclusive, where an asset possessed the features of both, the question was whether the asset could be more appropriately described as “plant” or as a “building or structure”: at [30] . 10 In determining whether an asset was a “plant” or a building, there was just one basic and overarching test – whether the item concerned was utilised for the purposes of the trade or business as “plant” or as a building. The following factors were pertinent in this inquiry: (a) the exact operational role which the asset played in the taxpayer’s business; (b) the physical nature and characteristics of the asset; (c) the intended permanence (or temporariness) of the asset; and (d) the asset’s connection to buildings. The court applied these factors in differentiating between “plant” and “structure”. In the final analysis, much would depend on the precise factual matrix and context concerned: at [3 4] , [35] and [37] . 11 The mutual exclusivity rule differentiating between “plant” and “building or structure” within our statutory framework was unique. Decisions from foreign jurisdictions should be treated with the appropriate degree of caution, especially where the wording of the foreign tax legislation was not identical with or not in materially the same terms as the local equivalent. This should not be misunderstood as a call to disregard foreign cases entirely. Rather, as the Judge correctly recognised, these cases “provide nuances and principles which may assist the court in assessing whether an asset has qualities of ‘plant’”. In the present context, these cases might be considered bearing in mind the distinctive objective under Singapore law, that was, to determine whether the asset was more appropriately described as a “plant” or a “building or structure”: at [3 9] to [4 1] . 12 The RTA and the Aerodrome Equipment should be evaluated separately and not as a single integrated asset. This was essentially because the RTA could function independently (even if not optimally) without the Aerodrome Equipment. The two groups of assets served distinct purposes in that the RTA provided the physical surface for aircraft movement while the Aerodrome Equipment handled aircraft navigation and safety. They were not sufficiently physically or functionally integrated such that they ought to be considered as an integrated asset. The fact that the RTA and the Aerodrome Equipment worked together and were so designed, were essential to the appellant’s business, generated revenue together and were subject to the same regulations did not make them one indivisible unit. There was no general or inflexible rule that different assets or components that served a common function when taken together had to be integrated into a single whole as “plant”: at [44] to [4 5] . 13 The determination of the Plant Issue rested on the ZF factors . The Board and the Judge correctly concluded that those factors weighed in favour of the RTA being classified as “structures” rather than “plant”. This was also consistent with the legislative intent, which preserved a clear and mutually exclusive distinction between plant and machinery on the one hand and buildings and structures on the other. The ZF factors did not support the more expansive interpretation of “plant” that the appellant sought to persuade the court to apply: at [58] . a. In terms of the RTA’s operational role, it primarily functioned as surfaces for aircraft movement. Even if a building was purpose-built and essential to the business, that did not automatically make it a “plant”. Being revenue-generating was not a decisive factor as there could be many structures which generate revenue: at [50] . b. As to the physical characteristics of the RTA, analogous cases involving surface structures had classified those relevant assets as premises or structures rather than “plant”, even when purpose-built for the business in question. A similar approach should be adopted in the case of the RTA. Further, the asset’s size, shape, durability, and the materials used to construct it were relevant. The more an asset resembled a conventional building or structure, the less likely it was “plant”. The physical characteristics of the RTA were clearly more similar to other pavement structures like roads: at [51] to [55] . c. The RTA, made of very durable materials, were designed for permanence: at [56] . 14 Apart from the ZF factors, the appellant advanced an argument on policy grounds. It argued that it was an unintended victim of a general legislative reform agenda after Parliament abolished the IBA scheme and replaced it with the Land Intensification Allowance scheme, the latter of which the appellant would not qualify for. While this might entail a competitive disadvantage for the appellant vis-à-vis airports in other countries, this could not in and of itself be the basis for adopting the interpretation or classification that the appellant sought. Tax laws should be interpreted objectively and not based on any claimed policy preferences. Further, taking an overly generous interpretation of “plant” in order for the RTA to qualify as “plant” would undermine the general prohibition against the deduction of expenses of a capital nature in the taxation of income: at [59] to [63] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.

case_name: DAN v PUBLIC PROSECUTOR
subject_tags: ["Criminal Procedure and Sentencing — Sentencing — Whether maximum sentence of life imprisonment justified — Whether worst type of cases of culpable homicide — Section 304(a) Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed)", "Criminal Procedure and Sentencing — Sentencing — Whether maximum sentence of four years’ imprisonment justified — Whether worst type of cases of ill-treatment — Section 5 Children and Young Persons Act (Cap 38, 2001 Rev Ed)"]
court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 19 September 2025 Case summary DAN v Public Prosecutor and another appeal [2025] SGCA 45 Criminal Appeals No 11 and 13 of 2024 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Judgment of the Court of Appeal (comprising Sundaresh Menon CJ, Steven Chong JCA, Judtih Prakash SJ) (delivered by Sundaresh Menon CJ): Outcome: The Court of Appeal (the “CA”) enhanced the sentence imposed on an offender who had brutally abused and killed his five-year-old daughter and was charged under s 304( a ) of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed) (the “Penal Code”), to a term of life imprisonment. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment •  It is relevant to distinguish between cases where an offender is charged for the lesser offence of culpable homicide not amounting to murder (a) because one of the partial defences to murder is made out; and (b) where none of the partial defences are engaged, but a lesser charge is nevertheless preferred. In the former category of cases, in light of the fairly high threshold that must be met to establish one or more of the partial defences, it may generally not be appropriate to impose a term of life imprisonment. However, in the latter category of cases, there is no basis to presumptively exclude the sentence of life imprisonment: at [37]–[40] . •  To assess whether a case falls within the “worst types” of its offence, the sentencing court should identify a set of defining characteristics or fundamental elements of the case at hand that cause it to stand out from the typical run of cases involving the same offence, and in the light of these, assess whether the offence was so egregious that it calls for the imposition of the maximum permissible sentence: at [42] . Background 1 The appellant was a father who brutally abused his two young children (“Ayeesha” and “[R]”) over the course of two years. Not only did he inflict brutal physical violence on the children, but he also confined them to cramped and unsanitary spaces. The children were starved to the point of having to eat their own faeces. This abuse was only put to a tragic end when the older daughter, Ayeesha, died at the appellant’s hands. She was only about five years old at that time and [R] was just under four years of age. 2 In the proceedings below, the appellant pleaded guilty to six charges with 20 further charges taken into consideration for sentencing. He was sentenced to an aggregate term of 34 and a half years’ imprisonment with six months’ imprisonment in lieu of caning, comprising: a. 15 years’ imprisonment and 12 strokes of the cane for a single charge of culpable homicide, not amounting to murder, punishable under s 304( a ) of the Penal Code . As the appellant was unfit to be caned, he was further sentenced to six months’ imprisonment in lieu of the 12 caning strokes. b. Four years’ imprisonment for each of four charges of ill-treatment of a child under s 5(1) of the Children and Young Persons Act (Cap 38, 2001 Rev Ed) (the “CYPA”). c. Three and a half years’ imprisonment for a single charge of causing the disappearance of evidence of the offence of culpable homicide, in breach of s 201 of the Penal Code. 3 The appellant appealed against both the aggregate sentence and the imprisonment that was ordered in lieu of caning. Facts The proceeded CYPA charges 4 In late 2015, when Ayeesha and [R] were aged three and two respectively, the appellant started his campaign of abuse. Two notable episodes of abuse were caught on video footage from the closed-circuit television cameras that the appellant set up to monitor them: a. On 27 March 2016, the appellant assaulted Ayeesha for 16 minutes, repeatedly slapping, punching, caning and kicking her without restraint. He grabbed her by the hair, lifted her by the neck with her back against the wall while punching her body, and even threatened her with a pair of scissors (the “12th Charge”). b. On 27 August 2016, the appellant caned and shouted at Ayeesha and [R] over the course of 24 minutes (the “17th Charge”). 5 From October 2016 to August 2017, a period of 10 months, both children were confined naked in the toilet of the flat. They were only permitted out for feeding or when the toilet was being used (the “19th Charge” and “20th Charge”). The culpable homicide charge 6 On 10 August 2017 at around 9.00pm, the appellant’s wife [W] complained to the appellant that Ayeesha was refusing to move her legs and that she had not been moving for the entire day. The appellant entered the toilet, pulled Ayeesha up from the ground by her arm, and beat her some 15 to 20 times across her face (the “10 August Attack”). The appellant placed Ayeesha back on the floor and noticed that her head was tilted backwards in an awkward position. Nevertheless, he left the toilet and went to bed. 7 On 11 August 2017 at around 3.00am, [W] informed the appellant that the children were sleeping in what seemed to her to be unusual positions. The appellant entered the toilet again and punched Ayeesha and [R] on their backs. He also kicked and stamped on Ayeesha’s buttocks and shoulder, turned her around, and slapped her on the face three or four more times (the “11 August Attack”). 8 About 15 hours after the 11 August Attack, in the evening of 11 August, [W] noticed that Ayeesha was lying unresponsive on the toilet floor, with her eyes closed and her body cold. The appellant attempted to administer cardiopulmonary resuscitation on Ayeesha, to no avail. The appellant and [W] realised that Ayeesha had died. 9 In the early hours of 12 August 2017, the appellant disposed of various items, which would connect him to the killing, in nearby rubbish bins. When the appellant took Ayeesha’s lifeless body to the hospital several hours later, he lied about the events that led to her death. The autopsy report revealed that Ayeesha’s death was caused by a head injury consistent with blunt force trauma to her head and face. It also stated that Ayeesha was severely undernourished, with numerous injuries to her head, trunk, upper and lower limbs. 10 Thereafter, the appellant provided multiple false statements to the police which contained fabricated accounts of the events leading to Ayeesha’s death. He only admitted to killing Ayeesha when confronted with the police camera footage of him disposing of evidence. 11 The appellant originally claimed trial to a charge for murder under s 300( c ) of the Penal Code. He only pleaded guilty after accepting the Prosecution’s offer to substitute the murder charge with one of culpable homicide, not amounting to murder, under s 304( a ) of the Penal Code. Decision on appeal 12 As prescribed in s 390(1)( c ) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (2020 Rev Ed) (the “CPC”), the appellate court has the power to enhance an offender’s sentence even in the absence of an appeal by the Public Prosecutor (the “Prosecution”). The inquiry is whether the “interests of justice” call for the enhancement of the sentence ordered at first instance, including where the trial judge ordered a sentence that was manifestly inadequate: at [34]–[35] . The fact that the Prosecution did not file an appeal, does not constrain the court from exercising its power to enhance a sentence: at [35] . The offender’s expectation on appeal is also irrelevant: at [34] . The sentence for the culpable homicide charge was enhanced to a term of life imprisonment 13 There are two broad categories of cases in which an offender will face a charge for the lesser offence of culpable homicide (under s 299 of the Penal Code) as opposed to one of murder (under s 300 of the Penal Code): a. The first is where the offender would ordinarily have been charged with murder, but where the charge is lowered either by the Prosecution or the court because one of the partial defences to murder under s 300 of the Penal Code is engaged: at [37(a )] . b. The second is where none of the partial defences is established, but where the Prosecution nevertheless prefers a charge of culpable homicide. This may be for a number of reasons, including to facilitate a plea agreement with the offender: at [37(b)] . 14 This distinction may have a bearing on the proper approach to sentencing: a. A case that falls within the “worst types of culpable homicides” will generally be devoid of mitigating circumstances. In the first category of cases (at [13(a)] above), in light of the fairly high threshold that must be met to fulfil one or more of the partial defences to murder, such cases will generally not be considered to be devoid of mitigating circumstances. Thus, a term of life imprisonment may not be warranted: at [38] . However, in cases involving mentally disordered offenders, the criteria set out in R v Rowland Jack Forster Hodgson (196 7) 52 Cr App Rep 113 (“ Hodgson ”) continue to be instructive in determining whether a term of life imprisonment would nonetheless be appropriate: at [39] . b. In the latter category of cases (at [13(b)] above) where none of the partial defences is engaged, there is no basis to presumptively exclude the sentence of life imprisonment. It should not be the default position that a term of life imprisonment will be excluded save where there is a danger of recurrence, upon applying the Hodgson criteria. The question is simply whether the offence is among the worst types of culpable homicide such that a sentence of life imprisonment is warranted: at [40] . 15 The worst type of culpable homicide does not mean the worst case of culpable homicide that may be imaginable. The role of the sentencing court is to identify a set of defining characteristics or fundamental elements of the case at hand that cause it to stand out from the typical run of cases involving the same offence, and in light of these, to assess whether the offence was so egregious that it warranted the imposition of the maximum permissible sentence: at [41] –[42] . 16 The CA identified five defining characteristics of this case which, viewed in their totality, made this one of the worst types of culpable homicide: at [44] : a. Cruelty and viciousness of the attack : The degree of cruelty inherent in an offence may be inferred from (a) the manner in which the attacks were carried out; (b) the frequency and recurrence of the attacks; and (c) the length of time over which they are carried out: at [45] . The true viciousness of the 10 and 11 August Attacks could only be appreciated by reference to the full range of circumstances under which they were perpetrated. In the 10 August Attack, Ayeesha was squatting on the toilet floor when the appellant pulled her up and slapped her 15 to 20 times. At this juncture, the appellant already noticed that Ayeesha’s head was tilted in an awkward position. He ignored this and went to bed. A few hours later, when [W] complained to him that Ayeesha was lying on the floor in a strange position, the appellant did not show any concern for her wellbeing. Rather, he proceeded to inflict further acts of violence on her in the 11 August Attack. Moreover, the appellant only became aware of Ayeesha’s death 15 hours after the 11 August Attack, in spite of the fact that he had been resting at home for most of that day. Viewed in this light, the 10 and 11 August Attacks were particularly cruel: at [46]–[47] . b. Prolonged period of escalating abuse : It was not disputed that the 10 and 11 August Attacks were the culmination of a two-year long period of abuse and neglect, where the appellant confined Ayeesha to cramped corners of the Flat, denied her sufficient food and care, and punched, caned and stamped on her body on several occasions. This ill-treatment caused Ayeesha to be severely undernourished with numerous existing injuries on her body. The 10 and 11 August Attacks were thus perpetrated against a victim who had already been abused in many and varied ways; rendering them especially heinous. Put another way, the severity of the 10 and 11 August Attacks was compounded by the appellant’s own prior acts of abuse and neglect: at [48] , [51] . c. Especial vulnerability of the victim : There will almost always be a gross physical disparity at play between an adult offender and a child victim that renders the child completely defenceless against the offender. This featured all the more prominently in the present case, since, as noted above, Ayeesha was severely undernourished and had multiple existing injuries: at [52] . d. Abuse of trust and repudiation of parental duty : Where a parent breaches the highest level of trust that is reposed in him or her and abuses and causes the death of his or her child, that parent must be dealt with by the most severe condemnation of the law. Since a parent stands in such a position of authority, instances of child abuse will also often be difficult to detect and prevent: at [54]–[55] . The appellant was Ayeesha’s primary caregiver and biological father. The 10 and 11 August Attacks were thus perpetrated in gross violation of the high degree of trust and authority that were reposed in him: at [53]–[54] . e. The case was devoid of mitigating factors : The offence was the result of a fully intentional set of actions and there was nothing to suggest that the appellant was not in control of his faculties: at [56] . Moreover, the CA disagreed that the appellant’s plea of guilt justified any sentencing discount. It was not indicative of any remorse on the appellant’s part, especially since he only pleaded guilty after the murder charge was lowered to one of culpable homicide: at [56] . 17 For these reasons, the CA was satisfied that this was one of the worst types of culpable homicide and enhanced the sentence to a term of life imprisonment. Regarding the 12strokes of the cane that were ordered, the CA declined to set this aside: at [57] –[58] . This was sufficient to dispose of the appeal since, as prescribed in s 307(2) of the CPC, the sentences for all other charges would run concurrently with the term of life imprisonment: at [59] . The sentences for the CYPA charges were left undisturbed 18 While there is no sentencing framework for ill-treatment offences under s 5 of the CYPA, a court may nevertheless take account of the following non-exhaustive factors in determining the appropriate sentence for this offence: (a) the extent of deliberation or premeditation; (b) the manner and duration of the ill-treatment; (c) the victim’s vulnerability; (d) the use of a weapon; (e) whether the attack was undertaken by a group; (f) whether there were any antecedents; and (g) any prior intervention by the authorities: at [62] . 19 There was no reason to disturb the maximum sentences for all four CYPA charges imposed by the Judge: [59] . 20 In relation to the 12th Charge (see [4(a)] above), this was the most egregious of the four CYPA charges. The appellant attacked Ayeesha relentlessly for 16 minutes and even held her in a chokehold for seven seconds. The scale and brutality of this abuse placed it within the worst types of ill-treatment offences: at [75]–[78] . 21 In relation to the 19th and 20th Charges (see [5] above), the ten-month long period of confinement caused Ayeesha and [R] to suffer severe physical and psychological repercussions. Ayeesha suffered many wounds and abrasions; [R] developed skin infections and was malnourished to the point that he required more than three months of hospitalization; [R] also suffered from global developmental delay due to social deprivation: at [79]–[81] . 22 In relation to the 17th Charge (see [4(b)] above), taken in isolation, the CA might have imposed a provisional starting sentence of about one and a half years’ imprisonment. However, on an application of the totality principle – which allows a court to enhance an individual sentence to ensure that the overall sentence imposed is commensurate with the totality of the offending conduct – the CA would nevertheless have increased the individual sentence for the 17th Charge to the maximum four-year imprisonment term. This was because sentencing on this charge in isolation would not have accurately reflected the gravity of the offence being committed as it was against the background of sustained violence and abuse, which would have made this especially unbearable from the perspective of young children aged between two and five: at [82] –[86] . The term of imprisonment in lieu of caning was left undisturbed 23 Regarding the appellant’s appeal against the Judge’s decision to impose a sentence of six months’ imprisonment in lieu of caning for the culpable homicide charge, this was rendered moot in light of the decision to enhance the sentence for this charge to a term of life imprisonment. In any event, the CA would have affirmed the Judge’s decision to order additional caning in lieu of imprisonment, given the emphasis on deterrence and retribution and the fact that the offences were committed against vulnerable victims: at [88]–[89] . 24 The CA dismissed the appeals and the aggregate sentence was enhanced to a term of life imprisonment: at [90] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.
