court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 18 September 2025 Case summary Zin Mar Nwe v Public Prosecutor [202 5] SGCA 44 Court of Appeal – Criminal Appeal No 10 of 2023 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Court of Appeal (delivered by See Kee Oon JAD): Outcome: The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal against the appellant’s conviction on a charge of murder and sentence of life imprisonment. The Court upheld the trial judge’s decision to reject the appellant’s partial defence of diminished responsibility but allowed her alternative partial defence of grave and sudden provocation. The appellant was therefore convicted on a substituted charge of culpable homicide not amounting to murder and sentenced to 17 years’ imprisonment. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment: • Although it is incumbent on accused persons and the Prosecution to proffer at trial all arguments they may wish to rely on, accused persons may invoke new defences for the first time on appeal provided those defences were reasonably available on the evidence led at trial. • Where the evidence discloses a defence not invoked by the accused person, it remains the trial judge’s duty – especially where capital charges are involved – to at least consider those alternative defences, barring any circumstances that would make it procedurally unfair to do so. • The partial defence of grave and sudden provocation was reasonably available to the appellant on the evidence led at her trial. The Deceased had verbally threatened the appellant, and the evidence sufficed to demonstrate that (a) the appellant had been deprived of self-control in consequence of that threat; and (b) an ordinary person of the same sex and age as the appellant, sharing her characteristics as could reasonably affect the gravity of the provocation, would have been so provoked as to suddenly lose self-control. • The sentencing court must first objectively assess the gravity and suddenness of the provocation before weighing that against any of the offender’s subjective characteristics that may have rendered him or her more susceptible to the provocation. The sentence must then be further adjusted for any other mitigating or aggravating factors not already taken into consideration. On that approach, a sentence of 17 years’ imprisonment was appropriate in the circumstances of the appellant’s case. Background 1 The appellant is a Burmese national who arrived in Singapore on 5 January 2018 seeking employment as a foreign domestic worker. In doing so, the appellant had falsely declared her age as 23. Bone-age tests performed on the appellant later revealed that she was closer to 17 years of age as at the date of the offence. 2 The appellant was employed in the household of one “ Mr S ” from 10 May 2018. Mr S was the appellant’s third employer in about four months after her arrival in Singapore. The other members of the household were Mr S’ wife and their two daughters. The deceased, Mdm M (the “ Deceased ”), was Mr S’ mother -in-law. She arrived in Singapore from India on 26 May 2018 for a month-long stay at Mr S’ residence (the “ Unit ”). 3 On the morning of 25 June 2018, the appellant and the Deceased were alone in the Unit by 11.27am. At around noon, the appellant brought a knife from the kitchen to the living room, where the Deceased lay on a sofa watching television. The appellant then stabbed the Deceased multiple times until the latter stopped moving. 4 The appellant would later explain to the police that the Deceased had physically and verbally abused her, both on the morning of the incident as well as prior to that day. The Deceased was said to have threatened the appellant in the moments before the fatal attack by uttering: “Tomorrow. You. Go. Agent.” The appellant understood this to mean that she would be sent back to her employment agency and consequently repatriated to Myanmar in debt to her agents, given that Mr S was already her third employer in about four months. According to the appellant, the Deceased’s threat made her “very angry” and was the trigger for the stabbing. 5 After having stabbed the Deceased, the appellant retrieved various personal effects and some money which belonged to her. She washed the knife which she had used to stab the Deceased and left it in the kitchen, where it was later retrieved by the police. The appellant then left the Unit after having changed her clothes and gathered some of her personal belongings. She first proceeded to her employment agency, where she requested for her passport. She left the agency, however, as soon as she heard that the agency’s staff were about to call her employers. The appellant then went to various locations across Singapore before returning to the agency, where she was arrested shortly thereafter. 6 An autopsy was performed on the Deceased the same day. The cause of the Deceased’s death was certified as “multiple stab wounds”. 26 stab wounds were observed on the Deceased’s body, three of which would have sufficed in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. 7 The appellant was charged with murder under s 300( c ) read with s 302(2) of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed) (the “ Penal Code ”) for having inflicted multiple stab wounds on the Deceased with a knife, with the intention of causing those injuries, which injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. The ingredients of the charge were not disputed by the appellant at her trial before a judge of the General Division of the High Court (the “ Judge ”) . She relied only on the partial defence of diminished responsibility under Exception 7 to s 300 of the Penal Code. 8 The material evidence that was adduced at trial included: (a) ten statements given by the appellant to the police in the course of investigations; and (b) psychiatric reports prepared by Dr Tommy Tan Kay Seng (“ Dr Tan ”) and Dr Alias Lijo (“ Dr Lijo ”) as expert witness for the appellant for the Prosecution respectively. 9 In his written report, Dr Tan took the view that the appellant had been in a “dissociative state” at the time of the stabbing and was both unaware and incapable of controlling her actions. Dr Tan also diagnosed the appellant with “mixed anxiety and depressive reaction” or “adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood” (the “ AD Diagnosis ”). Dr Lijo, on the other hand, disagreed with AD Diagnosis as well as Dr Tan’s opinion that the appellant had been in a dissociative state. In Dr Lijo’s view, the appellant suffered from no psychiatric illness that impaired her mental responsibility for her acts at the time of the offence. 10 The Judge rejected the appellant’s defence. In particular, the Judge was not persuaded that the appellant had been in a dissociative state at the material time. To the contrary, the evidence indicated that the appellant had remained conscious of her actions throughout. The Judge further rejected the AD Diagnosis and preferred Dr Lijo’s view that the appellant suffered from no mental illness. This led to the conclusion that the appellant’s mental responsibility for causing the Deceased’s death had not been substantially impaired. On that footing, the Judge convicted the appellant on the murder charge and sentenced her to life imprisonment. The punishment of death could not have been imposed in view of the appellant’s age. 11 On appeal, the appellant argued that the Judge had erred in rejecting her defence of diminished responsibility. She also argued that the Judge should have considered the partial defence of grave and sudden provocation (under Exception 1 to s 300 of the Penal Code) which, although never pursued in her defence at trial, was nevertheless reasonably available on the evidence. Decision of the court The partial defence of diminished responsibility 12 To succeed in her defence of diminished responsibility, the burden was on the appellant to prove on a balance of probabilities that: (a) she had been suffering from an abnormality of mind (“ Requirement 1 ”) ; (b) such abnormality of mind arose from a condition of arrested or retarded development, arose from any inherent causes, or was induced by disease or injury (“ Requirement 2 ”); and (c) the abnormality of mind substantially impaired her mental responsibility for her acts and omissions in causing the Deceased’s death (“ Requirement 3 ”) : at [ 29] . 13 On Requirement 1, the essential question was whether the Judge had obviously erred in finding that there was no “abnormality of mind” because the available evidence was overwhelmingly probative of the appellant having been in a dissociative state with a reduced capacity for self-control at the time of the offence: at [38] . 14 That question was answered in the negative. First, Dr Tan himself acknowledged that “dissociation” meant a disconnect between a person’s mind and actions. However, he also conceded at trial that the appellant had in fact been conscious of her actions at the time of the stabbing. That was the finding made by the Judge, which the appellant did not dispute on appeal. It thus followed that there could have been no disconnect between the appellant’s mind and her actions – and hence, no dissociation – at the time of the offence. This was significant because the only “abnormality of mind” posited by the appellant’s defence at trial was her alleged dissociation, and Dr Tan’s assessment of the appellant having been in a dissociative state was the sole basis for his opinion that she had suffered from an abnormality of mind: at [36] and [39] to [41] . 15 Second, Dr Tan’s written report was prepared solely on the basis of information provided to him by the appellant and her sister. Dr Tan also admitted that he took at face value what the appellant had said to him at their interviews. This further undermined the reliability of Dr Tan’s opinion that the appellant had been in a dissociative state: at [42] and [43] . 16 For these reasons, the Judge made no error in finding that Requirement 1 had not been satisfied. The evidence was not so probative of the appellant having been in a dissociative state that appellate intervention in that finding was warranted: at [46] . 17 On Requirement 2, the AD Diagnosis was advanced by Dr Tan as the aetiology or root cause of the appellant’s putative abnormality of mind ( ie , her dissociation at the time of the stabbing). The first difficulty with this assessment was that there was nothing in Dr Tan’s evidence that explained the connection between the AD Diagnosis and the appellant’s alleged dissociation. In fact, Dr Tan conceded under cross-examination that the appellant’s dissociation was irrelevant to the AD Diagnosis. This was fatal to the defence, given that the abnormality of mind had to have arisen from a qualifying psychiatric condition: at [50] to [53] . 18 Second, and in any event, the Judge had also rightly rejected the AD Diagnosis. This was again because Dr Tan had prepared his report on the basis of information supplied to him by the appellant and her sister some two years after the material events. There was also no corroboration of the details which formed the foundation for the AD Diagnosis. These gaps were striking in circumstances where there was no objective evidence of the prior abuse allegedly suffered by the appellant, that having been a part of the anecdotal evidence on which Dr Tan based his diagnosis: at [5 4] to [59] . 19 Having upheld the Judge’s findings on Requirement 1 and 2, it was unnecessary in the circumstances to consider Requirement 3: at [61] . The partial defence of grave and sudden provocation 20 The appellant was not precluded from raising the alternative defence of grave and sudden provocation on appeal simply because she had failed to do so at trial. Case law has established that, as a matter of fairness to accused persons, they should be permitted to rely on alternative defences on appeal provided those defences were reasonably available on the evidence before the court at the trial below. The Judge should have considered that alternative defence, especially since he had made a number of findings plainly relevant to it: at [63] , [64] and [102] . 21 To avail herself of the defence of grave and sudden provocation, there were two tests that the appellant had to satisfy. The first (the “ Subjective Test ” ) required proof that the appellant had been deprived of self-control by the Deceased’s provocation. The second (the “ Objective Test ” ) required proof that an ordinary person of the same sex and age as the appellant, sharing her characteristics as could reasonably affect the gravity of the provocation, would have been so provoked as to suddenly lose her self-control: at [67] . 22 The provocation in this case was the Deceased having said to the Appellant: “Tomorrow. You. Go. Agent.” The Judge was satisfied that the Deceased had made the utterance, which the appellant perceived as a threat. That finding was not seriously disputed on appeal, nor was there any disagreement that the provocation was “sudden” and proximate in time to the Appellant’s fatal attack: at [68] . 23 The Subjective Test was satisfied on the evidence led at trial. The appellant’s police statements offered a consistent, contemporaneous, and inherently reliable account of how she had lost control of herself at the material time. That account was consistent with the objective circumstances that surrounded the commission of the offence, which included the frenzied nature of the attack (reflected in the number and distribution of stab wounds on the Deceased’s body); the evident spontaneity of the offence and absence of any premeditation; and the appellant’s conduct in the aftermath of the killing: at [71] to [8 7] . 24 The Objective Test was also satisfied on the evidence. The Judge accepted that the Deceased had abused the appellant prior to the fateful incident. To the extent the Judge found that there had been acts of abuse that occurred on the morning of the incident prior to the attack, that finding was not plainly wrong or against the weight of evidence. Insofar as the Judge may have taken the view that the appellant had been abused in the period leading up the date of the killing, however, that finding was unsupported by the evidence. Apart from the appellant’s uncorroborated say-so, there was no objective evidence of abuse during that time: at [91] to [99] . 25 Weighing the Deceased’s acts of abuse alongside the appellant’s personal circumstances – in particular, her youth and immaturity; the challenge of adapting to living and working in a foreign country; her indebtedness to her employment agent; and her fear of being repatriated in those circumstances – the Court was satisfied that an ordinary person of the appellant’s age, sex and characteristics would have been so provoked in the circumstances as to suddenly lose self-control: at [100] . 26 The appeal against conviction was therefore allowed. The appellant’s conviction on the charge of murder under s 300( c ) of the Penal Code was substituted with one of culpable homicide not amounting to murder punishable under s 304( a ) : at [103] . The appropriate sentence on the substituted charge 27 As a starting point, the appropriate sentence had to account for the fact of the offence having been committed under grave and sudden provocation. As a partial defence to a charge of murder, grave and sudden provocation required a subjective loss of self-control by the offender. That factor had to be relevant to an assessment of the offender’s culpability, and therefore the punishment to be imposed: at [115] . 28 Where culpable homicide was committed under grave and sudden provocation, life imprisonment was generally warranted only where the offender presented a continuing threat to the safety of others. A sentence of life imprisonment was thus inappropriate in this case because the appellant presented no continuing threat to public safety or risk of re-offending: at [116] and [121] . 29 Where the offence called for a lesser sentence of up to 20 years’ imprisonment, the calibration of that sentence depended on the extent to which the offender’s culpability had been diminished by the provocation. In this connection, the sentencing court had to first objectively assess the gravity and suddenness of the provocation before weighing that against any of the offender’s subjective characteristics that may have rendered him or her more susceptible to the provocation. Where the provocation was extreme in both its objective and subjective aspects, a significant reduction from the upper limit of 20 years’ imprisonment might have been called for. By contrast, milder forms of provocation ought generally to attract only modest reductions in sentence or no reduction at all: at [117] and [118] . 30 Having ascertained the appropriate reduction (if any) to be given on account of the provocation, the sentence then had to be adjusted for any other mitigating or aggravating factors not already taken into consideration: at [119] . 31 In this case, the provocation was sudden and objectively grave insofar as it represented not only a threat to the appellant’s employment and livelihood, but also the inevitability of her repatriation to Myanmar in debt. On the other hand, the objective gravity of the provocation was tempered by the fact that it comprised a single verbal utterance by the Deceased: at [122] and [123] . 32 On the subjective aspect of the inquiry, the effect of the Deceased’s threat on the appellant would have been amplified by the latter’s youth, immaturity and financial vulnerability; her family’s circumstances in their troubled homeland; and, to a lesser extent, the physical and verbal abuse she had suffered at the hands of the Deceased prior to the commission of the offence: at [124] . 33 The appellant’s offence was aggravated by her use of a weapon; the brutal nature of the attack on the Deceased; and the context in which the offence had been committed ( ie , by a domestic helper in her employer’s household ). The Court rejected, however, the Prosecution’s argument that the appellant had attempted to conceal the offence or evade arrest: at [126] . 34 Having regard to the relevant sentencing considerations in this case, the Court considered it appropriate to impose a sentence of 17 years’ imprisonment on the appellant. The sentence was backdated to the date of the appellant’s arrest: at [127] and [129] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s judgment. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s judgment.

court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 30 September 2025 Case Summary DNO v DNP [2025] SGHC(I) 24 SIC/OA 4/2025 --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Singapore International Commercial Court (delivered by Anthony James Besanko IJ): Outcome: The SICC dismissed DNO’s application to set aside an arbitral award on the grounds of breach of natural justice and conflict with the public policy of Singapore. Background 1. Between February and May 2020, DNP (the respondent in the present proceedings) and a registered partnership (the “Partnership”) entered into eight contracts for the sale-and-purchase of raw cashew nuts by DNP, to the Partnership. Due to COVID-19 lockdowns, delivery dates were extended: [9]–[12]. 2. On 24 July 2020, the parties executed a Memorandum of Understanding (“MOU”) setting out, among others, the Partnership’s payment obligations. In essence, the MOU required the Partnership to (a) pay a 10% deposit of arrived cargo value to Company N (a subsidiary of DNP), and a 10% advance of arrived cargo value to DNP within 30 days of the date of the MOU (the “MOU Advances”); (b) pay all clearing costs, demurrages, warehouse rental, insurance and security charges to Company N within 10 days of clearing cargo (the “Clearing Charges”); and (c) clear all goods against payment within 90 days of the MOU ( ie , by 22 October 2020): [7], [15]–[21]. 3. The Partnership failed to make required payments under the MOU, leading DNP to terminate the agreement on 1 October 2020 and sell the cargo to third parties: [27]–[28]. 4. Company N received eight post-dated cheques from the Partnership in respect of the Clearing Charges. The Partnership later issued stop-payment instructions due to quality concerns and suspicions about cargo sales, and five cheques were dishonoured. Between January and April 2021, Company N commenced five proceedings in the Indian courts, seeking to recover INR30,300,000 in clearing charges (the “Indian Court Proceedings”): [31]–[32]. 5. DNP subsequently commenced arbitration against the Partnership. The arbitration was administered by the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (the “SIAC”). On 25 July 2024, the arbitral tribunal (the “Tribunal”) issued an award in favour of DNP, awarding DNP damages of US$33,009.53 and INR22,432,076.68 (the “Award”): [1], [5]. OA 4 6. On 21 October 2024, DNO applied to set aside the Award on grounds of breach of natural justice under s 24( b ) of the International Arbitration Act 1994 (2020 Rev Ed) (the “IAA), and conflict with the public policy of Singapore under Art 34(2)( b )(ii) of the UNCITRAL Model Law : [1], [3]. Issues before the Court 7. The court identified four issues for determination: [33]. a. The “Standing Issue”: Did DNO have standing to make the application for the setting aside of the Award? b. The “Natural Justice Issue”: i. Did the Tribunal’s refusal of the Partnership’s application to amend its Defence and Counterclaim in the arbitration (the “Amendment Application”) involve a breach of the rules of natural justice in connection with the making of the Award, whereby the rights of the Partnership/DNO were prejudiced? ii. With respect to four particular matters in the Award, did the Tribunal’s findings and conclusions as to those matters or any one of them involve a breach of the rules of natural justice in connection with the making of the Award whereby the rights of the Partnership/DNO were prejudiced? c. The “Public Policy Issue”: Did certain conduct of DNP mean that the Award was in conflict with the public policy of Singapore? The Standing Issue 8. The court identified the following legal principles as relevant to the Standing Issue: [37]–[41]. a. The law of the place of incorporation of a foreign corporation governed issues relating to incorporation ( JX Holdings Inc and another v Singapore Airlines Ltd [2016] 5 SLR 988 at [21]; Dicey, Morris and Collins on The Conflict of Laws vol 1 (Lord Collins of Mapesbury and Professor Jonathan Harris gen ed) (Sweet & Maxwell, 16th Ed, 2022) at paras 30-010–30-012). In this case, the court looked to the law of India. b. The legal test which DNO had to satisfy in order to establish standing was whether the legal personality of the Partnership merged into and was assumed by DNO such that they were, for all intents and purposes, the same entity ( National Oilwell Varco Norway AS (formerly known as Hydralift AS) v Keppel FELS Ltd (formerly known as Far East Levingston Shipbuilding Ltd) [2022] 2 SLR 115 at [24]–[25]). c. The content and effect of foreign law was a matter of fact and was to be proved in the same way as any other matter of fact ( EFT Holdings, Inc and another v Marinteknik Shipbuilders (S) Pte Ltd and another [2014] 1 SLR(R) 860 at [54]; Pacific Recreation Pte Ltd v SY Technology Inc and another appeal [2008] 2 SLR(R) 491 (“ Pacific Recreation ”) at [54]). “Raw sources” of foreign law may be admissible pursuant to s 59(1)( b ) of the Evidence Act 1893 (2020 Rev Ed) ( Pacific Recreation at [55]–[60]). However, the court was not obliged to accord evidentiary weight to raw sources. d. The Singapore International Commercial Court Rules 2021 (the “SICC Rules”) contained rules dealing with the adducing of expert evidence (O 14 of the SICC Rules) and proof of foreign law (O 16 of the SICC Rules). In this case, DNO did not pursue either avenue for the purpose of establishing Indian law. 9. In the supporting affidavit to the application, a representative of DNO (“Mr A”) stated that the Partnership had been dissolved under Indian laws and converted into a private limited company, DNO, on 31 March 2024: [43]. 10. In the response affidavit, a representative of DNP (“Mr Z”) adduced evidence demonstrating that the Partnership continued to file GST Returns even after its purported dissolution. This formed the basis of DNP’s submission that the Partnership continued to exist as a separate entity, and DNO accordingly had no standing to challenge the Award: [43]–[45]. 11. In a further reply affidavit, Mr A adduced the following items of evidence: [46]–[52]. a. DNO’s Certificate of Incorporation dated 30 March 2024; b. an application filed under s 366 of the Companies Act, 2013 (India) (the “Indian Companies Act”), along with various supporting documents; and c. a document signed by DNO’s chartered accountant, dated 21 May 2020, which referred to the conversion of the Partnership to DNO. 12. Section 366 of the Indian Companies Act, as DNO asserted, pertained to the power of a partnership firm to register as, among other alternatives, a company limited by shares: [48]. 13. Mr A also acknowledged that the Partnership had been filing GST Returns, but said that these were filed on a “zero-rated basis since June 2024”, and that DNO was in the process of deregistering the Partnership’s GST registration: [53]–[54]. 14. The court held that the legal personality of the Partnership had merged into and was assumed by DNO, such that they were, for all intents and purposes, the same entity: [58]–[59]. a. The court placed limited weight on s 366 of the Indian Companies Act; finding that the provision, together with the documents previously referred to above, established that there was power for a registered partnership to register as a company limited by shares in India: [56]. b. The application under s 366 of the Indian Companies Act, the documents accompanying the application, and the fact that DNO’s Certificate of Incorporation was issued almost immediately after the application, provided strong support for that conclusion: [58]. c. While the existence of the GST Returns had to be taken into account, it was significant that they recorded nil taxable supplies inward and outward, and that Mr A gave evidence that DNO was in the process of cancelling the Partnership’s GST registration: [58]. 15. Accordingly, DNO had standing to challenge the Award and apply to have it set aside: [60]. The Natural Justice Issue 16. DNO alleged two separate breaches of natural justice in relation to (a) the Tribunal’s denial of the “Amendment Application”; and (b) purportedly “inconsistent and/or defective” reasoning on the part of the Tribunal in the Award: [61]. The Amendment Application 17. In the Amendment Application, the Partnership sought to raise the Indian Court Proceedings as a defence to DNP’s claims. In essence, it argued that there was a risk of double recovery as Company N was already claiming for the Clearing Charges in Indian courts: [69]. 18. The Tribunal denied the Amendment Application and gave its reasons with respect to four relevant considerations, being (a) delay in making the application; (b) disruption in progressing the arbitration to a substantive hearing; (c) prejudice to DNP if the application was allowed; and (d) prejudice to the Partnership if the application was not allowed. Before the court, DNO advanced criticisms against the Tribunal’s reasons: [65], [74]–[84]. 19. In respect of the first three considerations, the court considered that DNO’s criticisms were not justified, and in any event, were far removed from a breach of natural justice: [80]–[81]. 20. In respect of the fourth consideration, DNO submitted that the Tribunal failed to deal with essential issues and failed to attempt to consider and comprehend the parties’ submissions. In this regard, DNO’s submission was that, by the proposed amendments, it sought to raise two matters which, if successful at trial, would constitute a defence to DNP’s claim for recovery of the Clearing Charges: [84]. 21. The court found, in respect of both matters, that the Tribunal had considered and addressed the matter. The court considered that the Tribunal complied with its duty to deal with the essential issues, and to consider and comprehend the parties’ submissions. Even if the Tribunal erred in fact or law, that was not sufficient to establish a breach of natural justice. Further, the court noted that the Tribunal had considered and rejected the matters raised by the proposed amendments in the Award: [94]–[103]. 22. Even if the breach of natural justice was made out, DNO was not entitled to rely on it as a ground for setting aside the Award: a. DNO had not established real or actual prejudice by the assumed breach of natural justice; it had not shown that the outcome of the arbitration would or could reasonably be different had the assumed breach not occurred. In fact, the Tribunal had addressed the very argument the Partnership sought to raise by the Amendment Application, in the Award: [107]– [114]. b. Further, DNO had waived its right to complain. Following China Machine New Energy Corp v Jaguar Energy Guatemala LLC and another [2020] 1 SLR 695 (“ China Machine ”) at [170], a party could not “hedge” against adverse results by warehousing a complaint of breach of natural justice until the outcome of the arbitration was known. The Amendment Application occurred at an interlocutory stage of the arbitration process and sometime before the evidentiary hearing. Thereafter, the Partnership proceeded on the basis that it was ready, willing and able to participate in the arbitration, which it subsequently did. It did not complain about the alleged breach of natural justice until after the Tribunal issued the Award: [115]–[12 6]. Four Matters 23. DNO identified four matters where it alleged the Tribunal's reasoning was inconsistent or defective: [12 8]. a. First, on contractual penalty: DNO argued the Tribunal failed to apply contractual penalties for a shipment of cargo which was below the contractually specified quality (the “Burkina Faso 023 Cargo”), which would have reduced the contract price, and the eventual damages awarded to DNP. b. Second, on discount: DNO contended there was an agreement that, in addition to the penalty, DNP would provide a discount to the contract price for the Burkina Faso 023 Cargo, and the Tribunal had incorrectly found otherwise. DNO pointed to an email dated 2 September 2020, which it contended that the Tribunal failed to consider. c. Third, on the agreement for termination of the MOU: DNO challenged the Tribunal's finding that parties agreed DNP could terminate for non-payment by 30 September 2020. DNO also argued that the Tribunal was inconsistent with the reasoning it applied in determining that there was no agreement on the discount, but that there was an agreemen t in relation to DNP’s right to terminate the MOU. The alleged inconsistency was that the Tribunal considered subsequent emails when finding that there was no agreement on a discount, but found an agreement regarding the termination of the MOU despite subsequent emails. d. Fourth, on alternative grounds for termination of the MOU: DNO disputed the Tribunal's conclusion that DNP had additional termination rights under the contractual documents. 24. The court found the following: a. In relation to the first matter, DNO did not identify how any of the arguments it raised constituted a breach of natural justice. Even if the Tribunal did err in its findings, those were errors of fact or law which do not constitute a breach of natural justice: [13 5]–[142]. b. In relation to the second matter, parties had, in formulating the list of issues, referred to the email dated 14 September 2020. The Tribunal considered the submissions which were put to it. The suggestion that the Tribunal “completely ignored” the fact that an agreement was reached on 2 September 2020 was unfair in view of the case put to it. Further, it was not correct to say that the Tribunal ignored the email dated 2 September 2020; the Tribunal referred to the email in a footnote: [14 3]–[155]. c. In relation to the third matter, DNO’s argument was not developed beyond an assertion that the Tribunal overlooked the subsequent emails dated 14, 21 and 25 September respectively. The court found that the Tribunal had referred to those emails in the Award. Further, in the ordinary case, a party would be hard-pressed to sustain such an argument where there were two different alleged agreements arising in two different factual circumstances: [15 7]–[165]. d. In relation to the fourth matter, although DNO challenged the Tribunal’s interpretation of clauses in the MOU, the court found that the Tribunal had considered the possible constructions of cl 1(a) and decided against the construction advanced by the Partnership. The court also found that there was no substance in DNO’s argument that the Tribunal erred in concluding that cll 4 and 6 of the MOU were conditions of the MOU. The Tribunal dealt with the arguments clearly and comprehensively: [16 6]–[170]. The Public Policy Issue 25. An award may be set aside where the court is satisfied that it is in conflict with the public policy of Singapore (Art 34(2)( b )(iii) of the Model Law). DNO argued that the Award was in conflict with the public policy of Singapore: [173]. a. DNP filed Import General Manifests (“IGMs”) with Indian customs authorities declaring Company N as owner of the Remaining Cargo (which arrived after the date of the MOU). DNO contended that (i) if DNP was the owner of the Remaining Cargo, it followed that the declarations or statements to the effect that Company N was the owner of the Remaining Cargo were false, and the provision of false declarations or statements was an offence under s 132 of the Customs Act, 1962 (India) (the “Indian Customs Act”); and (ii) assuming that the declarations or statements in the IGMs were correct, Company N was the owner of the Remaining Cargo and the party entitled to seek damages; DNP was not entitled to seek and recover damages: [17 4]–[176]. b. In respect of invoices issued by DNP to Company N for the Remaining Cargo (the “Invoices”), DNO submitted that the Invoices were backdated and fabricated; the Tribunal had erred in admitting the Invoices into evidence despite the Partnership’s objection that they were not authentic. Further, DNO submitted that the provision of backdated invoices to the Indian customs authorities was an act which meant that the Award was in conflict with the public policy of Singapore: [17 7]–[179]. 26. The court identified the following relevant principles: [18 1]–[185]. a. The public policy ground was a narrow one: PT Asuransi Jasa Indonesia (Persero) v Dexia Bank SA [2007] 1 SLR(R) 597 at [59]. b. The fact of illegality under foreign law was not sufficient to warrant the setting-aside of an arbitral award: DBX and another v DBZ [2023] SGHC(I) 18 at [133] . c. In Sacofa Sdn Bhd v Super Sea Cable Networks Pte Ltd and another [2025] 3 SLR 209 (at [52]–[53]), the court was not prepared to make a finding of a breach of a law of a foreign jurisdiction in the absence of expert evidence. 27. In respect of the IGMs, DNO did not call any evidence as to the content of Indian law. All it did was to identify s 132 of the Indian Customs Act and tender the IGMs. The court found that such an approach was insufficient. In the absence of expert evidence supporting DNO’s submission, a finding could not be made that DNP committed an offence under s 132 of the Indian Customs Act, in relation to the IGMs: [18 8]–[193]. 28. Further, even if DNP did commit an offence under s 132 of the Indian Customs Act, there were two other grounds for rejecting DNO’s submission . First, DNO did not show a sufficient nexus between the illegality and the Award. Secondly, a breach of foreign law was not sufficient by itself to establish that an award was in conflict with the public policy of Singapore. There was no evidence that the Award would have been contrary to the public policy of India. Further, the upholding of such an award could not be characterised as an act which would “shock the conscience” or “violate the forum’s most basic notion of morality and justice”, or was “clearly injurious to the public good” or “wholly offensive to the ordinary reasonable and fully informed member of the public”: [19 4]–[196]. 29. In respect of the Invoices, the court found that the Tribunal considered and rejected the Partnership’s argument that the Invoices should not have been admitted into evidence because the documents were not authentic. The court considered that it was difficult to see how the Tribunal’s ruling on the admissibility of evidence of that nature could amount to a breach of natural justice or bring the Award into conflict with public policy. In any event, the Tribunal had found that the Invoices were not fabricated nor backdated with a view to mislead: [19 7]–[199]. Further Submissions by DNO 30. DNO made further submissions arguing that DNP was not the proper party to claim damages and that only Company N, as cargo owner, could bring such an action. The court rejected these submissions. a. DNO submitted that the Tribunal had failed to consider the issue of the proper claimant for all of the claims made by the Partnership in the arbitration. The court found that the issues raised had been considered by the Tribunal: [202] –[203]. b. DNO submitted that the Tribunal, in addressing the issue of title, did not take into account the IGMs or the Invoices. The court found that the Tribunal had addressed the issue of title, and was not required to address every item of evidence relied on by the party who seeks a particular finding. Further, there was no prejudice to DNO: [20 4]. c. DNO also submitted that in circumstances where Company N was the owner of the Cargo (or at least, the Remaining Cargo), only Company N could bring an action for loss and damage in relation to the Cargo. The court considered that this was not an argument of a breach of natural justice, but an argument going to the merits of the Tribunal’s decision: [20 5]. Conclusion 31. The court dismissed OA 4 in its entirety: [20 6]. This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s judgment. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s judgment.

case_name: THE MANAGEMENT CORPORATION STRATA TITLE PLAN NO. 561 v KOSMA HOLDINGS PTE LTD
subject_tags: ["Land — Easements — Rights of way — Section 99 of the Land Titles Act 1993 (2020 Rev Ed)", "Land — Easements — Rights of way — Section 97A of the Land Titles Act 1993 (2020 Rev Ed)", "Injunctions — Mandatory injunction — Order to remove structures that have been installed", "Injunctions — Prohibitory injunction — Order to restrain from impeding or obstructing entry of vehicles", "Evidence — Admissibility of evidence — Secondary evidence when the original subdivision plan has been lost"]
court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 17 September 2025 Case Summary MCST Plan No 561 v Kosma Holdings Pte Ltd [2025] SGHC 185 General Division of the High Court — Originating Application No 608 of 2025 and Summons No 1687 of 2025 Philip Jeyaretnam J Decision of the General Division of the High Court Outcome: The General Division of the High Court declined to imply an easement over the respondent’s land under s 99 of the Land Titles Act 1993 (2020 Rev Ed) (“LTA”), but held that it would create an easement under s 97A if s 97A(2)( c ) (which requires the applicant to have made all reasonable prior attempts to obtain the easement) was fulfilled. It thus granted time for parties to exchange proposals concerning the easement, as well as leave to file supplementary submissions thereafter. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment •  The court could not imply an easement under s 99 of the LTA because the applicant was unable to produce the subdivision plan of the land (or any corresponding secondary evidence) to prove that it was appropriated or set apart for use as a service road. •  Easement of a right of way over the service road was reasonably necessary for the effective use of the mall, particularly, in connection with refuse collection as well as loading and unloading. Using the land as a mall was also not inconsistent with the public interest, and the respondent could be adequately compensated for any loss that might arise from the creation of the easement. Hence, it was appropriate to create an easement under s 97A if s 97A(2)( c ) was fulfilled. Introduction 1 This was an application by the management corporation of a mall (“the MCST”) for the grant of an easement on the respondent’s land. By way of background, the MCST managed the mall’s loading/unloading bay (the “Loading Bay”) and the rubbish centre located within the Loading Bay. The Loading Bay could only be accessed by vehicles via a service road, which the respondent owned. 2 The MCST contracted with a waste management company for refuse collection. However, the respondent refused to allow refuse collection trucks free entry into the Loading Bay. It also implemented measures which hindered refuse collection. Further, it began imposing administrative fees of $1,000 for each count of unauthorised entry. In short, the respondent had taken steps to fully monetise its ownership of the service road by charging access fees for refuse collection trucks. These measures caused great difficulty for the mall’s daily refuse removal and caused significant delay to the delivery of goods to the subsidiary proprietors of the mall. The MCST hence brought this application seeking: (a) the implication of an easement under s 99(1) of the land Titles Act 1993 (2020 Rev Ed) (“LTA”); or (b) the creation of an easement under s 97A(1) of the LTA. Decision on s 99(1) of the LTA 3 Section 99 of the LTA provided for the implication of easements, including rights of way, where land has been developed and subdivided as may be: (a) necessary for the reasonable enjoyment of the now subdivided lots (or buildings on them); in so far as these have been (b) “appropriated or set apart”; (c) on the subdivision plan: at [13] . The subdivision plan 4 The starting point was to look at the subdivision plan submitted to the competent authority. The party seeking to imply an easement needed to adduce said plan in evidence and show that the easement was appropriated or set apart on it. In this case, such plan was not adduced in evidence. Instead, only a certified plan was adduced: at [18]−[19] . 5 The certified plan was not the subdivision plan. While this was not in itself fatal to the application, it gave rise to the question as to whether the land for the easement had been “appropriated or set apart” on the subdivision plan. In this regard, since the subdivision plan could not be produced despite parties’ best efforts, s 67(1)( c ) of the Evidence Act 1893 (“EA”) was potentially relevant to allow secondary evidence to be given instead: at [21]−[23] . 6 However, the certified plan did not fall within the definition of “secondary evidence” under s 65 of the EA. The court therefore could not imply an easement through s 99 of the LTA: at [25] −[26] . Appropriated or set apart 7 For completeness, the court observed that had it been open to it to do so, it would have accepted the certified plan as secondary evidence to establish the inference that the approved subdivision plan “set apart” the service road using the label “service road”, as was done in the certified plan. Having regard to the Land Transport Authority’s Code of Practice for street work proposals relating to development works, the court observed that the service road catered to the servicing needs of the Loading Bay (including the bin centre): at [27]−[28] . Necessary for the enjoyment of the mall 8 Finally, the court observed that it would also have been necessary, for the reasonable enjoyment of the mall, that there be an implied right of way to and from the bin centre located within the Loading Bay, albeit limited to refuse trucks, such that either refuse trucks could enter without charge or rubbish bins could be wheeled out: at [30] and [38] . Decision on s 97A of the LTA 9 The purpose behind the introduction of s 97A of the LTA was to facilitate more efficient and optimal use of land: at [43] . Section 97A(1) of the LTA 10 The first question which had to be considered was whether an easement of a right of way over the service road was reasonably necessary for the effective use of the mall. Three considerations were relevant: (a) whether the proposed use of the land was reasonable compared to the alternative uses; (b) whether the proposed easement was reasonably necessary for that proposed use; and (c) the effect of the grant on the owner of the affected land: at [44]−[45] . 11 The court further observed that: (a) the qualifier “reasonably” applied to the word “necessary” loosened the requirement of necessity as compared to s 99 of the LTA, which had no such qualifier; (b) the phrase “effective use” focused the inquiry on the impact of the land in question, and carried an additional consideration of degree which was absent in s 99 of the LTA; and (c) the provision for adequate compensation allowed the creation of an easement even where it entailed some disadvantage to the land owner burdened by it, but permitted for adequate compensation to be made. However, (d) the court had to exercise caution in the creation of easements: at [47] . 12 Without access to the Loading Bay via the service road, the mall could not effectively function for its built purpose as a mall. Use of the service road in connection with refuse collection was categorically necessary while use of the service road for loading and unloading was at the very least reasonable and substantially preferable to alternative methods of loading and unloading. Moreover, the service road was always intended to serve the Loading Bay (including the bin centre). An easement of way over the service road to the Loading Bay was thus reasonably necessary for the use of the mall, satisfying s 97A(1) of the LTA: at [48]−[5 1] . Sections 97A(2)( a ) and ( b ) of the LTA 13 It was obvious that the use of the mall as a mall was not inconsistent with the public interest. Section 97A(2)( a ) of the LTA was thus satisfied. Section 97A(2)( b ) of the LTA was also satisfied, since t he respondent could be adequately compensated for the creation of the easement. In assessing adequate compensation under this subsection, the court could determine on whom the duty to maintain the land would lie: at [51] . Section 97A(2)( c ) of the LTA 14 Section 97A(2)( c ) of the LTA required the MCST to make all reasonable attempts to obtain the easement directly from the respondent prior to the court making the order. This was not yet done. Since this requirement was not a condition precedent to the application but only to the making of the order, the court granted the MCST time to fulfil this requirement, as well as to consider adequate compensation to the respondent for creation of the easement: at [52] . Conclusion 15 Having decided that it would not imply an easement under s 99 of the LTA, but would create an easement if s 97A(2)( c ) of the LTA was fulfilled, the court granted parties time to exchange proposals concerning the easement, as well as leave to subsequently file supplementary submissions: at [53] .
