case_name: NADARAJAN S/O CHIDAMBARAM v ESWARI D/O NATARAJAN
subject_tags: ["Insolvency Law — Bankruptcy — Statutory demand — Setting aside of statutory demand claiming judgment debt based on intended challenge to the judgment debt"]
summary:
**Facts**
The claimant, Nadarajan s/o Chidambaram, is the brother of the late Mr C Nathan. The defendant, Eswari d/o Natarajan, is the executrix of the Estate of C Nathan, Deceased. Ms Eswari previously commenced District Court Suit No 787 of 2022, claiming that Mr Nadarajan held $90,000 on trust for Mr Nathan, an arrangement recorded in Mr Nathan’s will. On 22 December 2025, the court entered judgment for the sum of $90,000 against Mr Nadarajan, who did not appeal the decision.

On 7 June 2026, Ms Eswari served a statutory demand on Mr Nadarajan for $128,316, comprising the judgment sum in DC 787, costs for the trial and various interlocutory applications and a registrar’s appeal, and interest. Under r 67(2)(b)(i) of the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution (Personal Insolvency) Rules 2020, Mr Nadarajan was required to apply to set aside the statutory demand by 21 June 2026, which he failed to do.

On 26 June 2026, Mr Nadarajan commenced Originating Application (Bankruptcy) No 64 of 2026, seeking an extension of time to apply to set aside the statutory demand and a stay of all enforcement proceedings until the conclusion of Family Court Originating Claim No 13 of 2025 (FC 13). In FC 13, Mr Nadarajan seeks to have the will declared null and void on the grounds that Mr Nathan was blind when he executed it and the legal requirements for such execution were not complied with. Mr Nadarajan contended that success in FC 13 would provide grounds to set aside the debts in the statutory demand. He explained his five-day delay in applying to set aside the statutory demand by claiming uncertainty regarding the consequences of bankruptcy on his claim in FC 13 and uncertainty as to whether the pending FC 13 proceedings constituted grounds for setting aside the statutory demand.

**Holding**
The court dismissed Originating Application (Bankruptcy) No 64 of 2026, refusing both the extension of time and the stay of enforcement. Costs were fixed at $2,109 (all-in) in favour of the defendant.

**Reasons**
The court noted that the application raised a point of principle regarding whether a debtor can set aside a statutory demand claiming a judgment debt when there is a pending challenge to that judgment debt, an issue the court observed had not been considered in reported case authorities.

Under r 67(4) of the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution (Personal Insolvency) Rules 2020, the court considers four factors when deciding whether to grant an extension of time: (a) the period of the delay; (b) the reasons for the delay; (c) the grounds for setting aside the statutory demand; and (d) the prejudice that might result from an extension of time, as established in Koh Kim Teck v Shook Lin & Bok LLP [2021] 1 SLR 596.

The court found the period of delay was short and not motivated by tactical reasons, and an extension would not prejudice Ms Eswari. However, the pivotal factor was the merit of the intended grounds for setting aside the statutory demand under r 68(2) of the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution (Personal Insolvency) Rules 2020. The court found Mr Nadarajan's case failed under every sub-paragraph of r 68(2):

1. Under r 68(2)(a), Mr Nadarajan had no valid counterclaim, set-off or cross-demand of equivalent value, as the relief sought in FC 13 was a declaration that the will was invalid, not a monetary sum.
2. Under r 68(2)(b), the debts were judgment debts. Citing Chia Kok Kee v Tan Wah [2024] SGHC 216 and paragraph 160(2) of the Supreme Court Practice Directions 2021, the court held that a court exercising bankruptcy jurisdiction will not go behind a judgment debt to inquire into its validity.
3. Under r 68(2)(c) and (d), there were no allegations that Ms Eswari held security in breach of the rules or that r 64 regarding the form of the demand had been breached.

case_name: The Tata Power Company Limited v Kleros Capital Partners Limited
subject_tags: ["Arbitration — Award — Recourse against award — Infra petita challenge", "Arbitration — Award — Recourse against award — Setting aside — Breach of natural justice", "Arbitration — Award — Recourse against award — Breach of natural justice — Whether tribunal demonstrated apparent bias"]
court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 26 August 2026 Case summary The Tata Power Company Limited v Kleros Capital Partners Limited [2026] SGHC(I) 15 Singapore International Commercial Court — Originating Application Nos 13, 24 and 25 of 2025 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of S Mohan J, Anthony Besanko IJ and Anthony Meagher IJ (grounds of decision delivered by S Mohan J): Outcome: The Singapore International Commercial Court (“ SICC ”) dismissed all three applications to set aside the tribunal majority’s quantum award. The applicants failed to establish that the tribunal had breached the rules of natural justice or failed to adhere to the agreed arbitral procedure by omitting to decide the issues of causation, remoteness and mitigation. The applicants also failed to establish that the majority of the tribunal was apparently biased by reason of, inter alia , undisclosed connections to the third-party funder financing the respondents’ claim. Background 1 The dispute arose from Tata’s breaches of a non-disclosure agreement, which breaches an arbitral tribunal (constituted under the SIAC Rules) found had deprived Kleros of the opportunity to secure a favourable outcome in relation to a coal mining project In Kamchatka, Russia. The tribunal issued a unanimous liability award finding Tata liable, and subsequently, a majority of the tribunal (the “ Majority ”) issued a quantum award (the “ Quantum Award ”) assessing Kleros’s loss on a loss of chance basis. Kleros’s claim in the arbitration was funded by Omni Bridgeway Limited (“ Omni Bridgeway ”). 2 Tata brought three originating applications seeking to set aside the Quantum Award and related relief. The applications raised two broad categories of challenge: first, that the Majority had failed to decide essential issues going to the quantum of Kleros’s loss; and second, that members of the Majority had undisclosed connections to Omni Bridgeway giving rise to apparent bias. 3 Specifically, Tata sought to set aside the Quantum Award on the following grounds: (a) that the Majority breached the rules of natural justice under s 24( b ) of the International Arbitration Act and/or failed to adhere to the agreed arbitral procedure under Article 34(2)( a )(iv) of the Model Law by failing to decide essential issues of causation, remoteness and mitigation (the “ Causation Issue ”, “ Remoteness Issue ” and “ Mitigation Issue ” respectively); and (b) that the Majority demonstrated apparent bias under s 24( a ) of the International Arbitration Act, by reason of undisclosed connections between members of the Majority and Omni Bridgeway (the “ Apparent Bias Issue ”). Decision On the Causation Issue, Remoteness Issue and Mitigation Issue 4 On the Causation Issue, a preliminary issue was whether Tata’s central argument that the Majority had failed to determine but-for causation by reference to an agreed “No Breach Scenario” counterfactual was a new ground of challenge not raised in the originating application or supporting witness statement, and therefore, whether it was time-barred. The SICC found that the thrust of Tata’s original case was that the Majority had failed to have regard to pre-March 2016 events and to conduct a breach-by-breach analysis, which was materially different from the complaint now advanced. All grounds of challenge must be clearly articulated with sufficient particularity in the originating application and supporting witness statement, and a party cannot rely on passing and undeveloped references therein to reserve the ability to formulate substantially different grounds at a later stage. Accordingly, the argument raised by Tata was a new argument that was time-barred: at [ 55] – [59] . 5 Substantively, neither party had specifically identified but-for causation as an issue to be decided in their respective versions of the Memorandum of Issues. Nor was there any reference to an agreed counterfactual or its precise content and parameters. The Tribunal’s own formulation of the remaining issues to be decided, which substantially adopted Kleros’s version, likewise contained no specific reference to but-for causation or the No Breach Scenario. The court nonetheless gave Tata the benefit of the doubt and proceeded to consider whether, on a close, commercial and reasonable reading of the Quantum Award, a virtually inescapable inference arose that the Majority had completely failed to determine but-for causation by reference to the “No Breach Scenario” counterfactual: at [ 64] – [ 71] . 6 On the Causation Issue, the SICC found that the Majority had applied its mind to and determined the issue, even if its reasoning was not always explicitly articulated. The Majority had accepted Kleros’s submissions on what the No Breach Scenario counterfactual specifically entailed and had proceeded on that basis when accepting the evidence of certain witnesses. The Majority had also addressed each of Tata’s numerous arguments on why Kleros could not have developed the project on its own or with a third party. The Majority’s repeated references to “a real and substantial chance”, together with the heading “But for Tata’s breaches…” and the express reference to the but-for test at in various paragraphs of the Quantum Award, constituted evidence demonstrative of the issue of causation being present in the Majority’s mind. As Tata’s complaint that the Majority failed to conduct a breach-by-breach analysis, that was not how Tata argued its case in the arbitration. On the Causation Issue, Tata’s complaints were in substance no more than a veiled attempt at challenging the merits of the Quantum Award, which was not justiciable before the court: at [72] – [85] . 7 On the Remoteness Issue, the SICC held that there is no requirement for a tribunal to address each issue in a clearly demarcated and separate section of its award. The Majority was entitled to deal with the issues in the manner it saw fit. The Majority had addressed remoteness, finding Tata’s remoteness arguments to be “much too wide” and accepting that loss of chance damages are recoverable wherever the essence of the breach includes depriving the claimant of the relevant opportunity. The Majority had analysed remoteness and foreseeability together with causation, and in any event, the Quantum Award made plain that the Majority had found that the loss of opportunity was not too remote. Tata’s challenge was again in substance an attempt to re-argue the merits of the case: at [ 86] – [ 98] . 8 On the Mitigation Issue, the SICC found Tata’s objections to be the clearest example of an attempt to challenge the merits of the Quantum Award under the guise of a due process challenge. The Majority had first addressed the anterior question of whether the mitigation principle was legally relevant, and concluded that it was not. The Majority was entitled to take a different view of the law even if the parties had proceeded on a different basis, as a tribunal is not bound to accept either party’s contentions on a point of law. In any event, the Majority went on to analyse the substance of the parties' arguments and evidence on mitigation, and expressly rejected Tata’s mitigation arguments. Whether that decision was right or wrong was entirely immaterial and not a question before the court. The SICC accordingly dismissed Tata's objections on the Mitigation Issue, finding no breach of natural justice by the Majority: at [99] – [103] . 9 Tata accepted that its objection on breach of the agreed arbitral procedure was inextricably bound up with its infra petita objection, and would fall if the court found no breach of natural justice. As the SICC dismissed all of Tata’s natural justice objections on the Causation, Remoteness and Mitigation Issues, the objection based on breach of the agreed arbitral procedure equally fell away. In light of the SICC’s conclusion that there was no breach of natural justice or of the agreed arbitral procedure, the question of remitting the Quantum Award was rendered moot: at [104] – [106] . On the Apparent Bias Issue 10 The SICC applied the well-established test of whether a reasonable, fair-minded and informed observer, knowing all the relevant facts, would have a reasonable suspicion that a fair determination of the dispute was not possible. Tata’s challenge was limited to three points: that Prof Boo had not disclosed his appointment in an ICSID arbitration where Omni Bridgeway was the funder of one of the parties; that Prof Boo had failed to disclose his close personal and professional relationship with Mr Benjamin Hughes, a member of Omni Bridgeway’s investment committee. Tata argued that Mr Hughes and Prof Boo were members of the same arbitration chambers, were also tenants in the same set of barrister’s chambers in the UK and also at one time lectured in the Faculty of Law at the National University of Singapore. Tata also complained that Mr Isaacs KC had not disclosed his appointment as sole arbitrator in an LCIA arbitration where Omni Bridgeway was similarly the funder of one of the parties. 11 As a preliminary matter, the SICC found that Tata’s (unsuccessful) challenge brought before the SIAC Court was time-barred, but did not find it necessary to decide whether the application before it was similarly time-barred: at [107] – [113] . 12 On the merits, the SICC dismissed Tata’s objections. None of the appointments of Prof Boo or Mr Isaacs KC had been made by or at the instance of Omni Bridgeway, any of the parties, or counsel involved in the Arbitration, and the mere fact that Omni Bridgeway happened to be the funder in those unrelated cases did not, without more, give rise to any apparent bias. As for the alleged close relationship between Prof Boo and Mr Hughes, their shared membership in the same chambers or university did not establish a relationship of the kind material to apparent bias. Prof Boo’s uncontroverted confirmation that he had never communicated with Mr Hughes about Omni Bridgeway’s involvement was given weight by the Court. The SICC found Tata’s complaints to be those of a party that was unduly sensitive rather than of a reasonable, fair-minded observer, and dismissed this ground accordingly: at [114] – [124] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s judgment. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court's judgment.
summary:
**Facts**
The applicant, The Tata Power Company Limited (“Tata”), is an Indian power generation and coal mining company. The respondent, Kleros Capital Partners Limited (“Kleros”), is a British Virgin Islands investment advisory firm. Kleros had identified a large-scale coal extraction project involving the Krutogorovo deposit (“Deposit”) in Russia, which required significant infrastructure and Russian federal government support. On 27 August 2013, Kleros approached Tata as a potential co-investor. The parties entered into two non-disclosure agreements (“NDAs”) dated 21 September 2013 and 16 September 2014 (the latter found by the tribunal to be an extension of the first).

The NDAs required Tata to maintain the confidentiality of “Confidential Information” (defined in clause 1.5) and included a “Non Circumvention” obligation (clause 20 of the 2013 NDA and clause 19 of the 2014 NDA) prohibiting Tata from exploiting the information or entering into transactions to circumvent Kleros’s economic interest. In the second half of 2015, the relationship strained over disputes regarding equity participation and leadership of the bid for the mining licence. By March 2016, the relationship effectively ended. While the 2014 NDA was still in force, Kleros unsuccessfully sought replacement partners. Kleros eventually did not bid for the licence in December 2017 and wound down its Russian operations. After the 2014 NDA expired on 15 September 2017, Tata’s Russian subsidiary, FENR, bid for and was granted the mining licence on 22 January 2018, though Tata later determined the project was not viable.

Kleros was restored to the company register in the British Virgin Islands on 17 November 2020 and commenced two arbitrations against Tata on 30 November 2020, alleging that Tata breached the NDAs by misusing confidential information and acting in bad faith to exclude Kleros from the project. The SIAC consolidated these into a single Arbitration on 11 February 2021. In 2021, Tata offered the mining licence to Kleros at the price Tata had paid for it, but Kleros rejected the offer. FENR subsequently requested to surrender the licence on 28 January 2022, which the Russian federal government accepted on 25 April 2022.

The arbitral tribunal consisted of Prof Lawrence Boo (presiding arbitrator), Mr A K Ganguli SA (nominated by Tata), and Mr Stuart Isaacs KC (nominated by Kleros). The proceedings were bifurcated. On 26 September 2023, the tribunal unanimously issued a Liability Award finding Tata liable for misusing confidential information in breach of clause 3.3 of the NDAs, circumventing Kleros in breach of clause 19 of the 2014 NDA, and breaching its contractual duty of good faith. Specifically, the tribunal found Tata misused confidential information to advance the project while intending to exclude Kleros, made false statements to Kleros, and concealed its intention to supplant Kleros. These findings were based on Tata excluding Kleros from dealings with third parties (including Geosolutions LLC, ROSMORPORT, KPMG, Sistema JSFC, RDIF, Sberbank, and FondVostok), misleading Kleros about meetings in Mumbai, and engineering the postponement of the mining licence auction.

On 1 July 2025, the tribunal issued the Quantum Award (Award No. 094 of 2025). A majority comprising Prof Boo and Mr Isaacs KC valued the project at US$1,021,500,000 as of the 2016 breach and fixed Kleros’s loss of chance at 60%. Tata was ordered to pay US$490,320,000 in damages (the average of two development scenarios), plus simple interest at 5.33% per annum from 30 November 2020. Tata was also ordered to pay Kleros’s legal costs of S$8,289,020.64 with interest. Mr Ganguli SA dissented, finding that Tata’s breaches did not deprive Kleros of the chance to bid or pursue the project, and instead proposed negotiating damages of US$13,500,000 plus interest, with each party bearing its own costs.

On 27 August 2025, the tribunal issued a Final Award (SIAC Award No. 129 of 2025) regarding costs.

**Holding**
The court dismissed OA 13, OA 24 and OA 25 in their entirety. It held that Tata’s challenge regarding the Majority’s alleged failure to decide the issue of causation on the basis of a “No Breach Scenario” counterfactual was time-barred. The court further found that Tata’s substantive submissions on the causation issue, the “Remoteness Issue”, and the “Mitigation Issue” were without merit, as there was no breach of natural justice or of any agreed arbitral procedure. The court also rejected Tata's allegations of apparent bias against Prof Boo and Mr Isaacs KC.

**Reasons**
The court found that the Majority’s detailed analysis of evidence and arguments in the Quantum Award demonstrated that the case was decided on its merits, and Tata failed to provide evidence of a danger that a fair determination of the dispute was not possible.

case_name: TAN SZE SHAN v GAIN CITY BEST-ELECTRIC PTE LTD
subject_tags: ["Civil Procedure — Judgments and orders — Enforcement — Whether judgment remains capable of enforcement after attempted performance by judgment debtor", "Civil Procedure — Judgments and orders — Enforcement — Whether judgment debtor’s inputs can be obtained before determining application for an enforcement order made without notice"]
summary:
**Facts**
Tan Sze Shan (the Applicant) purchased an ASUS Laptop Ryzen 7 4700U from Gain City Best-Electric Pte Ltd (the Respondent) for $1,586.00. Following a claim in the Small Claims Tribunal, an order (the SCT Order) was issued requiring the Respondent to provide a one-to-one replacement laptop by 25 February 2022 (the First obligation). In default of this, the Respondent was required to pay the Applicant $1,586.00 by the same date (the Second obligation). On or before 25 February 2022, the Respondent attempted to deliver a brand new replacement laptop of the same make and model, but the Applicant rejected the delivery because he believed it lacked the full manufacturer warranty. After more than four years of dormancy, the Applicant issued two Letters of Demand in May 2026 and subsequently filed an enforcement application without notice under O 22 r 2(3) of the Rules of Court 2021 to attach up to $2,586 from the Respondent’s bank accounts, comprising the $1,586 principal sum, $500 for the Bailiff, and $500 for the Applicant.

**Holding**
The application for an enforcement order is dismissed.

**Reasons**
The court found that the Respondent performed the First obligation by making a one-to-one replacement available to the Applicant within the stipulated time, as "provide" ordinarily means to make available. The Applicant’s rejection of the laptop based on a lack of warranty did not place the Respondent in default because the SCT Order did not expressly require the replacement to have a full manufacturer warranty, nor did the original purchase order. The court held that attributing such a requirement to the Tribunal Magistrate would be "wholly unreasonable and unjust" and would impermissibly enlarge the terms of the order. Consequently, the Second obligation to pay $1,586 never arose, leaving no unsatisfied obligation capable of enforcement under O 22 r 2(1) of the Rules of Court 2021.

In interpreting the SCT Order, the court characterized it as an ordinary court order rather than a contractual consent order. The court cited Hoban Steven Maurice Dixon and another v Scanlon Graeme John and others [2007] 2 SLR(R) 770 to support the principle that court orders must be interpreted reasonably. Additionally, the court cited GNC Holdings LLC v ONI Global Pte Ltd and another [2026] SGHC(I) 11 to emphasize that the court's role is to enforce an award, not to rehear an application to vary the award or grant improvements to the orders.

case_name: DUP v DUQ
subject_tags: ["Civil Procedure — Mareva injunctions — Real risk of dissipation", "Civil Procedure — Proprietary injunction — Balance of convenience", "Civil Procedure — Proprietary injunction — Fortification of damages"]
summary:
**Facts**
The claimant, DUP, is a British Virgin Islands incorporated company operating a crypto native neobank powered by its own native governance and utility token. The respondent, DUQ, is an Australian citizen and former Chief Strategy Officer of DUP, employed under an independent contractor agreement. In her role, DUQ provided ecosystem partnership services, managed relationships with overseas investors, coordinated exchange listings, and maintained designated sub-accounts and API access (including keys, secret keys, and passphrases) on various platforms for DUP.

The dispute concerns the beneficial ownership of 20,000,000 Tokens (“Disputed Tokens”) and 500,000 USDT (collectively, the “Disputed Coins”), valued at approximately US$1,250,107.43, which DUP transferred to accounts held by DUQ on 2 May 2025. DUP contends the transfer was for DUQ to provide liquidity for market making via designated sub-accounts to ensure segregation from DUQ's personal assets. DUQ contends the Disputed Coins were transferred as agreed compensation for her contributions—specifically for remaining with the company, closing a successful Series A funding round, and convincing two partners to purchase a block of Tokens on the secondary market—and that she is the beneficial owner. DUP alleges that DUQ refused to return the coins after becoming dissatisfied with her remuneration. On 16 February 2026, DUP obtained a proprietary injunction (PI) and a worldwide freezing order (WFO) against DUQ on an ex parte basis.

**Holding**
The court set aside the worldwide freezing order (WFO). However, the court ordered that the proprietary injunction (PI) be maintained, subject to the condition that DUP provide notional fortification of the undertaking as to damages in the amount of US$125,000 to be paid into court within three weeks, failing which the PI shall be discharged. The court further found that DUP had not abused the court's process and had not breached its duty of full and frank disclosure.

**Reasons**
The court determined that on the balance of convenience, the proprietary injunction should remain in place. The court applied the requirements for granting a PI as set out in American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd [1975] AC 396 and adopted in Bouvier, Yves Charles Edgar v Accent Delight International Ltd [2015] 5 SLR 558, which require that there be a serious question to be tried and that the balance of convenience lie in favour of the injunction.

Regarding the first stage of the test, the court cited Group Lease Holdings Pte Ltd (in liquidation) v Group Lease Public Co Ltd [2025] 3 SLR 1315 to note that the threshold for a serious question to be tried is modest; the court only considers whether the claim is not frivolous or vexatious. The court found a serious question to be tried because DUP provided contemporaneous messages regarding API access to sub-accounts and DUQ had admitted awareness that these sub-accounts were for market making.

For the second stage, the court applied the two-stage analysis from Group Lease Holdings to determine the balance of convenience: first, whether damages would be an adequate remedy and whether the respondent is in a financial position to pay them; and second, the overall balance of convenience. The court found that damages would not be an adequate remedy for DUP because the value of the Disputed Coins is difficult to quantify due to cryptocurrency-specific factors, and a potential "dump" of the Tokens by DUQ could cause irreparable harm. Conversely, the court found that DUQ could be adequately compensated in damages via the price difference of the Disputed Coins.

The court further noted that a Court of Appeal decision affirming the SICC's decision in Novo Nordisk regarding the dismissal of a setting aside application for a WFO did not impact the decision in the present case.

case_name: PT SRI REJEKI ISMAN TBK & 7 Ors
subject_tags: ["Insolvency Law — Cross-border insolvency — Recognition of foreign\ninsolvency proceedings"]
court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 26 August 2026 Case summary Re PT Sri Rejeki Isman Tbk [2026] SGHC(I) 16 Singapore International Commercial Court — Originating Application No 7 of 2026 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of Christopher S. Sontchi IJ: Outcome: The Singapore International Commercial Court (“SICC”) allowed the application to recognise Indonesian insolvency proceedings as foreign main proceedings under the UNCITRAL Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency (“Model Law”). Background to the dispute 1 The first to fourth applicants (“Sritex Indonesian Entities”) are companies in liquidation in Indonesia. The Sritex Indonesian Entities were part of a textile conglomerate. All of the Sritex Indonesian Entities were incorporated in Indonesia and headquartered in Central Java. The Sritex Indonesian Entities had undergone restructuring proceedings, but had since been declared bankrupt by the Semarang Commercial Court and Indonesian Supreme Court (“Indonesian Bankruptcy Proceeding”). 2 The fifth to eighth applicants (“Curators”) were appointed in the course of the Indonesian Bankruptcy Proceeding.  In the course of the Indonesian Bankruptcy Proceeding, the Curators were authorised to take “all necessary legal measures to enhance the bankruptcy estate in the Republic of Singapore”. 3 Prior to the Indonesian Bankruptcy Proceeding, certain subsidiaries of the Sritex Indonesian Entities had issued senior notes (“Notes”), which were listed on the main board of the Singapore Exchange Securities Trading Limited. The Curators had stated on affidavit that they were unaware of how the proceeds of the Notes were used, whether they flowed to the Sritex Indonesian Entities, or whether they had been held in Singapore. 4 The Curators therefore commenced SIC/OA 7/2026 to seek recognition of the Indonesian Bankruptcy Proceeding as foreign main proceedings under the Model Law. In addition to the automatic moratorium that follows the recognition of a foreign main proceeding under Art 20(1)( a ) of the Model Law, the applicants sought additional specific relief, which may be broadly categorised as follows: a. First, a stay of, among other things, the enforcement of security over any property of the Sritex Indonesian Entities situated in Singapore (“Extended Stay Relief”). This was sought pursuant to Art 21(1)( g ) of the Model Law. b. Second, the power to examine witnesses, to take evidence and to obtain delivery of information concerning the Sritex Indonesian Entities’ property, affairs, rights, obligations or liabilities in Singapore, specifically to trace the proceeds of the Notes and to ascertain how such proceeds were used (“Investigative Relief”). This was sought pursuant to Arts 21(1)( d ), 21(1)( g ) and, alternatively, Art 21(1), of the Model Law. c. Third, the power to exercise various rights in relation to the Sritex Indonesian Entities’ assets, such as the power to administer the Sritex Indonesian Entities’ property in Singapore and to take into custody and collect the documents and papers of the Sritex Indonesian Entities, among other things (“Administrative Relief”. This was sought pursuant to Art 21(1)( e ), or alternatively the chapeau of Art 21(1), of the Model Law. The court’s decision 5 The Indonesian Bankruptcy Proceeding was a foreign main proceeding under the meaning of the Model Law. The Indonesian Bankruptcy Proceeding was conducted under a law relating to insolvency, and the Curators were “foreign representatives” under the meaning of the Model Law. In addition, the centre of main interests of the Sritex Indonesian Entities was Indonesia. The Sritex Indonesian Entities had their registered offices in Indonesia, operated in Indonesia, and were managed in Indonesia. This meant that the automatic reliefs under Art 20 of the Model Law applied: at [20]–[24] . 6 The SICC found it appropriate to grant the Extended Stay Relief. While secured creditors generally stood outside of the collective insolvency process, such that it would normally be inappropriate to stay the enforcement of security, this was not invariably the case. Under Art 21(1) of the Model Law, the court is empowered to grant “any appropriate relief”. Although the Extended Stay Relief was ordinarily granted in judicial management and not liquidations, it was observed that the English courts have similarly viewed the Extended Stay Relief as appropriate depending on the facts of the case. The SICC observed that while the Extended Stay Relief should ordinarily not be granted, the court’s discretion to grant such a relief could be exercised where the facts before the court indicated that the enforcement of security may compromise or deplete the pool of assets that should be available for distribution to creditors, or where such relief would enhance or preserve the pool of assets available for distribution: at [26]–[38] . On the facts of the case, it was appropriate to grant the Extended Stay Relief. Key personnel of the Sritex Indonesian Entities had been investigated in Indonesia for fraud, embezzlement and corruption, and these allegations gave rise to a concern that security may have been granted illegitimately. Coupled with the fact that the Curators had thus far been unable to trace the use or receipt of the proceeds of the Notes, it was appropriate to grant the Extended Stay Relief, such that secured creditors would need to seek leave of the court before enforcing security: at [38] . 7 The SICC found it appropriate to grant the Investigative Relief. The SICC provided guidance on the appropriate test for the grant of such relief where foreign representatives sought general investigative powers to make inquiries, rather than disclosure orders against specific individuals. The appropriate test was found in the chapeau of Art 21(1), that the relief sought must be “necessary to protect the property of the debtor or the interests of the creditors”: at [42]–[51] . 8 The SICC found it appropriate to grant the Administrative Relief. Such relief was appropriate as it would allow the Curators to administer, collect, or liquidate the Sritex Indonesian Entities’ assets, thereby increasing their assets or reducing their debts. Such relief would not place the Curators on any different footing to Singapore-appointed liquidators. The Administrative Relief was granted subject to the condition that the applicants seek the leave of the court before distributing assets or funds, and before repatriating funds or assets out of Singapore: at [ 55]–[57] . 9 The SICC therefore allowed the application, recognised the Indonesian Bankruptcy Proceeding as foreign main proceedings under the Model Law, and granted the additional reliefs sought. This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.
summary:
**Facts**
The first to fourth applicants, PT Sri Rejeki Isman Tbk, PT Sinar Pantja Djaja, PT Bitratex Industries, and PT Primayudha Mandirijaya (collectively the "Sritex Indonesian Entities"), are Indonesian companies and members of the Sritex Group. Following financial difficulties in 2021, the Sritex Indonesian Entities entered into a court-supervised restructuring proceeding (PKPU) and obtained a composition plan ratified by the Semarang Commercial Court (the "Homologation Decision"). Upon the Sritex Indonesian Entities' failure to comply with the repayment schedules, the Semarang Commercial Court annulled the Homologation Decision and declared the Sritex Indonesian Entities bankrupt, a decision subsequently affirmed by the Indonesian Supreme Court (the "Indonesian Bankruptcy Proceeding"). The Sritex Indonesian Entities are currently being investigated by Indonesian authorities for corruption, fraud, and embezzlement, with former personnel arrested for the disbursement of fraudulent loans and embezzlement of loaned funds.

The fifth to eighth applicants, Denny Ardiansyah, Nur Hidayat, Fajar Romy Gumilar, and Nurma Candra Yani Sadikin (the "Curators"), were appointed in the Indonesian Bankruptcy Proceeding and authorised to take all necessary legal measures to enhance the bankruptcy estate in Singapore. The application sought to investigate the operations and finances of two subsidiaries, Golden Legacy Pte Ltd and Golden Mountain Textile and Trading Pte Ltd (collectively the "Sritex Singaporean Entities"). In 2016, 2017, and 2020, the Sritex Indonesian Entities and the Sritex Singaporean Entities issued senior notes ("Notes") listed on the Singapore Exchange Securities Trading Limited totaling US$725,000,000; the Curators seek to trace the use and flow of these proceeds.

**Holding**
The court granted the application to recognize the Indonesian Bankruptcy Proceeding as foreign main proceedings. The court also granted additional relief sought by the Curators, including Extended Stay Relief (a stay of the enforcement of security over any property of the Sritex Indonesian Entities in Singapore), Investigative Relief (the power to examine witnesses, take evidence, and obtain information to trace the proceeds of the Notes), and Administrative Relief (the power to administer the Sritex Indonesian Entities’ property in Singapore and to take into custody and collect their documents and papers), subject to the condition that no assets or proceeds thereof may be repatriated out of Singapore or distributed without the leave of the court.

**Reasons**
The court found that the requirements for granting recognition under the UNCITRAL Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency, as adopted in Singapore via s 252 and the Third Schedule of the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act 2018 (2020 Rev Ed) ("IRDA"), had been satisfied. Specifically, the procedural requirements in Art 15 of the Model Law were met.

The court determined that the centre of main interests (COMI) of the Sritex Indonesian Entities was Indonesia. Applying the presumption in Art 16(3) of the Model Law and the principles in Re Fullerton Capital Ltd [2025] 1 SLR 432, the court held that raising funds in Singapore did not displace the presumption that their registered office was their COMI. Consequently, the Indonesian Bankruptcy Proceeding was recognized as a "foreign main proceeding", triggering automatic reliefs under Art 20 of the Model Law.

Regarding Investigative Relief under Art 21(1)(d) and Administrative Relief under Art 21(1)(e), the court held that the appropriate test was whether the relief was "appropriate relief" and "necessary to protect the property of the debtor or the interests of the creditors" per the chapeau of Art 21(1).

case_name: Sean Kerwin Mathews & Anor  v Singapore Recreation Club & 11 Ors
subject_tags: ["Civil Procedure — Striking Out", "Unincorporated Associations and Trade Unions — Friendly Societies —Meetings"]
summary:
**Facts**
The claimants, Sean Kerwin Mathews and Mu Yee Shyong, are ordinary members of the billiards section of the first defendant, the Singapore Recreation Club. The second to 12th defendants are members of the 127th Management Committee of the Singapore Recreation Club. The dispute arises from a Statement of Claim filed by the claimants in HC/OC 968/2025, in which they seek a declaration that Resolution 1a was invalid, a declaration that the passing of Resolution 1a contravened r 37 of the Constitution, and an injunction to restrain the defendants from carrying out the proposed works under Resolution 1a.

The dispute relates to a Transformation Works Plan proposed by the Singapore Recreation Club on 2 February 2024, which included a Relocation Plan to move the billiards room from level two of the clubhouse to basement two and convert the level two space into a co-working space. On 24 March 2024, an extraordinary general meeting approved the Transformation Works Resolution, authorising the Management Committee to carry out the works with a maximum budget of $16,620,231, including a contingency sum of $1,510,930 for an anticipated Land Betterment Charge (LBC).

The actual LBC required was $4.9m, leading the Management Committee to determine that the Relocation Plan was not financially viable. Consequently, a notice was issued for an extraordinary general meeting (EOGM) on 18 October 2025 to vote on three options: Resolution 1 (approving the $4.9m LBC payment to proceed with the Relocation Plan), Resolution 1a (abandoning the Relocation Plan to convert the billiards room into a co-working space), or Resolution 1b (abandoning the Relocation Plan to integrate the billiards room within a co-working space on level two).

The voting mechanism used two voting slips. Voting Slip 1 required a “Yes” or “No” vote for Resolution 1 and included a directive that “Voting Slip 2 is not applicable for tick to ‘YES’ box”. Voting Slip 2 required members to tick “Yes” for either Resolution 1a or Resolution 1b. If Resolution 1 passed by a simple majority, votes for Voting Slip 2 would not be counted. If Resolution 1 failed, the Club would proceed with whichever resolution in Voting Slip 2 received the higher number of votes; in the event of a tie, the Club would proceed with either at its discretion. Members could abstain by leaving boxes unticked, while ticking both boxes for Resolution 1, or both for Resolutions 1a and 1b, would result in spoilt votes.

On 10 October 2025, the Management Committee published a “2nd EOGM of the 127th MC Q&A” document, stating that while members could reject both Resolutions 1a and 1b by abstaining, the Management Committee would proceed based on whichever option received the most votes to keep the Transformation Works on schedule. On 14 October 2025, 143 members petitioned the Club’s general manager, Mr James Lee, to table a resolution allowing members to reject both Resolutions 1a and 1b. At the EOGM, Mr Lee responded to similar requests by stating that members could reject a resolution either by not voting (blank vote/abstention) or by casting a “NO” vote.

Following the EOGM, the Management Committee announced the results: Resolution 1 failed (32 in favour, 514 against). For Voting Slip 2, Resolution 1a received 151 votes in favour and 125 against (with 183 spoilt and 55 blank votes), while Resolution 1b received 125 votes in favour and 151 against (with 192 spoilt and 46 blank votes). Consequently, Resolution 1a was declared passed.

The claimants' causes of action are: (a) the Simple Majority Voting Threshold Claim, asserting that r 37 of the Constitution required Resolution 1a to be decided by a majority of all members present (at least 280 of 559), which 151 votes did not meet; (b) the Blank Votes Claim, asserting that the 55 blank votes for Resolution 1a should be construed as votes against it per the Q&A instructions, meaning Resolution 1a failed; (c) the Invalidity of Q&A Instructions Claim, asserting that if blank votes are not counted as votes against, the Q&A instructions were contrary to r 37 of the Constitution; and (d) the Curtailment of Members’ Right to Vote Claim, asserting the outcome was illegitimate because there was no resolution to reject both 1a and 1b, and those voting for Resolution 1 were precluded from voting on 1a and 1b.

**Holding**
The court allowed the appeal against the Assistant Registrar’s decision and declined to strike out any of the claimants’ claims. The defendants were ordered to pay the claimants costs of $30,000 and disbursements of $1,901.83.

**Reasons**
The court found that the Curtailment of Members’ Right to Vote Claim was not an abuse of process.

case_name: YDF v YDG
subject_tags: ["Family Law — Custody", "Family Law — Custody — Access", "Family Law — Maintenance — Wife", "Family Law — Maintenance — Child", "Family Law — Matrimonial assets — Division"]
summary:
**Facts**
The parties, YDF (the Husband) and YDG (the Wife), are Indian nationals residing in Singapore. They married in India on 18 January 2013 and have one son, born in 2016. The Husband is an institutional trader, while the Wife is a homemaker holding an undergraduate degree and a Master of Science in International Management from the University of London. The parties previously resided in Hong Kong before moving to Singapore in 2019. On 5 August 2022, the Husband filed for divorce on the ground of the Wife's behaviour. An Interim Judgment (IJ) was granted on 12 October 2023. The current dispute concerns ancillary matters, specifically the custody, care and control of the son, the identification and valuation of the pool of matrimonial assets, the division of those assets, and maintenance for the Wife and the son. The court noted that the parties have been extremely litigious, filing over two dozen applications and 51 affidavits, and that both parties have been generally not forthcoming with evidence, lacking frank and full disclosure.

The Husband's employment history is as follows: he worked for the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation (“HSBC”) in India at the time of marriage (earning approximately S$4,166 per month), for HSBC in Hong Kong from 2016 to 2018 (approximately S$11,700 per month), for Natwest in Singapore in 2019 (approximately S$25,000 per month), for Bunge in Singapore from 2020 to 2021 (approximately S$20,000 per month), and for Barclays in Singapore (approximately S$25,000 per month). Following a period of unemployment from February 2023 to March 2024, he worked in India from April 2024 to June 2024 (approximately S$2,000 per month) before securing a post in Singapore in July 2024 earning approximately S$37,500 per month, with a contract ending in October 2026.

On 12 October 2023, the Family Courts issued an interim custody and access order (FC/ORC 5016/2023), which provided for joint custody with joint decision-making on education, religious upbringing, and medical treatment/vaccinations. The order granted the Husband specific weekday and weekend access to the son, remote access via video calls twice weekly, and prohibited either party from taking the son out of Singapore without the other's permission or a court order.

**Holding**
The court granted the Husband's request for joint custody, rejecting the Wife's request for sole custody. The court ordered that the Wife shall have sole care and control of the son. Regarding access, the court held that the provisions of the interim access order (FC/ORC 5016/2023) should stand, rejecting the Wife's request for supervised-only access and the Husband's request for overnight access and unsupervised access. The court further declined the Husband's request to bring the son overseas and ordered that during school holidays, the Husband shall have access thrice a week on mutually agreed days and times, with the son to be returned by 9.30pm if access occurs in the evening.

Regarding the pool of matrimonial assets, the court held that the appropriate date for identification is the date of the IJ, 12 October 2023. The court identified the following as matrimonial assets: (1) the contents of bank accounts in the Husband’s name as at the date of the IJ (totaling S$63,524.17 across accounts with HSBC Singapore, HSBC India, HSBC Hong Kong, DBS, ICICI Bank, State Bank of India, and Bank of India); (2) the Husband’s share portfolio (14,000 HSBC HK shares, 6,000 Mirion Technologies shares, and 150,000 Industrial and Commercial Bank of China shares), valued as at the date of the AM hearing at S$637,241.34; and (3) gold and jewellery, specifically a gold chain held by the Husband (S$1,000), a gold necklace (S$20,800), two jewellery purchases (S$5,000), and jewellery given by the Husband to the Wife (S$5,000), totaling S$31,800. The total value of the pool of matrimonial assets was determined to be S$732,565.51.

The court rejected the Wife's valuation of the pool (between S$23,486,834 and S$26,054,971), finding it based on projected earning capacity rather than actual evidence. The court further held that the Husband's Standard Chartered bank account was not a matrimonial asset as it was opened in July 2024, after the date of the IJ. The court also declined to include any properties or business interests in India, or other alleged undisclosed assets, into the matrimonial pool.

The court ordered the matrimonial assets to be divided 75% to the Husband and 25% to the Wife. The Husband is to pay the Wife S$152,341.43 (representing 25% of the pool less the value of jewellery in her possession). For maintenance, the Husband is to pay the Wife a lump sum of S$90,360. For the son, the Husband is to pay S$2,600 per month plus education costs for three years from the date of judgment; thereafter, the Husband and Wife shall bear 75% and 25% of the son's maintenance respectively.

case_name: Shipworks Engineering Pte Ltd and another v Sembcorp Marine Integrated Yard Pte Ltd and another and another appeal
subject_tags: ["Contract — Breach", "Civil Procedure — Striking out", "Contract — Contractual discretion"]
court_summary: SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 27 August 2026 Case summary Shipworks Engineering Pte Ltd and another v Sembcorp Marine Integrated Yard Pte Ltd and another and another appeal [2026] SGHC(A) 22 Appellate Division of the High Court — Civil Appeals Nos 36 and 42 of 2025 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of the Appellate Division of the High Court (delivered by Kannan Ramesh JAD): Outcome: The Appellate Division of the High Court ( “Appellate Division”) allowed both appeals in part. The plaintiffs’ appeal (AD/CA 36/2025 (“AD 36”)) succeeded on four substantive matters: (i) the plaintiffs were entitled to rely on the Plaintiffs’ Timesheets (“PT”s) in the Plaintiffs’ Set of Documents (“PSD”) as the operative documents for Manpower Jobs, save that any Matching PT (being a PT in the Defendants’ Set of Documents (“DSD”) identical to a PT in the PSD) tainted by a forged Section Engineer’s signature could not be relied upon to support the claim; (ii) the plaintiffs succeeded on their quantum meruit claim for eight of the twelve Sub-Task Jobs ( “STJs”) for which invoices had not been issued (“Non-Invoiced STJ”s); (iii) the plaintiffs succeeded on their Miscellaneous Jobs claim; and (iv) the defendants’ counterclaim in HC/S 1042/2020 (“Suit 1042”) for moneys paid on 19 Work Orders (“WO”s) in respect of which the plaintiffs brought no claims was dismissed. The defendants’ appeal (AD/CA 42/2025 (“AD 42”)) succeeded only on the question of how administrative charges were to be calculated (“Quantum Issue”). Both parties’ cross-appeals on pre-judgment interest were dismissed, save that the award of pre-judgment interest on the Suit 1042 counterclaim fell away consequentially with the dismissal of that counterclaim. Pertinent and significant points of the judgment • The PTs were the operative documents for Manpower Jobs, being more accurate and reliable than the Defendants’ Timesheets (“DT”s) and Weekly Timesheets (“WT”s), and having been accepted and acted upon by the defendants in making progress payments. • The defendants had not validly put the authenticity of the PTs in the PSD in issue, as their pleadings focused on documents in the DSD, and their Notice of Non-Admission was filed out of time without explanation. • In any event, the plaintiffs have established the authenticity of the PTs in the PSD. • The defendants could only impugn the PTs in the PSD by proving forgery of a Matching PT in the DSD; a forged signature of the defendants’ section engineer (“Section Engineer”) on a Matching PT was fatal, but a forged signature of the defendants’ section manager (“Section Manager”) alone was not. • By failing to challenge the authenticity of the Job Completion Reports (“JCRs”) or the Section Engineer’s signatures therein for the Non-Invoiced STJs, the defendants effectively conceded that the work had been verified and performed. • For Miscellaneous Jobs, the unsigned Work Completion Reports (“WCR”s) and Transport Supply Timesheets (“TST”s), read in context, constituted sufficient contemporaneous evidence of performance, and the defendants failed to discharge their evidential burden of showing that the work was not done. • Clause 9(a) of the Contractor’s Registration Agreement (“CRA”) and Subcontractor Registration Agreement (“SRA”) applied only to the valuation of work in progress, and not completed work; clause 17 was the operative provision for final payment, and any discretion thereunder had to be exercised in good faith and not arbitrarily or capriciously. • The defendants’ Suit 1042 counterclaim failed because the defendants did not discharge their burden of proving that the payments they sought to claw back were made on the basis of forged or fabricated operative documents, given the poor housekeeping of the defendants and the plaintiffs’ credible explanation that they had disposed of supporting documents for fully paid WOs. • The plaintiffs’ claim was not struck out for forgery, as the forgeries that were established did not corrupt the trial process to the degree that fair adjudication was impossible. • On the administrative charges, the defendants were entitled to levy the 1% administrative charge every time a new partial payment invoice or request was submitted after 27 July 2018. For the purpose of computing the quantum of each administrative charge, the 1% charge applied to the total partial payments made in relation to that WO thus far, whether or not the constituent partial payments were themselves made after 27 July 2018. However, the total administrative charge collected each time must not exceed 4% of the total amount of partial payments made within any given contract year starting from 27 July 2018. 1 AD 36 is the plaintiffs’ appeal and AD 42 is the defendants’ cross-appeal, both arising from the decision of a Judge of the High Court in HC/S 1040/2020 (consolidated with HC/S 1042/2020, HC/S 1051/2020 and HC/S 1052/2020) (“Suit 1040”). The plaintiffs are Shipworks Engineering Pte Ltd (“Shipworks”) and Lanka Marine Services Pte Ltd (“Lanka”). The defendants are Sembcorp Marine Integrated Yard Pte Ltd (“SMIY”) and Jurong Shipyard Pte Ltd (“Jurong”). Background to the appeal and material facts 2 The defendants engaged the plaintiffs to perform three categories of work: Manpower Jobs (supply of manpower), STJs (sub-tasks such as spray-painting and high-pressure washing), and Miscellaneous Jobs (miscellaneous services such as toilet cleaning and the supply of lorry cranes). The parties’ relationships were governed principally by a few agreements including (a) the SRA, entered into between Lanka and Jurong on 13 May 2009, (b) the CRA, entered into between Shipworks and Jurong on 10 April 2014, and (c) the Administrative Charges Agreements between SMIY and each of Shipworks and Lanka respectively, dated 27 July 2018: at [ 5]–[8] . 3 The plaintiffs claimed at trial a total of $26,589,879.95 for 203 unpaid invoices across the three categories of work and on quantum meruit for 12 completed Non-Invoiced STJs. The defendants counterclaimed for $20,822,519.59, comprising alleged overpayments on irregular invoices, administrative charges under the Administrative Charges Agreements, and a separate counterclaim in HC/S 1042/2020 (“Suit 1042”) for moneys paid on 19 WOs in respect of which the plaintiffs brought no claims: at [2]–[ 3] . 4 The Judge below partially allowed both the claim and the counterclaim. The Judge’s decisions are recorded in the Liability Judgment ( Shipworks Engineering Pte Ltd v Sembcorp Marine Integrated Yard Pte Ltd [2024] SGHC 325) and the Quantum Judgment ( Shipworks Engineering Pte Ltd v Sembcorp Marine Integrated Yard Pte Ltd [2025] SGHC 40). The Judge found that the plaintiffs’ claims stood or fell by the PTs in the PSD, that some of the PTs bore forged or fabricated signatures, that the defendants had a contractual discretion to value the plaintiffs’ works subject to a Wednesbury reasonableness standard, and that the plaintiffs’ entire claim should not be struck out for forgery. The Judge refused to award pre-judgment interest to the plaintiffs and partially allowed the defendants’ claim for pre-judgment interest on their counterclaim: at [7 0]–[85] . Decision on appeal Manpower Jobs 5 The Appellate Division agreed with the Judge that the PTs were the operative documents for Manpower Jobs. The PTs were more accurate and reliable than the DTs and the WTs because they were verified daily by the Section Engineer on site and weekly by the Section Manager, whereas the data in the Defendants’ Online System (the defendants’ internal digital system for recording manpower data) was shown to be inaccurate. The defendants made progress payments (not mere advance payments) on the basis of the PTs, and their multi-layered approval system repeatedly approved such payments without objection. The Manpower Quotations, which were agreements for the plaintiffs to supply additional manpower to the defendants, also provided a contractual basis for the submission of the PTs. The defendants’ assertion that the PTs were unauthorised was rejected as commercially implausible and unsupported by credible evidence: at [96]–[111] . 6 The Appellate Division agreed with the Judge that the originals of the PTs in the PSD were delivered to the defendants by the plaintiffs. Mr Navin Kumar, who oversaw the business and operations of the plaintiffs as the sole director of both Shipworks and Lanka, gave consistent and unchallenged evidence that the originals were delivered by hand to the defendants’ finance department. The defendants’ evidence on the chain of custody of the Received Documents (being the documents the defendants claimed were received from the plaintiffs, forming part of the DSD) was internally inconsistent and demonstrated haphazard housekeeping of documents. The DSD was therefore not a comprehensive record of all documents received from the plaintiffs. As the originals were in the defendants’ possession, the plaintiffs were entitled to prove the PTs in the PSD by secondary evidence under sections 67(1)( a )(i), 67(1)( a )(ii) and 67(1)( c ) of the Evidence Act 1893 (2020 Rev Ed) (“EA”): at [112]–[120] . 7 The Appellate Division held that the defendants had not validly put the authenticity of the PTs in the PSD in issue. The defendants’ pleadings focused exclusively on documents in the DSD, and their Notice of Non-Admission dated 27 September 2023 was filed approximately 14 months out of time under Order 27 rule 4(2) of the Rules of Court 2014, without any explanation for the delay. Even if authenticity had been properly put in issue, it was established on the evidence through Mr Navin Kumar’s unchallenged account of the lifecycle of the PTs from preparation through to delivery and retention of copies. The defendants’ unchallenged failure to challenge the signatures of their representatives on the PTs in the PSD meant that those signatures were to be treated as genuine endorsements of the number of workers and hours worked recorded therein: at [121]–[137] . 8 The Appellate Division held that the defendants could only impugn the PTs in the PSD by proving forgery of an identical Matching PT in the DSD, since the defendants’ handwriting expert Ms Lee Gek Kwee (“Ms Lee”) examined only documents in the DSD. Where a Matching PT existed and the Section Engineer’s signature was established to be a handwritten forgery, that PT could not support the plaintiffs’ claim, as the Section Engineer was the only representative who independently verified the number of workers and hours worked for the WO in question. However, a forged Section Manager’s signature alone did not invalidate a PT if the Section Engineer’s signature was genuine. The Corresponding PTs (being the PTs in the DSD that relate to the same WO as a PT in the PSD but are not identical to it) in the DSD were unaffected by the forgery findings. The Appellate Division also held that the Judge erred in treating Faint Signatures (being signatures on the PTs that Ms Lee was unable to examine for genuineness) as rendering the relevant PTs inauthentic; Ms Lee had merely stated she could not examine them for genuineness, not that they were forged: at [138]–[154] . 9 The Appellate Division declined to strike out the plaintiffs’ entire claim. Applying the test in McDonald v Excalibur & Keswick Groundworks Ltd [2023] 1 WLR 2139 (“ Excalibur ”), the court must ask whether the litigant’s conduct is of such a nature and degree as to corrupt the trial process so as to put the fairness of the trial in jeopardy. The forgeries were limited to the Matching PTs and did not involve the systematic falsification of all disclosed documents or the giving of false evidence that made it impossible to distinguish authentic from fabricated evidence. The defendants were able to identify specific forged documents with expert assistance, demonstrating that the trial process retained its integrity. The defendants’ own ability to identify specific forged documents undermined their contention that the forgery had corrupted the entire trial process. Striking out the entire claim would be a wholly disproportionate remedy: at [155]–[169] . Sub-Task Jobs 10 The Appellate Division allowed Lanka’s appeal on the eight Non-Invoiced STJs (valued at $366,463.49) with only partially signed JCRs. The relevant inquiry was not whether Lanka had complied with contractual invoicing requirements, but whether the work was in fact done, given that the claim was framed in quantum meruit : at [179]–[181] . 11 The copies of the partially signed JCRs were admissible as secondary evidence under section 67(1) of the EA. The originals were in the defendants’ possession, having been handed over at a meeting with the defendants’ representatives in February 2020. The Judge’s finding that it was illogical for partially signed JCRs to have been returned to Lanka was based on a misreading of Mr Navin Kumar’s evidence and was unsustainable in light of the fact that the defendants challenged neither the authenticity of the JCRs nor the Section Engineer’s signatures on them: at [1 82]–[186] . 12 Mr Navin Kumar testified that the work was performed. The JCRs for the eight WOs constituted contemporaneous first-hand verification by the Section Engineer that the work was carried out. Mr Woi Cha How’s evidence is further and independent corroboration that the work was performed, his only reservation being as to contractual preconditions for payment rather than whether the work was done. The defendants failed to challenge the authenticity of the JCRs or the Section Engineer’s signatures therein, or adduce any positive evidence of non-performance. Therefore, Lanka has proven that the works in respect of the eight WOs were performed: at [1 87]–[194] . Miscellaneous Jobs 13 The Appellate Division allowed the plaintiffs’ appeal on the Miscellaneous Jobs. The plaintiffs’ alternative claim was in quantum meruit , so the relevant question was whether the work was done. WOs were issued for each Miscellaneous Job, and there was no evidence of any complaint of non-performance or engagement of alternative contractors. The WCRs and TSTs constituted contemporaneous evidence of performance; the TSTs in particular carried evidentiary weight as summaries of data from delivery orders signed by SMIY’s own engineers on site. The defendants failed to discharge their evidential burden of showing that the work was not done: at [19 5]–[204] . Administrative charges 14 The Appellate Division agreed with the Judge on the Entitlement Issue (being the threshold question of when the defendants were entitled to levy the contractually stipulated 1% administrative charge on partial payments): these administrative charges applied only to works performed and invoiced after 27 July 2018, as the chapeau of those agreements referred to “sub-contract work to be performed” by the plaintiffs: at [206]–[208] . 15 The Appellate Division disagreed with the Judge on the Quantum Issue. The plain language of clause 5 provided that the 1% administrative charge was based on the “total amount of advance/progress payments made” on each account, meaning the 1% multiplier applied to the cumulative total of all partial payments made under a given WO each time a new partial payment invoice or request was submitted after 27 July 2018, and not merely to the particular payment that triggered the charge. The Judge’s construction would have rendered the 4% per annum cap entirely redundant. However, the defendants’ construction was also not entirely accepted: the total administrative charge collected each time must not exceed 4% of the total amount of partial payments made within any given contract year starting from 27 July 2018: at [209]–[215] . Contractual discretion 16 The Appellate Division held that clause 9(a) of the CRA and SRA applied only to the valuation of work in progress, not completed work. Its purpose was to assess whether the plaintiffs’ progress was satisfactory, and it gave teeth to clause 9(b)’s right to suspend work. Extending clause 9(a) to final payment would allow the defendants to disregard agreed quotations or rates even after services were rendered, which would be commercially absurd and render clause 17 meaningless. The defendants’ reliance on clause 36 (which provided that headings were for convenience only) did not assist, as the conclusion that clause 9(a) was confined to work in progress rested on the language and structure of clause 9 read as a whole, not on its heading: at [2 21]–[224] . 17 Clause 17 was the operative provision for final payment. A true gap existed in the contracts as to the circumstances in which the defendants’ discretion under clause 17 could be challenged, since clause 9(a)’s fraud carve-out did not extend to clause 17. The Appellate Division implied a term that the defendants’ discretion under clause 17 must be exercised in good faith and not arbitrarily or capriciously, consistent with settled Singapore law. The Appellate Division noted that while the Judge applied a Wednesbury unreasonableness standard, the proper basis for the implied term was rooted in contract law and did not depend on transposing administrative law principles which Wednesbury unreasonableness was from. Where the defendants’ own representatives had verified and signed off on supporting documents at the material time, there was no room to retroactively reassess the extent of works completed. Where rates had been approved or agreed, any departure from those rates was, absent strong justification, arbitrary and capricious: at [22 5]–[232] . Suit 1042 counterclaim 18 The Appellate Division dismissed the Suit 1042 counterclaim which was one of three parts of the counterclaim by the defendants. The defendants bore the burden of proving that the payments they sought to claw back were made on the basis of forged or fabricated operative documents. Since the PTs were the operative documents, the defendants had to show either that the payment was made on the basis of a specific PT that was forged, or that no PTs were in fact submitted for the relevant WOs. The defendants failed on both counts. Their inconsistent evidence on the retrieval of documents cast serious doubt on the comprehensiveness and completeness of the DSD. The plaintiffs’ explanation that they had disposed of supporting documents for fully paid WOs was credible and unchallenged. The Judge erred in failing to consider this explanation and in treating the plaintiffs’ inability to produce the documents as a deliberate choice. The verified PTs were submitted for those WOs and subsequently misplaced by the defendants due to poor housekeeping: at [23 3]–[241] . Pre-judgment interest 19 The Appellate Division dismissed both parties’ cross-appeals on pre-judgment interest, subject to the consequential setting aside of pre-judgment interest on the Suit 1042 counterclaim. The plaintiffs were not awarded pre-judgment interest on their claims, as the action remained tainted by the forgeries established on the Matching PTs. The defendants were not awarded an earlier start date or a broader scope for pre-judgment interest on their counterclaim; the Judge’s award of interest from the date of the first Defence and Counterclaim was upheld as falling between the dates proposed by both parties. The award of pre-judgment interest on the Suit 1042 counterclaim was set aside consequentially with the dismissal of that counterclaim. The award of pre-judgment interest on the administrative charges, at 5.33% per annum from the date of the Defence and Counterclaim (Amendment No 1) to the date of the Liability Judgment, was upheld: at [242]–[248] . Conclusion 20 The Appellate Division directed the parties to agree on the sums payable on the claim and counterclaim in accordance with the judgment within 14 days, so that judgment may be entered for the appropriate amounts. Liberty to apply was granted in the event the parties were unable to agree. The issue of costs was reserved pending resolution of the quantum: at [2 50] . The specific orders were as follows: a. In AD 42 (defendants’ appeal), the appeal succeeded only on the Quantum Issue relating to administrative charges: the 1% administrative charge is to be calculated on the cumulative total of all partial payments made under each WO each time a new partial payment invoice or request is submitted after 27 July 2018, subject to a 4% per annum cap calculated from 27 July 2018. The defendants did not otherwise succeed on their challenges to the Judge’s findings on work processes, operative documents, authenticity, forgery, the striking out application, or the contractual discretion issue: at [249 (a)] . b. In AD 36 (plaintiffs’ appeal), the appeal succeeded on four substantive matters: (i) the plaintiffs are entitled to rely on the PTs in the PSD as the operative documents for Manpower Jobs, save that any Matching PT tainted by a forged Section Engineer’s signature cannot stand; (ii) Lanka’s quantum meruit claim for the eight Non-Invoiced STJs supported by partially signed JCRs (valued at $366,463.49) is allowed; (iii) the plaintiffs’ claim for Miscellaneous Jobs is allowed; and (iv) the Suit 1042 counterclaim is dismissed: at [249(b)] . c. On pre-judgment interest: the plaintiffs do not obtain interest on the claims on which they succeeded; the defendants obtain neither an earlier start date nor a broader scope for pre-judgment interest on claims allowed under their counterclaim; the award of pre-judgment interest on the Suit 1042 counterclaim is set aside consequentially; and the award of pre-judgment interest on the administrative charges at 5.33% per annum from the date of the Defence and Counterclaim (Amendment No 1) to the date of the Liability Judgment stands: at [249(c)] . This summary is provided to assist in the understanding of the Court’s grounds of decision. It is not intended to be a substitute for the reasons of the Court. All numbers in bold font and square brackets refer to the corresponding paragraph numbers in the Court’s grounds of decision.
summary:
**Facts**
Shipworks Engineering Pte Ltd and Lanka Marine Services Pte Ltd (the plaintiffs) provided three categories of services to Sembcorp Marine Integrated Yard Pte Ltd and Jurong Shipyard Pte Ltd (the defendants): “Manpower Jobs” (supplying manpower), “Sub-Task Jobs” (STJs, such as spray-painting and high pressure washing), and “Miscellaneous Jobs” (such as cleaning toilets and supplying lorry cranes). The relationships were governed by several agreements, including the Subcontractor Registration Agreement (SRA), the Subcontractor Work Agreement, the Contractor Registration Agreement (CRA), the 2018 CRA, and the Administrative Charges Agreements.

The plaintiffs claimed $26,589,879.95, consisting of $26,048,727.76 for 203 unpaid invoices and $541,152.19 on quantum meruit for 12 completed STJs for which invoices had not been issued. The defendants disputed the claim and counterclaimed for $20,822,519.59, comprising $20,384,284.41 for alleged overpayments on irregular invoices and $438,235.18 for administrative charges. The counterclaim was segregated into three parts: (a) moneys overpaid on allegedly irregular invoices and supporting documents; (b) administrative charges pursuant to the Administrative Charges Agreements; and (c) payments made on irregular invoices and supporting documents submitted by the plaintiffs in relation to 19 WOs on which the plaintiffs brought no claims (pursued in HC/S 1042/2020 (“Suit 1042”)).

The dispute involved significant contention regarding the authenticity, reliability, and relevance of documents, with the defendants alleging that some signatures of their representatives had been forged or fabricated. For manpower supply, the documents included Plaintiffs’ Timesheets (PTs), Daily Timesheets (DTs), and Weekly Timesheets (WTs). For STJs, they included Job Completion Reports (JCRs), Sub-Task Work Lists (STWLs), and Payment Summaries. For Miscellaneous Jobs, they included Work Completion Reports (WCRs) for toilet cleaning and Transport Supply Timesheets (TSTs) for lorry crane supply.

The parties disagreed on the billing process. For full payment, the plaintiffs submitted the original invoice, WO and supporting documents to the defendants’ Finance Department for multi-level review. For partial payments, the parties disputed whether these were progress payments for work performed (plaintiffs' view) or advances/loans for liquidity (defendants' view). Regarding Manpower Jobs, the defendants used a biometric security system for clock-in clock-out (“CICO”) data and a “Defendants’ Online System” (“DOS”) to record workers and hours. The plaintiffs contended that PTs verified by defendants' engineers were the primary records, while the defendants maintained that claims must be supported by DTs and WTs generated via the DOS.

**Holding**
The provided excerpts note that the appeals are cross-appeals from a High Court Judge who partially allowed both the claim and the counterclaim in the Liability Judgment ([2024] SGHC 325) and Quantum Judgment ([2025] SGHC 40).

The Court of Appeal:
1. Dismissed the defendants' appeal on invoiced STJs, preferring the PSD over the DSD.
2. Allowed Lanka’s appeal regarding eight Non-Invoiced STJs (valued at $366,463.49), finding that Lanka proved the work was carried out.
3. Allowed the plaintiffs’ appeal regarding Miscellaneous Jobs, finding the Judge erred in dismissing the claim.
4. Partially allowed the defendants' appeal on the administrative charges counterclaim, correcting the Judge's findings on the quantum of the charges.
5. Dismissed the defendants' appeal regarding the scope of their discretion under cl 9(a) and cl 17 of the CRA and SRA.
6. Dismissed the defendants' Suit 1042 counterclaim and set aside the pre-judgment interest associated with it.
7. Dismissed the cross-appeals on pre-judgment interest: the plaintiffs do not obtain interest on their successful claims; the defendants do not obtain an earlier start date or a broader scope for their pre-judgment interest; and the award of interest on administrative charges stands.

**Reasons**
The High Court Judge in the Liability Judgment analyzed the dispute by determining, WO by WO, whether the work and amount claimed were proved and the evidential weight of supporting documents.

On the nature of partial payments, the Court of Appeal affirmed the Judge's finding that they were progress payments. The Court found the defendants' multi-layered approval system made it incredible that payments were repeatedly approved without anyone noticing that PTs, rather than DTs/WTs, were the supporting documents.

Regarding contractual discretion, the Court of Appeal addressed cl 9(a) and cl 17 of the CRA and SRA:
1. Clause 9(a): The Court held that cl 9(a) concerns “Work Progress” and applies only to the valuation of work in progress; it does not apply to the valuation of completed works at the final payment stage.
2. Clause 17: This is the operative provision for final payment. Applying *Leiman, Ricardo v Noble Resources Ltd* [2018] SGHC 166, *Sembcorp Marine Ltd v PPL Holdings Pte Ltd* [2013] 4 SLR 193, and *Foo Jong Peng v Phua Kiah Mai* [2012] 4 SLR 1267, the Court implied a term that the discretion under cl 17 must be exercised in good faith and not arbitrarily or capriciously. The Court rejected the *Wednesbury* unreasonableness standard, citing *Carlsberg South Asia Pte Ltd v Pawan Kumar Jagetia* [2022] SGHC 74 and *MGA International Pte Ltd v Wajilam Exports (Singapore) Pte Ltd* [2010] SGHC 319 for the good faith standard.
3. Application: Where defendants' representatives verified and signed timesheets, those signatures constitute acknowledgments of work done; retroactive reassessment would be in bad faith.

The Judge addressed the defendants’ pleaded irregularities as follows:
1. Manpower Jobs: The Court of Appeal agreed that PTs are the operative documents. The absence of a WT was not fatal if a PT or DT established the claim. However, a forged Section Engineer’s signature on a PT is fatal to that PT. The Court found the Judge erred in treating "Faint Signatures" as inauthentic.
2. Suit 1042 Counterclaim: The Court held the defendants failed to discharge their burden of proof regarding the existence of forgeries and/or fabrications on which they sought to claw back payments on the operative documents. The Judge erred in assuming the plaintiffs "chose" not to produce supporting documents; the plaintiffs credibly explained they had disposed of documents from 2014 after receiving final payment. Because PTs were the operative documents, the defendants had to prove that payments were made based on the impugned documents or that no PTs were submitted.
